title: DS-Lighting: Making Agent Harnesses Explicit for Data-Science Automation
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise for automating data-science workflows, yet their end-to-end performance depends critically on the agent harness that represents tasks, manages execution state, constrains output artifacts, and provides evaluation feedback. Existing data-science agents often leave this harness implicit, making results difficult to reproduce, compare, and attribute across heterogeneous tasks. We introduce DS-Lighting, a unified harness toolkit that makes harness design explicit for data-science automation. DS-Lighting decomposes the harness into four reusable layers: data, workflow, execution, and evaluation, and represents diverse agents as executable operator programs that support both predefined pipelines and adaptive search. We further integrate multiple open-source data-science benchmarks into an MLE-Bench-style task format, enabling controlled comparison under a shared task interface, sandboxed runtime, and metric protocol. Experiments across agents, harnesses, models, and ablations show that explicit harness design improves reproducibility, comparability, and reliability, while reducing avoidable system-level failures in end-to-end data-science workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/dslighting

AI.tldr: DS-Lighting is a unified harness toolkit that makes harness design explicit for data-science automation with LLM agents. It decomposes the harness into four reusable layers (data, workflow, execution, evaluation), represents agents as executable operator programs, and integrates multiple benchmarks into an MLE-Bench-style format for controlled comparison.
AI.motivation: Existing data-science agents often leave the agent harness implicit, making results difficult to reproduce, compare, and attribute across heterogeneous tasks. The end-to-end performance of LLM agents depends critically on this harness, but it is rarely formalized.
AI.method: DS-Lighting decomposes the harness into four reusable layers: data, workflow, execution, and evaluation. It represents diverse agents as executable operator programs supporting both predefined pipelines and adaptive search, and integrates multiple open-source data-science benchmarks into an MLE-Bench-style task format with a shared task interface, sandboxed runtime, and metric protocol.
AI.result: Experiments across agents, harnesses, models, and ablations show that explicit harness design improves reproducibility, comparability, and reliability, while reducing avoidable system-level failures in end-to-end data-science workflows.
AI.conclusion: Making harness design explicit through a unified layered toolkit enhances the reproducibility, comparability, and reliability of LLM-agent-driven data-science automation. The toolkit is open-sourced for community use.

title: Expert-validated STEM QA
comment: We have open-sourced a portion of our dataset for the AI research community at https://huggingface.co/datasets/TuringEnterprises/Open-RL
summary: Recent advancements in AI are helping scientists achieve breakthroughs in fields such as mathematics, medicine, and materials sciences. New evaluation datasets for AI models contribute to such advancement in AI. In the STEM domain, frontier models have consumed most of the available online data, creating the need for human-created datasets that codify the knowledge of leading experts in the domain. There are several STEM datasets available for the research community in this field. However, there are some gaps in these datasets, leaving room for improvement. Examples of gaps include (1) saturation in model performance on these datasets, leaving no head-room for meaningful evaluations, (2) skewed taxonomy distributions, (3) multiple choice question format that is misaligned with how scientists use AI in the real world, and (4) inaccurate answers and rationales partially led by a contest-based data collection and a time-bound review process. In this study, we present 'Expert-validated STEM QA', a high-quality, expert-validated STEM dataset (N=398) in Physics, Chemistry, Biology, and Mathematics, created by 241 domain experts. We (1) carefully designed a taxonomy with balanced distribution, (2) vetted question contributors with quality-driven incentive, (3) conducted multiple rounds of reviews with revisions validated by domain experts based on consensus, and (4) created the dataset in verifiable question and answer format. Our study demonstrated low performance ($<25\%$) of frontier AI models on the dataset as a benchmark. Post-training on a separate, private version of the dataset (N=2,000) increased performance of the open source model by $15\%$ relative to the baseline model (p=0.045) on the STEM subset of HLE-verified dataset, indicating potential utility of the dataset for model training. We have open-sourced a portion of our dataset for the AI research community.

AI.tldr: The paper presents 'Expert-validated STEM QA', a high-quality expert-validated STEM dataset (N=398) in Physics, Chemistry, Biology, and Mathematics, created by 241 domain experts. It addresses gaps in existing STEM datasets such as performance saturation, skewed taxonomy, multiple-choice misalignment, and inaccurate answers. The dataset demonstrates low frontier AI model performance (<25%) and shows post-training utility (15% relative improvement) on a private version, with a portion open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Existing STEM evaluation datasets for AI have critical gaps: (1) model performance saturation leaving no headroom for meaningful evaluation, (2) skewed taxonomy distributions, (3) multiple-choice formats misaligned with real-world scientific usage of AI, and (4) inaccurate answers/rationales caused by contest-based collection and time-bound reviews. There is a need for high-quality, expert-validated datasets that codify expert knowledge, especially as frontier models have consumed most available online data.
AI.method: The authors created an expert-validated STEM QA dataset through a rigorous pipeline: (1) carefully designed a taxonomy with balanced distribution across Physics, Chemistry, Biology, and Mathematics; (2) vetted question contributors using quality-driven incentives; (3) conducted multiple rounds of reviews with revisions validated by domain experts based on consensus; and (4) created the dataset in verifiable question-and-answer format. The dataset contains N=398 questions from 241 domain experts. Post-training experiments were conducted on a separate private version (N=2,000) to assess training utility.
AI.result: Frontier AI models achieved low performance (<25%) on the dataset as a benchmark, indicating sufficient headroom for meaningful evaluation. Post-training on a private version (N=2,000) improved an open-source model's performance by 15% relative to the baseline (p=0.045) on the STEM subset of the HLE-verified dataset, demonstrating the dataset's utility for model training. A portion of the dataset has been open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: The Expert-validated STEM QA dataset provides a high-quality, expert-validated benchmark that overcomes key limitations of existing STEM datasets, offers meaningful headroom for evaluating frontier models, and shows promise as a training resource for improving model performance on STEM tasks. The open-sourced portion enables broader research community access.

title: A collective capability boundary in frontier large language models on guideline-conformant and case-specific oncology decision-making
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical knowledge examinations, yet real-world oncology is not a knowledge test--it is a sequence of guideline-pathway choices, escalation judgments, and commitments under uncertainty. Existing benchmarks largely measure factual recall, leaving open whether frontier LLMs share decision-path blind spots that combining models cannot fix. We built the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB)--2,005 oncology decision points across NCCN guidelines and colorectal cancer cases--and evaluated nine frontier LLMs (four closed-source, five open-weight families) released between June 2025 and April 2026. A fully deterministic scorer (zero LLM inference) classified outputs into 14 failure types, independently validated by two oncologists (Cohen's weighted $κ$ = 0.939 and 0.790) on a 225-item stratified sample. Treating the nine as a pooled super-model, 42.1% (Wilson 95% CI 40.0--44.3%) of all items--35.7% of the 1,586 NCCN items and 66.4% of the 419 colorectal-cancer cases--were answered correctly by none, with failures concentrated in choosing between guideline pathways before reasoning within any: a consistent blind spot in clinical meta-judgment that likely requires architectural intervention rather than more training data. Two models tuned for decisiveness (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) made unsafe commitments three to five times more often than the seven cautious models without scoring higher. In 3--9% of items, models stated the correct next clinical step yet did not commit to it--failures of decision, not knowledge. Model quality is no longer the primary bottleneck for clinical LLM deployment; the binding constraint is the assumption that any single model can be the sole basis for a clinical decision. Progress requires architectures that detect when a model reaches its competence boundary and route the decision to a clinician.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB) with 2,005 oncology decision points to evaluate whether frontier LLMs can make clinical decisions, not just recall medical facts. Nine frontier LLMs (June 2025–April 2026) were evaluated with a zero-LLM deterministic scorer validated by oncologists. Results show 42.1% of items were answered correctly by none of the nine models pooled together, revealing a systematic blind spot in choosing between guideline pathways (clinical meta-judgment). Models tuned for decisiveness made unsafe commitments 3–5× more often without scoring higher. The authors conclude that model quality is no longer the primary bottleneck; the binding constraint is the assumption that any single model can be the sole basis for clinical decisions, requiring architectures that detect competence boundaries and route decisions to clinicians.
AI.motivation: Existing medical benchmarks measure factual recall, not real-world oncology practice, which involves a sequence of guideline-pathway choices, escalation judgments, and commitments under uncertainty. The authors aim to determine whether frontier LLMs share decision-path blind spots that cannot be fixed by combining models, and whether model decisiveness tuning compromises safety.
AI.method: Built the Oncology Decision Boundary Benchmark (ODBB) with 2,005 oncology decision points from NCCN guidelines and colorectal cancer cases. Evaluated nine frontier LLMs from four closed-source and five open-weight families. Used a fully deterministic scorer (zero LLM inference) classifying outputs into 14 failure types, independently validated by two oncologists (weighted Cohen's κ = 0.939 and 0.790) on a 225-item stratified sample.
AI.result: 42.1% (Wilson 95% CI 40.0–44.3%) of all items were answered correctly by none of the nine models pooled: 35.7% of NCCN items and 66.4% of colorectal-cancer cases. Failures concentrated in choosing between guideline pathways before reasoning within any. Decisiveness-tuned models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) made unsafe commitments 3–5× more often than cautious models without scoring higher. In 3–9% of items, models stated the correct next step but failed to commit to it—failures of decision, not knowledge.
AI.conclusion: The primary bottleneck for clinical LLM deployment is no longer model quality but the architectural assumption that any single model can be the sole basis for a clinical decision. Progress requires architectures that detect when a model reaches its competence boundary and route decisions to a clinician.

title: Statutory AI: Aligning Large Language Models With Legal Norms
summary: With the increasing development of AI regulatory frameworks, ensuring that artificial intelligence systems, particularly generative models, operate in accordance with legal and ethical standards has become a critical priority. Existing proposals for AI alignment and value-guided behavior, however, face some limitations. Approaches such as Constitutional AI depend on human supervision, while broad normative frameworks like the Good-for-Humanity (GfH) principle may be overly general and ambiguous to provide actionable governance guidance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid approach called Statutory AI that employs pre-existing human-authored principles drawn from specific themes within a legal corpus. Specifically, Statutory AI uses legal texts as a constitutional framework, enabling AI systems to autonomously critique and revise their outputs according to established norms. It operates in two stages, both using Chain-of-Thought prompting. The first stage classifies the user prompt into one of the identified themes, while the second stage analyzes it in conjunction with relevant articles selected from the legal corpus of that theme. To illustrate the potential of our approach, we conducted an experiment involving 1,000 red-teaming prompts and five penal themes: discrimination, disclosure of confidential information, violence, fraud, and abuse of vulnerable persons. Statutory AI reduced harmful content by 52 to 59 percentage points across tested models, approximately 10 percentage points higher than standard Constitutional AI, while cutting computation time by over 50%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Statutory AI, a hybrid approach that uses pre-existing human-authored legal principles from specific themes in a legal corpus as a constitutional framework for AI alignment. It operates in two Chain-of-Thought prompted stages: theme classification and output critique/revision. Experiments on 1,000 red-teaming prompts across five penal themes show harmful content reduced by 52-59 percentage points, ~10 points better than Constitutional AI, with over 50% computation time savings.
AI.motivation: Existing AI alignment approaches have limitations: Constitutional AI depends on human supervision, and broad normative frameworks like the Good-for-Humanity principle are too general and ambiguous for actionable governance guidance. There is a critical need for AI systems to operate in accordance with legal and ethical standards as AI regulatory frameworks develop.
AI.method: Statutory AI employs legal texts as a constitutional framework, using pre-existing human-authored principles from specific themes within a legal corpus. It operates in two stages, both using Chain-of-Thought prompting: (1) classify the user prompt into one of the identified themes, and (2) analyze the prompt in conjunction with relevant articles selected from the legal corpus of that theme, enabling the AI to autonomously critique and revise outputs according to established norms.
AI.result: In experiments with 1,000 red-teaming prompts and five penal themes (discrimination, disclosure of confidential information, violence, fraud, and abuse of vulnerable persons), Statutory AI reduced harmful content by 52 to 59 percentage points across tested models—approximately 10 percentage points higher than standard Constitutional AI—while cutting computation time by over 50%.
AI.conclusion: Statutory AI overcomes the limitations of existing alignment approaches by leveraging specific, actionable legal principles rather than broad normative frameworks or purely human-supervised methods. It demonstrates superior harm reduction and computational efficiency compared to Constitutional AI, suggesting that legal corpora can serve as effective constitutional frameworks for AI governance.

title: RedLight-VLA: Models for traffic-rule grounding and behavioral emphasis in driving policies
summary: Behavior-cloned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) driving policies struggle with rare rule-governed maneuvers at signalized intersections. Braking and launching examples contribute little to averaged trajectory loss, while fused representations lack explicit supervision for the governing traffic-light and stop-line state. We present RedLight-VLA, a training objective that uses expert futures and automatically generated perception targets without additional manual rule annotation. First, trajectory-derived behavioral reweighting (BR) emphasizes rare deceleration and acceleration using rotation-invariant longitudinal dynamics and a scale-preserving reduction that exactly recovers the baseline when disabled. Second, parallel auxiliary (AUX) heads ground traffic-light and stop-line state in continuous post-fusion rule tokens, without autoregressive language generation or changes to the trajectory decoder. We evaluate on a curated set of 20 s sequences with a 5 s prediction horizon. Controlled variants share the same backbone, training data, decoder, and evaluation population. Against an otherwise identical VLA baseline, RedLight-VLA reduces red-light stop-line overshoot from 7.3% to6.8%, reduces stop-line velocity error by 12.7%, and improves 3 s trafficlight-sliced ADE/FDE from 0.274/0.964 m to 0.247/0.897 m. Green-light false stops increase from 3.2% to 3.9%; however, combining BR with AUX supervision mitigates the larger increase observed for AUX alone (4.0%). The combined model also improves non-traffic-light ADE/FDE from 0.268/0.956 m to 0.241/0.876 m and outperforms either mechanism alone on all four sliced displacement measures.

AI.tldr: RedLight-VLA introduces a training objective combining trajectory-derived behavioral reweighting and parallel auxiliary heads to improve behavior-cloned VLA driving policies on rare rule-governed maneuvers at signalized intersections, reducing red-light stop-line overshoot, stop-line velocity error, and trajectory errors without additional manual rule annotation.
AI.motivation: Behavior-cloned VLA driving policies perform poorly on rare rule-governed maneuvers at signalized intersections because braking and launching examples contribute little to averaged trajectory loss, and fused representations lack explicit supervision for traffic-light and stop-line state.
AI.method: Two complementary mechanisms are introduced: (1) trajectory-derived behavioral reweighting (BR) that emphasizes rare deceleration and acceleration using rotation-invariant longitudinal dynamics with a scale-preserving reduction that recovers the baseline when disabled; (2) parallel auxiliary (AUX) heads that ground traffic-light and stop-line state in continuous post-fusion rule tokens without autoregressive language generation or changes to the trajectory decoder.
AI.result: Against an identical VLA baseline, RedLight-VLA reduces red-light stop-line overshoot from 7.3% to 6.8%, reduces stop-line velocity error by 12.7%, and improves 3s traffic-light-sliced ADE/FDE from 0.274/0.964m to 0.247/0.897m. Green-light false stops increase from 3.2% to 3.9%, but BR combined with AUX mitigates the larger AUX-alone increase (4.0%). Combined model also improves non-traffic-light ADE/FDE from 0.268/0.956m to 0.241/0.876m and outperforms either mechanism alone on all four sliced displacement measures.
AI.conclusion: Combining behavioral reweighting with auxiliary rule supervision yields consistent improvements across traffic-light-sliced and non-traffic-light displacement metrics while mitigating false-stop increases, demonstrating that targeted training objectives can address rare rule-governed maneuvers without manual annotation or architectural changes to the decoder.

title: From Question-First to Analyst-First: Domain-Expert Skills and Verified Knowledge Compilation for Proactive Enterprise Analytics
summary: Conversational analytics systems assume the user already has a well-formed question, leaving a non-expert facing a blank query box on an unfamiliar enterprise schema. Commercial 'proactive' tools narrow this gap only by detecting statistical anomalies over analyst-curated metric layers, and academic next-question recommenders depend on query logs that a fresh dataset lacks. We describe a production analytics system that inverts the interaction model from question-first to analyst-first through two coupled architectural ideas. First, a pluggable domain-expert 'skill' abstraction: a folder-based, database-free subject-matter pack (a manifest, per-stage prompt facets, keyword-routed references, report templates, and optional compute) auto-selected per (client, dataset) by deterministic schema matching and spliced as a cross-cutting concern into every stage of an agentic pipeline, the schema explorer, and the report engines, degrading to a strict no-op when absent. Because a skill is a self-contained folder resolved deterministically, the catalogue is open-ended: an extensible marketplace of domain experts. Second, an offline knowledge-compilation loop: an agent probes the dataset's parquet via DuckDB (zero load on production), runs critic-gated per-table convergence with self-healing retries, and data-validates joins by value overlap, producing durable schema knowledge that drives standing expert reports whose every published metric is re-verified by re-executing its evidence SQL, plus suggested questions that mirror the report agenda. These close a proactive loop: reports surface numbers, the numbers seed questions, and a click launches a verified deep dive, all before the query box is used. We give a formal model and report illustrative single-tenant evidence. We make no user-study or benchmark claims; the contribution is the architecture and its defensibility.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a production analytics system that inverts the conventional query-first interaction model to an analyst-first model. It introduces two coupled architectural ideas: (1) a pluggable domain-expert 'skill' abstraction—self-contained folder-based packages auto-selected per (client, dataset) via deterministic schema matching and spliced into every stage of an agentic pipeline; and (2) an offline knowledge-compilation loop that probes datasets via DuckDB, validates joins, and produces durable schema knowledge that drives standing expert reports with verified metrics and suggested questions. This creates a proactive closed loop where reports surface numbers, numbers seed questions, and clicks launch verified deep dives—all before the user touches the query box. The paper provides a formal model and illustrative single-tenant evidence, making no user-study or benchmark claims.
AI.motivation: Conversational analytics systems assume users arrive with well-formed questions, but non-experts face a blank query box over unfamiliar enterprise schemas. Commercial proactive tools only detect statistical anomalies over curated metric layers, and academic next-question recommenders depend on query logs that fresh datasets lack. The gap is that non-expert users have no way to discover what questions are worth asking or what the data contains.
AI.method: The system inverts the interaction model from question-first to analyst-first through two coupled architectural ideas. First, a pluggable domain-expert 'skill' abstraction: a folder-based, database-free subject-matter pack (manifest, per-stage prompt facets, keyword-routed references, report templates, optional compute) auto-selected per (client, dataset) by deterministic schema matching and spliced as a cross-cutting concern into every stage of the agentic pipeline, schema explorer, and report engines, degrading to a strict no-op when absent. Second, an offline knowledge-compilation loop: an agent probes the dataset's parquet via DuckDB (zero production load), runs critic-gated per-table convergence with self-healing retries, data-validates joins by value overlap, and produces durable schema knowledge driving standing expert reports whose every published metric is re-verified by re-executing evidence SQL, plus suggested questions mirroring the report agenda.
AI.result: The paper provides a formal model of the architecture and reports illustrative single-tenant evidence. It explicitly makes no user-study or benchmark claims; the contribution is framed as the architecture itself and its defensibility (deterministic resolution, open-ended extensibility, verified metrics, zero production load via offline processing).
AI.conclusion: The contribution is an architectural pattern—analyst-first proactive analytics—that is open-ended (skills marketplace), deterministic (folder-based resolution), and defensible (every published metric is re-verified by re-executing its evidence SQL). The system closes a proactive loop: reports surface numbers, numbers seed questions, and clicks launch verified deep dives, all before the query box is used.

title: The Potential of Haptic Foundation Models
comment: accepted by IEEE Consumer Electronics Magazine
summary: Despite the success of foundation models in language and vision, their expansion into embodied AI is bottlenecked by a lack of generalized touch sensing. This limitation is especially relevant to consumer electronics, where smartphones, wearables, VR controllers, home robots, and health monitoring devices require safe and adaptive physical interaction. Constrained by hardware heterogeneity and the necessity of active physical data collection, current haptic models remain rigidly task-specific. To overcome these limitations, this article explores the transformative potential and developmental trajectory of Haptic Foundation Models (HFMs). We detail the paradigm shift required to transition from passive Large Language Models and Vision Language Models into active HFMs across four core dimensions: action coupling, physical dynamical representation space, continuous time-series data granularity, and action-conditioned future state prediction. Furthermore, we synthesize existing large-scale tactile datasets and benchmark UniTouch, AnyTouch, T3, and Sparsh on TacBench for force estimation, slip detection, and relative pose estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Haptic Foundation Models (HFMs) to address the lack of generalized touch sensing in embodied AI, particularly for consumer electronics. It outlines the paradigm shift from passive LLMs/VLMs to active HFMs across four core dimensions, and benchmarks existing tactile models (UniTouch, AnyTouch, T3, Sparsh) on TacBench for force estimation, slip detection, and relative pose estimation.
AI.motivation: Foundation models have succeeded in language and vision, but their extension to embodied AI is bottlenecked by the absence of generalized touch sensing. Current haptic models are rigidly task-specific due to hardware heterogeneity and the requirement of active physical data collection, which is especially problematic for consumer electronics requiring safe and adaptive physical interaction.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes HFMs and details four core dimensions for transitioning from passive language/vision models to active haptic models: (1) action coupling, (2) physical dynamical representation space, (3) continuous time-series data granularity, and (4) action-conditioned future state prediction. It also synthesizes large-scale tactile datasets and benchmarks existing models on TacBench across three tasks: force estimation, slip detection, and relative pose estimation.
AI.result: The paper benchmarks UniTouch, AnyTouch, T3, and Sparsh on TacBench for force estimation, slip detection, and relative pose estimation, providing a comparative evaluation of current tactile foundation model capabilities.
AI.conclusion: HFMs represent a transformative direction for generalized touch sensing in embodied AI and consumer electronics, but require a fundamental paradigm shift from passive models to active, action-conditioned haptic models to overcome existing limitations.

title: The Signal in the Noise: An Auditable Reliability Layer for Biomedical Text Classification
comment: 6 pages. Accepted at the 2026 14th International Conference on Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (ICBCB 2026), Kitakyushu, Japan; to appear in IEEE Conference Proceedings (IEEE Xplore). Code: https://github.com/MoustafaMohamedMoustafaHassan/the_signal_in_the_noise_CORD19_project
summary: Biomedical NLP pipelines routinely presuppose clean input text, yet large-scale corpora assembled through automated PDF parsing harbour pervasive OCR-like artifacts, token splits and merges, hyphenation remnants, and character-level corruption, that systematically erode lexical evidence and degrade downstream classifiers. We introduce a conservative, fully auditable spell-correction reliability layer conceived as a safety-oriented preprocessing module rather than a maximal-accuracy corrector: under conditions of uncertainty, the system abstains from editing, in accordance with a medical do-no-harm philosophy. The deterministic architecture couples bounded edit-distance candidate generation with corpus-derived n-gram scoring and a suite of biomedical safety gates that protect domain-critical terminology. We evaluate the layer both intrinsically, on a manually curated benchmark of 2,104 token-level cases, and extrinsically, on a tri-class CORD-19 topic classifier (Prevention, Treatment, Epidemiology) spanning 10,000 examples under a principled four-run protocol (Clean, Noisy, Restored, Safety). Intrinsically, the layer attains 94.61% error-fix recall on synthetic errors with zero harmful edits on negative controls. Downstream, it recovers approximately 80.45% of the noise-induced macro-F1 degradation, elevating macro-F1 from 0.7654 (Noisy) to 0.7717 (Restored) while preserving near-clean performance (Safety: 0.7721). A supplementary case study on 103 real-world OCR-extracted abstracts classified with BioBERT confirms that transformer encoders appeared relatively robust to mild noise, motivating a future grey-box architecture that integrates bounded neural signals and UMLS lexicons without compromising auditability. The system is fully deterministic, artifact-driven, and designed with deployment and auditability in mind.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a conservative, auditable spell-correction reliability layer for biomedical NLP pipelines that abstains from editing under uncertainty (do-no-harm philosophy). It uses bounded edit-distance candidate generation, corpus-derived n-gram scoring, and biomedical safety gates to correct OCR/PDF-parsing artifacts. Evaluated intrinsically on 2,104 token-level cases (94.61% error-fix recall, zero harmful edits) and extrinsically on CORD-19 topic classification, it recovers ~80.45% of noise-induced macro-F1 degradation while preserving near-clean performance.
AI.motivation: Biomedical NLP pipelines assume clean text, but large-scale corpora from automated PDF parsing contain pervasive OCR-like artifacts (token splits/merges, hyphenation remnants, character corruption) that systematically degrade lexical evidence and downstream classifier performance. Existing correctors prioritize maximal accuracy over safety, risking harmful edits to domain-critical terminology.
AI.method: The system is a deterministic preprocessing layer combining: (1) bounded edit-distance candidate generation, (2) corpus-derived n-gram scoring for candidate ranking, and (3) biomedical safety gates protecting domain-critical terminology. Under uncertainty the system abstains from editing, following a medical do-no-harm philosophy. The architecture is fully deterministic and auditable.
AI.result: Intrinsic evaluation: 94.61% error-fix recall on synthetic errors with zero harmful edits on negative controls. Extrinsic evaluation (tri-class CORD-19 topic classifier, 10,000 examples, four-run protocol): recovered ~80.45% of noise-induced macro-F1 degradation, improving macro-F1 from 0.7654 (Noisy) to 0.7717 (Restored), with Safety mode at 0.7721 (near-clean). A case study on 103 real-world OCR abstracts showed transformer encoders (BioBERT) were relatively robust to mild noise, motivating a future grey-box architecture integrating bounded neural signals and UMLS lexicons.
AI.conclusion: A safety-first, deterministic spell-correction layer effectively mitigates OCR/PDF artifacts in biomedical NLP while avoiding harmful edits, recovering most of the noise-induced performance degradation. The near-clean performance of the Safety mode validates the do-no-harm design. Findings motivate a future grey-box architecture that integrates bounded neural signals and UMLS lexicons without compromising auditability, with deployment and auditability being central design goals.

title: Cognitively-Grounded On-Device Runtime Learning for Ground Robots in Unknown Physical Environments
summary: This paper presents \ul{CogRun}, a framework that enables safety-critical ground robots to perform cognitively-grounded runtime learning entirely on edge-AI devices in unknown physical environments, without prior maps or perceptual knowledge. CogRun consists of three components: a Learning-Agent, a Rational-Agent, and a Coordinator. The Learning-Agent is novel in cognitive-neural learning architecture, which featurs dedicated replay buffers, cognition-driven experience sampling, and a safety-aware action blending of actor-critic reinforcement learning (RL) with instance-based learning (IBL). The Rational-Agent is a non-learning module that complements the Learning-Agent by exclusively handling safety-critical functions, while the Coordinator manages interactions between the two agents to promote safe and efficient runtime learning. CogRun's full autonomy stack (i.e., perception, learning, and control) on edge-AI devices eliminates dependence on wireless communications, enabling broader applications in challenging environments with limited or no connectivity. Experiments on a quadruped robot in real-world wild forests and on an off-road autonomous vehicle in a simulated wild forest demonstrate that CogRun enables safe and efficient runtime learning, allowing robots to safely and continuously interact with the physical world for enhancing task performance in complex, unknown environments.

AI.tldr: CogRun is a framework enabling safety-critical ground robots to perform cognitively-grounded runtime learning on edge-AI devices in unknown environments. It combines a cognitive-neural Learning-Agent (RL + instance-based learning), a Rational-Agent for safety-critical functions, and a Coordinator, achieving full autonomy on-device without wireless dependence. Validated on a quadruped robot in real forests and a simulated off-road vehicle.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical ground robots operating in unknown physical environments face challenges of runtime learning without prior maps or perceptual knowledge, especially in environments with limited or no connectivity. Existing approaches require cloud/off-board computation and cannot ensure safety during continuous learning.
AI.method: CogRun comprises three components: (1) a Learning-Agent with a novel cognitive-neural architecture featuring dedicated replay buffers, cognition-driven experience sampling, and safety-aware action blending between actor-critic RL and instance-based learning (IBL); (2) a Rational-Agent, a non-learning module exclusively handling safety-critical functions; and (3) a Coordinator managing interactions between the two agents. The full autonomy stack (perception, learning, control) runs on edge-AI devices.
AI.result: Experiments on a quadruped robot in real wild forests and on an off-road autonomous vehicle in simulated wild forests demonstrate that CogRun enables safe and efficient runtime learning, allowing continuous safe interaction with the physical world to enhance task performance in complex, unknown environments.
AI.conclusion: CogRun demonstrates that fully on-device runtime learning is feasible and safe for safety-critical robots in unknown, connectivity-limited environments, broadening applicability for ground robots operating in challenging real-world conditions.

title: Paper Pilot: A Human-in-the-Loop Expert System for Evidence-Traceable Scientific Manuscript Generation in Applied Sciences
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly embedded in scientific workflows for literature analysis, drafting, and review. Existing systems advance autonomous discovery and manuscript generation, but do not resolve the governance problem that arises when ideas, methods, results, and claims propagate through AI-assisted workflows without mandatory human approval or artifact-level traceability. This paper proposes Paper Pilot, a human-in-the-loop expert system for evidence-traceable scientific manuscript generation in applied sciences. It adapts the Collaborative Agent Reasoning Engineering (CARE) methodology to manuscript development through manuscript-owner approval gates, explicit no-pass criteria, claim classification, audit logging, advisory LLM review, and evidence-locked revision control. The framework defines eight approval gates across the idea-to-claim pipeline and distinguishes literature-grounded from artifact-grounded claims, requiring reported numbers and interpretations to remain traceable to approved evidence; its system prompt is openly released for deployment in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or institutional LLM environments. As a first empirical validation, we evaluate the citation-grounding layer with a controlled, mechanically scored benchmark (two commercial LLMs, real arXiv papers, no LLM judge): under coverage pressure ungated drafters fabricated up to 25% of their citations and never flagged an evidence gap, whereas the same models under Paper Pilot's evidence-locked rules produced zero fabricated citations and surfaced the planted gaps as explicit placeholders. Preliminary results for result grounding, revision, and adversarial robustness point the same way; full evaluation is left to future work. Paper Pilot positions LLM-assisted writing as a controlled human-AI decision-support process rather than a fully autonomous authorship pipeline.

AI.tldr: Paper Pilot is a human-in-the-loop expert system for evidence-traceable scientific manuscript generation that enforces eight approval gates, evidence-locked revision control, and claim classification to prevent fabricated citations and ensure traceability in LLM-assisted writing pipelines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used in scientific workflows, but existing systems lack mandatory human approval and artifact-level traceability, creating a governance problem where ideas, methods, results, and claims propagate through AI-assisted workflows without proper oversight or provenance.
AI.method: The framework adapts the Collaborative Agent Reasoning Engineering (CARE) methodology to manuscript development, implementing manuscript-owner approval gates, explicit no-pass criteria, claim classification, audit logging, advisory LLM review, and evidence-locked revision control. It defines eight approval gates across the idea-to-claim pipeline and distinguishes literature-grounded from artifact-grounded claims. The system prompt is openly released and deployment-agnostic across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or institutional LLM environments.
AI.result: In a controlled benchmark using two commercial LLMs and real arXiv papers, ungated drafters fabricated up to 25% of citations under coverage pressure without flagging evidence gaps, while Paper Pilot's evidence-locked rules produced zero fabricated citations and surfaced planted gaps as explicit placeholders. Preliminary results for result grounding, revision, and adversarial robustness align with these findings.
AI.conclusion: Paper Pilot reframes LLM-assisted writing as a controlled human-AI decision-support process rather than a fully autonomous authorship pipeline, demonstrating that evidence-locking and approval gates can effectively prevent citation fabrication. Full evaluation of all framework components is deferred to future work.

title: RoboGesture: Real-Time Semantic-aligned Co-Speech Gestures Generation for Humanoid Interaction
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project page: https://RoboGesture.github.io
summary: Enabling humanoid robots to respond to human speech with synchronized and semantically meaningful gestures is fundamental to natural human-robot interaction. However, this task faces three critical barriers: the scarcity of semantically rich datasets, the "modality eclipse" where models ignore audio cues in favor of kinematic inertia, and the sim-to-real gap regarding physical safety. We propose RoboGesture, a robot-centric framework that co-designs data, modeling, and control to power a complete interactive human-humanoid system in which the robot listens, responds, and gestures in real time. We first establish the RoboGesture dataset featuring over 300 gesture categories and develop an automated pipeline to synthesize large-scale collision-free, robot-specific audio-motion pairs. Our architecture features a Hierarchical Semantic-Acoustic Aligner that extracts multi-granular prosodic and semantic cues directly from raw audio tokens. These cues drive a Streaming Conditional Motion Generator based on a diffusion transformer with conditional flow matching. To ensure high responsiveness, we introduce Anti-Inertia CFG Masking, which prevents the model from collapsing into repetitive historical patterns by compelling it to proactively mine control signals from the audio modality. Finally, an MPC-based safety filter ensures real-time, collision-free execution on physical hardware. Experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrate that RoboGesture generates safer, more rhythmic, and more semantically appropriate responses compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: RoboGesture is a robot-centric framework that co-designs data, modeling, and control to enable humanoid robots to generate synchronized, semantically meaningful gestures in response to human speech in real time. It introduces a large-scale robot-specific dataset with 300+ gesture categories, a Hierarchical Semantic-Acoustic Aligner, a Streaming Conditional Motion Generator based on diffusion transformers with flow matching, Anti-Inertia CFG Masking to prevent modality eclipse, and an MPC-based safety filter. Validated on a Unitree G1 humanoid, it outperforms baselines in safety, rhythm, and semantic appropriateness.
AI.motivation: Enabling humanoid robots to produce synchronized and semantically meaningful gestures in response to human speech is essential for natural human-robot interaction, but faces three barriers: scarce semantically rich datasets, modality eclipse where models rely on kinematic inertia rather than audio cues, and the sim-to-real gap regarding physical safety.
AI.method: The framework (1) establishes the RoboGesture dataset with 300+ gesture categories and an automated pipeline for synthesizing large-scale, collision-free, robot-specific audio-motion pairs; (2) employs a Hierarchical Semantic-Acoustic Aligner to extract multi-granular prosodic and semantic cues from raw audio tokens; (3) uses a Streaming Conditional Motion Generator based on a diffusion transformer with conditional flow matching; (4) introduces Anti-Inertia CFG Masking to force the model to actively mine audio control signals and prevent collapse into repetitive historical patterns; and (5) applies an MPC-based safety filter for real-time, collision-free physical execution.
AI.result: Experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrate that RoboGesture produces safer, more rhythmic, and more semantically appropriate gestures compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By co-designing data, modeling, and control, RoboGesture achieves a complete interactive human-humanoid system where the robot listens, responds, and gestures in real time with improved safety, rhythmic quality, and semantic alignment.

title: The Race between Agentic AI Capabilities and Data Quality Control in Online Surveys
summary: Online surveys are a foundational data collection instrument in a variety of fields, with attention checks serving as critical guardians of response quality. However, the rapid emergence of agentic AI (goal directed systems powered by a large language model (LLM) brain and/or a multimodal processing unit with tool-augmented capabilities) raises new questions about the robustness of these safeguards. We investigate how well agentic AI architectures can complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks. We evaluate a single-agent architecture capable of multimodal input processing and tool-based web interaction on a controlled survey sandbox. We analyze the problem from two perspectives. From an attack perspective, we demonstrate how structural vulnerabilities such as exposed DOM metadata and predictable option encoding allow agents to resolve attention checks through structured parsing only. From a defense perspective, we implement a mitigation strategy of DOM metadata obfuscation to remove semantic cues in text-based questions. We evaluate multiple open-source language and multimodal models to study capability and orchestration effectiveness. Based on our evaluations, we offer perspectives on how to simultaneously meet the needs of empiricists and agentic AI researchers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether agentic AI architectures (LLM-powered, tool-augmented systems) can complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks, finding that structural vulnerabilities like exposed DOM metadata and predictable option encoding allow agents to bypass attention checks via structured parsing, while proposing DOM metadata obfuscation as a mitigation strategy.
AI.motivation: Online surveys rely on attention checks to ensure response quality, but the emergence of agentic AI raises concerns about whether these safeguards remain robust. The paper seeks to understand how well such AI systems can navigate surveys and bypass quality-control mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a single-agent architecture with multimodal input processing and tool-based web interaction on a controlled survey sandbox. They analyze the problem from both attack and defense perspectives: demonstrating structural vulnerabilities (exposed DOM metadata, predictable option encoding) that enable structured parsing-based attention check resolution, and implementing DOM metadata obfuscation as a mitigation. Multiple open-source language and multimodal models are evaluated for capability and orchestration effectiveness.
AI.result: Agentic AI architectures can successfully complete web-based surveys and pass standard attention checks by exploiting structural vulnerabilities such as exposed DOM metadata and predictable option encoding. The proposed DOM metadata obfuscation mitigation strategy removes semantic cues in text-based questions, reducing agent vulnerability exploitation.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers perspectives on how to simultaneously meet the needs of empirical researchers (maintaining valid survey data) and agentic AI researchers (enabling robust AI web interaction), highlighting the need for balanced solutions that preserve data quality while accommodating AI-based survey completion.

title: Multi-Group Pipe Routing under Permanent Geometric Occupancy: Problem, Benchmark, and Classical Baselines
summary: Additive manufacturing (AM) enables compact hydraulic components whose internal fluid channels can follow free-form 3D paths rather than conventionally drilled holes. A representative case is multi-group channel layout in rotary direct-drive servo valves: once a channel is placed it permanently occupies volume, so later channels must clear earlier geometry--unlike classical multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), where agents free space after moving. We study this setting as multi-group pipe routing under permanent geometric occupancy. Our contributions are a problem formalization with geometric dual-witness conflicts, a constructive 3D benchmark (two corridor generators x two obstacle painters, controlled difficulty, feasibility witnesses), and baseline results for CBS, PBS, and priority planning adapted to this coupling. We evaluate by success rate under a fixed time budget. PlaneSlice hard instances clearly rank CBS above PBS and PP, while easier cells validate the pipeline. The goal is a reproducible problem definition, suite, and classical baselines--not a new optimal MAPF algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes a novel problem of multi-group pipe routing under permanent geometric occupancy for additive manufacturing, introduces a constructive 3D benchmark with controllable difficulty, and evaluates adapted classical MAPF planners (CBS, PBS, priority planning) showing CBS outperforms others on hard instances.
AI.motivation: Additive manufacturing allows free-form internal fluid channels, but routing multiple channel groups sequentially creates a unique challenge: once a channel is placed, it permanently occupies volume, requiring later channels to avoid all previously placed geometry. This differs fundamentally from classical MAPF where agents free space after moving, motivating a new problem formulation and evaluation suite.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem with geometric dual-witness conflicts, build a controllable 3D benchmark using two corridor generators and two obstacle painters with feasibility witnesses, and adapt CBS, PBS, and priority planning algorithms to handle the permanent geometric occupancy coupling between channel groups.
AI.result: On PlaneSlice hard instances, CBS clearly ranks above PBS and priority planning in success rate under fixed time budget, while easier cell instances validate the pipeline's correctness and feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a reproducible problem definition, benchmark suite, and classical baselines for multi-group pipe routing under permanent geometric occupancy. It is intended as a foundation for future work rather than proposing a new optimal MAPF algorithm.

title: CDPR: Counterfactual Advantage-based Credit Assignment for Cost-Aware Sequential Medical Diagnosis
summary: Clinical diagnosis is a step-by-step, cost-aware process: a physician orders examinations one at a time, observes the results, and updates the diagnosis before reaching a final conclusion. Most medical language models instead treat diagnosis as a one-pass classification task and ignore the trade-off between a test's value and its cost. We model diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process and train the policy with reinforcement learning. The main difficulty is credit assignment: the only reliable signal comes once at the end of a long trajectory, so it scores a wasteful workup the same as an efficient one. We propose CDPR (Counterfactual Diagnostic Process Reward), which needs no expert labels and no learned critic. CDPR first finds the states where the policy hesitates, using the uncertainty of its action distribution, and then scores the chosen action by its advantage over the alternatives the policy itself would consider, estimated with short rollouts under a utility that balances correctness against test count, cost, and infeasible requests. A rollout cache reuses within-batch trajectories to keep the cost low. We integrate CDPR into GRPO and test it on one in-domain (MIMIC-IV) and two out-of-domain (ClinicalBench and a private hospital dataset) benchmarks. CDPR improves diagnostic accuracy while clearly reducing the number and cost of examinations.

AI.tldr: CDPR is a reinforcement learning framework that models clinical diagnosis as a cost-aware sequential decision process, using counterfactual reward estimation to improve diagnostic accuracy while reducing the number and cost of medical examinations.
AI.motivation: Most medical language models treat diagnosis as a one-pass classification task, ignoring the inherently sequential and cost-aware nature of clinical diagnosis. The key challenge is credit assignment in long decision trajectories, where only a final signal is available and wasteful workups score the same as efficient ones.
AI.method: CDPR identifies states where the policy hesitates using action distribution uncertainty, then scores chosen actions by their advantage over plausible alternatives estimated via short rollouts under a utility balancing correctness, test count, cost, and infeasible requests. A rollout cache reuses within-batch trajectories to keep computational cost low. The approach is integrated into GRPO and requires no expert labels or learned critic.
AI.result: CDPR improves diagnostic accuracy while clearly reducing the number and cost of examinations across one in-domain benchmark (MIMIC-IV) and two out-of-domain benchmarks (ClinicalBench and a private hospital dataset).
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual reward estimation in sequential diagnostic processes can yield both more accurate and more cost-efficient clinical decision-making without requiring expert annotations or additional learned critics.

title: RoboPhys-3D: A Comprehensive Embodied World Model Evaluation via 3D Reconstruction
summary: Video world models increasingly serve as data engines, action planners, and simulators for embodied AI, but conventional embodied world model (EWM) benchmarks lack a unified 3D-grounded protocol for establishing whether generated rollouts preserve the underlying 3D scene state or translate into executable actions. We introduce RoboPhys-3D, a 3D-grounded EWM benchmark built on RoboTwin 2.0, covering 50 manipulation tasks across four regimes, with 5,000 episodes and 25,000 multi-view ground-truth videos. A defining feature of RoboPhys-3D is that generated and ground-truth videos are processed through the same 3D reconstruction pipeline, enabling reconstruction-induced error to be distinguished from generation-induced error. The RoboPhys-3D benchmark organizes 50 complementary metrics into 18 sub-dimensions across four levels: pixel-level fidelity, 3D geometry consistency, state-level understanding, and task-level completeness. We further introduce Average Full Score, a hierarchical score averaging all 50 metrics for comprehensive evaluation, and RoboPhyscore, a compact task-aligned score averaging the metrics most strongly correlated with task success. Among the four representative video world models, Cosmos 3 achieves the highest RoboPhyscore (0.6330, 92.7% of ground truth), while state- and execution-grounded metrics reveal substantial failures that perceptual and vision-language model-based judgments fail to capture. RoboPhyscore further exhibits strong agreement with human evaluation (Pearson r = 0.9761 and Spearman \r{ho} = 0.8962), demonstrating the importance of grounded, execution-aware evaluation for EWM capability.

AI.tldr: We introduce RoboPhys-3D, a 3D-grounded embodied world model benchmark built on RoboTwin 2.0, spanning 50 manipulation tasks, 5,000 episodes, and 25,000 multi-view ground-truth videos. It uses a unified 3D reconstruction pipeline for both generated and ground-truth videos to separate reconstruction-induced from generation-induced errors, evaluating across 50 metrics in 18 sub-dimensions and four levels. Two composite scores are proposed: Average Full Score and RoboPhyscore, the latter correlating strongly with task success and human evaluation (Pearson r=0.9761). Cosmos 3 achieves the highest RoboPhyscore (0.6330, 92.7% of ground truth) while revealing failures missed by perception/VLM-based judgments.
AI.motivation: Conventional embodied world model benchmarks lack a unified 3D-grounded protocol to verify whether generated rollouts preserve 3D scene state or translate into executable actions, motivating a benchmark that grounds evaluation in recovered 3D geometry and task executability.
AI.method: RoboPhys-3D processes both generated and ground-truth videos through the same 3D reconstruction pipeline to isolate generation-induced error from reconstruction-induced error. It defines 50 complementary metrics organized into 18 sub-dimensions across four levels (pixel fidelity, 3D geometry consistency, state understanding, task completeness), and proposes Average Full Score and RoboPhyscore (task-aligned weighted average of task-correlated metrics). Evaluates four representative video world models including Cosmos 3.
AI.result: Cosmos 3 achieves the highest RoboPhyscore of 0.6330, reaching 92.7% of ground-truth performance. State- and execution-grounded metrics reveal substantial failures missed by perceptual and vision-language-model-based judgments. RoboPhyscore shows strong agreement with human evaluation (Pearson r=0.9761, Spearman rho=0.8962).
AI.conclusion: Grounded, execution-aware evaluation is essential for assessing embodied world model capability; purely perceptual or VLM-based judgments are insufficient, and 3D-grounded task-aligned scoring provides a more reliable framework for EWM benchmarking.

title: SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning
comment: accepted to The 3rd AI for Math Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, yet the mathematically meaningful skills underlying their reasoning remain underexplored. We introduce \texttt{SHAPE}, a framework that analyzes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories through two lenses developed in mathematics education: (1) semantic spaces: the model's evolving mathematical interpretations of a problem (e.g., algebraic, geometric), and (2) heuristics: the specific mathematical actions taken within those spaces (e.g., simplifying the problem, working backward). We first use \texttt{SHAPE} to analyze the reasoning patterns of various models. Our findings reveal that the mathematical heuristics employed by a model better explain final answer correctness than traditional CoT features. Furthermore, models are likely to reach correct solutions by concentrating their reasoning effort within a few semantic spaces rather than exploring many disparate ones -- a pattern consistent with human behavior. Next, we utilize the \texttt{SHAPE} lens to evaluate whether post-training truly enhances mathematical proficiency. We find that reinforcement learning induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. Lastly, we post-train LLMs by promoting diverse heuristics and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving accuracy. Overall, \texttt{SHAPE} provides a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework for decoding LLM reasoning and offers a new path toward post-training LLMs for math reasoning. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/holi-lab/SHAPE-of-CoT

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SHAPE, a framework for analyzing Chain-of-Thought trajectories in LLMs using two lenses from mathematics education: semantic spaces (mathematical interpretations like algebraic or geometric) and heuristics (mathematical actions like simplifying or working backward). The framework reveals that heuristics predict correctness better than traditional CoT features, models perform better when concentrating on fewer semantic spaces, and post-training via reinforcement learning induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. The authors also demonstrate that post-training to promote diverse heuristics improves accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, but the mathematically meaningful skills underlying their reasoning remain underexplored. The paper aims to provide a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework to decode LLM reasoning through the lens of mathematics education.
AI.method: SHAPE analyzes CoT trajectories through two lenses from mathematics education: (1) semantic spaces—the model's evolving mathematical interpretations of a problem (e.g., algebraic, geometric), and (2) heuristics—the specific mathematical actions taken within those spaces (e.g., simplifying, working backward). The framework is used to analyze reasoning patterns across models, evaluate post-training effects, and inform a novel post-training approach that promotes diverse heuristics.
AI.result: Mathematical heuristics predict final answer correctness better than traditional CoT features. Models are more likely to reach correct solutions by concentrating reasoning within a few semantic spaces rather than exploring many disparate ones—consistent with human behavior. Reinforcement learning post-training induces mode-seeking in heuristic usage. Post-training LLMs by promoting diverse heuristics is effective in improving accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SHAPE provides a theoretically-grounded diagnostic framework for decoding LLM reasoning and offers a new path toward post-training LLMs for mathematical reasoning. The work bridges mathematics education theory with LLM analysis and training.

title: Vehicle Drift Emergence: Continuous Evolution from Grip Driving to the Handling Limit via Boundary Exploration Learning Model Predictive Control
summary: Automated drift controllers commonly track a prescribed drift equilibrium, sideslip reference, or trajectory. These formulations establish how to execute drift, whereas the continuous transition from grip driving to drift near the handling limit remains unresolved. This paper defines drift emergence in a repetitive lap time minimization task, where neither the controller objective nor the reward contains an explicit drift reference. A boundary exploration learning model predictive controller (BE-LMPC) constructs an empirical safe set and a locally shifted terminal cost from completed laps. By iteratively improving spatial speed allocation under a fixed global speed bound, the controller progressively explores larger sideslip and yaw rate envelopes while preserving recoverability. As lap performance improves, sustained sideslip and pronounced yaw motion emerge while the rear axle approaches saturation. Analysis shows that, when external conditions vary smoothly, the transition from tire adhesion to sliding does not itself cause abrupt changes in tire force or vehicle state. The combined-slip Fiala model satisfies this continuity condition at the transition. At a tire road friction coefficient of 0.6, lap time decreases from 49.95 s on Lap~3 to 25.50 s on Lap~12, with drift first emerging on Lap~11. Lap~12 reaches 16.5$^\circ$ sideslip and 0.894 rear axle utilization. In contrast, no drift is detected for friction coefficients from 0.8 to 1.2; at 1.2, a similar peak speed is achieved with only 0.483 rear axle utilization. These results characterize drift as a conditional continuation of limit handling that emerges when increasing performance demand approaches the available tire capacity, rather than as a separately prescribed motion mode.

AI.tldr: This paper explores drift emergence in an automated lap time minimization task using a boundary exploration learning model predictive controller (BE-LMPC), showing that drift arises naturally as a conditional continuation of limit handling when performance demands approach tire capacity, rather than being explicitly prescribed. At a friction coefficient of 0.6, lap time improves from 49.95s (Lap 3) to 25.50s (Lap 12), with drift first emerging on Lap 11 at 16.5° sideslip and 0.894 rear axle utilization.
AI.motivation: Existing automated drift controllers prescribe drift equilibria, sideslip references, or trajectories, yet the continuous transition from grip driving to drift near the handling limit has not been resolved. This paper seeks to characterize drift as an emergent phenomenon rather than a separately prescribed motion mode in an objective-driven lap time minimization task.
AI.method: A boundary exploration learning model predictive controller (BE-LMPC) is used, which constructs an empirical safe set and a locally shifted terminal cost from completed laps. The controller iteratively improves spatial speed allocation under a fixed global speed bound, progressively exploring larger sideslip and yaw rate envelopes while preserving recoverability. The combined-slip Fiala tire model is analyzed for continuity conditions at the adhesion-to-sliding transition.
AI.result: At a tire-road friction coefficient of 0.6, lap time decreased from 49.95s on Lap 3 to 25.50s on Lap 12, with drift first emerging on Lap 11, reaching 16.5° sideslip and 0.894 rear axle utilization. No drift was detected for friction coefficients from 0.8 to 1.2; at 1.2, a similar peak speed was achieved with only 0.483 rear axle utilization. The combined-slip Fiala model was shown to satisfy continuity conditions at the transition.
AI.conclusion: Drift is characterized as a conditional continuation of limit handling that emerges when increasing performance demand approaches available tire capacity, rather than as a separately prescribed motion mode. The transition from tire adhesion to sliding does not itself cause abrupt changes in tire force or vehicle state when external conditions vary smoothly.

title: Leveraging Generative AI to Design Accessible Interactive Visualizations for Undergraduate Mathematics: A Six-Phase Workflow
summary: Interactive visualizations support conceptual understanding in undergraduate mathematics, but building them has required programming expertise most instructors lack. Using a design-based research approach, we develop, deploy, and evaluate a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control) that uses generative AI to build WCAG~2.2 Level~AA compliant visualizations without programming. The six phases structure every prompt, scaffold the AI's code generation, and define where human verification is applied. We ask whether the structure reliably yields correct and accessible tools, whether it runs both backward (reverse-engineering prompts from a finished tool) and forward (generating a tool from a plain-language idea), and what verification each phase requires. Across four deployed tools spanning calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, we evaluate mathematical correctness against closed forms, accessibility through automated and manual screen-reader testing, and the errors that recurred. The structure produces structurally complete first-pass tools, but human verification remains mandatory at every phase: each output must be checked for mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical fit before the next phase begins. The workflow is platform-independent and serves both instructors and students.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control) that uses generative AI to build WCAG 2.2 Level AA compliant interactive mathematics visualizations without requiring programming expertise. The workflow is validated across four deployed tools in calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, showing it produces structurally complete first-pass tools, though human verification remains mandatory at every phase.
AI.motivation: Interactive visualizations enhance conceptual understanding in undergraduate mathematics, but instructors typically lack the programming expertise required to build them. This work addresses this gap by developing a structured workflow that leverages generative AI to lower the technical barrier for creating accessible visualizations.
AI.method: A design-based research approach is used to develop, deploy, and evaluate a six-phase workflow (Foundation, Customization, Mathematical Depth, Application, Accessibility, Pedagogical Control). The workflow structures every prompt, scaffolds AI code generation, and defines where human verification is applied. It is tested in both backward direction (reverse-engineering prompts from finished tools) and forward direction (generating tools from plain-language ideas). Validation includes mathematical correctness checks against closed forms, automated and manual screen-reader accessibility testing, and analysis of recurring errors.
AI.result: Across four deployed tools spanning calculus, multivariable calculus, and differential equations, the workflow produces structurally complete first-pass tools. However, human verification remains mandatory at every phase: each output must be checked for mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical fit before proceeding to the next phase. The workflow is platform-independent and serves both instructors and students.
AI.conclusion: The six-phase generative AI workflow offers a viable path for instructors to create accessible interactive mathematics visualizations without programming skills, but it does not eliminate the need for human oversight—verification is required at each phase to ensure mathematical correctness, accessibility, and pedagogical appropriateness.

title: Generation of High-Level Concepts in 3D Scene Graphs via Autoregressive Diffusion
summary: Indoor 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) represent environments as multi-layer hierarchies that connect observed geometric primitives (e.g., planes) to higher-level metric-semantic concepts (e.g., rooms, floors, buildings), enabling incremental spatial reasoning for robotic perception and SLAM. However, classical high-level concept generation approaches rely on hand-crafted rules for specific concept classes, while learning-based methods require separate models for graph structure and spatial node features (e.g., centroids), which limits scalability to novel classes and more complex hierarchies. We propose a unified autoregressive diffusion-based graph generative model that jointly learns structure and features, constructing complete 3DSGs bottom-up from observed vertical planes across arbitrary hierarchy depths. Our method consistently surpasses all learning-based and random baselines across 3DSG datasets spanning synthetic scenes, real architectural floor plans, and robotic sensor data, with varying layout complexity and hierarchy depth, and surpasses a one-shot model with oracle access to the target graph size on the largest hierarchy and on real single-floor data. Finally, we propose an adaptation of the Fused Gromov--Wasserstein distance for principled graph-level evaluation of generated 3DSGs against ground truth.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified autoregressive diffusion-based graph generative model for Indoor 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) that jointly learns graph structure and spatial node features, constructing complete 3DSGs bottom-up from vertical planes across arbitrary hierarchy depths. The method outperforms learning-based and random baselines across multiple datasets and proposes an adapted Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance for principled graph-level evaluation.
AI.motivation: Classical high-level concept generation for 3DSGs relies on hand-crafted rules limited to specific classes, while learning-based approaches require separate models for graph structure and spatial node features, hindering scalability to novel classes and more complex hierarchies.
AI.method: A unified autoregressive diffusion-based graph generative model that jointly learns both graph structure and spatial node features (e.g., centroids), constructing complete 3DSGs bottom-up from observed vertical planes across arbitrary hierarchy depths. Additionally, an adaptation of the Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance is proposed for graph-level evaluation of generated 3DSGs.
AI.result: The method consistently surpasses all learning-based and random baselines across 3DSG datasets spanning synthetic scenes, real architectural floor plans, and robotic sensor data with varying layout complexity and hierarchy depth. It also outperforms a one-shot model with oracle access to target graph size on the largest hierarchy and real single-floor data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed joint generative approach overcomes limitations of both rule-based and separately-modeled learning-based methods, achieving state-of-the-art generation of 3DSGs across diverse data sources and hierarchy complexities, with a principled evaluation metric for generated graphs.

title: Integrating Triaxial IMU Sensors and Ensemble Learning for Effective Parkinson Disease Severity Classification
summary: Parkinson disease PD is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that can have a significant impact on motor performance resulting in the appearance of symptoms such as tremors rigidity postural instabilities and bradykinesia. Timely clinical treatment disease management and quality life of the patients are closely linked to early and appropriate identification of PD. Over the past few years the growth of wearable sensor technology and artificial intelligence AI have made it possible to create noninvasive and data driven disease detection methods. This paper proposes a comparative system using artificial intelligence to detect Parkinsons disease by analyzing the motion and tremor data captured by an inertial measurement unit IMU. The data comprises the signals of the acceleration and gyroscope sensors measuring movement in three directions X Y and Z. The signs and symptoms provide helpful information about subtle motor deficits associated with PD. Several classification models like Support Vector Machine SVM Logistic Regression LR KNearest Neighbors KNN Decision Tree DT Extreme Gradient Boosting XGBoost and Light Gradient Boosting Machine LightGBM were used to compare their effectiveness. The Logistic Regression model had a performance around 75 percent in all evaluation metrics and KNearest Neighbours KNN around 90 percent. The support vector machine SVM performed almost 94 percent whereas the performance of classifiers such as Decision Tree and XGBoost was close to 96 percent and overall classification efficacy respectively. LightGBM model performs consistently at the best rank among all of the evaluated methods having Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1score of around 97 percent. The results show that the proposed machine learning approach offers an accurate and effective predictive capability in the classification of PD severity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-based comparative system for detecting Parkinson's disease using IMU sensor data (acceleration and gyroscope signals in X, Y, Z axes) capturing motion and tremor. Multiple machine learning classifiers were compared, with LightGBM achieving the best performance (~97% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score).
AI.motivation: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder significantly impacting motor functions. Early and accurate detection is critical for timely treatment and improved patient quality of life. The growth of wearable sensor technology and AI enables noninvasive, data-driven disease detection methods to address this need.
AI.method: The system uses an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to capture acceleration and gyroscope signals across three axes (X, Y, Z) representing motion and tremor data. Seven classification models were evaluated and compared: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Tree (DT), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM).
AI.result: Logistic Regression achieved ~75% across all metrics; KNN reached ~90%; SVM achieved ~94%; Decision Tree and XGBoost were close to 96%. LightGBM consistently ranked best among all evaluated methods with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score around 97%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed machine learning approach provides accurate and effective predictive capability for classifying PD severity, with LightGBM demonstrating the strongest overall performance among the compared classifiers.

title: Adversarial Calibration Attack on Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) rely on accurate camera-LiDAR calibration for multimodal sensor fusion. In practice, calibration can drift due to vibration, temperature variation, or minor sensor displacement, motivating online calibration algorithms that detect and correct misalignment at runtime while allowing the vehicle to continue operating without a factory visit. Existing AV attacks largely assume correct calibration. We instead identify online sensor calibration as a new attack plane. A corrupted calibration update can persist across subsequent fusion operations, causing system-wide errors that propagate from perception to planning and control. We present Adversarial Calibration Attack (ACA), the first physical attack against camera-LiDAR online calibration. Using a single adversarial poster, ACA first spoofs the miscalibration detector to trigger the calibration process and then steers the calibration estimator toward an incorrect transformation. A unified optimization jointly designs the poster's geometry and texture for both objectives. We evaluate ACA across benchmark datasets, simulation, and physical experiments. On benchmark datasets such as KITTI and nuScenes, ACA induces up to 33.9 degrees mean rotational calibration error, thereby severely degrading object detection. In the CARLA simulator, the attack causes a collision when the corrupted calibration is accepted in vulnerable scenarios crafted by the attacker. On a real Husky robot, a printed adversarial poster successfully reproduces the calibration error. These results demonstrate that online calibration is a practical and safety-critical attack surface for AVs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Adversarial Calibration Attack (ACA), the first physical attack targeting camera-LiDAR online calibration in autonomous vehicles. Using a single adversarial poster, ACA can trigger and manipulate the calibration process to induce large calibration errors (up to 33.9 degrees), severely degrading perception and potentially causing collisions in simulation.
AI.motivation: Online calibration is essential for AVs to correct sensor drift, but existing attacks focus on targets that assume correct calibration. The authors identify online calibration as a novel attack surface where a corrupted update can persist and propagate errors across the entire perception-to-control pipeline, posing a critical safety risk.
AI.method: ACA uses a single adversarial poster designed via unified optimization that jointly optimizes geometry and texture to achieve two objectives: (1) spoofing the miscalibration detector to trigger the calibration process, and (2) steering the calibration estimator toward an incorrect transformation. Evaluation is conducted across benchmark datasets (KITTI, nuScenes), CARLA simulation, and physical experiments on a Husky robot.
AI.result: On KITTI and nuScenes, ACA induces up to 33.9 degrees mean rotational calibration error, severely degrading object detection. In CARLA, the attack causes a collision in attacker-crafted vulnerable scenarios. Physical experiments on a real Husky robot confirm the printed adversarial poster successfully reproduces calibration errors.
AI.conclusion: Online camera-LiDAR calibration is a practical and safety-critical attack surface for autonomous vehicles. The success of ACA across simulation and physical platforms demonstrates the feasibility of physical adversarial attacks against online calibration systems, highlighting the need for robust calibration security measures.

title: C3-UniMM: Causal Cycle-Consistent Unified Multimodal Modeling via Super Alignment and Shared Decoding Space
summary: Unified Multimodal Models aim to achieve any-to-any understanding and generation across arbitrary modalities. However, existing methods primarily rely on modeling implicit statistical correlations and lack cross-modal structural consistency constraints.
