This deficiency leads to profound issues, including semantic drift, poor compositional generalization, and instability under interventions. In this paper, we propose C3-UniMM, a unified multimodal modeling framework based on Causal Cycle Consistency and Super Alignment. Specifically, we introduce a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) as a shared cross-modal semantic space and design unified multimodal encoding blocks, enabling understanding and generation to be synergistically optimized within the identical causal semantic structure. Furthermore, we propose a Unified Decoding Space to enforce structural preservation and semantic invertibility during the cross-modal generation process. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances both the invertibility and mechanism invariance of cross-modal mappings. Extensive experimental results across multiple understanding, generation, and compositional generalization tasks indicate that C3-UniMM substantially outperforms existing unified multimodal baselines.

AI.tldr: C3-UniMM proposes a unified multimodal framework that introduces a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) as a shared cross-modal semantic space, along with a Unified Decoding Space enforcing structural preservation and semantic invertibility, achieving causal cycle consistency and super alignment across understanding and generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing unified multimodal models rely on implicit statistical correlations and lack cross-modal structural consistency constraints, leading to semantic drift, poor compositional generalization, and instability under interventions.
AI.method: The framework introduces a Structured Latent Causal Graph (SLCG) as a shared cross-modal semantic space with unified multimodal encoding blocks, enabling synergistic optimization of understanding and generation within an identical causal semantic structure. It also proposes a Unified Decoding Space to enforce structural preservation and semantic invertibility during cross-modal generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple understanding, generation, and compositional generalization tasks show C3-UniMM substantially outperforms existing unified multimodal baselines. Theoretical analyses demonstrate enhanced invertibility and mechanism invariance of cross-modal mappings.
AI.conclusion: Causal cycle consistency and structural constraints in a shared latent causal semantic space significantly improve unified multimodal understanding and generation, offering a principled alternative to purely statistical correlation-based approaches.

title: Dual Park-Ravani Interpolation of Rigid Motions: Acceleration-Field Continuity and Holonomic Hermite Repair
comment: 12 pages. Ancillary Python programs reproduce the numerical verification
summary: The Park-Ravani construction generates a twice continuously differentiable, frame-invariant spline on SO(3) by exponentiating cubic canonical-coordinate polynomials. We show that the construction transfers, without changing form, to the group of orthogonal dual tensors, a representation of rigid displacements. The transferred recurrence is stated compactly through the dual extension of the right Jacobian of the exponential map and its first Fréchet derivative. This yields interpolation of prescribed rigid poses and continuity of the body dual twist and its first derivative. Using the higher-order rigid-body kinematics of dual spatial twists, we then prove that the resulting curve has a continuous physical acceleration field, not merely a continuous quantity obtained by formally differentiating the dual part of a twist. We also distinguish algebraic dual transfer from temporal differential prolongation: their simultaneous first-order use takes place in a hyper-dual algebra, and interpolation of arbitrary prolonged nodal data need not be holonomic. A noncommuting three-pose example verifies the recurrence, all knot continuity statements, and dimensional covariance under a change from meters to millimeters. We define and analyze the first-order holonomy defect of a generic hyper-dual interpolant, exhibit an exact counterexample, and remove the defect by cubic or quintic Hermite interpolation in dual logarithmic coordinates.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Park-Ravani spline construction from SO(3) to the group of orthogonal dual tensors (representing rigid displacements), enabling interpolation of prescribed rigid poses with continuity of the body dual twist and its first derivative. The authors prove the resulting curve has a continuous physical acceleration field via higher-order rigid-body kinematics of dual spatial twists, distinguish algebraic dual transfer from temporal differential prolongation in hyper-dual algebras, analyze holonomy defects of hyper-dual interpolants, and remove these defects using cubic/quintic Hermite interpolation in dual logarithmic coordinates.
AI.motivation: To generalize a well-established frame-invariant spline construction on SO(3) to the dual orthogonal group that represents rigid body displacements, while ensuring not just formal algebraic continuity but physically meaningful kinematic properties such as continuous acceleration.
AI.method: The construction transfers the Park-Ravani cubic canonical-coordinate exponential scheme to orthogonal dual tensors using the dual extension of the right Jacobian of the exponential map and its first Fréchet derivative. The authors leverage higher-order rigid-body kinematics of dual spatial twists to establish physical acceleration continuity, and employ hyper-dual algebras to analyze the interplay between algebraic dual transfer and temporal differential prolongation. Holonomy defects are examined and removed via Hermite interpolation in dual logarithmic coordinates.
AI.result: The recurrence successfully interpolates prescribed rigid poses with continuous body dual twist and first derivative. A noncommuting three-pose example verifies the recurrence, knot continuity, and dimensional covariance (meters to millimeters). The paper defines and analyzes the first-order holonomy defect of generic hyper-dual interpolants, provides an exact counterexample, and demonstrates defect removal via cubic or quintic Hermite interpolation in dual logarithmic coordinates.
AI.conclusion: The Park-Ravani construction extends naturally to dual orthogonal tensors, providing smooth interpolation of rigid motions with genuine physical acceleration continuity. Key subtleties arise when combining algebraic dual transfer with temporal prolongation, requiring hyper-dual algebra and Hermite interpolation in logarithmic coordinates to resolve holonomy defects.

title: MedTVL: Harnessing Vision and Language for Medical Time Series Classification
summary: Recent advancements in multimodal learning for medical time series (MedTS) classification highlight the benefits of integrating complementary modalities for clinical decision. However, existing methods typically focus on bi-modal interactions (e.g., time series and text), leaving the tri-modal synergy between time series, vision, and language largely unexplored. Inspired by diagnostic practice synergizing numerical assessment, visual inspection and clinical context, we introduce MedTVL, a text-guided dual-pathway architecture tailored for MedTS classification. Specifically, it synergizes a convolution-based temporal pathway for fine-grained temporal dynamics from raw numerical sequences and a transformer-based visual pathway for holistic morphological structures from time-series-derived images. Such combination of cross-modal and architectural heterogeneity provides a comprehensive diagnostic perspective. To further resolve potential diagnostic ambiguity, both pathways are guided by adaptive medical textual semantics. Finally, a Mixture-of-Experts mechanism dynamically routes each instance to specialized fusion experts, capturing instance-specific reliance on the temporal and visual pathway outputs. In addition, MedTVL supports multimodal contrastive learning to mitigate the clinical label scarcity challenge. Extensive experiments across multiple medical datasets and tasks, spanning supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings, demonstrate the superiority and transferability of MedTVL, highlighting its potential for robust clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedTVL is a text-guided dual-pathway architecture for medical time series classification that synergizes a convolution-based temporal pathway and a transformer-based visual pathway, guided by adaptive medical text semantics and facilitated by a Mixture-of-Experts fusion mechanism and multimodal contrastive learning, demonstrating superior performance across supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal medical time series classification methods primarily focus on bi-modal interactions (e.g., time series and text), leaving tri-modal synergy between time series, vision, and language largely unexplored, despite diagnostic practice naturally integrating numerical assessment, visual inspection, and clinical context.
AI.method: MedTVL uses a convolution-based temporal pathway for fine-grained temporal dynamics from raw numerical sequences and a transformer-based visual pathway for holistic morphological structures from time-series-derived images. Both pathways are guided by adaptive medical textual semantics to resolve diagnostic ambiguity, and a Mixture-of-Experts mechanism dynamically routes each instance to specialized fusion experts for instance-specific reliance weighting. Multimodal contrastive learning is also supported to address clinical label scarcity.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple medical datasets and tasks spanning supervised, few-shot, and contrastive learning settings demonstrate the superiority and transferability of MedTVL for robust clinical decision support.
AI.conclusion: The combination of cross-modal and architectural heterogeneity provides a comprehensive diagnostic perspective, and MedTVL's text-guided dual-pathway design with MoE-based fusion and contrastive learning shows strong potential for robust clinical decision support in medical time series classification.

title: Brain-Language-Action (BLA) Models: Language-Conditioned EEG for Robotics Control
summary:
Electroencephalography (EEG)-based robotic control is commonly formulated as a direct classification problem, in which electrical neural signals are mapped to a fixed set of discrete actions. However, the limited separability and high noise of EEG signals make it difficult to scale this approach to fine-grained robotic control spaces. We introduce Brain-Language-Action (BLA) models, a framework in which language conditions the interpretation of neural representations for robotic action generation. In a BLA, a small set of reliably distinguishable brain states can be dynamically associated with different actions through a language-defined control mapping, allowing a small number of neural classes to apply to a larger global action space.
  We develop a proof-of-concept BLA for drone control using motor-imagery EEG from the BCI Competition IV 2a dataset. The system is trained in two stages. First, we evaluate multiple candidate EEG encoder architectures using subject-specific four-class motor-imagery classification, converting 250Hz, 3.5-second, 22-channel EEG samples into five 128-dimensional brain-token embeddings. Second, these embeddings are projected into the embedding space of a pretrained large language model (LLM) and jointly fine-tuned with language instructions to autoregressively generate structured three-token drone actions. Across 840 possible language-defined mappings between four neural states and seven flight action combinations, the resulting BLA achieves 90% per-token accuracy during evaluation. These results provide an initial demonstration that language conditioning can expand the effective control range of EEG-based robotic interfaces without requiring a corresponding increase in the number of directly distinguishable neural states.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Brain-Language-Action (BLA) models, a framework that uses language to condition the interpretation of EEG neural representations for robotic control. By mapping a small set of distinguishable brain states to a larger action space via language-defined control mappings, the authors demonstrate a proof-of-concept BLA for drone control achieving 90% per-token accuracy across 840 possible language-defined mappings, showing language conditioning can expand the effective control range of EEG-based interfaces without requiring more neural classes.
AI.motivation: Traditional EEG-based robotic control treats the problem as direct classification from neural signals to a fixed set of discrete actions. However, EEG signals suffer from limited separability and high noise, making it difficult to scale this approach to fine-grained robotic control spaces that require many distinct actions.
AI.method: The BLA framework is built in two stages. First, multiple candidate EEG encoder architectures are evaluated using subject-specific four-class motor-imagery classification on the BCI Competition IV 2a dataset, converting 250Hz, 3.5-second, 22-channel EEG samples into five 128-dimensional brain-token embeddings. Second, these embeddings are projected into the embedding space of a pretrained large language model (LLM) and jointly fine-tuned with language instructions to autoregressively generate structured three-token drone actions.
AI.result: Across 840 possible language-defined mappings between four neural states and seven flight action combinations, the resulting BLA model achieves 90% per-token accuracy during evaluation. This demonstrates that language conditioning can expand the effective control range of EEG-based robotic interfaces without a corresponding increase in the number of directly distinguishable neural states.
AI.conclusion: Language conditioning provides an effective mechanism for decoupling the number of distinguishable brain states from the size of the actionable control space in EEG-based robotic interfaces. The BLA framework offers an initial proof-of-concept that a small set of reliable neural classes can be dynamically associated with a much larger global action space through language-defined control mappings.

title: RegDivergence-101: An LLM Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdiction Regulatory Contradiction Detection in Life Sciences
summary: Pharmaceutical sponsors developing a drug for both the United States and the European Union must reconcile guidance issued independently by the FDA and the EMA. Where the two agencies require substantively the same thing, a sponsor can file once; where they diverge, a single trial design risks rejection in one region; where one agency is silent on a point the other regulates, the sponsor must infer obligations. Today this reconciliation is performed manually by regulatory-affairs experts. We introduce cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection: given an FDA requirement and an EMA requirement on the same topic, classify their relationship as AGREE, DIVERGE, or SILENT. SILENT is inherently directional (SILENT_FDA vs. SILENT_EMA); we record direction per pair and report per-direction F1 alongside the collapsed label. We release RegDivergence-101, a 101-pair expert-grounded pilot evaluation benchmark (labels grounded in three peer-reviewed FDA/EMA comparison studies and primary FDA/EMA/ICH guidance text; dual-annotation inter-annotator kappa = 0.85), and systematically characterise a four-method baseline hierarchy: lexical heuristic (0.511 macro-F1, 95% CI [0.411-0.605]), NLI cross-encoder (0.233), obligation-level Graph-RAG (0.663 [0.570-0.747]), and flat LLM judge / Claude Haiku (0.830 [0.747-0.908]). Three directional observations emerge at pilot scale (n = 101): SILENT is semantically detectable but invisible to entailment-only formulations; pair-level obligation graphs improve over lexical methods but trail flat-LLM context (CIs partially overlapping); and corpus-level graph construction is the indicated architectural target for large-scale silent-detection. RegDivergence-101 is a pilot release establishing the task formulation and baseline hierarchy; four unrepresented regulatory domains and an expansion roadmap are described in Section 7.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the task of cross-jurisdiction regulatory divergence detection for FDA vs. EMA pharmaceutical requirements, classifying pairs as AGREE, DIVERGE, or SILENT (directionally). It releases RegDivergence-101, a 101-pair expert-grounded benchmark (κ=0.85), and benchmarks four baseline methods, finding that a flat LLM judge (Claude Haiku) achieves best macro-F1 (0.830), with corpus-level graph construction identified as the next architectural target.
AI.motivation: Sponsors developing drugs for both the US and EU must manually reconcile independent FDA and EMA guidance. Manual regulatory-affairs expert review is time-consuming and error-prone; no automated task formulation existed for detecting where agency requirements agree, diverge, or are unilateral/silent.
AI.method: Defines a three-class classification task (AGREE, DIVERGE, SILENT) with directional SILENT labels. Releases RegDivergence-101: a 101-pair benchmark grounded in three peer-reviewed FDA/EMA comparison studies and primary regulatory guidance text, with dual annotation (κ=0.85). Evaluates a four-method baseline hierarchy: lexical heuristic, NLI cross-encoder, obligation-level Graph-RAG, and flat LLM judge (Claude Haiku), reporting per-direction F1 and macro-F1.
AI.result: Lexical heuristic achieves 0.511 macro-F1 (95% CI [0.411-0.605]); NLI cross-encoder 0.233; obligation-level Graph-RAG 0.663 ([0.570-0.747]); flat LLM judge (Claude Haiku) 0.830 ([0.747-0.908]). Three observations: SILENT is semantically detectable but invisible to entailment-only formulations; graph-based methods improve over lexical baselines but trail flat-LLM context with partially overlapping CIs; corpus-level graph construction is the indicated target for large-scale silent detection.
AI.conclusion: RegDivergence-101 establishes the task formulation and baseline hierarchy for automated regulatory divergence detection at pilot scale (n=101). Flat LLM judges are currently best; future work should target corpus-level graph construction for scalable SILENT detection, with four unrepresented regulatory domains and an expansion roadmap described in Section 7.

title: Hydra: A Navigation World Action Model with Discrete Latent Planning and Continuous Flow-Matching Execution
summary: World models let robots imagine possible futures, but exploiting this capability for real-time control is bottlenecked by a representation misalignment: the generative model and the planner operate on decoupled manifolds, so the planner has no shared structure to search over and must instead decode every candidate back into high-dimensional pixel space to evaluate it. This decoding step is a major obstacle to real-time control on physical hardware. In this paper, we present Hydra, a discrete World Action Model that closes this gap by moving the planner, both the sampler and the evaluator, inside the model. Hydra establishes a unified latent manifold over visual states, physical poses, and control actions, then compresses this manifold through modality-specific Vector-Quantized bottlenecks into discrete vocabularies of kinodynamic intents and visual states. Because candidates are now drawn directly from this shared manifold, sampling is informed by the model's own understanding of the observation rather than proposed blind, and evaluation happens natively within the discrete space: candidates are ranked by a Kinematic-Perceptual Cost, without ever decoding to pixels. We term this Discrete Latent Planning (DLP). Because planning over discrete intents alone cannot supply the smooth, continuous commands physical actuation requires, Hydra pairs DLP with conditional Flow Matching, which maps each selected intent to a continuous trajectory for execution. Evaluated on two physical robotic platforms, Hydra outperforms state-of-the-art world models in goal-directed planning, while matching or exceeding the closed-loop execution capabilities of leading reactive foundation policies.

AI.tldr: Hydra is a discrete World Action Model that unifies visual states, physical poses, and control actions into a shared latent manifold, compressed via modality-specific VQ bottlenecks into discrete vocabularies. It enables Discrete Latent Planning (DLP) where sampling and evaluation happen natively in discrete space without decoding to pixels, paired with conditional Flow Matching to produce continuous execution trajectories. It outperforms SOTA world models on goal-directed planning and matches/exceeds reactive foundation policies on physical robots.
AI.motivation: World models enable robots to imagine futures but suffer from representation misalignment: the generative model and planner operate on decoupled manifolds, forcing the planner to decode every candidate back into high-dimensional pixel space for evaluation—a computational bottleneck preventing real-time control on physical hardware.
AI.method: Hydra establishes a unified latent manifold over visual states, physical poses, and control actions, compressed through modality-specific Vector-Quantized bottlenecks into discrete vocabularies of kinodynamic intents and visual states. It performs Discrete Latent Planning (DLP) where candidates are sampled from this shared manifold and ranked by a Kinematic-Perceptual Cost entirely in discrete space. Conditional Flow Matching then maps each selected discrete intent to a continuous trajectory for physical execution.
AI.result: Evaluated on two physical robotic platforms, Hydra outperforms state-of-the-art world models in goal-directed planning and matches or exceeds the closed-loop execution capabilities of leading reactive foundation policies.
AI.conclusion: By moving the planner inside the generative model and unifying the planning and generative manifolds, Hydra eliminates the pixel-decoding bottleneck, enabling efficient real-time world-model-based control on physical hardware while retaining strong closed-loop execution performance.

title: TPvG: A Moral Decision Framework for Large Language Models from One-Shot to Sequential Feedback
summary: Existing LLM moral evaluations typically present models with isolated moral vignettes and elicit a single-shot decision, neglecting a factor known to profoundly influence human moral behavior: consequence feedback. We introduce TPvG (Text-based Pain-versus-Gain), adapted from a human moral paradigm, which embeds consequence feedback into an everyday moral dilemma of not harming others versus maximising self-gain. TPvG comprises five moral decision tasks, progressing from minimal-context one-shot choices to sequential decisions with explicit consequence feedback. Our results show that LLM moral decisions were strongly affected by decision format (one-shot versus sequential), and explicit receiver feedback produced heterogeneous effects across models. Furthermore, LLM responses to explicit receiver feedback diverged from the human reference pattern, suggesting potentially different decision processes. These findings highlight the need to evaluate whether LLM moral behavior remains stable in high-stakes interactive settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TPvG (Text-based Pain-versus-Gain), a benchmark adapted from a human moral paradigm that embeds consequence feedback into moral dilemmas. Testing five tasks from one-shot to sequential decisions with feedback, the authors find that LLM moral decisions are strongly affected by decision format and that model responses to feedback diverge from human patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM moral evaluations rely on isolated vignettes with single-shot decisions, ignoring consequence feedback—a factor known to profoundly shape human moral behavior. This limits ecological validity and may misrepresent how LLMs behave in interactive, high-stakes settings.
AI.method: TPvG adapts a human moral paradigm into text, embedding consequence feedback into the moral dilemma of not harming others versus maximizing self-gain. The benchmark comprises five moral decision tasks that progress from minimal-context one-shot choices to sequential decisions with explicit consequence feedback.
AI.result: LLM moral decisions were strongly affected by decision format (one-shot versus sequential), explicit receiver feedback produced heterogeneous effects across models, and LLM responses to feedback diverged from human reference patterns, suggesting different underlying decision processes.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the need to evaluate whether LLM moral behavior remains stable in high-stakes interactive settings, where consequence feedback is present and decisions unfold sequentially.

title: Coding What Matters: A Semantic-Aware Memory Interface for Energy-Efficient Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles stream high-resolution surround-camera frames into memory before perception runs. This sensor-to-memory path consumes energy when cells store ones and adjacent bytes toggle on the data bus, so its cost follows bit-1 density and switching activity rather than pixel semantics. We present MotiMem-Omega, a semantic-aware memory-interface coder that lowers this cost while preserving perception predictions. Its semantic importance field protects traffic participants, especially vulnerable road users, while assigning lower fidelity to sky and empty background. Cross-dataset bit-sensitivity sweeps determine class weights, with a safety floor for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorcyclists. Each image block then selects a precision tier by minimizing a joint energy-distortion cost. When ego pose is available, a motion-compensated prior carries protected regions between frames. We estimate interface-energy reduction from the two measured proxies using a coefficient-swept memory-energy model. Across 29 detectors on 12 driving datasets, 5 occupancy models, and 5 segmentation networks, MotiMem-Omega retains about 90% of detection mean average precision, 91% of vulnerable-road-user recall, over 98% of occupancy accuracy, and the strongest segmentation retention among energy-reducing methods. It reduces front-camera bit-1 density by 52%, corresponding to a modeled memory-interface energy reduction near 36%, with a lower end of 27% under the literature coefficient sweep. It also gives higher retention than the baseline and energy-matched truncation at the same or lower bit-1 density, whereas image codecs preserve accuracy without reducing memory-interface energy.

AI.tldr: MotiMem-Omega is a semantic-aware memory-interface coder that reduces memory energy consumption in autonomous vehicle perception pipelines by exploiting the observation that memory write costs follow bit-1 density and switching activity rather than pixel semantics. It protects traffic participants while assigning lower fidelity to unimportant regions, achieving ~52% reduction in bit-1 density and ~36% modeled memory-interface energy reduction while retaining ~90% of detection mAP, 91% of vulnerable-road-user recall, and over 98% of occupancy accuracy across a broad experimental sweep.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles stream high-resolution surround-camera frames into memory before perception runs. This sensor-to-memory path consumes energy proportional to bit-1 density and data-bus switching activity, not pixel semantic value. Existing approaches either preserve accuracy without energy benefit (codecs) or reduce fidelity without semantic awareness. There is a need for a semantic-aware coder that minimizes memory-interface energy while protecting safety-critical perception targets.
AI.method: MotiMem-Omega constructs a semantic importance field that protects traffic participants (especially vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists) while lowering fidelity for sky and background. Class weights are determined via cross-dataset bit-sensitivity sweeps with a safety floor for vulnerable road users. Each image block selects a precision tier by minimizing a joint energy-distortion cost. When ego pose is available, a motion-compensated prior carries protected regions between frames. Energy is estimated from two measured proxies (bit-1 density and switching activity) using a coefficient-swept memory-energy model.
AI.result: Across 29 detectors on 12 driving datasets, 5 occupancy models, and 5 segmentation networks, MotiMem-Omega retains ~90% detection mAP, 91% vulnerable-road-user recall, >98% occupancy accuracy, and the strongest segmentation retention among energy-reducing methods. It reduces front-camera bit-1 density by 52%, corresponding to a modeled memory-interface energy reduction near 36% (27% lower bound under literature coefficient sweep). It outperforms baseline and energy-matched truncation at the same or lower bit-1 density, whereas image codecs preserve accuracy without reducing memory-interface energy.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aware memory-interface coding is an effective approach for reducing the energy footprint of the sensor-to-memory path in autonomous driving perception. By aligning fidelity allocation with semantic importance and optionally exploiting ego-motion priors, MotiMem-Omega achieves substantial energy savings while preserving perception performance for safety-critical classes, outperforming both naive truncation and accuracy-preserving codec baselines.

title: InternReviewer & InternAdvocate: Objective Reward and Evaluation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning in Peer Review and Rebuttal
summary: Generating professional scholarly content, such as peer reviews and rebuttals, requires an intricate synergy between domain reasoning and factual grounding. This work presents a comprehensive framework for the development and evaluation of specialized scholarly agents, InternReviewer and InternAdvocate. We first establish a large-scale, high-quality scholarly dataset and integrate a high-efficiency arXiv retrieval tool to enable active evidence gathering. To optimize these agents, we implement an agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm driven by a unified objective metric and reward system. This system avoids the biases of subjective model-based judging by employing multi-dimensional criteria, including reference-anchored semantic alignment, structural compliance, and a strict verification mechanism that cross-checks citations against real-time interaction logs to eliminate hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that agents trained within this closed-loop framework exhibit significant improvements in reasoning depth and citation accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for developing and evaluating specialized scholarly agents (InternReviewer and InternAdvocate) using a large-scale dataset, arXiv retrieval, and an agentic Reinforcement Learning paradigm with a unified reward system based on multi-dimensional criteria to improve reasoning depth and citation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Generating professional scholarly content like peer reviews and rebuttals requires both domain reasoning and factual grounding, which is challenging. Existing approaches rely on subjective model-based judging that introduces biases, highlighting the need for a more objective, multi-criteria evaluation framework.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) construction of a large-scale high-quality scholarly dataset, (2) integration of a high-efficiency arXiv retrieval tool for active evidence gathering, (3) implementation of an agentic Reinforcement Learning paradigm driven by a unified objective metric and reward system, and (4) multi-dimensional evaluation criteria including reference-anchored semantic alignment, structural compliance, and strict citation verification against real-time interaction logs to eliminate hallucinations.
AI.result: Agents trained within the closed-loop framework demonstrate significant improvements in reasoning depth and citation accuracy, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop RL framework with objective multi-dimensional rewards successfully enhances scholarly agent performance in both reasoning quality and factual grounding, offering a robust alternative to subjective model-based evaluation.

title: A Degradation-Tolerance Benchmark for Camera-Only End-to-End Driving
summary: Camera-only end-to-end (E2E) driving models are nearing deployment, where the camera stream is degraded by blur, noise, low light, weather, frame loss, and memory faults. How much a policy tolerates before its driving breaks is unclear. Corruption-robustness benchmarks target detection or bird's-eye-view perception, not the planning output that drives the car. We present DriveDegrade, a benchmark for image-degradation tolerance in camera-only E2E driving. Sixteen corruption families at five severities are injected on the fly inside the image loader, one operator reaching fifteen policies, and we evaluate open-loop planning on nuScenes and NAVSIM plus a CARLA closed-loop anchor. First, mild degradation barely affects planning, and the families that break it have a clear threshold at mid severity. Second, fragility is corruption-dependent: blur, JPEG, and raindrop damage planning most, while weather and bit error are tolerated far into the range. Third, a flat curve is ambiguous, so we separate corruptions that degrade the image from those that remove it. A planner that reads its camera must lose accuracy when information is deleted, whatever it does under quality loss. On these two axes the planners separate sharply, quantifying the ego-status shortcut without mistaking indifference for robustness. A released vision-language-action planner is flat on both axes, and blinding all six of its cameras costs it only 11.5 percent.

AI.tldr: DriveDegrade is a benchmark for evaluating how camera-only end-to-end driving models tolerate image degradations (16 corruption families, 5 severities) across 15 policies, finding that mild degradation barely affects planning, corruption impacts are family-dependent (blur/JPEG/raindrops most damaging), and flat robustness curves can mask shortcuts—e.g., a vision-language-action planner loses only 11.5% even when all cameras are blinded.
AI.motivation: Camera-only end-to-end driving models are nearing deployment but will face degraded camera inputs (blur, noise, weather, frame loss, memory faults). Existing corruption-robustness benchmarks target detection or BEV perception, not the planning output that actually drives the car, leaving a gap in understanding how much degradation a driving policy can tolerate.
AI.method: The authors build DriveDegrade, which injects 16 corruption families at 5 severities on the fly inside the image loader of 15 camera-only E2E driving policies. They evaluate open-loop planning on nuScenes and NAVSIM, plus a CARLA closed-loop anchor. They also introduce a diagnostic distinction: separating corruptions that degrade image quality from those that remove information, and measuring robustness curves to detect shortcuts (e.g., ego-status reliance) rather than mistaking flat curves for true robustness.
AI.result: Mild degradation barely affects planning with a clear severity threshold where performance breaks; fragility is corruption-dependent (blur, JPEG, raindrop damage planning most; weather and bit error tolerated longer); separating degradation from information-removal corruptions reveals planners diverge sharply, quantifying the ego-status shortcut. A released vision-language-action planner is flat on both axes, losing only 11.5% when all six cameras are blinded.
AI.conclusion: DriveDegrade reveals that corruption robustness in E2E driving is corruption-specific and thresholded, and that flat robustness curves can hide shortcuts. The benchmark's diagnostic framework distinguishes genuine resilience from policies that ignore the camera, providing a more honest evaluation of camera-only E2E driving robustness before deployment.

title: Preference Elicitation for Policy Optimization and Application to Aligning Heart Transplantation with Human Values
summary: Preference elicitation is essential for aligning AI systems with human values. Prior approaches (e.g., for organ allocation) often ask stakeholders to compare the decisions of an algorithm (e.g., patient A vs. patient B). Such a decision-level approach conflates the means with the ends. Instead, we elicit preferences directly over allocation outcomes to learn a utility function for policy optimization. We construct a novel preference elicitation algorithm for linear utilities that outperforms prior techniques in practice. Our algorithm has two phases. The first phase learns cutting planes through pairwise comparisons to rapidly shrink the space of possible attribute weights and warm-starts the second phase by eliminating dominated regions. The second phase then provably converges to the user's utility function. We apply our technique to heart transplant allocation where a policy must balance competing objectives such as post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geographic ease, and equity. Using our algorithm, we conduct a user study to learn and aggregate a community-aligned utility function, and use it to optimize heart transplant policies that are significantly better aligned with human values. Compared to the hindsight optimum, the status quo policy achieves a competitive ratio of just 0.54, while our method is near-optimal with a competitive ratio of 0.95.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel preference elicitation algorithm for linear utilities that learns utility functions by eliciting preferences directly over allocation outcomes (rather than decisions), and demonstrates its effectiveness in heart transplant allocation. The method uses cutting planes for rapid weight-space reduction, followed by a provably convergent second phase, achieving a competitive ratio of 0.95 compared to 0.54 for the status quo policy.
AI.motivation: Prior preference elicitation approaches for aligning AI systems with human values (e.g., in organ allocation) ask stakeholders to compare algorithm decisions (patient A vs. patient B), which conflates means with ends. The authors argue that preferences should be elicited directly over allocation outcomes to learn a utility function for policy optimization, rather than over intermediate algorithmic decisions.
AI.method: The algorithm has two phases: (1) a cutting-plane phase that learns through pairwise comparisons over allocation outcomes, rapidly shrinking the space of possible attribute weights and warm-starting the second phase by eliminating dominated regions; (2) a second phase that provably converges to the user's utility function. The technique is applied to heart transplant allocation, where a policy must balance post-transplant outcomes, waitlist mortality, geographic ease, and equity, with a user study to learn and aggregate a community-aligned utility function.
AI.result: Compared to the hindsight optimum, the status quo policy achieves a competitive ratio of only 0.54, while the proposed method is near-optimal with a competitive ratio of 0.95, demonstrating significantly better alignment with human values in heart transplant allocation policy.
AI.conclusion: Eliciting preferences over outcomes rather than decisions enables the learning of utility functions that better align AI policies with human values. The two-phase cutting-plane algorithm is both practical and provably convergent, achieving near-optimal performance in a real-world heart transplant allocation setting, substantially outperforming the status quo.

title: Teaching Robot Policies to Humans Using Erroneous Examples
summary:
Human-robot collaboration describes the process of humans and autonomous agents working together to accomplish common goals. This process is facilitated best when robot policies, or behaviors in different situations, are made transparent to humans. Demonstration-based explanations have been a focus of human-robot collaboration research, and the field has frequently drawn upon literature from education to improve how humans are taught robot policies. However, no single teaching method has been proven effective across domains, difficulties, learners, and other variables; the question of how humans can most effectively be taught robot policies remains open.
  In traditional classrooms, learners are shown erroneous examples, in which they reflect on and correct incorrect responses to understand common pitfalls when learning a concept. We propose using erroneous examples to teach robot policies, extending an existing policy teaching framework. We conduct a user study in which participants view incorrect demonstrations of robot behavior and correct the actions to align with the actual policy. Our findings suggest that viewing these incorrect demonstrations and verbalizing one's reasoning in predicting a robot's actions improves retention of the policy over time, in agreement with the effect of erroneous examples in classrooms. We also categorize participants into distinct learning styles and establish that participants using inverse reinforcement learning-like reasoning perform best on policy prediction tasks. With this work, we aim to advance the methods by which robots educate humans on their policies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using erroneous examples—incorrect demonstrations of robot behavior that humans correct—to teach robot policies to humans, extending an existing policy teaching framework. A user study shows that viewing incorrect demonstrations and verbalizing reasoning improves policy retention over time, and that participants using inverse reinforcement learning-like reasoning perform best.
AI.motivation: Demonstration-based explanations are a central approach in human-robot collaboration, but no single teaching method has been proven effective across all domains, difficulties, and learners. The question of how to most effectively teach robot policies to humans remains open, motivating the exploration of new pedagogical techniques.
AI.method: The authors extend an existing policy teaching framework by incorporating erroneous examples—incorrect demonstrations of robot behavior. They conduct a user study where participants view incorrect demonstrations and correct the actions to match the actual policy. Participants are also categorized into learning styles based on their reasoning approaches.
AI.result: Viewing incorrect demonstrations and verbalizing reasoning about predicting a robot's actions improves retention of the policy over time, consistent with the effect of erroneous examples in education. Participants using inverse reinforcement learning-like reasoning performed best on policy prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Erroneous examples are an effective method for teaching robot policies to humans, corroborating findings from educational literature. This work advances the methods by which robots can educate humans about their policies, contributing to more transparent and effective human-robot collaboration.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Tabu Search for Tactical Wireless Network Design
summary: Designing high-performance tactical wireless networks under realistic operational constraints gives rise to challenging combinatorial optimization problems, where the evaluation of candidate solutions relies on detailed physical and traffic-aware models. Although classical metaheuristics such as Tabu Search offer effective mechanisms for exploring large search spaces, their computational cost remains high because numerous candidate moves must be evaluated at every iteration. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework that improves the efficiency of Tabu Search by learning to guide its move selection process. Rather than altering the neighborhood structure, our approach exploits the information contained in the search trajectories generated during the optimization process. At each iteration, we record both improving and non-improving edge-based transformations together with a set of descriptive features capturing the structural, geometric, and performance characteristics of the network. This information is used to train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that predicts the impact of candidate moves on the objective function. The trained model is then integrated into the Tabu Search algorithm to rank candidate transformations according to their predicted quality, thereby reducing the number of costly objective evaluations while maintaining an effective exploration of the search space. Experimental results on synthetic benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed learning-assisted Tabu Search notably reduces computation time while consistently producing higher-quality solutions than the standard algorithm. These findings highlight the potential of combining machine learning with metaheuristics by leveraging the implicit knowledge embedded in search trajectories, paving the way for more efficient solution methods for large-scale network design problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a data-driven framework that enhances Tabu Search for tactical wireless network design by training a Graph Neural Network (GNN) on search trajectory data to predict the quality of candidate moves, thereby reducing costly objective evaluations while improving solution quality and computation time.
AI.motivation: Tactical wireless network design under realistic constraints involves challenging combinatorial optimization problems where evaluating candidate solutions requires expensive physical and traffic-aware models. Classical metaheuristics like Tabu Search explore large search spaces effectively but incur high computational cost because many candidate moves must be evaluated at each iteration.
AI.method: The approach trains a Graph Neural Network (GNN) on information gathered from search trajectories of Tabu Search. At each iteration, both improving and non-improving edge-based transformations are recorded along with descriptive features capturing structural, geometric, and performance characteristics of the network. The trained GNN predicts the impact of candidate moves on the objective function, and is integrated into Tabu Search to rank candidate transformations by predicted quality, reducing the number of costly objective evaluations while maintaining effective exploration.
AI.result: Experimental results on synthetic benchmark instances show that the learning-assisted Tabu Search notably reduces computation time while consistently producing higher-quality solutions than the standard Tabu Search algorithm.
AI.conclusion: Combining machine learning with metaheuristics by leveraging implicit knowledge embedded in search trajectories shows strong potential for more efficient solution methods in large-scale network design problems.

title: DREAM: Deployment-Time Demonstration Generation via Real-to-Sim for Scalable Policy Adaptation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made strong progress in language-conditioned robot manipulation, but improving their performance in a new workspace still often requires action-labeled data from that environment. Collecting such data by human teleoperation is costly, especially when each workspace, object arrangement, or task may require new demonstrations. We present DREAM, a framework that generates fine-tuning data for a pretrained VLA from a captured workspace and a language instruction, without requiring a task-specific human demonstration. DREAM reconstructs the workspace, automatically translates the instruction into symbolic task goals and success criteria using a large language model, and uses task-and-motion planning to generate feasible robot trajectories. The planned trajectories are augmented across randomized object configurations, verified by the generated success criteria, and rendered into image-action examples for VLA fine-tuning. Through real-robot experiments on language-conditioned manipulation tasks, we study whether DREAM can serve as a scalable data-collection system for the deployment workspace by examining whether fine-tuning on its automatically generated data improves success over direct deployment and how its data-collection cost compares with human teleoperation when adapting a VLA to a new workspace.

AI.tldr: DREAM is a framework that automatically generates fine-tuning data for pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models in a new workspace using a single captured scene and a language instruction, without requiring task-specific human demonstrations. It reconstructs the workspace, translates instructions into symbolic goals via LLM, plans feasible trajectories with task-and-motion planning, augments data across randomized configurations, and renders image-action examples for fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Adapting VLA models to new workspaces typically requires action-labeled data collected via costly human teleoperation, which is impractical as each workspace, object arrangement, or task may need new demonstrations.
AI.method: DREAM consists of four stages: (1) workspace reconstruction from a captured scene; (2) automatic translation of language instructions into symbolic task goals and success criteria using a large language model; (3) task-and-motion planning to generate feasible robot trajectories; and (4) augmenting planned trajectories across randomized object configurations, verifying them with generated success criteria, and rendering them into image-action examples for VLA fine-tuning.
AI.result: The paper evaluates DREAM through real-robot experiments on language-conditioned manipulation tasks, studying whether fine-tuning on automatically generated data improves success over direct deployment and comparing data-collection cost against human teleoperation when adapting a VLA to a new workspace.
AI.conclusion: DREAM demonstrates the potential to serve as a scalable, low-cost data-collection system for deploying VLAs in new workspaces by reducing or eliminating the need for human demonstrations while maintaining or improving task success.

title: CDEP Agent: Connecting Meteorologically Detected Temporal Compound Events to Real-World Documentary Evidence
summary: Compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation (CDEP) events are recognized in climate science as a growing driver of extreme impact, but whether this recognition carries over into real-world early warning and post-event documentation is unknown, so a meteorologically real CDEP event may pass with neither advance warning nor any later record. Here we present CDEP Agent, an auditable LLM-agent framework that tests this mismatch directly by linking CDEP candidates detected from meteorological reanalysis to real-world hazard and impact evidence across sources with different spatial scales, temporal resolutions, and reporting conventions. Using California as a case study, we identify 408 candidate CDEP events from ERA5 observations during 2021-2025 and evaluate each against the U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events, and public webpages along five dimensions: antecedent drought, extreme rainfall, local impact, hazard-impact attribution, and explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage. Only 34.3% of candidates are corroborated on both hazard components, and just 1.5% are ever explicitly linked to their antecedent drought, indicating that most meteorologically detected CDEP events go undocumented and their compound nature almost never enters the record at all. Our framework gives climate scientists a way to test physical event definitions against what actually gets documented, and gives social scientists, economists, and disaster-response agencies a provenance-linked evidence base for compound events that current warning and reporting systems largely fail to capture.

AI.tldr: CDEP Agent is an auditable LLM-agent framework that links meteorologically detected compound drought-to-extreme-precipitation (CDEP) events to real-world documentation. Using California 2021-2025, it found only 34.3% of 408 candidates were corroborated on both hazard components and just 1.5% explicitly linked to antecedent drought, revealing that most CDEP events go undocumented.
AI.motivation: While CDEP events are increasingly recognized in climate science as major impact drivers, it is unknown whether this recognition reaches real-world early warning and post-event documentation. A meteorologically real CDEP event may pass without warning or record, creating a critical mismatch between scientific understanding and operational practice.
AI.method: CDEP Agent is an auditable LLM-agent framework that links CDEP candidates from meteorological reanalysis (ERA5) to real-world hazard and impact evidence across multiple sources with differing spatial scales, temporal resolutions, and reporting conventions. 408 candidate CDEP events were identified in California during 2021-2025 and evaluated against the U.S. Drought Monitor, NOAA Storm Events, and public webpages along five dimensions: antecedent drought, extreme rainfall, local impact, hazard-impact attribution, and explicit drought-to-rainfall linkage.
AI.result: Only 34.3% of candidate CDEP events were corroborated on both hazard components, and just 1.5% were ever explicitly linked to their antecedent drought. This indicates that most meteorologically detected CDEP events go undocumented, and their compound nature almost never enters official or public records.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides climate scientists a way to test physical event definitions against what is actually documented, and gives social scientists, economists, and disaster-response agencies a provenance-linked evidence base for compound events that current warning and reporting systems largely fail to capture.

title: GHOST in the Robots: Real-Time Exocentric Dual-Robot VR Teleoperation from Onboard Cameras
summary: Teleoperating multiple robots simultaneously enables additional views and coordinated control. Yet, it poses fundamental challenges: the system must present sensor data cohesively and allow operators to manage multiple robot bases, arms, and cameras while maintaining low latency. Current multi-robot teleoperation systems require multiple operators, rely on autonomy, or restrict operators to high-level commands. We present GHOST: an open-source VR teleoperation system that enables single operator control of two mobile manipulators via direct lowlevel commands using only onboard sensing. GHOST creates an exocentric 3D workspace by aligning real-time point clouds from the robots' RGB-D cameras, where scene coverage is improved through learning-based completion to aid operator spatial awareness. For control, the operator uses a mode-switching architecture to command either robot individually or both robots simultaneously. Experiments with 15 novice participants demonstrate 1.6-4x the success rate of an off-the-shelf tablet interface. For experts across nine challenging dual-robot tasks, our system enabled completion of two tasks that were infeasible with the tablet, and was 1.47x faster on average than the tablet. Website and code: https://h2r.github.io/GHOST/.

AI.tldr: GHOST is an open-source VR teleoperation system enabling a single operator to control two mobile manipulators via direct low-level commands using only onboard sensing, leveraging aligned real-time point clouds with learning-based completion for spatial awareness and a mode-switching architecture for individual or simultaneous robot control. Experiments show 1.6-4x higher success rates over a tablet interface for novices and 1.47x faster task completion for experts.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot teleoperation is challenging because current systems require multiple operators, depend on autonomy, or restrict operators to high-level commands. There is a need for a system that allows a single operator to control multiple robots directly at the low level while presenting sensor data cohesively and maintaining low latency.
AI.method: GHOST constructs an exocentric 3D workspace by aligning real-time point clouds from onboard RGB-D cameras of two mobile manipulators, with learning-based completion to improve scene coverage and operator spatial awareness. Control is achieved via a mode-switching architecture that permits commanding either robot individually or both simultaneously through direct low-level commands.
AI.result: With 15 novice participants, GHOST achieved 1.6-4x the success rate of an off-the-shelf tablet interface. For experts across nine challenging dual-robot tasks, the system enabled completion of two tasks infeasible with the tablet and was 1.47x faster on average than the tablet.
AI.conclusion: GHOST demonstrates that a single operator can effectively teleoperate multiple mobile manipulators at the low level in VR with only onboard sensing, outperforming conventional tablet interfaces in both success rate and speed, while enabling tasks infeasible with prior approaches.

title: CrossAudit: A Git-Native, Cross-Vendor Audit Loop for Agentic Science
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, 22 references. Reference implementation, audit ledger, and experiment artefacts: https://github.com/dongzhaohe321418-lab/crossaudit
summary:
An AI scientist should not grade its own homework. Yet in the systems we examined, the agent that reviews the work usually comes from the same model family as the agent that produced it, or at least from the same vendor. Model evaluators are known to favour their own generations. Whether models trained alike also share blind spots is a conjecture, not a settled finding, but if they do, the reviewer inherits the author's. The record of what was flagged and what was waved through often sits in platform logs that nobody outside can replay.
  We present CrossAudit, a protocol for supervising autonomous research pipelines. It rests on three commitments. Each increment of work is audited by an agent from a different vendor against a rulebook a human wrote and versioned. Reports, verdicts, disputes and rulings are git commits, so the supervision history can be re-read and cited; raw model exchanges are not yet part of that record. Scripted checks run before any model does. Advisory judgement never gates the pipeline: a model blocks only by citing a rule, and no model may waive a deterministic failure. Blockers that survive a bounded number of revision rounds go to a person.
  We state the protocol as eight invariants. We describe a reference implementation built from GitHub Actions and a few hundred lines of Python, and report a live deployment of a closely related variant in a computational-chemistry pipeline. We also ran a seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 seeded defects, one run per configuration). A cross-vendor audit of our own repository then voided its blinding. We adopt that audit's findings and report the corrected results. The trial shows that two vendors read the same rulebook differently. It does not show that either is better. The strongest evidence here is the committed, uncontrolled record of cross-vendor audits of this paper itself.

AI.tldr: CrossAudit is a protocol for supervising autonomous research pipelines where every increment of work is audited by an agent from a different vendor against a human-written, versioned rulebook. The protocol mandates that reports, verdicts, disputes, and rulings are git commits for traceability, scripted checks run before any model does, advisory judgement never gates the pipeline (a model blocks only by citing a rule), and blockers surviving bounded revision rounds escalate to a human. The paper reports a reference implementation in GitHub Actions/Python, a live deployment in computational chemistry, and a seeded-defect trial (30 increments, 43 defects) revealing that two vendors read the same rulebook differently without demonstrating either is superior.
AI.motivation: AI systems that evaluate their own or same-family/same-vendor generated work are biased toward their own generations and may share blind spots. The supervision history is often opaque in platform logs that outsiders cannot replay. Thus there is a need for trustworthy, cross-vendor, human-grounded, and transparent auditing of autonomous research pipelines.
AI.method: CrossAudit protocol: (1) each work increment is audited by an agent from a different vendor; (2) human-written versioned rulebooks define the audit criteria; (3) reports, verdicts, disputes and rulings are stored as git commits; (4) scripted deterministic checks run before any model; (5) models cannot gate the pipeline except by citing a rule, and cannot waive deterministic failures; (6) blockers surviving a bounded number of revision rounds escalate to humans; (7) the protocol is stated as eight invariants; (8) validated via a reference implementation (GitHub Actions + Python), a live computational-chemistry deployment, and a seeded-defect trial.
AI.result: A cross-vendor audit of the authors' own repository voided its blinding; the authors adopted the audit's findings and report corrected results. The seeded-defect trial shows two vendors read the same rulebook differently, but does not demonstrate that either vendor is better. The strongest evidence is the committed, uncontrolled record of cross-vendor audits of the paper itself.
AI.conclusion: Cross-auditing across vendors is a viable mechanism for supervisory integrity in autonomous research pipelines. The protocol's strongest contribution is demonstrating—through its own committed audit trail—that cross-vendor variance exists and is observable, even if neither vendor proved superior. The work positions committed, reproducible supervision records as central to trust in AI-driven research.

title: Agri-Sim: Agricultural Simulation Platform for Embodied Intelligence Evaluation in Greenhouse Robotics
summary: Agricultural-robot development requires simulation environments that can jointly support realistic scene construction, virtual sensing, autonomous navigation, motion planning, and manipulation-task execution. This paper presents Agri-Sim, a Unity and ROS2-based simulation platform for the closed-loop development and functional evaluation of agricultural robots. The platform contains a configurable tomato-greenhouse environment, a mobile dual-arm harvesting robot, virtual RGB-D, LiDAR, IMU, and joint sensors, and a bidirectional communication interface between Unity and ROS2. Unity is responsible for scene rendering, rigid-body dynamics, collision detection, virtual sensing, and task-state execution, whereas ROS2 and MoveIt 2 provide localization, navigation, collision-aware motion planning, inverse kinematics, and trajectory generation. Autonomous greenhouse navigation and dual-arm tomato harvesting were used to evaluate the complete simulation workflow. The experiments covered virtual sensor publication, ROS2-based navigation, collision-aware motion planning, mobile-base control, tomato acquisition, inter-arm handover, and box placement. The results demonstrate that Agri-Sim supports closed-loop integration and repeatable functional evaluation of navigation and manipulation workflows in a controlled virtual greenhouse, providing a practical foundation for subsequent algorithm development and Sim-to-Real studies.

AI.tldr: Agri-Sim is a Unity and ROS2-based simulation platform for agricultural robots, featuring a configurable tomato-greenhouse environment, a mobile dual-arm harvesting robot, virtual sensors, and a bidirectional Unity-ROS2 interface. It supports closed-loop navigation and manipulation workflows and was validated through autonomous greenhouse navigation and dual-arm tomato harvesting experiments.
AI.motivation: Agricultural-robot development requires a simulation environment that jointly supports realistic scene construction, virtual sensing, autonomous navigation, motion planning, and manipulation-task execution—capabilities that are typically fragmented across existing tools.
AI.method: The platform leverages Unity for scene rendering, rigid-body dynamics, collision detection, virtual sensing, and task-state execution, while ROS2 and MoveIt 2 handle localization, navigation, collision-aware motion planning, inverse kinematics, and trajectory generation. A bidirectional communication interface links the two frameworks.
AI.result: Experiments covering virtual sensor publication, ROS2 navigation, collision-aware motion planning, mobile-base control, tomato acquisition, inter-arm handover, and box placement demonstrated that Agri-Sim supports closed-loop integration and repeatable functional evaluation in a controlled virtual greenhouse.
AI.conclusion: Agri-Sim provides a practical foundation for agricultural-robot algorithm development and subsequent Sim-to-Real studies by enabling closed-loop, repeatable evaluation of navigation and manipulation workflows in a virtual greenhouse.

title: AutoScientist-Quant: Self-Evolving Coding Agents for Automatic Research in Quantitative Investment
summary: Large language model agents can discover alphas, yet current methods have three weaknesses. The search cannot adapt during the run, automation usually ends at alpha generation while library selection and model choice stay manual, and alpha discovery can read the test window through loop feedback or code problems. We present AutoScientist-Quant, a self evolving search process that regards quantitative research as one budgeted search problem. A single controller conditions every decision on the remaining budget, choosing at each round whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop, which node to expand, how many alphas to generate, and how to retrieve past trajectories from the shared memory. The same core then selects from the library and tunes the model, closing the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. We also review the evaluation pipeline reused from prior work, fix two lookahead problems, and keep the feedback window disjoint from the held out test window, so every comparison tests true generalization. On CSI universes, the framework attains the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and these conclusions hold across several backbones and markets.

AI.tldr: AutoScientist-Quant is a self-evolving search framework for quantitative alpha discovery that treats the entire research pipeline as a single budgeted search problem, addressing three weaknesses in prior LLM agent methods: non-adaptive search, incomplete automation, and test-window leakage.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents for alpha discovery suffer from three key weaknesses: (1) the search cannot adapt during execution, (2) automation stops at alpha generation while library selection and model choice remain manual, and (3) alpha discovery can leak information from the test window through loop feedback or code issues.
AI.method: The framework uses a single controller that conditions all decisions on the remaining budget. At each round, the controller chooses whether to improve, combine, pivot, or stop; which node to expand; how many alphas to generate; and how to retrieve past trajectories from shared memory. The same core also handles library selection and model tuning, closing the loop from hypothesis to deployable strategy. The evaluation pipeline is reviewed to fix two lookahead problems, keeping the feedback window disjoint from the held-out test window.
AI.result: On CSI universes, the framework achieves the best value of nearly every metric in every setting, and these results hold across multiple backbones and markets.
AI.conclusion: Treating quantitative research as a unified budgeted search problem with a self-evolving controller enables adaptive, fully automated, and leakage-free alpha discovery, yielding state-of-the-art performance across diverse markets and model backbones.

title: From Multi-Modal Paths to Executable Trajectories: A Trajectory Planning Framework for 4WIS Robots
summary: Four-wheel independent steering (4WIS) mobile robots support multiple motion modes, offering high maneuverability in narrow and complex environments. However, existing planning methods often fail to fully exploit these capabilities, leading to suboptimal trajectory quality. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a multi-modal global trajectory planning framework that couples mode-augmented front-end search with mode-consistent segment-wise trajectory optimization. In the front-end stage, Hybrid A* is extended to a four-dimensional state space incorporating motion modes, while mode-switching-aware cost and heuristic functions embed mode decisions into the global search process. Multi-modal Reeds-Shepp curves and an intelligent terminal connection strategy are further designed to improve search efficiency. In the back-end stage, a segment-wise trajectory optimization framework based on an improved iterative safe corridor scheme is developed to convert discrete multi-modal paths into smooth, kinematically feasible trajectories with stationary mode transitions. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves the best overall performance in safety, arrival time, terminal accuracy and computation time. Real-world experiments on a physical 4WIS robot further validate the practical effectiveness and executability of the generated trajectories, providing a flexible and high-performance solution for multi-modal mobile robot trajectory planning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-modal global trajectory planning framework for four-wheel independent steering (4WIS) mobile robots, coupling a mode-augmented front-end search (extended Hybrid A* with motion modes) with a mode-consistent segment-wise back-end optimization using an improved iterative safe corridor scheme, validated through simulations and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing planning methods for 4WIS mobile robots fail to fully exploit their multiple motion modes, leading to suboptimal trajectory quality in narrow and complex environments.
AI.method: The framework consists of (1) a front-end stage that extends Hybrid A* to a four-dimensional state space incorporating motion modes, with mode-switching-aware cost and heuristic functions, multi-modal Reeds-Shepp curves, and an intelligent terminal connection strategy; and (2) a back-end stage using a segment-wise trajectory optimization framework based on an improved iterative safe corridor scheme to convert discrete multi-modal paths into smooth, kinematically feasible trajectories with stationary mode transitions.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method achieves the best overall performance in safety, arrival time, terminal accuracy, and computation time. Real-world experiments on a physical 4WIS robot further validate the practical effectiveness and executability of the generated trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-modal trajectory planning framework provides a flexible and high-performance solution for multi-modal mobile robot trajectory planning, fully leveraging the capabilities of 4WIS robots.

title: AI Scientist Mission Control (AIMC): Visual Analytics for Human Oversight of Autonomous Scientific Discovery
summary: Autonomous scientific discovery systems can generate large numbers of research ideas, experiments, and manuscripts with minimal human intervention. As these systems become increasingly capable, scientists require effective mechanisms to monitor output quality, identify recurring failure modes, understand research evolution, and prioritize promising discoveries for review. We present AIMC, a visual analytics framework for human oversight of autonomous scientific discovery. AIMC combines semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations to support the exploration of AI-generated research artifacts. We demonstrate the framework through a case study of the papers generated by an autonomous AI Scientist (FARS), together with their associated review feedback. Our analysis reveals recurring methodological weaknesses, evolving research themes, domain-specific differences in quality, and a small set of highly novel papers that warrant deeper human inspection. These findings illustrate how visual analytics can support transparency, diagnosis, and human AI collaboration in emerging autonomous scientific discovery workflows.

AI.tldr: AIMC is a visual analytics framework for human oversight of autonomous scientific discovery, combining semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations to help scientists monitor, diagnose, and prioritize AI-generated research artifacts.
AI.motivation: Autonomous scientific discovery systems can produce large volumes of research ideas, experiments, and manuscripts with minimal human intervention, creating a need for effective mechanisms to monitor output quality, identify recurring failure modes, understand research evolution, and prioritize promising discoveries for human review.
AI.method: AIMC integrates semantic embeddings, automated weakness extraction, temporal analysis, and interactive visualizations within a visual analytics framework, demonstrated through a case study on papers generated by the FARS autonomous AI Scientist along with associated review feedback.
AI.result: The analysis reveals recurring methodological weaknesses, evolving research themes, domain-specific differences in quality, and a small set of highly novel papers warranting deeper human inspection.
AI.conclusion: Visual analytics can support transparency, diagnosis, and human-AI collaboration in emerging autonomous scientific discovery workflows.

title: CGFM-Nav: Cognitive Graph-Field Memory for Semantic-Guided Lifelong Multimodal Embodied Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to reason over accumulated observations while continuously exploring unseen regions. However, existing environment representations often struggle to jointly support explicit semantic memory and continuous exploration guidance. To address this challenge, we propose Cognitive Graph-Field Memory (CGFM), a persistent multimodal scene representation that couples explicit relational memory with continuous spatial intuition. CGFM organizes objects, spatial relations, and visual observations into a multimodal scene graph, enabling target retrieval and long-horizon reasoning across navigation tasks. When no reliable target match is identified, graph-based evidence is projected into a goal-conditioned semantic-frontier field to guide exploration toward semantically promising frontiers and regions. Building upon CGFM, we introduce CGFM-Nav, a foundation-model-based framework for lifelong multimodal navigation that integrates task-relevant subgraph selection, VLM reasoning, and verification feedback into a closed decision loop. Preliminary experiments on GOAT-Bench show that, under the same Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, CGFM-Nav improves the overall success rate from 53.2% to 63.0% and SPL from 30.0% to 39.6%, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining explicit semantic memory with semantic-guided exploration.

AI.tldr: CGFM-Nav uses a Cognitive Graph-Field Memory that combines explicit relational scene graphs with continuous semantic-frontier fields for lifelong vision-and-language navigation, improving success rate from 53.2% to 63.0% and SPL from 30.0% to 39.6% on GOAT-Bench under the same Qwen3-VL-8B backbone.
AI.motivation: Existing environment representations in VLN struggle to simultaneously support explicit semantic memory for reasoning and continuous exploration guidance for navigating unseen regions.
AI.method: CGFM couples a multimodal scene graph (organizing objects, spatial relations, visual observations) with a goal-conditioned semantic-frontier field. When no reliable target match is identified, graph-based evidence is projected into the frontier field to guide exploration. CGFM-Nav is a foundation-model-based framework integrating task-relevant subgraph selection, VLM reasoning, and verification feedback in a closed decision loop.
AI.result: On GOAT-Bench, with the same Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, CGFM-Nav improves overall success rate from 53.2% to 63.0% and SPL from 30.0% to 39.6%.
AI.conclusion: Combining explicit semantic memory with semantic-guided exploration effectively enhances lifelong multimodal navigation performance.

title: Self-Evolving Skills via Surrogate-Guided Solve-and-Reproduce
summary: Agent skills are portable packages of instructions and resources an agent consults at deployment. Self-evolving them fails in two ways today. First, skills evolved from scratch underperform human-curated ones and, on a weak model, using no skill at all. Second, an evolution-time pass records one lucky trajectory that a fresh stochastic agent often fails to reproduce at deployment. We present reSolve, a per-task, oracle-in-the-loop framework built on three components. It decouples interactive solving from a self-contained deliverable that is independently re-executed in a fresh container, a protocol we call solve-and-reproduce. It enhances the sparse reward signal with a surrogate verifier that cannot access hidden tests or reference answers. It then runs verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph. Within a fixed harness, a cheap model self-evolves skills that reach $74.9\%$ mean-of-3, $+14.8$ points over the $60.1\%$ human-curated baseline, exceeding the strongest official curated-skill result ($67.3\%$, GPT-5.5/OpenHands). We also report observed failure cases and domain-level results, including performance on the 14 Natural Science tasks, to clarify when the approach does and does not help.

AI.tldr: reSolve is a per-task, oracle-in-the-loop framework for self-evolving agent skills that decouples interactive solving from a self-contained re-executable deliverable (solve-and-reproduce), enhances sparse rewards with a surrogate verifier, and uses verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph. A cheap model self-evolves skills reaching 74.9% mean-of-3, +14.8 points over the 60.1% human-curated baseline and exceeding the 67.3% GPT-5.5/OpenHands curated-skill result.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agent skills currently fail in two ways: (1) skills evolved from scratch underperform human-curated ones, and on a weak model, using no skill at all; (2) an evolution-time pass records one lucky trajectory that a fresh stochastic agent often fails to reproduce at deployment.
AI.method: reSolve is built on three components: (1) solve-and-reproduce, which decouples interactive solving from a self-contained deliverable independently re-executed in a fresh container; (2) a surrogate verifier that enhances sparse reward signals without accessing hidden tests or reference answers; (3) verifier-guided beam search over a solution-construction graph.
AI.result: Within a fixed harness, a cheap model self-evolves skills reaching 74.9% mean-of-3, +14.8 points over the 60.1% human-curated baseline, exceeding the strongest official curated-skill result of 67.3% (GPT-5.5/OpenHands). The paper also reports failure cases and domain-level results, including performance on 14 Natural Science tasks.
AI.conclusion: The approach clarifies when oracle-in-the-loop self-evolution does and does not help, reporting observed failure cases and domain-level results to establish the boundaries of the method's effectiveness.

title: Systematic Lightweight Method for Robotics Based on Strain Energy Distribution Optimization
