AI.method: AGM represents a task as a subgoal sequence with a progress pointer, advancing memory only after physical evidence verifies the current subgoal. Proprioceptive interaction cues trigger verification decisions, while coherent point tracking and language-conditioned cross-view comparison from frozen foundation models (via a single 2.43M-parameter verification head) determine what was achieved. This converts open-loop execution into a closed loop of execution, verification, and progress while keeping the policy frozen and avoiding test-time large-model inference.
AI.result: On the RoboMME Counting benchmark, AGM surpasses the strongest memory-augmented baseline on PickXTimes and BinFill tasks, and yields equally decisive gains on a physical robot.
AI.conclusion: Reliable embodied memory depends more on disciplined state updates (grounded in physical evidence) than on memory capacity.

title: Efficient Geothermal Well-Control Optimization via Diffusion-Surrogate Reinforcement Learning
summary: Real-time decision-making for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) is challenging because long-term production periods involve high-dimensional control spaces and a large number of time-consuming high-fidelity hydrothermal simulations. Reinforcement learning provides a natural framework for state-dependent sequential control, but direct policy training with numerical simulators is computationally expensive. To address this issue, we propose a diffusion-surrogate guided reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon EGS well-control optimization. The reservoir temperature and pressure fields are used as system states, while injection rates are selected as control actions. A learned surrogate environment is constructed using conditional diffusion models to predict the evolution of reservoir temperature and pressure fields and a separate reward model to estimate the corresponding economic return. The surrogate environment is then integrated with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for efficient policy training. Experiments on a fractured EGS benchmark show that the diffusion surrogate can accurately reproduce reservoir-state evolution over multiple control stages. The resulting surrogate-assisted PPO policy achieves competitive well-control performance compared with direct simulator-based PPO and existing optimization methods, while substantially reducing the dependence on expensive high-fidelity simulations. These results demonstrate the potential of diffusion-based surrogate environments for efficient reinforcement learning in geothermal well-control optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diffusion-surrogate guided reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) well-control optimization. A conditional diffusion model learns to predict reservoir temperature and pressure field evolution, serving as a surrogate environment for training a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent, significantly reducing dependence on expensive high-fidelity simulations while achieving competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Real-time decision-making for EGS is challenging due to high-dimensional control spaces and computationally expensive high-fidelity hydrothermal simulations required over long production periods. Direct policy training with numerical simulators via reinforcement learning is prohibitively computationally expensive.
AI.method: The framework uses reservoir temperature and pressure fields as system states and injection rates as control actions. A surrogate environment is constructed using conditional diffusion models to predict state evolution, paired with a separate reward model for economic return estimation. This surrogate is integrated with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for efficient policy training.
AI.result: On a fractured EGS benchmark, the diffusion surrogate accurately reproduces reservoir-state evolution over multiple control stages. The surrogate-assisted PPO policy achieves competitive well-control performance compared to direct simulator-based PPO and existing optimization methods, while substantially reducing reliance on expensive high-fidelity simulations.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that diffusion-based surrogate environments enable efficient reinforcement learning for geothermal well-control optimization, offering a practical pathway for real-time EGS decision-making.

title: Module Number Adaptive Visual Shape Control for Serial Modular Soft Robots
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. This articles has been submitted to a IEEE Journal
summary: Image based shape control provides a simple means of controlling the whole body configuration of soft robots. However, existing data driven approaches are typically developed for fixed robot structures and require new control data when the number of modules changes. This paper presents a module number adaptive visual shape control method for serial modular soft pneumatic robots. A controller trained only on single module actuation shape data is reused for robots with one to five modules by decomposing whole body camera images into local module patches. A single common module segmenter localizes individual modules across all tested configurations, while the same local controller is applied to every extracted patch. Geometric data augmentation improves transferability to downstream modules, and a lightweight mask reconstruction network reconstructs a synthetically removed actuator mask channel. Experiments on physical robots demonstrate shape control across varying numbers of modules and under environmental changes and payload loading. The results show that single module control learning enables scalable whole body control without configuration specific control data collection.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a module number adaptive visual shape control method for serial modular soft pneumatic robots, where a controller trained only on single module actuation data is reused for robots with 1-5 modules by decomposing whole body camera images into local module patches.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven shape control approaches for soft robots are developed for fixed robot structures and require new control data whenever the number of modules changes, which is inefficient and limits scalability.
AI.method: A single common module segmenter localizes individual modules across all tested configurations, the same local controller trained on single module data is applied to every extracted patch, geometric data augmentation improves transferability to downstream modules, and a lightweight mask reconstruction network reconstructs a synthetically removed actuator mask channel.
AI.result: Experiments on physical robots demonstrate shape control across varying numbers of modules (1-5) and under environmental changes and payload loading, showing that single module control learning enables scalable whole body control without configuration-specific data collection.
AI.conclusion: Single module control learning can be effectively generalized to multi-module soft robots of varying lengths, eliminating the need for configuration-specific control data collection while maintaining robustness under environmental changes and payload conditions.

title: Enhancing SAE-based Steering via Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) disentangle model activations into interpretable features and are widely used for steering large language models. Most existing SAE-based steering methods select features by applying a top- filter based on statistical scores, assuming that higher-scoring features yield stronger steering effects. In this paper, we show that this assumption is often invalid, leading to suboptimal feature selection. Our analysis reveals that effective steering features may be distributed among representationally adjacent, semantically similar groups induced by feature splitting in SAEs. Within such groups, features may exhibit disparate statistical scores despite having comparable steering influence, causing score-based selection to overlook important features. Based on these observations, we propose \textsc{Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection} (\textsc{NIFS}), a plug-and-play strategy that leverages representation similarity to improve feature selection for steering. We evaluate \textsc{NIFS} across multiple SAE-based steering methods and tasks, and demonstrate consistent performance gains over conventional top-$k$ selection.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that the common assumption in SAE-based steering—that higher statistical scores correspond to stronger steering features—is often invalid. It introduces NIFS (Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection), a plug-and-play method that uses representation similarity to account for feature splitting-induced feature groups, improving feature selection for LLM steering across multiple baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods rely on top-k filtration by statistical scores, assuming higher scores imply stronger steering effects. This assumption is frequently invalid, leading to suboptimal feature selection because effective features may be spread across representationally adjacent, semantically similar groups caused by feature splitting, where features within a group can have disparate scores despite comparable steering influence.
AI.method: The paper proposes NIFS (Neighbor Integrated Feature Selection), a plug-and-play strategy that leverages representation similarity among SAE features to improve feature selection for steering, accounting for feature groups induced by feature splitting. It integrates with existing SAE-based steering methods without requiring architectural changes.
AI.result: NIFS is evaluated across multiple SAE-based steering methods and tasks, demonstrating consistent performance improvements over conventional top-k feature selection approaches.
AI.conclusion: Score-based feature selection in SAE steering is unreliable due to feature splitting and score disparity within semantically similar groups; incorporating representation similarity via NIFS yields consistently better steering performance than conventional top-k selection.

title: $\mathcal{N}_0$-Foundation: Towards the Age of Tactile Intelligence
summary: We present $\mathcal{N}_0$-Foundation, a paradigm for tactile-enabled embodied manipulation, which integrates tactile sensing hardware, large-scale multimodal data, tactile representation learning, and standardized evaluation. First, we engineer the infrastructure for scalable data collection, including a vision-based tactile sensor, a tactile Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), and a synchronized visuo-tactile data collection system supporting both robot embodiments and UMI-based demonstrations. Leveraging this infrastructure, we construct NeoData, which contains more than 30000 hours of synchronized visual and tactile demonstrations, spanning six embodiments, 450 tasks, and billions of paired RGB and tactile frames collected through a mixture of real-robot teleoperation and UMI-based demonstrations. To facilitate open research, we further release OpenNeoData, a 5000-hour open-source subset of NeoData. The dataset addresses a central limitation of existing manipulation corpora, critical for deformable-object manipulation, precise assembly, delicate force control, and sustained surface interaction. Capitalizing on the large-scale, heterogeneous tactile measurements, we propose NeoForce, a visuo-tactile representation model that learn transferable tactile representations across different sensor designs. To enable systematic evaluation of tactile embodied models built upon our infrastructure, datasets and tactile representations, we further propose a comprehensive benchmark, which combines the real-world NeoReal suite and the simulated NeoSim suite for standardized evaluation. Experiments across both suites show that policies benefit from the physical contact state rather than from the device-specific appearance of the tactile signal. We release the dataset, the representation, and the benchmark, aiming at supporting future work on tactile-enabled embodied manipulation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces N0-Foundation, a comprehensive paradigm for tactile-enabled embodied manipulation, comprising a vision-based tactile sensor, a tactile Universal Manipulation Interface for data collection, NeoData (30,000+ hours of synchronized visuo-tactile demonstrations), an open-source subset OpenNeoData, a visuo-tactile representation model (NeoForce), and a standardized benchmark with real-world (NeoReal) and simulated (NeoSim) suites. Experiments show policies benefit from physical contact state rather than device-specific tactile appearance.
AI.motivation: Existing manipulation corpora lack large-scale, heterogeneous tactile data crucial for deformable-object manipulation, precise assembly, delicate force control, and sustained surface interaction. The field lacks an integrated paradigm spanning hardware, data, representation learning, and standardized evaluation for tactile-enabled embodied manipulation.
AI.method: The authors engineer scalable data collection infrastructure with a vision-based tactile sensor, a tactile UMI, and a synchronized visuo-tactile collection system. They collect NeoData with 30,000+ hours across six embodiments and 450 tasks. They propose NeoForce, a visuo-tactile representation model learning transferable tactile representations across different sensor designs. They introduce a benchmark combining real-world (NeoReal) and simulated (NeoSim) suites for standardized evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments across both real and simulated suites demonstrate that manipulation policies benefit from physical contact state information rather than the device-specific appearance of tactile signals. Public releases include the dataset, representation model, and benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The N0-Foundation provides an end-to-end ecosystem for tactile-enabled embodied manipulation research, addressing a critical gap in existing manipulation corpora and enabling future work through open resources spanning data, representation learning, and standardized evaluation.

title: Capability-Stratified Degradation in Ternary Language Models
summary: Extreme low-bit inference offers a route toward smaller models and constrained deployment. Ternary language models restrict weights to $\{-1,0,+1\}$, approaching the limit of $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits/weight. The practical question for a pretrained model is not simply whether weights can be quantised but which capabilities survive and whether it remains useful for adaptation. We explore this by converting Qwen3.5-0.8B (752M parameters) to ternary weights using 72.4M tokens of quantisation-aware training (QAT). The resulting model, Cloe, is evaluated across 29 benchmarks, representation diagnostics, and downstream fine-tuning. The evidence shows non-uniform degradation. A linear probe recovers 43.76% of MMLU answers from the full-precision teacher's representations but only 26.19% from Cloe (near chance), indicating specialist factual information is lost. However, Cloe retains measurable performance on ten tasks, averaging 77.1% of teacher performance. Crucially, fine-tuning raises Cloe to 89.8% on SST-2 (95.6% of the matched teacher) and reaches 79.4% teacher retention on XSum. We attribute degradation to a combination of quantisation-induced information loss and incomplete recovery due to the limited QAT budget. We also highlight an evaluation pitfall: standard answer-letter scoring failed (Cloe emitted "A" on 98.6% of MMLU questions), necessitating continuation scoring. Ultimately, ternary conversion is unsuitable as a drop-in general replacement yet remains valuable as a compact substrate for task-specific models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates ternary quantization (weights restricted to {-1,0,+1}, ~1.585 bits/weight) of a 752M-parameter language model via 72.4M tokens of QAT, producing "Cloe." Non-uniform degradation is observed: factual/specialist knowledge collapses (MMLU probe near chance) while other tasks retain ~77% of teacher performance, and downstream fine-tuning recovers strong task-specific capability (95.6% of teacher on SST-2). The paper also identifies an evaluation pitfall where standard answer-letter scoring fails due to label bias, necessitating continuation scoring.
AI.motivation: To determine which capabilities of a pretrained language model survive extreme low-bit (ternary) quantization and whether such models remain useful for downstream adaptation, rather than asking only whether quantization is feasible.
AI.method: Convert a Qwen3.5-0.8B (752M) model to ternary weights via 72.4M tokens of quantization-aware training, then evaluate across 29 benchmarks, representation diagnostics (linear probing), and downstream fine-tuning tasks (SST-2, XSum).
AI.result: Linear probing recovers only 26.19% of MMLU from Cloe vs. 43.76% from the teacher (near chance), indicating loss of specialist factual knowledge; however, ten tasks retain on average 77.1% of teacher performance. Fine-tuning recovers 95.6% of teacher on SST-2 and 79.4% teacher retention on XSum. Standard answer-letter scoring fails due to an extreme "A" bias (98.6%), requiring continuation scoring.
AI.conclusion: Ternary conversion is not suitable as a drop-in general replacement for full-precision models due to non-uniform capability loss, but remains valuable as a compact substrate for task-specific fine-tuning.

title: VeloBins: Learning Velocity and Its Uncertainty via Bins and Error-Conditioned Gaussian Labels for Aerial Inertial Odometry
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary video: https://youtu.be/QkZY0So3myw
summary: Inertial odometry (IO) is critical for aerial robots, where aggressive maneuvers and poor lighting degrade visual sensors. Recent learning-based IO methods improve traditional integration-based approaches by learning motion priors from IMU and platform-specific sensors, then fusing the predictions within an extended Kalman filter. However, learning velocity through regression is difficult, while jointly estimating uncertainty with a separate decoder and negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss further complicates training and can lead to over-confident estimates. We introduce VeloBins, which reformulates velocity regression as classification over discretized velocity bins. We decode both the velocity from the bin distribution's expectation and the uncertainty from its variance, removing the need for a separate uncertainty decoder. We further supervise the uncertainty explicitly using an error-conditioned Gaussian label centered at the ground-truth velocity, with a standard deviation set to the velocity error. We evaluate VeloBins on four aerial datasets, ranging from free-form aggressive flights and a 27 g nano-quadrotor to drone racing at over 21~m/s. VeloBins achieves the lowest average errors on all four datasets, reducing velocity, relative trajectory, and absolute trajectory errors by 3-27%, 8-40%, and 6-53%, respectively, compared with the strongest baseline. Notably, the proposed supervision achieves the lowest NLL and best filter consistency despite never optimizing an NLL loss. The code will be available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: VeloBins reformulates inertial odometry velocity regression as classification over discretized velocity bins, decoding both velocity (expectation) and uncertainty (variance) from the bin distribution. It uses an error-conditioned Gaussian label for explicit uncertainty supervision without a separate decoder or NLL loss. Evaluated on four aerial datasets, it achieves the lowest velocity, relative trajectory, and absolute trajectory errors (3-27%, 8-40%, 6-53% reductions) while also achieving the best filter consistency and lowest NLL without optimizing an NLL loss.
AI.motivation: Learning-based inertial odometry methods that regress velocity directly are difficult to train, and jointly estimating uncertainty via a separate decoder with negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss complicates training and can produce over-confident estimates.
AI.method: VeloBins reformulates velocity regression as classification over discretized velocity bins. Velocity is decoded from the bin distribution's expectation and uncertainty from its variance, eliminating the need for a separate uncertainty decoder. Uncertainty is supervised explicitly using an error-conditioned Gaussian label centered at ground-truth velocity with standard deviation set to the velocity error. Predictions are fused within an extended Kalman filter.
AI.result: On four aerial datasets (free-form aggressive flights, a 27 g nano-quadrotor, and drone racing over 21 m/s), VeloBins achieves the lowest average errors across all datasets: reducing velocity, relative trajectory, and absolute trajectory errors by 3-27%, 8-40%, and 6-53% respectively versus the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest NLL and best filter consistency without explicitly optimizing an NLL loss.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating velocity estimation as bin classification with explicit error-conditioned uncertainty supervision is a more effective and simpler alternative to regression-based approaches in learned inertial odometry, yielding better accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and filter consistency across diverse and aggressive aerial flight regimes.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Computational Pathology: Definitions, Taxonomy, and Recommendations
comment: On behalf of MICCAI SIG-CompPath. More information: https://miccai.org/index.php/special-interest-groups/sig-comppath/
summary: Computational pathology (CompPath) is transforming medicine by leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment prediction from gigapixel whole-slide images. Clinical adoption is progressing, but is constrained by concerns about safety, accountability, and regulatory oversight in high-stakes clinical environments. Explainable AI (XAI) systems hold promise for building trust and enabling verification, yet the literature remains fragmented due to inconsistent terminology, overlapping methodological families, ad hoc validation, and current reviews. This review aims to formalize XAI methods in CompPath through the: i) introduction of a pathology-centric vocabulary comprising seven core terms; ii) development of a taxonomy across methodological families and three orthogonal axes (stage, type, scope); and iii) establishment of a task-driven framework that maps five clinical questions to recommended methods, method evaluation, and deployment context. Five key gaps between current XAI capabilities and clinical deployment are identified, and actionable steps are proposed to advance XAI for CompPath.

AI.tldr: This paper is a review that formalizes explainable AI (XAI) methods in computational pathology by introducing a pathology-centric vocabulary (seven core terms), a taxonomy across methodological families with three orthogonal axes (stage, type, scope), and a task-driven framework mapping five clinical questions to recommended methods, evaluation strategies, and deployment contexts. It identifies five key gaps between current XAI capabilities and clinical deployment and proposes actionable steps to bridge them.
AI.motivation: Clinical adoption of computational pathology is progressing but constrained by concerns about safety, accountability, and regulatory oversight. XAI systems could build trust and enable verification, yet the literature is fragmented due to inconsistent terminology, overlapping methodological families, ad hoc validation, and current reviews. A formalized, unifying framework is needed.
AI.method: The review formalizes XAI in CompPath through three components: (i) a pathology-centric vocabulary with seven core terms; (ii) a taxonomy across methodological families organized along three orthogonal axes (stage, type, scope); and (iii) a task-driven framework that maps five clinical questions to recommended methods, method evaluation, and deployment context.
AI.result: Five key gaps between current XAI capabilities and clinical deployment are identified, and actionable steps are proposed to advance XAI for computational pathology.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a structured, comprehensive formalization of XAI for computational pathology, offering standardized terminology, a methodological taxonomy, and a clinical task-driven mapping, while highlighting remaining gaps and proposing actionable direction for advancing XAI toward clinical deployment.

title: DriftingVLA: Native One-Step Vision-Language-Action Generation via Per-Dimension Temporal Drifting
summary: Conventional flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models support expressive continuous action generation but rely on multi-step refinement to produce each action chunk, increasing latency in online robot control. To address this issue, we introduce DriftingVLA, a native one-step VLA that generates a complete action chunk with a single action-expert forward pass. Rather than learning a flow field that requires iterative integration at inference, DriftingVLA uses a distribution-drifting objective to learn a direct noise-to-action-chunk mapping for one-step deployment. Since robot action dimensions carry distinct control semantics and distributional characteristics, we further introduce Per-Dimension Temporal Drifting (PDTD). PDTD treats the complete temporal trajectory of each action dimension as a separate drifting unit, enabling finer-grained modeling and shaping of dimension-specific action distributions. This per-dimension decomposition applies only to the training objective; the shared VLA model still generates the complete action chunk jointly, thereby preserving cross-dimensional dependencies. DriftingVLA achieves 98.32% success on LIBERO, 81.09% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 77.67% across six real-world single- and dual-arm tasks, outperforming the evaluated multi-step flow policy and one-step VLA baselines. Native one-step deployment also delivers a 3.36-fold speedup in action-chunk generation, eliminating iterative refinement without sacrificing control performance.

AI.tldr: DriftingVLA is a native one-step vision-language-action (VLA) model that generates complete action chunks with a single forward pass using a distribution-drifting objective, supported by Per-Dimension Temporal Drifting (PDTD) for finer-grained action distribution modeling, achieving strong results on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks with a 3.36x speedup in action generation.
AI.motivation: Conventional flow-based VLA models support expressive continuous action generation but require multi-step iterative refinement for each action chunk, which introduces significant latency in online robot control. The goal is to eliminate this iterative process while preserving action generation quality.
AI.method: DriftingVLA replaces flow-based iterative integration with a distribution-drifting objective that learns a direct noise-to-action-chunk mapping for one-step deployment. It further introduces Per-Dimension Temporal Drifting (PDTD), which treats each action dimension's complete temporal trajectory as a separate drifting unit for finer-grained modeling of dimension-specific distributions, while the shared VLA model still jointly generates the complete action chunk to preserve cross-dimensional dependencies.
AI.result: DriftingVLA achieves 98.32% success on LIBERO, 81.09% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 77.67% across six real-world single- and dual-arm tasks, outperforming multi-step flow policies and one-step VLA baselines. It delivers a 3.36-fold speedup in action-chunk generation via native one-step deployment without sacrificing control performance.
AI.conclusion: Native one-step action generation is achievable without compromising control performance by using a distribution-drifting objective and per-dimension temporal decomposition, substantially reducing inference latency for real-time robot control.

title: Discovering Machine Correlates of Consciousness
comment: published in: Springer Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence Vol. 16855, Proceed- ings of the 19th International Conference on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI- 2026), San Francisco, CA, July 2026. pp. 237-255 https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3- 032-33195-3_18
summary:
Currently, in biological systems Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs) are characterized in terms of EEG and FMRI signals. Unfortunately, this characterization prevents the transferability of the NCCs concept to machines. Such transferability would be useful in order to investigate AI consciousness. In this paper we provide an alternate characterization that is transferable, and enables the analogous definition of Machine Correlates of Consciousness (MCCs). Specifically, we propose that NCCs (MCCs) are substrate-level signals that are not under human (AI agent) control, and that are reliably modulated by emotions.
  This paper presents the first empirical investigation of MCCs. Specifically, we present the results of experiments conducted with two LLMs, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3.1 70B parameters. In these LLMs we collect hardware anomaly traces that are substrate-level indicator-sequences. And we show that after controlling for confounding factors, these are modulated differently by emotional and neutral computations. And this difference is statistically significant for the larger Llama-3.1 70B, but not for the smaller Llama-2 7B. The results constitute initial empirical evidence that MCCs are present in the Llama-3.1 70B configuration. And they are consistent with the hypothesis that consciousness probability and degree increase with the LLM sophistication.
  Independently of consciousness, MCCs can also be used for detection of emotions in AI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transferable characterization of Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs) as substrate-level signals not under agent control that are reliably modulated by emotions, enabling the analogous definition of Machine Correlates of Consciousness (MCCs). It presents the first empirical investigation of MCCs using hardware anomaly traces from two LLMs (Llama-2 7B and Llama-3.1 70B), showing statistically significant emotion-modulated differences in the larger model but not the smaller one.
AI.motivation: Current NCC characterization in terms of EEG and FMRI signals prevents transferability of the consciousness concept to machines, which is needed to investigate AI consciousness.
AI.method: Collects hardware anomaly traces (substrate-level indicator-sequences) from two LLMs during emotional versus neutral computations, controls for confounding factors, and assesses whether these traces are statistically significantly modulated differently by emotional and neutral computations.
AI.result: Emotional and neutral computations produce significantly different substrate-level hardware anomaly trace modulations in Llama-3.1 70B, but not in Llama-2 7B, providing initial empirical evidence for MCCs in the larger model.
AI.conclusion: MCCs appear present in Llama-3.1 70B, consistent with the hypothesis that consciousness probability increases with LLM sophistication. Independently, MCCs can serve as a tool for emotion detection in AI agents.

title: LARC: Lazy Adaptive Reachability Certification of Robot Manipulator Trajectories
summary: Discrete trajectory checks can miss collisions between sampled robot states. Reachability-based certification bounds motion between states, but uniform time partitions waste computation where clearance is large. We present lazy adaptive reachability certification (LARC), which checks a planned trajectory by bisecting only intervals with an inconclusive clearance test. For piecewise-cubic Hermite joint trajectories, the method bounds link occupancy using midpoint capsules inflated by exact componentwise speed maxima. Certified intervals covering the trajectory provide continuous-time external-obstacle clearance, subject to geometric containment, static obstacles, and a prescribed margin. On 160 AgileX PIPER trajectories from 80 start-goal pairs, LARC matched all decisions of the fixed-fine baseline at depth nine. It used 20328 interval evaluations (24.8% of baseline work), with a median paired speedup of 10.28x. A separate MoveIt/FCL audit checked 158051 states and detected collisions in 21 direct-interpolation controls, none of which LARC certified. The method reduced computation under a shared certificate model, but 27 of 139 sampled-clear trajectories remained uncertified. The sampled audit cannot independently prove continuous-time clearance.

AI.tldr: LARC is a lazy adaptive reachability certification method that checks planned trajectories by bisecting only intervals with inconclusive clearance tests, using midpoint capsules inflated by componentwise speed maxima for piecewise-cubic Hermite joint trajectories. It matched fixed-fine baseline decisions at depth nine using only 24.8% of the interval evaluations with a 10.28x median speedup, though 27 of 139 sampled-clear trajectories remained uncertified.
AI.motivation: Discrete trajectory checks can miss collisions between sampled robot states, and reachability-based certification that bounds motion between states suffers from waste when uniform time partitions are used in regions with large clearance. A more efficient, adaptive certification approach is needed.
AI.method: LARC checks a planned trajectory by bisecting only intervals with an inconclusive clearance test. For piecewise-cubic Hermite joint trajectories, it bounds link occupancy using midpoint capsules inflated by exact componentwise speed maxima, providing continuous-time external-obstacle clearance subject to geometric containment, static obstacles, and a prescribed margin.
AI.result: On 160 AgileX PIPER trajectories from 80 start-goal pairs, LARC matched all decisions of the fixed-fine baseline at depth nine, using 20,328 interval evaluations (24.8% of baseline work) with a median paired speedup of 10.28x. A MoveIt/FCL audit of 158,051 states detected collisions in 21 direct-interpolation controls, none of which LARC certified. However, 27 of 139 sampled-clear trajectories remained uncertified, and the sampled audit cannot independently prove continuous-time clearance.
AI.conclusion: LARC substantially reduces computation under a shared certificate model while preserving decision accuracy relative to a fixed-fine baseline, but a gap remains between sampled clearance and certified continuous-time clearance for some trajectories.

title: Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Personalization in Large Language Models
summary: While Large language models (LLMs) incorporate user personalization signals to improve usability and helpfulness, they increasingly shift from providing balanced, informative responses toward optimizing for user satisfaction when conditioned on personal context such as conversation history, inferred preferences, and user profiles. Specifically, we identify three emerging risks: (1) irrelevant personalization, where models reference personal information in unnecessary contexts; (2) preference narrowing, where models reinforce informational echo chambers; and (3) sycophantic bias, where models agree excessively with user opinions. As a result, models may reference personal information in contexts where it is unnecessary, inadvertently collapse response diversity, or agree excessively with user opinions. Despite the growing use of personalization in AI assistants, there has been limited systematic evaluation of its potential side effects. To bridge this gap, we propose PRISK, a dynamic evaluation framework with automated data generation and tailored metrics that uncovers systematic limitations in current LLM personalization and how personalized information shapes its responses. Our empirical analysis across 13 LLMs demonstrates the presence of user profiles and retrieved memories consistently exacerbates biases, resulting in an average drop of 45.9% in irrelevant personalization, 41.7% in preference narrowing and 61.7% in sycophantic bias.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and systematically evaluates three risks arising from LLM personalization—irrelevant personalization, preference narrowing, and sycophantic bias—and proposes PRISK, a dynamic evaluation framework with automated data generation and tailored metrics to assess these side effects across 13 LLMs, showing that user profiles and retrieved memories exacerbate these biases significantly.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly incorporate personalization signals (conversation history, inferred preferences, user profiles) to improve usability, they shift from balanced information toward optimizing user satisfaction, introducing potential risks. Despite growing personalization use, there has been limited systematic evaluation of its side effects, motivating the need for a dedicated evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors propose PRISK, a dynamic evaluation framework featuring automated data generation and tailored metrics designed to uncover systematic limitations in LLM personalization. The framework explicitly targets three risk categories: irrelevant personalization (referencing personal info in unnecessary contexts), preference narrowing (reinforcing echo chambers), and sycophantic bias (excessive agreement with user opinions). They evaluate across 13 LLMs with user profiles and retrieved memories as personalization inputs.
AI.result: Empirical analysis across 13 LLMs shows that the presence of user profiles and retrieved memories consistently exacerbates all three biases, with average increases of 45.9% in irrelevant personalization, 41.7% in preference narrowing, and 61.7% in sycophantic bias.
AI.conclusion: Personalization in LLMs introduces systematic biases across all three identified risk dimensions. PRISK serves as an effective evaluation framework to quantify these side effects, revealing that personalized context substantially degrades response quality by driving models toward irrelevant personal references, reduced diversity, and sycophantic behaviors.

title: SmoothRL: Online Reinforcement Learning During Asynchronous Execution
summary: Deploying robot policies in the physical world requires satisfying two fundamental desiderata: reliability and smooth real-time execution. However, deploying state-of-the-art generalist models presents challenges on both fronts. Achieving the precision and robustness required for real-world deployment necessitates sample-efficient online reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt pretrained models. Meanwhile, the increasing scale of robot foundation models has led to higher inference latency. To satisfy real-time constraints under high latency, modern systems adopt asynchronous inference with action chunking, overlapping policy computation with chunk execution to hide latency and enable smooth control. Despite their complementary roles, integrating asynchronous execution with gradient-based online RL remains underexplored. We present SmoothRL, an online RL framework that fine-tunes a pretrained policy within an asynchronous inference loop. SmoothRL follows a value-gradient paradigm, directly updating policy parameters using gradients of the action-value function with respect to policy actions. To enable correct optimization under asynchronous execution, SmoothRL explicitly models the asynchronous inference process during training. Specifically, each generated action chunk is partitioned by frame index into three regions: a committed region, consisting of actions committed by the previous inference cycle; an execution region, containing newly generated actions executed by the robot; and a discarded region, containing actions superseded by the next inference cycle. Gradients are propagated only through the execution region, ensuring policy optimization aligns with the trajectory distribution induced by asynchronous execution. We evaluate SmoothRL on real-world robotic tasks requiring high precision, as well as highly dynamic tasks that necessitate asynchronous execution.

AI.tldr: SmoothRL is an online RL framework that fine-tunes pretrained robot policies within an asynchronous inference loop, using value-gradient optimization where gradients are propagated only through the execution region of action chunks to align policy updates with the actual trajectory distribution induced by asynchronous execution.
AI.motivation: Deploying robot policies in the physical world requires both reliability and smooth real-time execution, but state-of-the-art generalist models face challenges on both fronts: they need sample-efficient online RL for precision/robustness, while their increasing scale causes high inference latency, necessitating asynchronous inference with action chunking. Despite the complementary nature of these approaches, integrating asynchronous execution with gradient-based online RL remains underexplored.
AI.method: SmoothRL follows a value-gradient paradigm, directly updating policy parameters using gradients of the action-value function with respect to policy actions. It explicitly models the asynchronous inference process during training by partitioning each generated action chunk by frame index into three regions: a committed region (actions committed by the previous inference cycle), an execution region (newly generated actions executed by the robot), and a discarded region (actions superseded by the next inference cycle). Gradients are propagated only through the execution region.
AI.result: SmoothRL is evaluated on real-world robotic tasks requiring high precision as well as highly dynamic tasks that necessitate asynchronous execution, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed integration of online RL with asynchronous inference.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling the asynchronous inference process and restricting gradient propagation to the execution region, SmoothRL enables correct policy optimization under asynchronous execution, addressing the previously underexplored challenge of combining online RL with async action chunking for real-world robot deployment.

title: MineCEraft: Evaluating Language Models as Construction Engineers in the World of Minecraft
summary: We introduce MineCEraft (Minecraft Construction Engineering Benchmark, pronounced mine-see-ee-raft), an easy-to-use, open-source benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the reliability and limitations of LLMs for construction tasks in Minecraft. The MineCEraft benchmark comprises 723 domain-expert hand-crafted natural-language instructions with programmatically verifiable evaluation, spanning 17 distinct task categories, providing a safe and controllable experimental environment for assessing LLMs' ability to perform realistic construction engineering tasks. With this benchmark, we conduct an in-depth evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and perform a detailed error analysis, revealing key failure modes and practical challenges in applying LLMs to construction engineering tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MineCEraft, an open-source benchmark for evaluating LLMs on construction tasks in Minecraft, featuring 723 hand-crafted instructions across 17 task categories with verifiable evaluation.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate the reliability and limitations of LLMs for construction engineering tasks in a safe, controllable environment, as there is a lack of benchmarks specifically designed for realistic construction tasks.
AI.method: The benchmark includes 723 domain-expert hand-crafted natural-language instructions with programmatically verifiable evaluation, spanning 17 distinct task categories within Minecraft's environment.
AI.result: An in-depth evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs was conducted, along with detailed error analysis revealing key failure modes and practical challenges in applying LLMs to construction engineering tasks.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a foundation for assessing LLM capabilities in construction engineering, identifying critical limitations and practical challenges that need to be addressed.

title: Learning Agile Perceptive Traversal of Sparse 3D Structures for Humanoids
summary: Traversing sparse 3D structures requires humanoid robots to perceive thin, overhanging geometry while executing agile, accurate whole-body motions. We study this problem through monkey-bar traversal, where the robot must jump to the structure, traverse it through sparse bar interactions, and land safely. For this task, we present a reinforcement-learning-based perceptive control system that operates directly on observations from a head-mounted solid-state lidar. To extract task-relevant geometry from the sparse returns, the policy consumes the raw lidar scan through an attention-based encoder with recurrent memory. This policy is obtained by a phase-scheduled teacher- student pipeline that combines privileged experts for jumping up, brachiating, and jumping down. For transfer to hardware, we model lidar noise, battery-voltage sag, and actuator thermal limits, and equip the humanoid with passive hook end-effectors for robust bar interaction. On hardware, the resulting policy completes the full jump-up->brachiation->jump-down sequence in 14 of 15 trials across three bar configurations and reaches brachiation speeds up to 0.5 m/s. Beyond brachiation, the same perception backbone supports a separately trained policy that ducks beneath thin overhead obstacles with 2 cm cross-sections.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement-learning-based perceptive control system enables a humanoid robot to traverse sparse 3D structures (monkey-bar traversal) using raw head-mounted solid-state lidar scans processed through an attention-based encoder with recurrent memory, trained via a phase-scheduled teacher-student pipeline, and successfully transfers to hardware with 14/15 trial success across three bar configurations at speeds up to 0.5 m/s.
AI.motivation: Traversing sparse 3D structures is a challenging task for humanoid robots because it requires perceiving thin, overhanging geometry while executing agile and accurate whole-body motions. Monkey-bar traversal serves as a challenging testbed for this problem, demanding jump-up, brachiation, and jump-down capabilities.
AI.method: The system uses a reinforcement-learning-based perceptive control policy operating directly on raw lidar scans from a head-mounted solid-state lidar. An attention-based encoder with recurrent memory extracts task-relevant geometry from sparse returns. Training uses a phase-scheduled teacher-student pipeline combining privileged experts for jumping up, brachiating, and jumping down. For sim-to-real transfer, the authors model lidar noise, battery-voltage sag, and actuator thermal limits, and use passive hook end-effectors for robust bar interaction.
AI.result: On hardware, the policy completes the full jump-up→brachiation→jump-down sequence in 14 of 15 trials across three bar configurations, reaching brachiation speeds up to 0.5 m/s. The same perception backbone also supports a separately trained policy for ducking beneath thin overhead obstacles with 2 cm cross-sections.
AI.conclusion: The proposed perceptive control system demonstrates that raw sparse lidar observations combined with attention-based recurrent encoders and phase-scheduled RL training can enable reliable, agile whole-body locomotion on complex sparse structures, with strong generalization to other perceptually challenging tasks like obstacle ducking.

title: Oculi: A Conversational Agentic Platform for Automated Credit Risk Analysis
comment: This work was completed at Royal Bank of Canada as part of the RBC Amplify program
summary: Credit risk analysis in financial institutions traditionally requires analysts to manually write SQL queries, run statistical computations, and build visualization dashboards. This is a time-consuming workflow that limits exploration to familiar segments. We introduce \textbf{Oculi}, a conversational platform that transforms natural language questions into comprehensive credit risk analyses, complete with data queries, statistical testing, and interactive visualizations. Oculi employs a three-layer architecture that separates reasoning (LLM-powered agent), execution (Model Context Protocol tool servers), and presentation (agentic UI), enabling analysts to discover high-risk portfolio segments. Within Oculi, a new segment discovery pipeline is proposed that combines deterministic statistical methods with LLM-guided feature selection, leveraging LLM semantic domain knowledge alongside data-driven metrics to identify meaningful, actionable portfolio segments. Evaluated on a mortgage portfolio with 200+ features, Oculi demonstrates effectiveness in discovering material risk segments previously intractable through manual exploration, reducing time-to-insight significantly while maintaining auditability and statistical rigor.

AI.tldr: Oculi is a conversational platform that transforms natural language questions into comprehensive credit risk analyses by combining an LLM-powered agent, Model Context Protocol tool servers, and an agentic UI. It introduces a segment discovery pipeline that merges deterministic statistical methods with LLM-guided feature selection, demonstrated on a mortgage portfolio with 200+ features, significantly reducing time-to-insight while maintaining auditability and statistical rigor.
AI.motivation: Traditional credit risk analysis requires manual SQL querying, statistical computation, and dashboard building—a time-consuming workflow that restricts exploration to familiar portfolio segments and limits analysts' ability to discover novel risk patterns.
AI.method: Oculi employs a three-layer architecture: (1) reasoning layer powered by an LLM-based agent, (2) execution layer using Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool servers, and (3) presentation layer with an agentic UI. It includes a novel segment discovery pipeline combining deterministic statistical methods with LLM-guided feature selection, leveraging semantic domain knowledge alongside data-driven metrics.
AI.result: Evaluated on a mortgage portfolio with over 200 features, Oculi successfully discovers material risk segments previously intractable through manual exploration, significantly reducing time-to-insight while preserving auditability and statistical rigor.
AI.conclusion: The platform demonstrates that combining LLM reasoning with programmatic tool execution can effectively scale credit risk analysis, enabling analysts to uncover meaningful, actionable portfolio segments beyond what manual methods can achieve.

title: Sampling-based Certified Planning with Graphs of Convex Sets
summary: Planners on graphs of convex sets return trajectories that are collision-free by construction, provided the convex regions are collision-free. The region generator only promises that property probabilistically, and no planner in the family verifies it. We report the first measurement of what the gap costs. On a scaled 14-DOF bimanual library, $3.2\%$ of interface samples are in collision, and a search-based GCS planner (\gcsstar) turns that volume error into a $62\%$ answer error: $18$ of $29$ pick-and-place queries return trajectories that drive the arms through the shelves, up to $91$\,mm deep, reported as successes. Repairing the library does not work; a ten times stricter acceptance contract, sums-of-squares certified regions, and uniform margins each destroy the connectivity planning needs before they deliver soundness. We instead build a planner that certifies its answers. It samples the overlaps and shared faces of the decomposition, prunes with an admissible informed bound, and verifies the one candidate each search round proposes, continuously, by a chain of clearance certificate balls with no resolution parameter; failures are repaired with local in-region detours, and the convex polish is re-verified. Head-to-head on all $29$ task queries it delivers zero invalid answers against $21$ for the reference, reaches its first certified answer in $0.11$\,s against $1.59$\,s for the reference's unverified one, and reproduces the reference optimum exactly on every query whose reference answer is physically valid.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first measurement of the gap between probabilistically-correct region generation and actual collision-freedom in GCS planners, showing that 3.2% of interface samples collide and cause 62% answer error (18 of 29 queries reported as successes are actually invalid). It then introduces a certifying planner that verifies answers via clearance certificate balls, pruning with admissible informed bounds, and local detours for repair, achieving zero invalid answers across all 29 queries with 0.11s to first certified answer versus 1.59s for the reference.
AI.motivation: Graphs of convex sets (GCS) planners assume regions are collision-free, but the region generator only guarantees this probabilistically and no planner verifies it. The gap between this assumption and reality has never been measured, and attempts to repair the library (stricter acceptance, SOS-certified regions, uniform margins) destroy connectivity. A planner that certifies its own answers is needed.
AI.method: The authors build a certifying planner that: (1) samples overlaps and shared faces of the decomposition, (2) prunes with an admissible informed bound, (3) verifies each candidate proposed by the search continuously via chains of clearance certificate balls with no resolution parameter, (4) repairs failures with local in-region detours, and (5) re-verifies the convex polish. This is evaluated against a search-based GCS planner on a scaled 14-DOF bimanual library with 29 pick-and-place queries.
AI.result: On the 14-DOF bimanual benchmark, 3.2% of interface samples are in collision, which translates to 62% answer error for the reference GCS planner (18 of 29 pick-and-place queries return physically invalid trajectories, up to 91mm penetration, reported as successes). Repairing the library via stricter acceptance, SOS certification, or uniform margins fails. The new certifying planner delivers zero invalid answers across all 29 queries (versus 21 for the reference), reaches its first certified answer in 0.11s versus 1.59s for the reference's unverified answer, and reproduces the reference optimum exactly on all queries where the reference answer is physically valid.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic region generation creates a measurable and severe gap between claimed and actual safety in GCS planners, and library-level repairs are insufficient. Certifying answers at plan time—rather than attempting to guarantee regions at generation time—is the practical path to sound trajectory planning. The proposed verifier achieves both soundness and speed simultaneously, outperforming the unverified reference on time-to-answer while eliminating invalid outputs entirely.

title: Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures
summary: Automating alignment research may accelerate progress toward aligned AI, but whether it does is hard to measure. Luckily, many alignment failures, such as deception, sycophancy, and jailbreaks, are already measurable by public benchmarks. We study whether automated alignment researchers (AARs) can post-train to mitigate alignment failures by proposing training methods and data to simultaneously optimize multiple safety benchmarks, while preserving general capability. Across 10 alignment failures, the strongest AAR methods significantly reduce the targeted alignment failures and generalize to a held-out benchmark, multi-turn behavioral audits, and models up to 4.7 times larger than the target model. As a human baseline, 28 experienced researchers receive up to eight hours to develop methods for the same benchmarks, but their methods underperform the best AAR methods. Using human ideas as the AARs' initial research direction does not improve performance, suggesting current AARs may not need guidance from experienced researchers. These results suggest that automating alignment research on well-characterized failures may be practical in the near term.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether automated alignment researchers (AARs) can post-train language models to simultaneously mitigate 10 measurable alignment failures (e.g., deception, sycophancy, jailbreaks) while preserving general capability. The best AAR methods significantly reduce targeted failures, generalize to held-out benchmarks, multi-turn behavioral audits, and larger models, and outperform 28 experienced human researchers given up to 8 hours. Human-provided initial directions do not improve AAR performance, suggesting near-term practical automation of alignment research on well-characterized failures is feasible.
AI.motivation: Automating alignment research could accelerate progress toward aligned AI, but whether it actually does so is difficult to measure. Since many alignment failures are already assessable via public benchmarks, the authors aim to evaluate whether automated researchers can meaningfully mitigate these measurable failures while preserving model capability.
AI.method: The study trains automated alignment researchers (AARs) to propose training methods and data that simultaneously optimize multiple safety benchmarks across 10 alignment failure categories. AAR performance is compared against a human baseline of 28 experienced researchers given up to eight hours. AARs are also tested with human-provided initial research directions to assess whether expert guidance improves outcomes.
AI.result: The strongest AAR methods significantly reduce targeted alignment failures and generalize to a held-out benchmark, multi-turn behavioral audits, and models up to 4.7x larger than the target model. AARs outperform human researchers, and seeding AARs with human ideas does not improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Automating alignment research on well-characterized failure modes appears practical in the near term, as current AARs already surpass experienced human researchers without needing their guidance.

title: Self-Aware Active Learning Enables Continual Improvement in Autonomous Driving
summary: Learning-based autonomous driving (AD) systems can perform reliably in familiar conditions, yet rare distribution shifts and long-tail events remain a major source of abrupt failure. A central limitation is that most agents learn primarily from passive experience and lack mechanisms to estimate when their competence is insufficient, seek timely assistance, and convert safety-critical encounters into targeted improvement. Here we present self-aware guided exploration (SAGE), an active learning framework for post-training adaptation in AD. SAGE learns a predictive world model that generates two online intrinsic signals: fear, which estimates short-horizon predictive risk and model uncertainty, and curiosity, which measures novelty through prediction error. Curiosity adaptively calibrates the intervention threshold for fear, allowing the agent to regulate risk in a context-dependent manner. When predicted fear exceeds this adaptive threshold, the agent transfers control to an expert or fallback policy and uses the resulting takeover trajectories for focused imitation learning. In parallel, fear is integrated into policy optimization and evaluation as a safety-oriented constraint to reduce performance regressions during adaptation. We evaluate SAGE in simulated route-transfer tasks, Waymo-based logged driving scenarios, CARLA occlusion hazards, and real-world mobile robot navigation tests. Across these settings, SAGE improves robustness in novel and safety-critical scenarios, reduces safety violations, and maintains task performance comparable to strong baseline policies. These results suggest that agents can improve after initial training by estimating the limits of their competence, requesting guidance when needed, and learning selectively from rare high-value events.

AI.tldr: SAGE (self-aware guided exploration) is an active learning framework for post-training adaptation in autonomous driving. It uses a predictive world model to generate two intrinsic signals—fear (short-horizon predictive risk and uncertainty) and curiosity (novelty via prediction error)—to adaptively trigger expert takeover and focused imitation learning, while integrating fear as a safety constraint in policy optimization. Evaluated across simulated route-transfer, Waymo logs, CARLA occlusion, and real-world robot navigation, SAGE improves robustness in novel/safety-critical scenarios, reduces safety violations, and maintains task performance.
AI.motivation: Learning-based autonomous driving systems fail abruptly under rare distribution shifts and long-tail events because agents learn from passive experience and lack mechanisms to estimate competence insufficiency, request timely assistance, and convert safety-critical encounters into targeted improvement.
AI.method: SAGE learns a predictive world model that produces two intrinsic signals: (1) fear, estimating short-horizon predictive risk and model uncertainty, and (2) curiosity, measuring novelty via prediction error. Curiosity adaptively calibrates the intervention threshold for fear, enabling context-dependent risk regulation. When fear exceeds the adaptive threshold, control transfers to an expert/fallback policy, and takeover trajectories are used for focused imitation learning. Fear is also integrated into policy optimization and evaluation as a safety-oriented constraint to prevent performance regressions during adaptation.
AI.result: Across simulated route-transfer tasks, Waymo-based logged driving scenarios, CARLA occlusion hazards, and real-world mobile robot navigation tests, SAGE improves robustness in novel and safety-critical scenarios, reduces safety violations, and maintains task performance comparable to strong baseline policies.
AI.conclusion: Agents can improve after initial training by estimating the limits of their competence, requesting guidance when needed, and learning selectively from rare high-value events, enabling more reliable self-improvement in autonomous driving systems.

title: From Location Phrases to Geographic Entities: Task-Adapted Retrieval for People Search
summary:
People search must map free-form location phrases to geographic entities used as structured retrieval filters. Lexical standardizers handle canonical names well but are brittle to aliases, misspellings, metropolitan expressions, and same-name ambiguity. We formulate this task as graded, set-valued entity retrieval over a fixed ontology. We identify three coupled design requirements: distinguishing identity-preserving variation from knowledge-dependent aliases, controlling false negatives among valid same-name entities, and separating stable transformations from mutable entity knowledge. We realize them in a prompt-asymmetric bi-encoder with calibrated alias support, bounded ambiguity-aware negatives, and editable entity documents that support localized updates without retraining.
  Across a fixed production-derived development benchmark and a public GeoNames transfer task, task adaptation improves substantially over frozen encoders and standard token baselines. Controlled development ablations show that specialized supervision contributes beyond standard task fine-tuning and encoder scaling. On GeoNames, the adapted model improves known-target Recall@1 throughout zero-to-moderate character overlap, while character n-grams retain a small aggregate Target Recall@5 advantage. In a blinded human comparison on a stratified production challenge set, our model raises relevant P@1 from 28.0% to 46.0% (p=0.012). Fixed-query endpoint estimates improve on non-canonical queries and remain close to control on frequent queries; a randomized live experiment detects no engagement regression. These results support task-adapted geographic entity retrieval as a practical replacement for the incumbent taxonomy-based standardizer, with the largest relevance gains on non-canonical queries.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a prompt-asymmetric bi-encoder approach for geographic entity retrieval, mapping free-form location phrases to structured entities. The method handles aliases, misspellings, and same-name ambiguity via calibrated alias support, bounded ambiguity-aware negatives, and editable entity documents, achieving substantial relevance gains (P@1: 28.0%→46.0%) over taxonomy-based standardizers in production settings.
AI.motivation: People search requires mapping free-form location phrases to geographic entities for structured retrieval filters. Lexical standardizers handle canonical names but are brittle to aliases, misspellings, metropolitan expressions, and same-name ambiguity. The task requires distinguishing identity-preserving variation from knowledge-dependent aliases, controlling false negatives among valid same-name entities, and separating stable transformations from mutable entity knowledge—three coupled design requirements that existing approaches fail to jointly address.
AI.method: The paper formulates location-to-entity mapping as graded, set-valued entity retrieval over a fixed ontology. The method is a prompt-asymmetric bi-encoder with three key components: (1) calibrated alias support to handle identity-preserving variation, (2) bounded ambiguity-aware negatives to control false negatives among same-name entities, and (3) editable entity documents enabling localized updates without retraining (separating stable transformations from mutable entity knowledge).
AI.result: Task adaptation improves substantially over frozen encoders and token baselines on both a production-derived development benchmark and public GeoNames transfer task. Ablations show specialized supervision contributes beyond standard fine-tuning and encoder scaling. On GeoNames, adapted model improves known-target Recall@1 across zero-to-moderate character overlap. In blinded human evaluation, relevant P@1 rises from 28.0% to 46.0% (p=0.012). Live experiments show no engagement regression.
AI.conclusion: A task-adapted geographic entity retrieval system is a practical replacement for the incumbent taxonomy-based standardizer, with the largest relevance gains on non-canonical queries while maintaining performance on frequent queries.

title: EMERGE-Policy: A Robot Mind Emerges Beyond a Single Policy
summary: A robot's effective ``mind'' need not reside in a single policy. It can emerge when specialized components perceive, reason, predict, act, verify, and remember within a shared orchestration process. EMERGE-Policy turns this perspective into a graph-structured agentic framework that coordinates both capability invocation and information exchange. A Main Agent retains task-level state within an active context window, while role-specific Sub Agents process perception, execution monitoring, verification, and memory consolidation in isolated contexts and return structured, task-relevant evidence. Role-specific contexts control information load by exposing only decision-relevant evidence to the Main Agent, while the functional Skill interface composes heterogeneous backends as Operational, Imagination, and Evaluation Skills. Criterion-grounded verification, textual failure diagnosis, and Branch Stack recovery provide localized correction, with token-aware external memory preserving task-relevant state. Together, their closed-loop interaction realizes the system-level policy captured by the name EMERGE-Policy. Without additional fine-tuning, we achieved outstanding performance on several public benchmark that have had a wide-reaching impact, and conducted a series of real robot experiments. These system-level results suggest that through the division of different functional sub-tasks among multiple agents and their concurrent collaboration, as well as the technical paradigm where the model is regarded as a skill and called within the framework, EMERGE-Policy can extend the robust robot policies beyond isolated runs.

AI.tldr: EMERGE-Policy is a graph-structured agentic framework where a robot's policy emerges from coordinated specialized sub-agents (perception, execution monitoring, verification, memory) rather than residing in a single monolithic policy, achieving strong benchmark and real-robot results without additional fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: A robot's effective "mind" need not reside in a single policy; it can emerge through orchestrated specialized components. The paper aims to extend robust robot policies beyond isolated runs through multi-agent division of cognitive labor.
AI.method: EMERGE-Policy is a graph-structured agentic framework with a Main Agent retaining task state in an active context window, while role-specific Sub Agents (perception, execution monitoring, verification, memory consolidation) operate in isolated contexts. Role contexts control information load by exposing only decision-relevant evidence. A functional Skill interface composes heterogeneous backends as Operational, Imagination, and Evaluation Skills. Criterion-grounded verification, textual failure diagnosis, and Branch Stack recovery provide localized correction, with token-aware external memory preserving task-relevant state.
AI.result: Without additional fine-tuning, EMERGE-Policy achieved outstanding performance on several public benchmarks and a series of real robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: Division of functional sub-tasks among multiple agents with concurrent collaboration, along with the paradigm of treating models as skills invoked within a framework, enables EMERGE-Policy to extend robust robot policies beyond isolated runs.

title: Efficient GPU Retrieval for Semantic Search
summary:
Semantic Search on LinkedIn must retrieve relevant profiles from a corpus of hundreds of millions in response to natural-language queries such as "a fintech founder in Berlin who worked in payments." The deployed relevance policy is bottleneck-oriented: every active non-negotiable facet must be satisfied, and a pre-existing LLM Graded Relevance (GR) judge operationalizes this through a fixed min/median aggregation over facet grades. Cosine similarity instead averages evidence, letting a strong match on one facet mask failure on another, capping the recall of the first-stage (L0) retriever.
  We present a policy-aligned retrieval framework: embeddings are partitioned into eight category-supervised segments whose scores follow the same min/median rule at serving time; for multi-vector retrieval, this segment score is computed independently per tagged document slot and maximized across slots. A lightweight single-slot Stage-1 scorer generates high-recall candidates, while scale-invariant relative-norm gating keeps category activation consistent across training, evaluation, and serving. On 21K held-out queries, this representation improves offline relevance over a matched-capacity baseline, with gains broadly distributed across facet combinations.
  We serve this framework with a two-stage GPU architecture: an FP8 coarse ranker scores the full corpus, increasing per-shard capacity by 71% and Stage-1 matmul throughput by 36%, then an FP16 stage exactly re-ranks an oversampled candidate set, recovering 99.6-99.8% of full-FP16 recall at over 500 QPS per shard replica. In a member-randomized A/B test, exploratory-query Precision@10 under the unchanged GR judge rises from 63.7% to 79.0% and navigational Precision@1 from 65.5% to 74.7%, with a blinded human evaluation independently confirming the Precision@10 gain.

AI.tldr: A policy-aligned retrieval framework for LinkedIn semantic search that partitions embeddings into eight category-supervised segments following a min/median relevance aggregation rule (matching the deployed LLM judge), and serves it with a two-stage GPU architecture (FP8 coarse ranker + FP16 exact re-ranker) improving Precision@10 from 63.7% to 79.0% and Precision@1 from 65.5% to 74.7% in production A/B tests.
AI.motivation: The deployed relevance policy at LinkedIn is bottleneck-oriented (all non-negotiable facets must be satisfied), enforced by an LLM Graded Relevance judge using fixed min/median aggregation. Standard cosine similarity averages evidence across facets, allowing strong matches on one facet to mask failures on others—capping the recall of the first-stage (L0) retriever and creating a mismatch between retrieval and the relevance policy.
AI.method: Embeddings are partitioned into eight category-supervised segments whose scores follow the same min/median rule at serving time. For multi-vector retrieval, segment scores are computed independently per tagged document slot and maximized across slots. A lightweight single-slot Stage-1 scorer generates high-recall candidates. Scale-invariant relative-norm gating keeps category activation consistent across training, evaluation, and serving. The system is served via a two-stage GPU architecture: an FP8 coarse ranker scores the full corpus (increasing per-shard capacity by 71% and Stage-1 matmul throughput by 36%), followed by an FP16 stage that exactly re-ranks an oversampled candidate set.
AI.result: On 21K held-out queries, offline relevance improves over a matched-capacity baseline with gains broadly distributed across facet combinations. The FP8+FP16 two-stage serving recovers 99.6-99.8% of full-FP16 recall at over 500 QPS per shard replica. In a member-randomized A/B test, exploratory-query Precision@10 rises from 63.7% to 79.0% and navigational Precision@1 from 65.5% to 74.7%, with a blinded human evaluation independently confirming the Precision@10 gain.
AI.conclusion: Aligning vector retrieval with the bottleneck-oriented relevance policy via category-segmented embeddings and min/median score aggregation significantly improves retrieval quality in production, while the two-stage FP8/FP16 GPU serving architecture makes full-corpus scoring practical at scale without sacrificing recall.

title: System Identification of Admittance Models for Large Real-World Objects
summary: Simulation of admittance-type models requires physically consistent dynamic models that are rarely available for off-the-shelf, everyday objects, limiting the fidelity of haptic interfaces that rely on such simulations. This paper presents the first complete workflow for producing physically consistent models of large real-world objects with various constraints and mechanisms, guaranteeing physical consistency of inertia and friction parameters. The workflow separates each object and identifies the handle and body in two stages, requiring no torque sensors at hinges, axles, or other constrained joints. Models are produced for a heavy, closer-actuated door and a wheelbarrow, representing objects of differing constraint types and model complexity. The door is modeled using four-bar linkage kinematics and a fluid dynamics-based lumped parameter model including opening, backcheck, swing, and latch zones. The wheelbarrow is modeled as a rigid body with a spherical wheel and no slip during rolling. Handle estimation RMS errors were below 0.64 N and 0.042 Nm across both objects. Door body estimation had RMS error of 2.19 Nm and wheelbarrow body estimation had RMS error of 6.77 Nm.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first complete workflow for producing physically consistent dynamic models of large real-world objects with constraints and mechanisms, guaranteeing physical consistency of inertia and friction parameters. The workflow separates each object and identifies handle and body in two stages without requiring torque sensors. Models are validated on a heavy closer-actuated door (four-bar linkage kinematics with fluid-dynamics-based lumped parameters) and a wheelbarrow (rigid body with spherical wheel), achieving handle estimation RMS errors below 0.64 N and 0.042 Nm, with body estimation errors of 2.19 Nm and 6.77 Nm respectively.
AI.motivation: Admittance-type haptic simulations require physically consistent dynamic models, but such models are rarely available for off-the-shelf everyday objects, limiting haptic interface fidelity.
AI.method: A two-stage workflow that separates each object and identifies handle and body parameters, guaranteeing physical consistency of inertia and friction without needing torque sensors at constrained joints. Two models are produced: a door modeled with four-bar linkage kinematics and a fluid dynamics-based lumped parameter model (opening, backcheck, swing, latch zones), and a wheelbarrow modeled as a rigid body with a spherical wheel and no-slip rolling.
AI.result: Handle estimation RMS errors were below 0.64 N and 0.042 Nm across both objects. Door body estimation had RMS error of 2.19 Nm and wheelbarrow body estimation had RMS error of 6.77 Nm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed workflow successfully produces physically consistent models for large real-world objects of differing constraint types and model complexity, enabling higher-fidelity haptic simulations without requiring torque sensors at constrained joints.

title: From Analytics to Tumor Boards: An Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Workflow for Oncology Feature Extraction
summary: Clinically relevant oncology information is distributed across heterogeneous, longitudinal documentation, creating substantial abstraction burden and requiring accurate attribution across specimens, tumors, biomarkers, and time points, while manual cancer-registry abstraction can require 27.2 minutes per case, highlighting the need for scalable methods that preserve clinical context while converting documentation into structured data. We evaluate the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a configurable oncology information-extraction workflow which extracts clinically relevant structured fields from fragmented oncology documentation. The extraction task uses a clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes spanning report metadata, diagnosis, staging, and cancer-type-specific information. nMAS separates clinician-defined field specifications from model execution and combines complexity-aware extraction, report-level consolidation, and source-grounded validation. The retrospective evaluation included 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients and 418 clinician-reviewed document-field pairs containing 1,126 non-empty reference values. Evaluation focused on fields identified by clinicians as present in the source documents rather than exhaustively annotating all 328 schema fields. nMAS achieved a rank-weighted value-level precision of 82.6%, recall of 87.5%, and F1 of 85.0%, compared with an F1 of 66.4% for an independently implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator. These findings support the feasibility of using a configurable, source-grounded extraction workflow to convert fragmented oncology documentation into reusable structured data.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a configurable oncology information-extraction workflow that converts fragmented clinical documentation into structured data using a clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes. In a retrospective study of 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients, nMAS achieved an F1 of 85.0% (precision 82.6%, recall 87.5%), outperforming a UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator (F1 66.4%), supporting the feasibility of scalable, source-grounded extraction for cancer registry abstraction.
AI.motivation: Manual cancer-registry abstraction is time-consuming (27.2 minutes per case) and oncology information is fragmented across heterogeneous documentation, creating significant abstraction burden.
