Scalable methods are needed that preserve clinical context while converting documentation into structured data for reuse.
AI.method: nMAS is a configurable multi-agent extraction workflow that separates clinician-defined field specifications from model execution. It uses a 328-attribute schema spanning report metadata, diagnosis, staging, and cancer-type-specific information, combined with complexity-aware extraction, report-level consolidation, and source-grounded validation. The evaluation used 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients and 418 clinician-reviewed document-field pairs containing 1,126 non-empty reference values, focusing on fields clinicians identified as present in source documents.
AI.result: nMAS achieved a rank-weighted value-level precision of 82.6%, recall of 87.5%, and F1 of 85.0%, compared with an F1 of 66.4% for an independently implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the feasibility of using a configurable, source-grounded extraction workflow to convert fragmented oncology documentation into reusable structured data, offering a scalable alternative to manual abstraction.

title: Training-Free Action Correction for VLA Model Failures via Language Feedback
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models demonstrate strong semantic understanding yet exhibit systematic failures during deployment. The conditions under which these failures occur, and whether they can be corrected without retraining, remain poorly understood. In this paper, we take steps toward addressing this gap. We present CorrectVLA, a framework that translates task-level natural language corrections into additive action magnitude adjustments without modifying policy weights. A human provides a single task-level correction, applied uniformly across all rollouts without per-episode intervention. In simulation, CorrectVLA recovers execution misalignment failures across both in-distribution and OOD tasks. In real-robot experiments on a UFactory xArm7 under environment shift, CorrectVLA restores near-perfect success where the base policy almost entirely breaks down, generalizing across object locations and identities. Through a taxonomy of failure modes on LIBERO-90, we find that execution misalignment failures, where the policy reaches the correct target but miscalibrates action magnitudes, represent the correctable subset, while other failure modes where semantic comprehension itself breaks down are not amenable to this approach. The approach succeeds when policies possess strategic correctness and fails when fundamental comprehension is absent, establishing a practical operational boundary for inference-time correction.

AI.tldr: CorrectVLA is a framework that translates task-level natural language corrections into additive action magnitude adjustments without retraining, recovering execution misalignment failures in VLA models across simulation and real-robot experiments.
AI.motivation: VLA models show strong semantic understanding but systematically fail during deployment. The conditions under which these failures occur and whether they can be corrected without retraining are poorly understood, motivating a framework for inference-time correction.
AI.method: CorrectVLA translates a single task-level natural language correction into additive action magnitude adjustments applied uniformly across all rollouts, without modifying policy weights or requiring per-episode intervention.
AI.result: In simulation, CorrectVLA recovers execution misalignment failures on both in-distribution and OOD tasks. In real-robot experiments on a UFactory xArm7 under environment shift, it restores near-perfect success where the base policy almost entirely breaks down, generalizing across object locations and identities.
AI.conclusion: Through a taxonomy of failure modes on LIBERO-90, execution misalignment failures (where the policy reaches the correct target but miscalibrates action magnitudes) are correctable, while semantic comprehension failures are not. The approach succeeds when policies possess strategic correctness and fails when fundamental comprehension is absent, establishing a practical operational boundary for inference-time correction.

title: The Role of Network Topology and Opponent Information in Shaping Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems
summary: Several works have investigated the influence of graph topology on cooperation among artificial agents, while the majority of the literature has focused on modelling agents' adaptation through strategy imitation, which relies solely on the cumulative payoffs of others. This paper investigates scenarios in which each agent learns to play the two-player Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) using deep reinforcement learning. Each agent is represented as a node in a graph, where its neighbours constitute the pool of opponents with whom it can interact. During each IPD episode, agents are provided with different types of information about their opponent, consisting of action history and opponent identity. Experimental results across different graph topologies show that the number of neighbours per node and the average path length are the main factors affecting the emergence of cooperation. We also show that, while partner selection fosters mutual cooperation by limiting the diversity of the opponent pool, providing agents with the identity of their opponent hinders the proliferation of cooperative strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how graph topology and opponent information affect cooperation in multi-agent Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma games where agents learn via deep reinforcement learning, finding that node degree and average path length are key factors, partner selection promotes cooperation, and opponent identity hinders it.
AI.motivation: Previous research on graph topology and cooperation has largely relied on strategy imitation based on cumulative payoffs, overlooking scenarios where agents learn strategies independently via deep reinforcement learning. This paper investigates how different graph structures and information availability affect the emergence of cooperation when agents learn through deep RL.
AI.method: Each agent is represented as a node in a graph, with neighbors as potential opponents. Agents learn to play the two-player Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma using deep reinforcement learning, receiving either action history alone or action history plus opponent identity during gameplay. Experiments are conducted across different graph topologies to assess how structural properties and information types affect cooperative behavior.
AI.result: The number of neighbours per node (degree) and the average path length of the graph are the dominant factors influencing the emergence of cooperation. Partner selection, which limits the diversity of the opponent pool, fosters mutual cooperation. Conversely, providing agents with opponent identity hinders the proliferation of cooperative strategies.
AI.conclusion: Graph structural properties such as node degree and average path length critically shape cooperation in RL-based IPD agents. Information design matters: restricting opponent pool diversity (via partner selection) aids cooperation, while revealing opponent identity undermines it.

title: MiBOT: A head-worn robot that modulates cardiovascular responses through human-like soft massage
comment: Published at 2024 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: Massage therapy is helpful for the rehabilitation of various diseases, such as headaches caused by migraines and stress. Existing robotic systems have focused on massage therapy on the torso and limbs, but performing massage motions through suitable actuation on a person's head has been a challenge. In this paper, we present MiBOT, a head-worn massage robot that actuates two soft tactors to produce touch motions mimicking human massage. A key design principle behind MiBOT is its silent actuation, which we achieve through pneumatic artificial muscles in conjunction with a controller loop to respond to contact pressure. We evaluated the effectiveness of MiBOT in a controlled study and assessed subjects' blood pressure and heart rate levels while applying MiBOT. We found that our mechanical system generated positive and conclusive quantitative outcomes that are similar to the human-administered massage, decreasing participants' mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 2.8 mmHg and 1.7 mmHg, respectively, as well as calming their heart rate by 8-10% on average.

AI.tldr: MiBOT is a head-worn massage robot using pneumatic artificial muscles with silent actuation and closed-loop pressure control to mimic human massage. In a controlled study, it reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 2.8 mmHg and 1.7 mmHg respectively, and lowered heart rate by 8-10%, matching the efficacy of human-administered massage.
AI.motivation: Existing massage robots focus on torso and limbs, but head massage—useful for migraines and stress—remains a challenge due to the difficulty of suitable actuation on the head.
AI.method: The authors present MiBOT, a head-worn massage robot that drives two soft tactors via pneumatic artificial muscles. Silent actuation is achieved through a controller loop that responds to contact pressure.
AI.result: In a controlled study, MiBOT produced quantitative outcomes similar to human-administered massage: mean systolic blood pressure decreased by 2.8 mmHg, diastolic by 1.7 mmHg, and heart rate was calmed by 8-10% on average.
AI.conclusion: MiBOT effectively replicates human head massage outcomes with measurable physiological benefits, demonstrating the feasibility of head-worn robotic massage systems.

title: Selective Forgetting: A Graph-Based Memory Framework for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary:
Knowledge graphs have been proposed as a structured alternative to flat retrieval-augmented generation for long-term agent memory, on the assumption that representing conversations as entities and relations improves recall. We evaluate that assumption directly. Our framework extracts each conversational turn into typed nodes and attributed edges, answers questions from a two-hop subgraph, and periodically prunes nodes that score low on a weighted combination of recency, access frequency, degree centrality, and age. On LongMemEval, the graph does not outperform a flat vector baseline at a matched candidate-generation budget of five retrieval roots: token F1 is $0.417$ against $0.468$, and a paired bootstrap over 500 questions gives
$Δ= -0.050$ (95\% CI $[-0.085, -0.016]$). The gap is widest on questions that require recalling a specific prior assistant turn, where judged correctness falls from $0.911$ to $0.607$, suggesting that decomposing a turn into entities discards the surface form these questions depend on. The forgetting module is more successful. Applied once to a persistent 27{,}021-node graph, it removes 9.8\% of nodes and 9.5\% of stored bytes; token F1 is unchanged ($+0.001$, 95\% CI $[-0.015, +0.016]$) and judged correctness falls by $1.6$ points, with the 95\% interval bounding any loss at $3.8$ points ($[-0.038, +0.006]$). Because our extractor is a single small model evaluated on one benchmark, these results characterise this extraction-based pipeline rather than graph-structured memory in general. Code: https://github.com/skhanzad/Selective-Amnesia

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates whether knowledge-graph-based agent memory outperforms flat retrieval-augmented generation for long-term conversational recall. Using a framework that extracts conversational turns into typed nodes/edges, answers questions from two-hop subgraphs, and periodically prunes low-scoring nodes, the authors find the graph underperforms a flat vector baseline at matched budget (token F1 0.417 vs 0.468), with the largest gap on questions requiring recall of specific prior assistant turns. However, the forgetting/pruning module is effective: it removes ~10% of nodes/bytes with negligible performance loss.
AI.motivation: Knowledge graphs have been proposed as a structured alternative to flat retrieval-augmented generation for long-term agent memory, based on the assumption that representing conversations as entities and relations improves recall. The authors aim to directly evaluate this assumption empirically.
AI.method: The framework extracts each conversational turn into typed nodes and attributed edges, answers questions from a two-hop subgraph, and periodically prunes nodes scoring low on a weighted combination of recency, access frequency, degree centrality, and age. Evaluation is on LongMemEval against a flat vector baseline at a matched candidate-generation budget of five retrieval roots, with paired bootstrap significance testing over 500 questions.
AI.result: The graph underperforms flat vector retrieval: token F1 0.417 vs 0.468 (Δ=-0.050, 95% CI [-0.085, -0.016]). The gap is largest on questions needing recall of a specific prior assistant turn (judged correctness 0.911→0.607). The forgetting module removes 9.8% of nodes and 9.5% of bytes from a 27,021-node graph with token F1 unchanged (+0.001) and judged correctness loss bounded at 3.8 points.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing conversational turns into graph entities discards surface-form information that certain recall questions depend on, explaining the graph's deficit. Selective forgetting via node pruning is effective and nearly lossless. Results are specific to this extraction-based pipeline on one benchmark and do not generalise to graph-structured memory in general.

title: Rethinking Language's Role in Efficient VLA for Autonomous Vehicles: Toward Smarter, Trustworthy Driving
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are reshaping autonomous driving (AD) by unifying perception, reasoning, and control through language, enabling semantic grounding, interpretable decisions, and better long-tail generalization. But language is expensive onboard: latency and memory budgets are tight, and autoregressive decoding is inherently sequential. This work reframes the central question as when and where language should act at inference, since inference cost recurs at every deployed frame while training cost is paid once. We introduce the Language Residue taxonomy to organize methods by their inference-time use of language: train-time-only supervision (L1), latent non-textual reasoning (L2), conditional invocation (L3), and full per-frame generation (L4). We review representative methods and tag each across five deployment axes (latency, parameters, memory, FLOPs, tokens), analyzing them on major open- and closed-loop driving benchmarks (e.g., nuScenes, NAVSIM, Bench2Drive). We further trace how efficient methods from NLP/LLM are adapted in AD, identifying the constraints and motivations driving these adaptations. A continuously updated repository will be available at Github.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a survey/taxonomy of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving, with a focus on inference-time efficiency. It introduces the "Language Residue" taxonomy categorizing methods by when/where language is used at inference (L1: train-only supervision, L2: latent non-textual reasoning, L3: conditional invocation, L4: full per-frame generation), evaluates methods across five deployment axes (latency, parameters, memory, FLOPs, tokens) on major driving benchmarks, and traces how efficient NLP/LLM techniques are adapted for AD.
AI.motivation: While VLA models improve autonomous driving by unifying perception, reasoning, and control via language (enabling semantic grounding and better long-tail generalization), language is expensive at inference time—autoregressive decoding is inherently sequential and latency/memory budgets on-vehicle are tight. Since inference cost recurs at every deployed frame while training cost is paid only once, the authors argue the central question should shift to when and where language is used at inference, motivating a systematic taxonomy and efficiency analysis.
AI.method: The paper proposes the Language Residue taxonomy that classifies VLA-AD methods into four levels based on inference-time language usage: L1 (train-time-only supervision), L2 (latent non-textual reasoning), L3 (conditional invocation), and L4 (full per-frame generation). Representative methods are reviewed and tagged across five deployment axes (latency, parameters, memory, FLOPs, tokens) and analyzed on open- and closed-loop driving benchmarks such as nuScenes, NAVSIM, and Bench2Drive. The authors also trace adaptations of efficient NLP/LLM methods for AD.
AI.result: The taxonomy and analyses provide a structured framework for understanding the inference-efficiency trade-offs of different VLA approaches in AD. The paper maps representative methods onto the four language-residue levels, quantifies their costs across the five deployment axes, and characterizes how efficiency techniques from NLP/LLM have been adapted to the autonomous driving setting, identifying the specific constraints and motivations behind these adaptations.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by reframing VLA-based autonomous driving research around inference-time efficiency, arguing that the decision of when and where language acts at deployment is the crucial design choice. It positions the Language Residue taxonomy as a unifying organizing principle and points to a continuously updated GitHub repository for keeping pace with the rapidly evolving field.

title: Agentic AI uncovers conserved cross-tissue protein co-abundance programs inaccessible to single-dataset analysis
summary: Protein co-abundance clusters preserved across tissues can reveal shared disease mechanisms and candidate therapeutic targets, particularly when proteins implicated in organ-confined diseases converge in peripheral or accessible tissues. However, previous cross-tissue studies have focused on biologically pre-selected tissue pairs, leaving most possible combinations and non-obvious relationships unexplored. We present an LLM-agent framework for large-scale, evidence-grounded comparison of tissue-specific protein co-abundance networks. The framework constructs tissue networks, derives pairwise consensus clusters, and integrates evidence from expression atlases, protein interaction and complex databases, pathway annotations, disease catalogues, and literature. Applied to all 820 pairwise combinations of 41 human tissues and fluids, it identified 1,833 conserved co-abundance clusters across 406 tissue pairs. Colon, synovial fluid, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bone marrow were the most broadly connected tissues, while the most cluster-rich pairs were dominated by bone marrow. The analysis also highlighted non-obvious relationships: skin-bone marrow exceeded the anatomically adjacent bone-bone marrow pair, while colon-breast contained cancer-relevant clusters involving extracellular-matrix remodeling, lipid metabolism, and immune modulation. Cluster-level analyses generated further mechanistic hypotheses, including a brain-gut extracellular-vesicle/redox/serotonin-cofactor axis and a liver-bone marrow stress-response axis involving genes linked to white matter disease. These results provide a global, comparable landscape of conserved protein co-abundance and a hypothesis-generating resource for mechanistic and therapeutic exploration. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Gry1005/AgenticAI-conserved-cross-tissue-protein-co-abundance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-agent framework for large-scale cross-tissue comparison of protein co-abundance networks, applied to all 820 pairwise combinations of 41 human tissues and fluids, identifying 1,833 conserved co-abundance clusters across 406 tissue pairs and generating mechanistic hypotheses for shared disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
AI.motivation: Previous cross-tissue studies of protein co-abundance networks have been limited to biologically pre-selected tissue pairs, leaving most possible combinations and non-obvious relationships unexplored. A systematic, evidence-grounded comparison across all tissue pairs could reveal shared disease mechanisms and candidate therapeutic targets that converge in accessible tissues.
AI.method: The framework constructs tissue-specific protein co-abundance networks, derives pairwise consensus clusters across all 820 combinations of 41 human tissues and fluids, and integrates multi-source evidence including expression atlases, protein interaction and complex databases, pathway annotations, disease catalogues, and literature via an LLM-agent architecture. Cluster-level downstream analyses generate mechanistic hypotheses.
AI.result: Identified 1,833 conserved co-abundance clusters across 406 tissue pairs. Colon, synovial fluid, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bone marrow were the most broadly connected tissues, while bone marrow dominated cluster-rich pairs. Non-obvious relationships were highlighted (e.g., skin-bone marrow surpassing anatomically adjacent bone-bone marrow; colon-breast revealing cancer-relevant clusters). Mechanistic hypotheses included a brain-gut extracellular-vesicle/redox/serotonin-cofactor axis and a liver-bone marrow stress-response axis linked to white matter disease.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a global, comparable landscape of conserved protein co-abundance across human tissues and serves as a hypothesis-generating resource for mechanistic and therapeutic exploration. Code and data are publicly available.

title: Contrast-Free Autonomous Navigation of Untethered Endovascular Microrobots Using Single-Plane Fluoroscopy
summary: Reliable three-dimensional (3D) navigation of magnetically actuated untethered microrobots remains a major barrier to clinical translation. X-ray fluoroscopy is the standard real-time imaging modality for endovascular procedures, but single-plane fluoroscopy provides only a two-dimensional (2D) projection, eliminating depth information and complicating autonomous navigation. Recovering this information through biplane imaging or repeated contrast-enhanced angiography increases procedural complexity, radiation exposure, or contrast burden. Here, we introduce VISTA (Virtual Integration for Spatial Tracking and Autonomy), a digital twin framework enabling contrast-free autonomous navigation under single-plane fluoroscopy. VISTA reconstructs vascular anatomy as a 3D digital twin, discretizes the vessel centerline into navigation milestones, and assigns the detected 2D robot position to the nearest projected milestone. Consecutive milestones define the local vessel orientation used to generate magnetic actuation commands, converting single-plane fluoroscopic observations into topology-constrained navigation states without requiring contrast injection during navigation. VISTA is demonstrated across anatomically distinct vascular phantoms under continuous flow and within the inferior vena cava of a live rat in vivo. Compared with conventional fluoroscopic human-in-the-loop control, VISTA reduced navigation time by up to 62%, corrective actuation commands by up to 98%, and radiation exposure by up to 57%. These results establish VISTA as a digital twin-guided framework for contrast-free autonomous navigation of untethered endovascular microrobots using widely available single-plane fluoroscopy.

AI.tldr: VISTA is a digital twin framework that enables contrast-free autonomous navigation of magnetically actuated untethered microrobots under single-plane X-ray fluoroscopy by reconstructing 3D vascular anatomy, discretizing vessel centerlines into milestones, and mapping 2D robot detections onto projected milestones to generate topology-constrained magnetic actuation commands.
AI.motivation: 3D navigation of untethered microrobots is hindered by single-plane fluoroscopy providing only 2D projections without depth information. Biplane imaging or contrast-enhanced angiography adds complexity, radiation exposure, or contrast burden, presenting a major barrier to clinical translation.
AI.method: VISTA reconstructs vascular anatomy as a 3D digital twin, discretizes the vessel centerline into navigation milestones, and assigns the detected 2D robot position to the nearest projected milestone. Consecutive milestones define local vessel orientation to generate magnetic actuation commands, converting single-plane fluoroscopic observations into topology-constrained navigation states without contrast injection during navigation.
AI.result: VISTA was demonstrated across anatomically distinct vascular phantoms under continuous flow and in the inferior vena cava of a live rat in vivo. Compared to conventional fluoroscopic human-in-the-loop control, VISTA reduced navigation time by up to 62%, corrective actuation commands by up to 98%, and radiation exposure by up to 57%.
AI.conclusion: VISTA establishes a digital twin-guided framework for contrast-free autonomous navigation of untethered endovascular microrobots using widely available single-plane fluoroscopy, overcoming the depth information limitation of 2D imaging without requiring additional contrast or imaging modalities.

title: Verification abundance, adjudication scarcity: what happens to mathematical knowledge when proof checking becomes free
summary:
In May 2026 an OpenAI model produced a counterexample to the Erdős unit distance conjecture. Five mathematicians published a human-verified version the same day, and the result entered the literature within weeks. In August 2026 the same laboratory published ten mathematical and theoretical computer science results, each accompanied by a machine-checkable Lean 4 certificate with no unproved steps. Four weeks later, one remained the subject of an unresolved dispute over whether its formalization meant what it claimed.
  We argue that this difference is structural. We distinguish three layers of verification: derivational validity, which a kernel checks; representational fidelity, whether the formal statement means the intended question; and epistemic significance. Only the first is mechanizable. Making it effectively free therefore does not eliminate verification work but shifts the burden to layers dependent on scarce expert attention.
  Measurements of the August corpus illustrate the shift. The kernel-checked proofs total 20.6 MB, while the statements requiring human audit total 55.6 KB, a ratio of 379 to 1. Yet those statements contain 218 bespoke definitions rather than relying on community-vetted ones. The audit surface is therefore small in volume but irreducibly expert. We argue that machine checking produces verification abundance while leaving adjudication scarce. We propose a six-category taxonomy of representational mismatch, a disclosure schema for machine-generated mathematical claims, and implications for software, cryptography, and regulated decision systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a hypothetical future scenario where AI-generated mathematical results with machine-checkable Lean 4 certificates shift verification burden from derivational validity (mechanizable) to representational fidelity and epistemic significance (expert-dependent). It proposes a taxonomy and disclosure schema for machine-generated mathematical claims.
AI.motivation: The paper observes that AI-generated proofs with formal certificates create "verification abundance" while leaving "adjudication scarce"—the burden shifts from mechanical proof checking to expert judgment about whether formal statements mean what they claim.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the August 2026 corpus of ten AI-generated mathematical results, distinguishing three verification layers (derivational validity, representational fidelity, epistemic significance). It measures the corpus: kernel-checked proofs totaling 20.6 MB versus human-audited statements totaling 55.6 KB (379:1 ratio) containing 218 bespoke definitions, and proposes a six-category taxonomy of representational mismatch plus a disclosure schema.
AI.result: The audit surface is small in volume (55.6 KB) but irreducibly expert, with 218 bespoke definitions not relying on community-vetted ones. One of ten results remained disputed over interpretability of its formalization.
AI.conclusion: Machine checking produces verification abundance while adjudication remains scarce. The paper proposes a taxonomy of representational mismatch, a disclosure schema for machine-generated claims, and implications for software, cryptography, and regulated decision systems.

title: Optimized Modular Design and Development of a Tilt-Rotor Bicopter Drone
comment: 7 pages, conference, Index terms -Tilt-Rotor Bicopter Drone, Optimal Modular Design, Static Analysis, Dynamic Flight Analysis
summary: Hybrid systems like tilt-rotor bicopter drones combine the beneficial characteristics of both fixed-wing and rotary-wing technology, enabling long endurance and VTOL capability. However, such drones also require an optimum design to ensure both static and dynamic stability. The modular design of a traditional bicopter is developed in this paper based on extensive analysis and in-depth structural and aerodynamic simulations. The structural analysis has been performed to ensure that the aircraft's structure withstands the stresses encountered during different flight modes. Controlling the relative positions of the Center of Gravity (CG) and Neutral Point (NP) is an essential aspect of the design, ensuring stability during hover and positive stability during forward flight. The thrust and power analyses have been conducted to assess the flight performance and endurance. After analysis, the drone has been developed, and flight tests with a basic flight controller were conducted to validate the performance metrics obtained in the simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the modular design and development of a tilt-rotor bicopter drone, combining fixed-wing and rotary-wing benefits for long endurance and VTOL capability, validated through structural, aerodynamic, thrust/power analyses and flight tests.
AI.motivation: Hybrid UAVs like bicopters offer long endurance and VTOL capability, but they require careful design to ensure both static and dynamic stability across different flight modes.
AI.method: The approach involves a modular bicopter design supported by extensive structural analysis (to withstand stresses across flight modes), aerodynamic analysis controlling CG and NP positions for stability, and thrust/power analysis to assess flight performance and endurance.
AI.result: A physical drone was developed and flight-tested with a basic flight controller, validating the performance metrics obtained from simulations.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates a complete design-to-validation workflow for a tilt-rotor bicopter, confirming that simulation-based analyses can reliably predict real-world flight performance, ensuring both hover stability and positive forward-flight stability.

title: Multi-Step Forecasting of Grape Berry Temperature based on LSTM Model with Feed-Forward Attention
summary: Accurate forecasting of grape berry temperature (Tb) is essential for enabling timely heat stress management in vineyards. In this study, a feed-forward attention mechanism integrated with a Long Short-Term Memory network (FAM-LSTM) was developed and evaluated for multi-step, high-resolution Tb prediction. Models were trained using environmental data from 2023 and 2024 at Prosser, WA, USA, and validated on 2025 summer data. FAM-LSTM was benchmarked against LSTM, GRU, RNN, and Random Forest (RF) across horizons ranging from 15 minutes to 72 hours (288 time steps). Two input scenarios were evaluated: nearest open-field weather station observations and in-vineyard microclimate measurements. FAM-LSTM consistently outperformed all benchmark models across all horizons and input scenarios. Incorporating in-vineyard microclimate data significantly improved forecasting accuracy at longer horizons. Using open-field data, FAM-LSTM achieved MAE and RMSE ranges of 0.58 to 1.70 deg C and 0.65 to 2.07 deg C, respectively. In-vineyard observations further improved performance, with MAE and RMSE in the ranges of 0.51 to 1.55 deg C and 0.71 to 1.87 deg C. Error analysis showed prediction uncertainty was highest during peak daytime periods (11:00 to 18:00) and increased progressively with forecast horizon. Overall, the FAM-LSTM framework offers robust Tb forecasting to support precision heat stress management in vineyards.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FAM-LSTM, a feed-forward attention mechanism integrated with Long Short-Term Memory networks, for multi-step high-resolution grape berry temperature forecasting. Evaluated against LSTM, GRU, RNN, and Random Forest across horizons from 15 minutes to 72 hours using both open-field weather station and in-vineyard microclimate data, FAM-LSTM consistently outperformed all benchmarks, with in-vineyard data providing further improvements, particularly at longer horizons.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of grape berry temperature (Tb) is critical for enabling timely heat stress management in vineyards, yet existing forecasting approaches lack the precision and multi-step capability needed for practical viticultural decision-making.
AI.method: A feed-forward attention mechanism integrated with a Long Short-Term Memory network (FAM-LSTM) was developed for multi-step, high-resolution Tb prediction. Models were trained on environmental data from 2023-2024 at Prosser, WA, USA and validated on 2025 summer data. Two input scenarios were compared: nearest open-field weather station observations versus in-vineyard microclimate measurements, across horizons spanning 15 minutes to 72 hours (288 time steps).
AI.result: FAM-LSTM outperformed LSTM, GRU, RNN, and Random Forest across all horizons and input scenarios. With open-field data, MAE ranged from 0.58 to 1.70 deg C and RMSE from 0.65 to 2.07 deg C. With in-vineyard observations, MAE ranged from 0.51 to 1.55 deg C and RMSE from 0.71 to 1.87 deg C. Error analysis revealed highest prediction uncertainty during peak daytime periods (11:00-18:00) with error increasing progressively with forecast horizon.
AI.conclusion: The FAM-LSTM framework provides robust grape berry temperature forecasting and can support precision heat stress management in vineyards, with in-vineyard microclimate data significantly enhancing accuracy at longer forecast horizons.

title: Motus2: A Self-Evolving General World Model for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: General embodied agents should perceive, predict, act, evaluate, and improve within a unified system. World models have shown great promise in building such agents, yet existing models typically append an action output head to a world simulator, without coupling them into a closed decision-and-learning loop for policy improvement. We present Motus2, a self-evolving general world model for dexterous manipulation. Motus2 advances world modeling through model scaling and data scaling. For model scaling, a single model with shared weights exposes three control interfaces: a policy (world-action model), a simulator (action-conditioned world model), and an evaluator (value model). The policy proposes candidate action chunks, the simulator predicts their visual consequences, and the evaluator assesses the predicted outcomes. Their coupling forms a closed decision-and-learning loop for policy improvement. This formulation uses curated expert demonstrations for action learning, while failed and suboptimal interactions provide valuable evidence for dynamics modeling and value learning. For data scaling, Motus2 progresses from large-scale monocular egocentric data to synchronized stereo egocentric data, followed by robot-domain adaptation with robot trajectories and supplementary human-robot alignment data. Motus2 further studies global-autoregressive and hybrid-memory extensions of its sliding-window context, adds tactile feedback for contact-aware control, and is instantiated on a fully biomimetic platform with stereo vision, dual arms, dual dexterous hands, and tactile sensing. Together, egocentric data scaling and closed-loop general world model scaling provide a general path toward self-evolving dexterous manipulation.

AI.tldr: Motus2 is a self-evolving general world model for dexterous manipulation that unifies policy, simulator, and value functions in a single shared-weight model, forming a closed decision-and-learning loop. It advances via model scaling (three coupled control interfaces) and data scaling (from monocular egocentric to stereo egocentric data, robot-domain adaptation), and is instantiated on a biomimetic platform with stereo vision, dual arms/hands, and tactile sensing.
AI.motivation: Existing world models for embodied agents typically append an action output head to a world simulator without coupling them into a closed decision-and-learning loop for policy improvement. This limits the agent's ability to self-evolve through experience rather than relying solely on curated demonstrations.
AI.method: Motus2 uses a single shared-weight model exposing three control interfaces: a policy (world-action model) that proposes candidate action chunks, a simulator (action-conditioned world model) that predicts visual consequences, and an evaluator (value model) that assesses predicted outcomes—coupled into a closed decision-and-learning loop. It uses expert demonstrations for action learning and failed/suboptimal interactions for dynamics and value learning. It scales data from monocular to stereo egocentric data with robot-domain adaptation, and adds global-autoregressive/hybrid-memory context extensions, tactile feedback, and full biomimetic embodiment with stereo vision, dual arms, dual dexterous hands, and tactile sensing.
AI.result: Motus2 demonstrates that egocentric data scaling combined with closed-loop general world model scaling provides a general path toward self-evolving dexterous manipulation, enabling agents to learn from both successful demonstrations and failed/suboptimal experiences within a unified system.
AI.conclusion: The coupled policy-simulator-evaluator architecture within a single world model, together with scalable egocentric data pipelines, constitutes a general and promising approach for building self-evolving embodied agents capable of dexterous manipulation.

title: Frequency Selective Neural Networks as a Foundation Architecture for Time Series Learning
summary: Time-series data across physical and biological domains are fundamentally driven by complex, non-stationary oscillatory modes. While deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks, and Transformers, have dominated sequential analysis, they remain fundamentally "spectral-blind". By mapping continuous physical waves into unconstrained spatial or discrete token spaces, these architectures suffer from severe spectral entanglement, acting as opaque black boxes that decouple predictive accuracy from physical reality. In this paper, we introduce the Frequency Selective Neural Network (FSNN), pioneering a foundation architecture guaranteeing physical interpretability without sacrificing expressive power of deep learning. FSNN addresses spectral entanglement by explicitly embedding the rigorous mathematics of advanced signal processing into its neural topology. Through a fully differentiable Wiener-like filter bank optimized via complex-domain backpropagation, FSNN autonomously discovers and isolates the precise physical modes of a given task. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FSNN establishes state-of-the-art predictive performance, achieving $77.0\%$ average accuracy on the standard 10 multivariate UEA datasets and leading across all major metrics on the highly imbalanced PTB-XL clinical ECG benchmark. Crucially, in contrast to yielding abstract feature maps, FSNN converges directly on physically meaningful frequency bands, such as isolating the cardiac QRS complex, providing a highly scalable, interpretable paradigm for robust pattern recognition in complex temporal domains. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ad6174hhhh/FSNN.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Frequency Selective Neural Network (FSNN), a foundation architecture that addresses the "spectral blindness" of existing deep learning models (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) by explicitly embedding advanced signal processing mathematics into the neural topology via a fully differentiable Wiener-like filter bank trained with complex-domain backpropagation. FSNN achieves 77.0% average accuracy on 10 multivariate UEA datasets and leads on the PTB-XL clinical ECG benchmark, while converging on physically meaningful frequency bands such as the cardiac QRS complex.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning architectures for time-series analysis are "spectral-blind" — they map continuous physical waves into unconstrained spatial or discrete token spaces, causing spectral entanglement and acting as opaque black boxes that decouple predictive accuracy from physical reality. This separates model performance from physical interpretability.
AI.method: FSNN embeds rigorous signal processing mathematics into its neural topology through a fully differentiable Wiener-like filter bank trained via complex-domain backpropagation. This allows the network to autonomously discover and isolate the precise physical oscillatory modes of a given task, explicitly addressing spectral entanglement.
AI.result: FSNN achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance with 77.0% average accuracy on the standard 10 multivariate UEA datasets and leads across all major metrics on the highly imbalanced PTB-XL clinical ECG benchmark. The model converges on physically interpretable frequency bands, such as the cardiac QRS complex, rather than abstract feature maps.
AI.conclusion: FSNN provides a highly scalable, interpretable paradigm for robust pattern recognition in complex temporal domains, proving that physical interpretability and deep learning expressive power can coexist. It sets a foundation for spectral-aware neural architectures that align with physical reality.

title: CanonNav: Disentangling Navigation Behavior from Camera Geometry in Cross-Platform Visual Navigation
summary: While visual navigation has advanced through imitation learning from cross-platform demonstrations, fully leveraging such data remains challenging. First, directly learning from image-trajectory pairs entangles navigation behavior with platform-dependent camera geometry. This hinders consistent learning by forcing the policy to implicitly infer camera geometry from visual observations, an inherently ill-posed problem. Second, imitation learning from demonstrated trajectories captures the expert's chosen motion but leaves the intermediate decisions underlying that motion implicit. To address these issues, we propose CanonNav, a visual navigation framework that disentangles navigation behavior from camera geometry and incorporates complementary planning supervision into learning from cross-platform demonstrations. CanonNav introduces camera geometry canonicalization, which transforms visual observations and trajectories into a camera-consistent representation space. Building on this representation, we derive safety and local-progress supervision using pseudo-labels from an offline traversability estimator. Safety supervision penalizes unsafe trajectories, while local-progress supervision guides where the robot should advance. Experiments across diverse camera configurations and environments show that, despite using only RGB at inference, CanonNav consistently outperforms RGB-based baselines and even surpasses RGB-D-based methods in challenging scenarios.

AI.tldr: CanonNav is a visual navigation framework that addresses cross-platform imitation learning challenges by canonicalizing camera geometry and adding safety/local-progress supervision from pseudo-labels, outperforming RGB baselines and RGB-D methods despite using only RGB at inference.
AI.motivation: Visual navigation from cross-platform demonstrations is hindered by entangled camera geometry that forces ill-posed implicit inference, and demonstrated trajectories leave intermediate decision-making implicit.
AI.method: CanonNav disentangles navigation behavior from camera geometry via camera geometry canonicalization, transforming visual observations and trajectories into a camera-consistent space, then augments learning with safety supervision (penalizing unsafe trajectories from offline traversability pseudo-labels) and local-progress supervision (guiding where the robot should advance).
AI.result: Experiments across diverse camera configurations and environments show CanonNav consistently outperforms RGB-based baselines and surpasses RGB-D-based methods in challenging scenarios, using only RGB at inference.
AI.conclusion: Cross-platform visual navigation can be improved by decoupling camera geometry from behavior and injecting complementary planning supervision, achieving superior performance without requiring depth sensors at test time.

title: Disentangling Representation using Attributes-based Gaussian Estimation for Medical Sound Diagnosis
comment: 4 figures, 2 tables, code is available at: https://github.com/ZhaoKe1024/DisentangledRepr
summary: Deep learning has a powerful capability of feature extraction. However, the lack of fairness and interpretability in deep neural networks poses limitations to their adoption in the medical domain. This paper proposes a disentangled representation learning (DisenRL) framework, named the Attributes-based Gaussian Estimation for Disentangled Representation (AGEDR), which incorporates Attribute Mapping Embedding (AME) modules designed to map attributes into vectors and align them with a subset of the latent vectors in a Variational AutoEncoder (VAE). This part of the latent vector will be disentangled from the remaining latent vectors by minimizing mutual information. A classifier is then trained using the mean parameters of the latent vectors from the VAE. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AGEDR outperforms both conventional classification models and existing disentangled representation learning methods. The ablation experiments also indicate the disentangling capability and fairness of AGEDR. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZhaoKe1024/DisentangledRepr.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AGEDR, a disentangled representation learning framework that incorporates Attribute Mapping Embedding (AME) modules into a Variational AutoEncoder to map attributes into latent vectors and disentangle them from remaining latent representations via mutual information minimization, enabling fair and interpretable classification that outperforms conventional models and existing DisenRL methods in medical contexts.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks have powerful feature extraction capabilities but lack fairness and interpretability, which limits their adoption in the medical domain where transparency and equitable decision-making are critical.
AI.method: AGEDR (Attributes-based Gaussian Estimation for Disentangled Representation) is a disentangled representation learning framework that uses Attribute Mapping Embedding (AME) modules to map attributes into vectors aligned with a subset of latent vectors in a VAE. Mutual information is minimized to disentangle this attribute-correlated portion from the remaining latent vectors, and a classifier is trained on the mean parameters of the VAE latent vectors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show AGEDR outperforms both conventional classification models and existing disentangled representation learning methods. Ablation experiments further demonstrate the disentangling capability and fairness of the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: AGEDR effectively enhances fairness and interpretability in deep learning models for medical applications through attribute-guided disentangled representation learning, achieving superior classification performance while maintaining controllable and transparent latent representations.

title: CometVLA: Co-Training on an Embodied Data Pyramid towards Physical Understanding
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models remain brittle in manipulation tasks that require physical commonsense. Current physical VQA data is typically disembodied and misaligned with robot action domains. Egocentric videos are used only as auxiliary pre-training. It remains unclear whether improved VLM physical understanding actually benefits downstream action generation. Therefore, we present CometVLA to close this gap. We construct CometData and CometBench, an embodied physical VQA corpus and benchmark strictly aligned with the robot's action data and embodiment. We introduce Global Action Prior (GAP) tokens, a compact learnable bottleneck that isolates task-agnostic motion regularities and lets the action head consume physical commonsense without corrupting the pre-trained VLM backbone. We co-train CometVLA across the embodied data pyramid, spanning teleoperation, simulation, egocentric trajectories, and VQA layers. On real-world manipulation tasks and RoboTwin simulation, CometVLA consistently outperforms strong VLA baselines. Correlation analysis shows that stronger VLM performance on CometBench indicates higher VLA success rates. Results demonstrate that physical understanding pre-training genuinely benefits downstream manipulation.

AI.tldr: CometVLA bridges the gap between physical VQA and robot action learning by introducing an embodied physical VQA corpus/benchmark (CometData/CometBench) aligned with robot action domains, and a Global Action Prior (GAP) token mechanism that enables the action head to leverage physical commonsense without corrupting the VLM backbone, demonstrating that physical understanding pre-training genuinely improves downstream manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models are brittle in manipulation tasks requiring physical commonsense. Current physical VQA data is disembodied and misaligned with robot action domains, egocentric videos are used only as auxiliary pre-training, and it remains unclear whether improved VLM physical understanding actually benefits downstream action generation.
AI.method: The authors construct CometData and CometBench (an embodied physical VQA corpus and benchmark aligned with robot action data and embodiment), introduce Global Action Prior (GAP) tokens (a compact learnable bottleneck isolating task-agnostic motion regularities), and co-train CometVLA across teleoperation, simulation, egocentric trajectories, and VQA layers.
AI.result: CometVLA consistently outperforms strong VLA baselines on real-world manipulation tasks and RoboTwin simulation. Correlation analysis shows that stronger VLM performance on CometBench indicates higher VLA success rates.
AI.conclusion: Physical understanding pre-training genuinely benefits downstream manipulation, and the study provides both data/benchmark resources and an architectural mechanism (GAP tokens) for integrating physical commonsense into VLA models.

title: Facts Without Rules: Boundary Metadata Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems often coordinate by compressing an upstream interaction into a handoff artifact that downstream agents treat as shared state. We show that this handoff step is a structural source of privacy leakage: summaries preferentially preserve operational facts while weakening the boundary metadata that governs how those facts may be used---a failure mode we call \emph{summary collapse}. On a controlled multi-agent coordination testbed we measure marker survival with a human-validated judge ($κ= 0.74$), where $σ_b = 1$ means every boundary marker survives verbatim and $σ_b = 0$ means all are lost. Boundary-marker and operational-fact survival are nearly uncorrelated at the handoff level on both GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B (Pearson $r$ near zero): uncompressed free-text handoffs preserve boundaries at $σ_b \approx 0.80$, whereas a $25$-word budget drops $σ_b$ to ${\approx}0.57$ while operational-fact survival stays near ceiling. Controlled downstream tests reveal that protection depends on \emph{boundary explicitness}: vague languages leak in $73\%$ of GPT and $50\%$ of DeepSeek cases, while explicit constraints reduce leakage to under $15\%$ across all three tested models. A no-handoff single-agent control further shows the failure is not reducible to multi-agent topology as direct full-marker access still leaks more often than the operationalized handoff. Prompt-only mitigation and exact-string redaction only partially address the problem, while a gold-derived audience allowlist nearly eliminates leakage across models, showing that correctly identifying audience boundaries is the key factor.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "summary collapse"—a privacy failure mode in multi-agent LLM systems where handoff summaries disproportionately preserve operational facts while losing the boundary metadata that governs how those facts may be used. Measurements show boundary-marker and operational-fact survival are nearly uncorrelated (Pearson r near zero), compression drops boundary survival from σ_b≈0.80 to ≈0.57, and the key mitigation is correctly identifying audience boundaries (gold-derived allowlist nearly eliminates leakage) rather than prompt-only or exact-string-redaction fixes.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems coordinate by compressing upstream interactions into handoff artifacts treated as shared state. The authors posit that this handoff step is a structural source of privacy leakage, and seek to characterize and quantify the failure mode where summaries preserve facts but lose the boundary metadata governing usage permissions.
AI.method: The authors build a controlled multi-agent coordination testbed and measure marker survival using a human-validated judge (κ=0.74). They quantify boundary-marker survival (σ_b) vs operational-fact survival across two LLM backends (GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1-32B), test varying compression budgets (free-text vs 25-word), run controlled downstream leakage tests comparing vague vs explicit boundary language across three models, include a no-handoff single-agent control, and evaluate mitigations including prompt-only constraints, exact-string redaction, and a gold-derived audience allowlist.
AI.result: Boundary-marker and operational-fact survival are nearly uncorrelated at the handoff level (Pearson r near zero). Uncompressed free-text handoffs preserve boundaries at σ_b≈0.80, while a 25-word budget drops σ_b to ≈0.57 while operational-fact survival stays near ceiling. Vague language leaks in 73% of GPT and 50% of DeepSeek cases, while explicit constraints reduce leakage to under 15% across all three models. A single-agent control shows leakage is not reducible to multi-agent topology—direct full-marker access leaks more. Prompt-only and exact-string redaction partially help, but a gold-derived audience allowlist nearly eliminates leakage.
AI.conclusion: Summary collapse is a structural privacy failure in multi-agent LLM handoffs: summaries preferentially preserve operational facts while degrading boundary metadata. Correctly identifying audience boundaries (via allowlist mechanisms) is the key factor in controlling leakage, outperforming compression-based, prompt-based, and redaction-based mitigations.

title: Data-Centric Neuromotor Interfaces for Portable Human-Machine Interaction
summary: Dexterous human-machine interaction requires intuitive and expressive interfaces that can be efficiently deployed on constrained edge devices. Flexible material-based neuromotor interfaces hold considerable promise, as they decode human movement intention into natural control. Although emerging flexible electronic skins enable wearable high-fidelity data acquisition, practical deployment inevitably involves trade-offs between computational resources and portability. We present a data-centric paradigm where physiological features yield fundamental separability, providing sufficient discriminative cues for recognition. A wireless, high-bandwidth system developed for collecting various electrophysiological signals, when integrated with muscle-specific electrodes, forms a surface electromyography-based interface. Exploiting highly separable data, a 2,210-parameter model achieves 94.36% accuracy across 34 gestures and can be rapidly deployed on edge devices, establishing a new thousand-parameter benchmark for dexterous decoding. The underlying data-algorithm interactions in the data-centric paradigm are further clarified, demonstrating its feasibility in real-world scenarios. This study provides a principled and validated pathway for practical deployment of reliable neuromotor interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a data-centric paradigm for dexterous human-machine interaction using flexible material-based neuromotor interfaces. A wireless, high-bandwidth surface electromyography (sEMG) system collects physiological signals that exhibit fundamental separability, enabling a remarkably compact 2,210-parameter model to achieve 94.36% accuracy across 34 gestures, deployable on constrained edge devices—establishing a thousand-parameter benchmark for dexterous decoding.
AI.motivation: Dexterous human-machine interaction requires intuitive, expressive interfaces deployable on constrained edge devices. While flexible electronic skins enable high-fidelity wearable data acquisition, practical deployment faces trade-offs between computational resources and portability. The authors seek to overcome this by demonstrating that if physiological data is inherently separable, a dramatically small model can suffice for accurate gesture recognition.
AI.method: The authors adopt a data-centric paradigm, prioritizing data quality over model complexity. They develop a wireless, high-bandwidth system integrated with muscle-specific electrodes to form an sEMG-based neuromotor interface. The system collects multiple electrophysiological signals that exhibit fundamental separability, and the authors exploit this property with an extremely compact 2,210-parameter neural model for 34-gesture classification. They further analyze the data-algorithm interactions underlying this paradigm.
AI.result: The compact 2,210-parameter model achieves 94.36% accuracy across 34 gestures on the highly separable sEMG data, establishing a new thousand-parameter benchmark for dexterous decoding. The model is rapidly deployable on edge devices, and the data-algorithm interactions are clarified, demonstrating feasibility in real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The study validates a principled data-centric pathway for practical deployment of reliable neuromotor interfaces, showing that physiological feature separability can dramatically reduce model complexity without sacrificing decoding accuracy on constrained edge devices.

title: Learning to Follow In-Context Watermark Instructions via Self-Distillation
summary: In-context watermarking (ICW) prepends an instruction to a query asking the model to embed a statistically detectable signal in its response. It thus equips LLMs with a watermarking interface that third parties can invoke without access to model internals. Its reliability hinges on the LLM following the instruction without degrading answer quality, yet how well current LLMs do so has not been measured. We introduce $\mathsf{ICWBench}$, a benchmark of three verifiable ICW instruction families, each scored on both detectability and answer quality. Evaluating 14 frontier proprietary and open-source LLMs, we find that none of the evaluated LLMs achieves both objectives across all three families. To address this, we propose a self-contained two-stage training method, requiring no distillation from a stronger model, no manual annotation, and no pre-existing ICW IF ability. The first stage, self-distillation with logits perturbation (SDLP), uses the same base LLM as both teacher and student: an instruction-equivalent decoding-time logits perturbation makes the teacher follow the ICW instruction, and the student is trained to match the teacher's output distribution. The second stage applies reinforcement learning with the automatic verifier as the reward. Applied to Qwen3-14B and GPT-OSS-20B, our method raises average TPR@$1\%$FPR across three ICW instructions from $0.100$ to $0.974$ and from $0.337$ to $0.968$, respectively, while maintaining high response quality under both perplexity evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ICWBench, a benchmark for evaluating in-context watermarking (ICW) in LLMs across three verifiable instruction families, testing both detectability and answer quality. It finds that none of 14 evaluated LLMs achieves both objectives across all families, and proposes a two-stage training method (self-distillation with logits perturbation followed by reinforcement learning with an automatic verifier) that significantly improves watermark detectability on Qwen3-14B and GPT-OSS-20B while preserving response quality.
AI.motivation: In-context watermarking provides a watermarking interface that third parties can invoke without model internal access, but its reliability depends on the LLM following watermark instructions without degrading answer quality. This has not been systematically measured, motivating the need for a benchmark and a method to improve LLM ICW ability.
AI.method: The paper proposes ICWBench with three verifiable ICW instruction families scored on detectability and answer quality, evaluates 14 LLMs, and introduces a two-stage training approach: (1) Self-distillation with logits perturbation (SDLP) where the same base LLM acts as both teacher and student with instruction-equivalent decoding-time logits perturbation, and (2) reinforcement learning using the automatic verifier as reward.
AI.result: None of the 14 evaluated LLMs achieves both detectability and answer quality across all three ICW instruction families. Applying the proposed training to Qwen3-14B and GPT-OSS-20B raises average TPR@1%FPR from 0.100 to 0.974 and from 0.337 to 0.968 respectively, while maintaining high response quality under perplexity evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit insufficient in-context watermarking capability, but the proposed self-contained two-stage training method can substantially improve detectability without requiring distillation from stronger models, manual annotation, or pre-existing ICW instruction-following ability, all while preserving answer quality.

title: SpectraTac: A Compact Camera-Free Optical Tactile Sensor with Distributed Color Sensing
summary: Tactile sensing is essential for physical interaction in robotics and human--machine systems. However, combining rich tactile information with compact hardware, low cost, and low computational overhead remains challenging. This work presents SpectraTac, a compact, camera-free optical tactile sensor that combines active red--green--blue (RGB) illumination with spatially distributed color sensing. Contact deforms a compliant transparent elastomer and modulates its internal light field, producing spatially differentiated changes in color and intensity. Three distributed color sensors capture these responses as low-dimensional spatio-spectral features, avoiding cameras, imaging optics, and high-dimensional image processing. The device measures 19.2 mm in diameter and 4 mm in height, with a material cost below USD~5. A data-driven decoding framework simultaneously estimates three-dimensional (3D) force and the contact region from the optical measurements. For 3D force prediction, the sensor achieved mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 0.161, 0.164, and 0.429 N along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. The nine-region contact-classification accuracy was 99.9%. We further evaluated real-time 3D force tracking and contact-region-based human--machine interaction through an interactive control task. These results indicate that distributed color-resolved optical sensing offers a compact, low-cost alternative to camera-based tactile sensing for robotics, wearable sensing, and interactive systems.

AI.tldr: SpectraTac is a compact, camera-free optical tactile sensor (19.2 mm diameter, under USD $5) that uses RGB illumination and distributed color sensors to estimate 3D force and contact region, achieving MAEs of 0.161/0.164/0.429 N along x/y/z axes and 99.9% contact classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tactile sensing is critical for robotics and human-machine interaction, but existing solutions struggle to simultaneously achieve rich tactile information, compact hardware, low cost, and low computational overhead—particularly camera-based approaches which are bulky and computationally expensive.
AI.method: SpectraTac employs active RGB illumination with a compliant transparent elastomer that deforms under contact, modulating the internal light field. Three distributed color sensors capture low-dimensional spatio-spectral features without cameras or imaging optics. A data-driven decoding framework jointly estimates 3D force and contact region from these optical measurements.
AI.result: The sensor achieves 3D force prediction MAEs of 0.161 N (x), 0.164 N (y), and 0.429 N (z), plus 99.9% accuracy in nine-region contact classification. Real-time force tracking and contact-region-based human-machine interaction were demonstrated through an interactive control task.
AI.conclusion: Distributed color-resolved optical sensing provides a compact, low-cost, low-complexity alternative to camera-based tactile sensing, well-suited for robotics, wearable sensing, and interactive systems.

title: EmoLASP: Emotion Recognition with Language Models and Answer Set Programming
comment: 13 pages. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Emotion recognition in conversations is increasingly tackled with language models, but these models can be unstable and expensive to fine-tune or to prompt with long dialogue histories. We propose EmoLASP, a framework that combines a language model with declarative reasoning via Answer Set Programming (ASP) to predict VAD scores (Valence-Arousal-Dominance) in conversations. Experiments on a widely used benchmark dataset (IEMOCAP) across six open-source LLMs (3B-120B) and two PLMs (BERT, RoBERTa) show that EmoLASP improves prediction performance compared to using the language model alone, even when the LLMs/PLMs are given no dialogue history in their prompts or input vectors. The gains are largest for prompt-only LLMs, which EmoLASP uses without any fine-tuning. However, for fine-tuned PLMs, the reasoner adds little once dialogue history is available. EmoLASP's LLM pipeline demonstrates the potential advantages of using a reasoning approach to ensure emotion prediction consistency and to reduce both the cost of fine-tuning and the cost of prompting with long dialogue histories.

AI.tldr: EmoLASP combines language models with Answer Set Programming (ASP) declarative reasoning to predict Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) scores in conversational emotion recognition, improving performance across six LLMs and two PLMs on IEMOCAP without requiring dialogue history or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Language models used for emotion recognition in conversations are often unstable and expensive to fine-tune or prompt with long dialogue histories. There is a need for a more efficient and consistent approach that reduces computational cost while maintaining or improving prediction quality.
AI.method: EmoLASP integrates a language model with Answer Set Programming (ASP) for declarative reasoning to predict VAD scores in conversations. It is evaluated on the IEMOCAP benchmark across six open-source LLMs (3B-120B) and two PLMs (BERT, RoBERTa), comparing prediction performance with and without dialogue history in prompts or input vectors.
AI.result: EmoLASP improves VAD prediction performance over using language models alone across all tested models, even when LLMs/PLMs receive no dialogue history. The largest gains are achieved for prompt-only LLMs used without fine-tuning. However, for fine-tuned PLMs, the ASP reasoner adds marginal benefit once dialogue history is available.
AI.conclusion: The declarative reasoning approach in EmoLASP offers a cost-effective alternative to fine-tuning and long-context prompting for conversational emotion recognition, ensuring prediction consistency while reducing both fine-tuning and prompting costs. Its benefits are most pronounced for prompt-only LLM pipelines.

title: PAVE: Predictive Alignment and Value-Guided Evolution for World-Action Policies
summary: Direct vision-language-action policies generate continuous robot actions efficiently, but standard behavior cloning leaves two complementary gaps: their representations are not explicitly required to describe how the scene evolves over multiple time scales, and deployment trajectories of unequal quality are often reused without separating useful dynamics from undesirable behavior. We introduce \method, a direct world-action policy that combines outcome-agnostic predictive learning with outcome-aware policy improvement. \method first retains a local fixed-offset JEPA objective and adds trajectory-relative multi-horizon transition alignment at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the remaining episode. These training-only targets require the current policy representation to preserve both local physical changes and longer-range task progress, without supplying explicit future tokens to the action head. \method then trains an independent distributional value critic on cumulative deployment trajectories, computes action-chunk-aligned $N$-step advantages, and converts them into positive, negative, or null text conditions for a flow-matching actor. Thus, every valid trajectory can teach what physically happened, while the actor is deployed only under the condition associated with relatively better actions. The multi-horizon predictor and critic are removed from online execution, preserving direct action generation from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioception. \redclaim{Across the three simulation benchmarks, \method achieves the strongest overall performance while preserving the direct actor's online execution path.}

title: Let Prompts Bridge Defense Knowledge: Transferable Graph Purification via Vulnerability-Aware GPL
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26). 10 pages, 7 figures, and 4 tables. Shuomin Xue and Jingyuan Li contributed equally to this work
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a cornerstone for representing complex relational dependencies in diverse multimedia tasks, particularly in cross-platform user interest modeling and cross-modal semantic alignment. In the real world, a practical defense against graph adversarial perturbations is needed. However, we observe that the prevailing adversarial purification methods are essentially domain-restricted defenses, which leads to the following shortcomings: (1) single-domain data provides insufficient structural and semantic diversity for learning robust purification criteria; (2) training of domain-specific defense strategies from scratch consumes substantial computational cost. To address the above limitations, we propose a transferable graph purification scheme, named ProGAP, to bridge adversarial defense knowledge via vulnerability-aware graph prompt learning. Firstly, to capture universal adversarial patterns, a perturbation-capture edge detector is pretrained on data-rich graphs by jointly modeling topological and semantic information. Subsequently, to achieve more knowledge transfer w.r.t. robustness, vulnerability-aware prompts are designed that inject targeted purification guidance into biased nodes, during which the pretrained detector adapts to distribution shifts in downstream graphs without parameter-laborious updates. Experimental results demonstrate that compared with state-of-the-art baselines, our ProGAP achieves 1%-9% improvement, and reduces the time consumption by up to 2.2x. The code for ProGAP is available at https://github.com/Lieyoufffff/ProGAP.

AI.tldr: ProGAP is a transferable graph purification framework that uses vulnerability-aware graph prompt learning to bridge adversarial defense knowledge across domains, overcoming the limitations of domain-restricted defenses in GNNs for multimedia tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial purification methods for GNNs are domain-restricted, suffering from insufficient structural/semantic diversity in single-domain data for learning robust purification criteria, and incurring high computational costs when training domain-specific defenses from scratch.
AI.method: ProGAP pretrains a perturbation-capture edge detector on data-rich graphs by jointly modeling topological and semantic information to capture universal adversarial patterns. It then designs vulnerability-aware prompts that inject targeted purification guidance into biased nodes, allowing the pretrained detector to adapt to distribution shifts in downstream graphs without costly parameter updates.
AI.result: Experiments show ProGAP achieves 1%-9% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines and reduces time consumption by up to 2.2x.
AI.conclusion: ProGAP demonstrates that transferable graph purification via vulnerability-aware prompt learning effectively bridges adversarial defense knowledge across domains, achieving better robustness with significantly lower computational cost.

title: A Hybrid PEM-GP Framework for Uncertainty-Aware System Identification of Quadcopters
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. Published in International Journal of Control, Automation, and Systems, Vol. 24, No. 8, pp. 2047-2057, 2026
summary:
Accurate dynamic models play a central role in achieving reliable control of quadcopters. Classical system identification methods remain widely used, mainly because of their interpretability. However, they often fail to capture important nonlinear effects, especially in small-scale aerial platforms where such effects become more pronounced.
  Data-driven approaches offer a different perspective. They can represent complex nonlinear dynamics more effectively, but this comes at the cost of reduced interpretability and the absence of well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
  In this work, we propose a framework that combines physics-based modeling with data-driven learning, while explicitly accounting for uncertainty. A physics-based model is first identified using the Prediction Error Method (PEM), which captures the main structure of the system. The remaining dynamics are then modeled using a Gaussian Process (GP), allowing the residual behavior to be learned directly from data. This separation makes it possible to distinguish between known physical effects and unmodeled dynamics.
  The proposed framework is validated on a Duckiedrone-like experimental setup. The results show that the PEM-GP model achieves prediction accuracy comparable to that of a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, while additionally providing calibrated uncertainty estimates. This combination improves model reliability and supports uncertainty-aware decision-making.

AI.tldr: A hybrid PEM-GP framework combines physics-based system identification with Gaussian Process residual learning to model quadcopter dynamics, achieving LSTM-comparable prediction accuracy while providing calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: Classical system identification methods are interpretable but fail to capture nonlinear effects in small-scale quadcopters, while purely data-driven approaches represent complex dynamics well but lack interpretability and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.method: First identify a physics-based model using the Prediction Error Method (PEM) to capture the main system structure, then model the remaining residual dynamics using a Gaussian Process (GP) learned directly from data, enabling a clear separation between known physical effects and unmodeled dynamics.
AI.result: Validated on a Duckiedrone-like experimental setup, the PEM-GP model achieves prediction accuracy comparable to an LSTM network while additionally providing calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: The combination of physics-based modeling with data-driven residual learning improves model reliability and supports uncertainty-aware decision-making for quadcopter control.

title: Agent2UCB: Agentic System for Generative Engine Optimization
summary: Large language model driven search engines such as Google AI Overviews and Perplexity have created new opportunities for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) the practice of refining content to increase its likelihood of being cited or summarized by generative systems. We demonstrate Agent2UCB, an agentic GEO system that autonomously improves content visibility through customized, feedback-driven optimization. For each content item, the system evaluates nine GEO strategies, identifies the most effective method, and accelerates selection using a bandit-based Agent2UCB policy that integrates LLM priors with online reward signals. To monitor side effects, the system also provides a lightweight, text-only SEO readiness evaluation covering readability, topical coverage, and EEAT-style credibility. Experiments on GEO-Bench show consistent visibility gains while preserving SEO quality. The demo allows users to choose the websites of interest, observe the optimization workflow, and compare GEO/SEO outcomes across methods.

AI.tldr: Agent2UCB is an agentic Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) system that autonomously improves content visibility in LLM-driven search engines by evaluating nine GEO strategies, using a bandit-based UCB policy with LLM priors for efficient strategy selection, and providing a lightweight SEO readiness evaluation. Experiments on GEO-Bench demonstrate consistent visibility gains while preserving SEO quality.
AI.motivation: With the rise of LLM-driven search engines (e.g., Google AI Overviews, Perplexity), there is a new need to optimize content for citation by generative systems. Existing GEO methods lack autonomous, feedback-driven optimization that adapts strategy selection per content item while monitoring side effects on traditional SEO quality.
AI.method: Agent2UCB is an agentic GRO system that: (1) evaluates nine distinct GEO strategies for each content item; (2) identifies the most effective strategy via a bandit-based Agent2UCB policy that combines LLM priors with online reward signals for accelerated selection; (3) provides a lightweight, text-only SEO readiness evaluation covering readability, topical coverage, and EEAT-style credibility to monitor side effects.
AI.result: Experiments on GEO-Bench show consistent visibility gains across content while preserving SEO quality. A demonstration allows users to select websites of interest, observe the optimization workflow, and compare GEO/SEO outcomes across methods.
AI.conclusion: Agent2UCB demonstrates that autonomous, bandit-driven GEO optimization can effectively improve content visibility in generative search engines without degrading traditional SEO readiness, offering a practical and demonstrable framework for content creators.

title: Anomaly Detection on Small Industrial Components via Vision-Based Tactile Sensing
