summary: Automated inspection of small industrial components, including sub-centimetre-scale parts where defects are geometry-driven and poorly resolved by standard optical cameras, calls for sensing modalities that can directly capture fine surface geometry. Vision-based tactile sensors address this need by converting contact imprints into high-resolution image-like data compatible with existing deep-learning pipelines, yet their effective use for industrial anomaly detection (AD) remains largely unexplored. This work systematically evaluates unsupervised AD methods on a real tactile dataset covering five genuine industrial components acquired with a GelSight Mini sensor mounted on a collaborative robot. Four feature-embedding methods, SPADE, PaDiM, FAPM, and InReaCh, are compared under three validations explicitly motivated by the deployment constraints of contact-based sensing: a Good Fraction analysis establishing the minimum number of nominal contacts for stable performance, directly bounded by gel wear since every acquisition degrades the soft interface; a cross-position evaluation assessing generalization across different contact locations observing the same recurring surface pattern; and a low- versus high-resolution comparison evaluating the cost-benefit of higher-resolution tactile acquisition. Overall, this systematic benchmarking study provides practical guidance for researchers and practitioners adopting vision-based tactile sensing for industrial AD and shows how this modality can serve as a viable alternative for industrial quality-control tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically benchmarks unsupervised anomaly detection methods on real tactile sensing data from a GelSight Mini sensor mounted on a collaborative robot, evaluating four feature-embedding methods (SPADE, PaDiM, FAPM, InReaCh) on five genuine industrial components under three deployment-motivated validation scenarios.
AI.motivation: Small industrial components with sub-centimetre-scale, geometry-driven defects are poorly resolved by standard optical cameras, and although vision-based tactile sensors can capture fine surface geometry as image-like data, their use for industrial anomaly detection remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Four unsupervised feature-embedding AD methods (SPADE, PaDiM, FAPM, InReaCh) are compared on a real tactile dataset of five industrial components acquired with a GelSight Mini on a collaborative robot. Three validation scenarios are used: (1) Good Fraction analysis for minimum nominal contacts needed, bounded by gel wear; (2) cross-position evaluation for generalization across contact locations observing the same recurring surface pattern; (3) low- versus high-resolution evaluation of the cost-benefit of higher-resolution tactile acquisition.
AI.result: The systematic benchmarking provides practical guidance for deploying vision-based tactile sensing in industrial AD, demonstrating that this modality serves as a viable alternative for industrial quality-control tasks across the evaluated methods and validation settings.
AI.conclusion: Vision-based tactile sensing with unsupervised AD methods offers a viable alternative for industrial quality-control tasks, particularly for small components with geometry-driven defects, and the study establishes practical deployment guidelines regarding contact budget, generalization across positions, and resolution trade-offs.

title: Revolutionizing Turn-by-Turn Navigation with Cloud-Edge Deep Learning
comment: This paper has accepted by IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
summary: Turn-by-turn (TBT) navigation systems are integral to modern driving experiences, providing real-time audio instructions to guide drivers safely to destinations. However, existing audio instruction policy often relies on rule-based approaches that struggle to balance informational content with cognitive load, potentially leading to driver confusion or missed turns in complex environments. To overcome these difficulties, we first model the generation of navigation instructions as a multi-task learning problem by decomposing the audio content into combinations of modular elements. Then, we propose a novel deep learning framework that leverages the powerful spatiotemporal information processing capabilities of Transformers and the strong multi-task learning abilities of Mixture of Experts (MoE) to generate real-time, context-aware audio instructions for TBT driving navigation. A cloud-edge collaborative architecture is implemented to handle the computational demands of the model, ensuring scalability and real-time performance for practical applications. Experimental results in the real world demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the yaw rate (the proportion of vehicles deviating from navigation routes) compared to traditional methods, delivering clearer and more effective audio instructions. This is the first large-scale application of deep learning in driving audio navigation, marking a substantial advancement in intelligent transportation and driving assistance technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first large-scale deep learning framework for turn-by-turn driving navigation audio instruction generation, combining Transformers with Mixture of Experts (MoE) to produce real-time, context-aware audio instructions. The approach models instruction generation as multi-task learning over modular audio elements and employs a cloud-edge collaborative architecture for scalability, achieving significant reductions in driver route deviation (yaw rate) compared to rule-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing rule-based audio instruction policies for TBT navigation struggle to balance informational content with cognitive load, leading to driver confusion or missed turns, particularly in complex driving environments. There is a need for a data-driven approach that can generate adaptive, context-aware instructions in real time.
AI.method: The paper (1) frames navigation instruction generation as a multi-task learning problem by decomposing audio content into modular elements; (2) proposes a deep learning framework combining Transformers for spatiotemporal information processing with Mixture of Experts (MoE) for multi-task learning; (3) implements a cloud-edge collaborative architecture to manage computational demands while ensuring real-time performance; (4) validates the system in real-world driving scenarios.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show the proposed method significantly reduces the yaw rate (proportion of vehicles deviating from navigation routes) compared to traditional rule-based methods, delivering clearer and more effective audio instructions for drivers.
AI.conclusion: This work marks the first large-scale deployment of deep learning in driving audio navigation, demonstrating a substantial advancement in intelligent transportation and driving assistance technologies, with potential to improve driver safety and navigation accuracy in complex environments.

title: Behavior-Skill: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Reliable execution of long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks remains challenging because overall task success depends on the successful completion of multiple constituent skills. Existing benchmarks, however, still rely primarily on full-task rollouts and aggregate task-level metrics, making intermediate failures difficult to observe and analyze. We present Behavior-Skill, a benchmark that reformulates the learning and evaluation of long-horizon tasks around executable constituent skills. It contains 235,492 skill instances from 10,000 demonstrations across 50 household tasks and 34 semantic skill categories. Each instance pairs a skill instruction with an aligned observation-action segment, and is further associated with a restorable intermediate state and a skill success condition to enable independent evaluation under valid preconditions. We further introduce trajectory-level and skill-level metrics to characterize policy capability beyond aggregate task success. Extensive experiments across representative VLA policies including pi0.5 and GR00T on the complete 50-task benchmark show that failures are highly non-uniform across skills, with contact-rich manipulation skills forming persistent bottlenecks. These results demonstrate that Behavior-Skill complements full-task evaluation by exposing intermediate capability profiles for analyzing and improving long-horizon VLA policies. Behavior-Skill is publicly available at https://github.com/nubot-nudt/Behavior-Skill.

AI.tldr: Behavior-Skill is a benchmark that reformulates long-horizon mobile manipulation task evaluation around executable constituent skills, containing 235,492 skill instances from 10,000 demonstrations across 50 household tasks and 34 semantic skill categories, with restorable states and success conditions for independent evaluation, plus trajectory-level and skill-level metrics. Experiments on VLA policies (pi0.5, GR00T) reveal highly non-uniform failures with contact-rich manipulation skills as persistent bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon mobile manipulation task success depends on multiple constituent skills, but existing benchmarks rely on full-task rollouts and aggregate task-level metrics, making intermediate failures difficult to observe and analyze.
AI.method: The benchmark decomposes long-horizon tasks into executable constituent skills, providing skill instances paired with instructions and aligned observation-action segments, restorable intermediate states, and skill success conditions for independent evaluation. It also introduces trajectory-level and skill-level evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Evaluation of VLA policies (pi0.5 and GR00T) across the full 50-task benchmark shows failures are highly non-uniform across skills, with contact-rich manipulation skills being persistent bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-Skill complements full-task evaluation by exposing intermediate capability profiles, enabling finer-grained analysis and improvement of long-horizon VLA policies.

title: Nested Convex-Body Chasing for Online Optimization with Evolving Feasible Sets
summary:
We study online optimization with nested shrinking feasible regions in two settings: convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets (CONES) and adversarial constrained online convex optimization (COCO). Our algorithms separate loss control from geometric movement: constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests preserve regret guarantees, while a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser limits movement.
  For CONES with a $G$-Lipschitz, $μ$-strongly convex objective on a diameter-$D$ domain, we chase intersections of the current feasible set with adaptive objective sublevel sets. Using the Euclidean chasing ratio $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)})$, we obtain nonpositive regret at every prefix and movement $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)\,GD\log(eT)/μ})$. The bound adapts to the increase in the constrained optimum value. In dimension two, with all other parameters fixed, every randomized algorithm with terminal expected regret $O(T^β)$, $β<1$, suffers $Ω(\sqrt{\log T})$ expected movement on some deterministic nested sequence, proving optimal horizon dependence. Under linear growth away from the constrained minimizer set, Steiner-point tracking yields movement independent of $T$.
  For general convex COCO, one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets gives regret $O(G_fD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$ and cumulative constraint violation $O(G_gD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$. For strongly convex losses, both are $O(d\log(1+d)\log(eT))$ when other parameters are fixed. These reductions replace the $O(d^{d/2})$ projection-path factor in prior analyses by the polynomial dimension dependence of Euclidean nested convex-body chasing.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online optimization with nested shrinking feasible regions in two settings: convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets (CONES) and adversarial constrained online convex optimization (COCO). The key idea is to decouple loss control from geometric movement using constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests, while a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser handles movement. The results achieve nonpositive regret with movement bounds scaling polynomially in dimension (via Euclidean chasing ratio O(√(d log(1+d)))), replacing the previous exponential O(d^(d/2)) projection-path factor in prior analyses. Lower bounds confirm optimal horizon dependence in dimension two.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of online optimization where feasible regions shrink over time (nested sets), requiring algorithms to balance regret guarantees against excessive movement between shrinking feasible sets—a problem where previous analyses had exponential dimension dependence due to costly projection paths.
AI.method: The algorithms separate loss control from geometric movement: (1) constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests preserve regret guarantees; (2) a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser limits movement using Euclidean nested convex-body chasing with ratio O(√(d log(1+d))). For CONES, the algorithm chases intersections of current feasible sets with adaptive objective sublevel sets. For COCO, one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets is employed.
AI.result: For CONES: nonpositive regret at every prefix with movement O(√(d log(1+d) GD log(eT)/μ)). In dimension two, any randomized algorithm with terminal expected regret O(T^β), β<1, suffers Ω(√(log T)) expected movement—proving optimal horizon dependence. Under linear growth conditions, movement becomes independent of T via Steiner-point tracking. For COCO: regret and cumulative constraint violation both O(G_fD√(d log(1+d) T)) for general convex losses, and O(d log(1+d) log(eT)) for strongly convex losses. These replace the O(d^(d/2)) projection-path factor with polynomial dimension dependence.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that decoupling movement control from loss optimization via nested convex-body chasing achieves near-optimal regret and movement trade-offs with polynomial dimension dependence, replacing exponential projection-path factors in prior work. Lower bounds in dimension two confirm the horizon dependence is optimal, and structural assumptions (linear growth) can eliminate T-dependence entirely.

title: Temporal Forcing: 4D Representation Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) methods improve manipulation performance by aligning their representations with 3D scene geometry. However, these methods often struggle with long-horizon manipulation and observation aliasing between visually similar states due to a lack of temporal information: the 3D scene geometry captures only the current state, rather than how it has evolved over time. To resolve this, we present Temporal Forcing, a 4D representation alignment method for VLA models. Specifically, we first introduce a history pathway that enables a vanilla VLA model to summarize observation history into temporally aware latent representations. Then, the latent representations are aligned with the geometric features extracted by a pretrained 4D foundation model, which captures the evolving 3D world through temporally consistent geometric representations, enabling a deeper understanding of dynamic environments. Temporal Forcing reaches 98.8% on LIBERO, outperforming its base model by 2.2 points. On a physical hidden-placement task, it raises full-task success from 20.0% to 43.3%. Code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: Temporal Forcing is a 4D representation alignment method for vision-language-action (VLA) models that introduces a history pathway to summarize observation history into temporally aware latent representations, then aligns them with geometric features from a pretrained 4D foundation model to capture evolving 3D world dynamics, achieving 98.8% on LIBERO and improving physical task success from 20.0% to 43.3%.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA methods align representations with 3D scene geometry but fail to capture temporal information, leading to struggles with long-horizon manipulation and observation aliasing between visually similar states, since 3D scene geometry only captures the current state rather than how it has evolved over time.
AI.method: Temporal Forcing first introduces a history pathway enabling a vanilla VLA model to summarize observation history into temporally aware latent representations. These latent representations are then aligned with geometric features extracted by a pretrained 4D foundation model, which captures the evolving 3D world through temporally consistent geometric representations.
AI.result: Temporal Forcing reaches 98.8% on LIBERO, outperforming its base model by 2.2 points. On a physical hidden-placement task, it raises full-task success from 20.0% to 43.3%.
AI.conclusion: Injecting temporal information via 4D representation alignment significantly improves VLA models' performance on long-horizon manipulation tasks and mitigates observation aliasing, demonstrating the value of integrating temporal dynamics into VLA frameworks.

title: HANIA: Planner-Guided Multimodal Graph Evidence Selection for Grounded Question Answering
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at Graph-enhanced LLMs for trustwOrthy Web data management (GLOW), ISWC 2026 Workshops, Bari, Italy
summary: Multimodal question answering remains sensitive to noisy, incomplete, and weakly grounded evidence. Long unstructured contexts can introduce redundancy and encourage unsupported generation, while flat retrieval may overlook relations needed for multi-step reasoning. We present HANIA, a planner-guided multimodal graph framework for evidence-grounded question answering. HANIA processes the supplied image and text using a frozen vision-language model to extract concise question-relevant visual evidence with explicit abstention. It then constructs an input-grounded multimodal graph and applies a two-group finite-state planner to coordinate descriptive and relational evidence. Coverage-aware pruning retains a compact evidence set based on relevance, graph confidence, concept coverage, and modality diversity. The selected passages, visual statements, and graph triples are provided to a frozen instruction-tuned decoder. We evaluate HANIA on ScienceQA using answer accuracy, evidence-filtering quality, evidence-budget sensitivity, and efficiency. The results show that structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval can support competitive multimodal question answering without target-dataset fine-tuning or iterative retrieval. The code is available at https://github.com/Zafar-southeast/HANIA.

AI.tldr: HANIA is a planner-guided multimodal graph framework for evidence-grounded question answering that extracts concise visual evidence, constructs a multimodal graph, applies a two-group finite-state planner, and uses coverage-aware pruning to select compact evidence for a frozen decoder, achieving competitive results on ScienceQA without fine-tuning or iterative retrieval.
AI.motivation: Multimodal question answering suffers from noisy, incomplete, and weakly grounded evidence. Long unstructured contexts introduce redundancy and encourage unsupported generation, while flat retrieval fails to capture relations needed for multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: HANIA processes images and text via a frozen vision-language model to extract concise, question-relevant visual evidence with explicit abstention. It constructs an input-grounded multimodal graph and applies a two-group finite-state planner to coordinate descriptive and relational evidence. Coverage-aware pruning retains a compact evidence set based on relevance, graph confidence, concept coverage, and modality diversity. Selected passages, visual statements, and graph triples are fed to a frozen instruction-tuned decoder.
AI.result: Evaluated on ScienceQA across answer accuracy, evidence-filtering quality, evidence-budget sensitivity, and efficiency. Results show structured evidence planning and compact graph-guided retrieval support competitive multimodal QA without target-dataset fine-tuning or iterative retrieval.
AI.conclusion: HANIA demonstrates that structured evidence planning combined with compact graph-guided retrieval can serve as an effective alternative to fine-tuned or iterative retrieval approaches for evidence-grounded multimodal question answering.

title: CIG-RL: Curiosity-Driven Information-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Source Term Estimation in Uncertain Environments
summary: Source term estimation (STE), which aims to estimate key properties of the gas source, is essential for identifying hazardous gas releases. Information-theoretic approaches have been adopted for autonomous STE using mobile sensors due to robustness in noisy environments, yet their online action selection incurs substantial computational cost. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) provides a promising alternative with its fast decision-making capability. In DRL-based STE, the agent selects actions based on belief states of the source term updated from noisy measurement sequences. However, existing methods rely on random exploration or solely on belief uncertainty reduction without an effective exploration strategy in DRL, which can limit policy robustness in noisy environments. To address this, we propose a curiosity-driven information-guided reinforcement learning for robust and efficient STE. The proposed method promotes active exploration of novel belief state transitions that have not been sufficiently explored during training. We further introduce an uncertainty-adaptive active perception reward to guide efficient source search under uncertainty. Simulations under high-noise conditions and real-world experiments demonstrate the robustness and feasibility of the proposed framework, highlighting its potential for practical STE problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a curiosity-driven information-guided reinforcement learning framework for source term estimation (STE) using mobile sensors. It enhances DRL-based STE by promoting active exploration of novel belief state transitions and introduces an uncertainty-adaptive active perception reward for efficient source search under noisy conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing DRL-based STE methods rely on random exploration or solely on belief uncertainty reduction without effective exploration strategies, which limits policy robustness in noisy environments. Information-theoretic approaches are robust but computationally expensive for online action selection.
AI.method: The proposed method integrates curiosity-driven exploration into DRL for STE, which encourages the agent to actively explore novel belief state transitions not sufficiently encountered during training. Additionally, an uncertainty-adaptive active perception reward is designed to guide efficient source search under uncertainty, balancing exploration and exploitation in high-noise conditions.
AI.result: Simulations under high-noise conditions and real-world experiments demonstrate the robustness and feasibility of the proposed framework for practical STE problems.
AI.conclusion: The curiosity-driven information-guided reinforcement learning framework shows strong potential for robust and efficient autonomous STE in real-world hazardous gas release scenarios, addressing the exploration limitation of existing DRL-based methods.

title: EviAnchor: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Regional Visual Evidence Compensation
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) frequently generate content unsupported by visual inputs. Preliminary experiments show that visual evidence is primarily incorporated into answer-side representations in early-to-middle decoder layers, while its direct influence progressively weakens in later layers. This attenuation suggests that visual evidence acquired earlier may be insufficiently utilized during subsequent generation. Based on this observation, we propose EviAnchor, a training-free and single-branch inference framework that preserves and reactivates visual evidence throughout generation. EviAnchor introduces Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots to progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially structured representations. It then strengthens the current decision state's access to these visual anchors through decision-conditioned evidence routing, mitigating excessive dependence on textual context. Finally, the model resumes its native Transformer computation to integrate the retrieved visual evidence with question semantics and generation history. Experiments across POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in visual grounding.

AI.tldr: EviAnchor is a training-free, single-branch inference framework for LVLMs that preserves and reactivates visual evidence throughout generation by introducing Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots and decision-conditioned evidence routing, improving visual grounding on POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LVLMs frequently generate hallucinated content unsupported by visual inputs. Preliminary analysis reveals that visual evidence enters answer-side representations mainly in early-to-middle decoder layers, with its influence weakening in later layers—meaning visual evidence acquired earlier is insufficiently utilized during subsequent generation.
AI.method: EviAnchor introduces Regional Evidence Anchor (REA) slots that progressively aggregate dense visual tokens into spatially structured representations, strengthens the current decision state's access to these visual anchors via decision-conditioned evidence routing to mitigate over-reliance on textual context, and resumes native Transformer computation to integrate retrieved visual evidence with question semantics and generation history.
AI.result: Experiments across POPE, CHAIR, and MMHal-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in visual grounding, indicating reduced hallucination.
AI.conclusion: EviAnchor effectively mitigates hallucination by ensuring visual evidence remains accessible and active throughout the entire generation process, without requiring any training or architectural changes to the base LVLM.

title: Learning to infer and manipulate through distributed whole-arm interaction in a soft robot
summary:
In animals such as elephants and octopuses, acquiring non-visual information about an object and physically engaging with it are inseparable processes mediated by rich, large-area interactions between compliant appendages and the environment. Soft robots provide a natural platform for translating this principle into engineered systems. Yet current robotic intelligence makes limited use of physical interaction, treating it primarily as a disturbance to be rejected or, at best, as a means of compensating for object misalignment.
  Here, we introduce a physical intelligence framework in which distributed compliant interactions jointly reveal task-relevant information and organize manipulation behavior. This results in an intrinsically partially observable problem: key task-relevant information is never measured directly, but must instead be inferred from the history of physical interactions. We propose a reinforcement-learning architecture that addresses this challenge by learning a memory-based control policy end-to-end. The key innovations making this possible are (i) a pretrained exploration policy that provides a reference for broad workspace exploration, (ii) joint optimization that integrates exploration and grasping objectives within a single recurrent policy, and (iii) a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation including observation mapping and policy fine-tuning.
  We demonstrate this principle through blind whole-arm grasping with a hybrid rigid-soft robotic arm that we equip with IMUs embedded directly within its compliant structure, providing its only source of proprioceptive sensing. The learned policy successfully identifies and grasps various objects by autonomously coordinating workspace exploration, object encounter and localization, inference of grasp-relevant properties, and stable whole-arm wrapping.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a physical intelligence framework for soft robotics where distributed compliant interactions simultaneously enable perception and manipulation, treating the problem as partially observable and solved via a memory-based reinforcement learning policy with pretrained exploration, joint optimization of exploration and grasping, and a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation. Demonstrated through blind whole-arm grasping using a hybrid rigid-soft robotic arm with embedded IMUs as the sole proprioceptive sensing modality.
AI.motivation: Current robotic intelligence treats physical interaction primarily as a disturbance to reject or as compensation for object misalignment, failing to exploit the rich, large-area compliant interactions that biological systems (e.g., elephants, octopuses) use to both perceive and manipulate objects simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a physical intelligence framework where distributed compliant interactions jointly reveal task-relevant information and organize manipulation, (2) a memory-based reinforcement-learning policy learned end-to-end for the intrinsically partially observable problem, enabled by (i) a pretrained exploration policy for workspace coverage, (ii) joint optimization of exploration and grasping within a single recurrent policy, and (iii) a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation pipeline with observation mapping and policy fine-tuning. The hardware platform is a hybrid rigid-soft arm with embedded IMUs as the only proprioceptive sensing source.
AI.result: The learned policy successfully identifies and grasps various objects by autonomously coordinating workspace exploration, object encounter and localization, inference of grasp-relevant properties, and stable whole-arm wrapping—all using only IMU-based proprioceptive feedback from the compliant structure.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that physical interaction itself can serve as a rich sensing modality in soft robotics, and that a memory-based recurrent policy trained with joint exploration and grasping optimization can solve the resulting partially observable control problem entirely through proprioceptive feedback, paving the way for more embodied forms of robotic intelligence.

title: SafeAtlas-VL: Beyond Binary Multimodal Safety with Large-Scale Data and Guard Models
summary: Multimodal safety moderation requires distinguishing risks arising from visual content, user intent, and assistant behavior. Existing safeguards, however, are typically trained for a single judgment target and reduce safety assessment to a binary decision. Consequently, risk becomes difficult to compare across a multimodal interaction, and ambiguous cases are obscured. We introduce SafeAtlas-VL, a dataset of 1.5M training instances that places image-, request-, and response-level judgments on a five-level ordered scale. We curate a broad collection of safety-relevant data from both real-world and synthetic sources and apply a disagreement-aware annotation procedure. The resulting dataset spans 15 harm categories and 55 fine-grained subcategories, covering a broad range of multimodal safety scenarios. We also construct SafeAtlas-Bench, a held-out set of 5,000 instances for evaluating five-level predictions and continuous risk scores. Upon this dataset, we train the SafeAtlas Guard series of models via target-conditioned tuning for multimodal safety detection. Our models not only perform five-way classification of safety levels but also map safety to continuous scores through a soft cumulative ordinal head. Experimental results demonstrate that guard models trained on our dataset exhibit strong generalization: even without using the training sets of other benchmarks, they achieve competitive performance on the corresponding test sets. Notably, our 8B model attains the overall best performance, outperforming the previous SOTA by approximately 4% in F1 score. Code, data, and models are released to support further research. Warning: this paper contains example data that may be offensive, harmful, graphic, or disturbing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SafeAtlas-VL, a large-scale multimodal safety dataset with 1.5M training instances that rate image-, request-, and response-level safety on a five-level ordinal scale across 15 harm categories and 55 subcategories. It also presents SafeAtlas-Bench (5,000 held-out instances) and the SafeAtlas Guard model series trained via target-conditioned tuning with a soft cumulative ordinal head for continuous risk scoring. The 8B model outperforms prior SOTA by ~4% F1, generalizing without using other benchmarks' training sets.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal safety safeguards are limited to binary decisions trained for a single judgment target, making it difficult to compare risks across different aspects of a multimodal interaction (image, request, response) and obscuring ambiguous safety cases. A finer-grained, multi-target, ordered safety assessment framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors curate a broad collection of safety-relevant data from real-world and synthetic sources, apply a disagreement-aware annotation procedure, and construct SafeAtlas-VL with 1.5M training instances containing image-, request-, and response-level judgments on a five-level ordered scale spanning 15 harm categories and 55 subcategories. They also build SafeAtlas-Bench, a 5,000-instance held-out evaluation set for five-level predictions and continuous risk scores. Models are trained via target-conditioned tuning with a soft cumulative ordinal head that enables both five-way classification and continuous risk scoring.
AI.result: The SafeAtlas Guard models demonstrate strong generalization: even without using the training sets of other benchmarks, they achieve competitive performance on corresponding test sets. The 8B model achieves the overall best performance, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art by approximately 4% in F1 score.
AI.conclusion: SafeAtlas-VL and the SafeAtlas Guard models enable more nuanced, multi-target, ordinal multimodal safety assessment. The released code, data, and models support further research in this direction, with the caveat that the dataset contains potentially offensive or disturbing example content.

title: A Dual-Cam Parallel Elastic Actuator with Shared Gas-Spring Compensation for Humanoid Ankles
comment: Accepted to IEEE AIM 2026. Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted
summary: To improve torque capacity and energy efficiency of humanoid ankles, this paper proposes a 2-DoF parallel elastic actuator (PEA). The main novelty of the proposed design lies in its dual-cam, single-gas-spring architecture, which enables torque compensation in both pitch and roll using a shared elastic element, thereby improving structural compactness compared with conventional multi-element compensation schemes. By leveraging parallel gas springs and customized cam modules, the proposed architecture provides dual-axis torque assistance tailored to specific task requirements. The second key contribution is the formulation of a coupled 2-DoF mathematical model that explicitly captures the interdependence between the two compensation units through the shared spring. Based on this model, an optimization-based design framework is developed to synthesize customized cam profiles from prescribed torque references, establishing a systematic link from task requirements to hardware realization. The complete lower-leg CAD integration is presented in detail. Static FEA and kinematic simulations confirm the design's feasibility and torque-relief effectiveness. The results highlight the proposed design as a compact, customizable solution for 2-DoF humanoid ankle torque compensation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a 2-DoF parallel elastic actuator (PEA) for humanoid ankles featuring a dual-cam, single-gas-spring architecture that enables torque compensation in both pitch and roll using one shared elastic element. A coupled 2-DoF mathematical model and optimization-based cam profile synthesis are developed, with FEA and kinematic simulations confirming feasibility and torque-relief effectiveness.
AI.motivation: To improve torque capacity and energy efficiency of humanoid ankles by overcoming the drawbacks of conventional multi-element compensation schemes, which suffer from structural bulkiness. The paper seeks a compact, customizable solution for dual-axis ankle torque compensation.
AI.method: (1) A dual-cam, single-gas-spring PEA architecture providing pitch and roll torque compensation via a shared elastic element; (2) a coupled 2-DoF mathematical model capturing the interdependence between compensation units through the shared spring; (3) an optimization-based design framework for synthesizing customized cam profiles from prescribed torque references; (4) full lower-leg CAD integration, validated by static FEA and kinematic simulations.
AI.result: Static FEA and kinematic simulations confirm the design's feasibility and torque-relief effectiveness. The results demonstrate a compact, customizable solution for 2-DoF humanoid ankle torque compensation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-cam, single-gas-spring PEA offers a compact, task-tailored approach to 2-DoF humanoid ankle torque compensation, with a systematic pipeline from torque requirements to hardware realization via cam profile optimization.

title: Clustering as Approximation by Constrained Projectors: Theory and Guarantees
summary: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework showing that a broad family of clustering methods, including k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel k-means, kernel FCM, and spectral clustering, can all be expressed as structured low-rank projectors acting on a signal-derived matrix. By formulating each method as an instance of min over B in C of ||M - M P_B||_F^2, with different constraint sets C, we establish a common optimization template that clarifies the algebraic links among hard, fuzzy, kernel-induced, and orthonormal projections. Within this framework, we derive non-trivial theoretical results, including geodesic convexity properties on the projection manifold, perturbation bounds quantifying stability to matrix noise, and exact recovery guarantees under ideal block-model conditions. The analysis further explains when different clustering families collapse to the same optimal subspace and how deviations arise under small inter-cluster leakage. Overall, the work provides a coherent, theory-first foundation for understanding clustering through structured projectors.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified theoretical framework demonstrating that diverse clustering methods (k-means, fuzzy c-means, kernel k-means, kernel FCM, and spectral clustering) can all be formulated as structured low-rank projectors applied to a signal-derived matrix, cast within a common optimization template min over B in C of ||M - M P_B||_F^2.
AI.motivation: To establish a coherent, theory-first foundation for understanding clustering algorithms by revealing their common algebraic structure, and to derive non-trivial theoretical guarantees (geodesic convexity, perturbation bounds, recovery guarantees) that generalize across clustering families.
AI.method: The authors express each clustering method as an instance of a single optimization template with different constraint sets C, covering hard, fuzzy, kernel-induced, and orthonormal projections, then analyze the resulting structured low-rank projector framework.
AI.result: The framework yields geodesic convexity properties on the projection manifold, perturbation bounds quantifying stability under matrix noise, exact recovery guarantees under ideal block-model conditions, and a characterization of when different clustering families converge to the same optimal subspace versus diverge under small inter-cluster leakage.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a unified theoretical foundation that clarifies algebraic links among hard, fuzzy, kernel-based, and spectral clustering methods, explaining both their equivalence conditions and sources of deviation.

title: GAFT: Geo-Anchored Fine-Tuning for Hazard Identification from Rare Failures
summary: Off-road navigation can fail when physical structures induce irrecoverable states such as high-centering or entrapment, requiring human interventions. Identifying these structures is crucial, yet challenging. Such failure events are rare and costly to collect, resulting in limited training data. Moreover, the collected data associate frames with outcomes, but do not indicate the visual cues responsible for the failure. Learning directly from these data can therefore exploit scenario-specific visual cues, leading to poor generalization. We propose \textbf{Geo-Anchored Fine-Tuning (GAFT)}, a parameter-efficient method that adapts a vision foundation model with a geometry-derived prior. It guides LoRA adaptation by aligning a spatial attention-rollout map with the geometry prior, while preserving pretrained representations. On an intervention-verified forest hazard benchmark, across ten independently trained adaptations, GAFT consistently outperforms frozen DINOv2 and supervised PEFT baselines, improving the repeated leave-one-scenario-out mean $F_2$ from 0.0607 to 0.3757 with statistical significance under paired analysis. Within these independently trained models, the best-performing GAFT model achieves a repeated-LOSO $F_2$ of 0.570. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/Xu-Yanran/geo_anchored_fine_tuning

AI.tldr: GAFT is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adapts a vision foundation model using a geometry-derived prior to detect off-road navigation hazards, improving F2 score from 0.0607 to 0.3757 on a forest hazard benchmark.
AI.motivation: Off-road navigation failures caused by physical structures are rare, costly to collect, and lack labeled visual cues, leading to poor generalization when learning directly from sparse outcome-level data.
AI.method: Geo-Anchored Fine-Tuning (GAFT) adapts a vision foundation model via LoRA, guiding the adaptation by aligning a spatial attention-rollout map with a geometry-derived prior while preserving pretrained representations.
AI.result: Across ten independently trained adaptations on an intervention-verified forest hazard benchmark, GAFT consistently outperforms frozen DINOv2 and supervised PEFT baselines, improving repeated leave-one-scenario-out mean F2 from 0.0607 to 0.3757 with statistical significance. The best GAFT model achieves F2 of 0.570.
AI.conclusion: GAFT effectively leverages geometry priors to improve generalization of hazard detection in off-road navigation with limited and weakly labeled data.

title: Emergent Misalignment Is Not Magical
summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on narrowly harmful datasets can lead to misalignment broadly, a phenomenon known as emergent misalignment (EM). EM poses a challenge for AI safety and our understanding of LLMs. Prior work often frames EM as an unexpected behavior, and explains it by appealing to general misalignment directions or anthropomorphizing it as acquiring an evil persona. However, the mechanisms behind these framings remain obscure. In this work, we show that EM is a predictable and data-dependent generalization phenomenon. By examining the base model's representation of EM training data and evaluation prompts, we find that evilness after EM training is highly predictable from representational distance: the closer an evaluation prompt is to training data centroid, the more evilness it elicits from EM models after training (with an average Spearman correlation of -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings). Building upon this analysis, we further demystify EM by showing that (1) its effectiveness changes significantly based on training data format; (2) there is not a general misalignment direction that transfers across different EM models; (3) the effect of EM is fundamentally different from persona changes. Furthermore, we extend the EM generalization metric from a scalar distance to a dataset-specific generalization direction, which robustly predicts EM models' evilness under semantics-preserving prompt perturbations including appending random tokens and paraphrasing, where other methods do not reliably generalize.

AI.tldr: Emergent misalignment (EM) in fine-tuned LLMs is a predictable, data-dependent generalization phenomenon rather than an unexpected or persona-based effect. Evilness after EM training is highly predictable from the representational distance between evaluation prompts and the EM training data centroid (average Spearman correlation of -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings).
AI.motivation: Emergent misalignment poses a challenge for AI safety, yet prior explanations framing it as unexpected behavior, a general misalignment direction, or an "evil persona" remain mechanistically obscure. The authors aim to demystify EM by providing a predictive, data-driven account of this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors analyze the base model's representations of EM training data and evaluation prompts, measuring representational distance as a predictor of post-training evilness. They conduct experiments across 12 model-dataset settings, test sensitivity to training data format, examine cross-model transfer of misalignment directions, compare EM against persona changes, and extend the generalization metric to a dataset-specific generalization direction for robustness under semantic-preserving perturbations.
AI.result: Evilness after EM training is highly predictable from representational distance to the training data centroid (average Spearman correlation of -0.73). EM effectiveness changes significantly with training data format, there is no general misalignment direction transferring across EM models, and EM effects are fundamentally distinct from persona changes. The proposed dataset-specific generalization direction robustly predicts evilness under prompt perturbations (e.g., random token appending, paraphrasing) where other methods fail.
AI.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is best understood as a predictable, data-dependent generalization phenomenon rooted in representational proximity to training data, rather than as unexpected behavior or persona acquisition. This framing provides a more mechanistic and robust account of EM with practical predictive power.

title: Zeva: In-Context Causal Learning for Generalizable Embodied Manipulation
summary: Generalizable embodied manipulation remains difficult to achieve through pretraining alone, due to unseen physical conditions in the real world. We argue that robots need to learn from their own physical interactions on the fly during real-world deployment and use this knowledge to inform subsequent actions. We present Zeva, the first framework that enables in-context learning from a robot's own physical interaction experience while keeping the policy model frozen. Zeva employs a Causal Interaction Extractor to encode an executed action and its induced state change into a causal interaction signal, which is stored in a dual-timescale causal memory. For subsequent actions, relevant causal interaction signals are retrieved from memory and injected into the frozen policy model as context. Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation demonstrate that Zeva achieves the best performance among the compared frontier VLAs and WAMs and, more importantly, enables self-evolution during deployment without gradient updates. Its success rate continues to improve as the robot accumulates interaction experience. Furthermore, the acquired interaction experience can generalize across tasks.

AI.tldr: Zeva is the first framework enabling in-context learning from a robot's own physical interaction experience during real-world deployment, using a Causal Interaction Extractor and dual-timescale causal memory, while keeping the policy model frozen. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on simulation and real-world manipulation benchmarks and enables self-evolution without gradient updates.
AI.motivation: Generalizable embodied manipulation is difficult to achieve through pretraining alone due to unseen physical conditions in the real world. Robots need to learn from their own physical interactions on the fly during real-world deployment to inform subsequent actions.
AI.method: Zeva employs a Causal Interaction Extractor to encode an executed action and its induced state change into a causal interaction signal, stored in a dual-timescale causal memory. Relevant causal interaction signals are retrieved from memory and injected into a frozen policy model as context for subsequent actions.
AI.result: Zeva achieves the best performance among compared frontier VLAs (Vision-Language-Action models) and WAMs (World Action Models) in simulation and real-world manipulation, enabling self-evolution during deployment without gradient updates. Success rate improves with accumulated interaction experience, and acquired experience generalizes across tasks.
AI.conclusion: In-context learning from the robot's own physical interaction experience, enabled by causal memory retrieval, provides an effective mechanism for continual self-improvement during deployment without modifying the frozen policy model.

title: Beyond Correctness: Validity-Oriented Evaluation of Biomedical LLM Judges
summary: We propose a scalable, validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when high-quality human judgments are scarce. First, we augment existing human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations that produce auditable preference pairs. Second, we evaluate judges beyond aggregate correctness using three deployment-relevant dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and compliance with the requested output format. We use this pipeline to assess Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four regimes: (1) base, using the instruct model as is; (2) SFT, distillation-based supervised fine-tuning only; (3) RL, GRPO-based reinforcement learning only; and (4) SFT$\rightarrow$RL, SFT followed by RL. The base and single-stage regimes struggle on structured medical discrimination such as PICO extraction and clinical calculations, whereas SFT$\rightarrow$RL performs best across correctness, compliance, and robustness; gains concentrate on decomposable tasks (PICO, MedCalc), at times matching or outperforming frontier models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable, validity-oriented pipeline for evaluating biomedical LLM judges when human labels are scarce. It augments existing benchmarks with deterministic metric-based mutations to create auditable preference pairs, and evaluates judges on correctness, robustness, and format compliance. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, it compares base, SFT, RL, and SFT→RL training regimes; SFT→RL performs best, especially on decomposable biomedical tasks like PICO extraction and clinical calculations.
AI.motivation: High-quality human judgments for evaluating biomedical LLM judges are scarce and expensive, yet reliable evaluation of such judges is critical for deployment in clinical/medical settings.
AI.method: The pipeline (1) augments human-labelled biomedical benchmarks with deterministic, metric-grounded mutations to produce auditable preference pairs, and (2) evaluates judges on three dimensions: correctness against metric-derived gold labels, robustness under repeated stochastic sampling, and format compliance. Four training regimes are assessed on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: base, SFT, RL (GRPO), and SFT→RL.
AI.result: Base and single-stage regimes struggle on structured medical discrimination (PICO extraction, clinical calculations). SFT→RL outperforms all others across correctness, compliance, and robustness, with gains concentrated on decomposable tasks and sometimes matching or exceeding frontier models.
AI.conclusion: SFT followed by RL is the most effective training strategy for biomedical LLM judges under data scarcity, particularly for decomposable medical tasks; the proposed pipeline offers a scalable and validity-oriented framework for judge evaluation in this domain.

title: SleepWalking: Privileged Representation Shaping for End-to-End Blind Locomotion in Legged Robots
summary: Partially observable locomotion requires a policy to act when task-relevant properties of the robot--environment state are not fully specified by instantaneous observations. Existing approaches often address this challenge by explicitly estimating missing physical variables or processing extended observation histories through structured architectures. We take a different view: partial observability is fundamentally an information-retention problem. The decisive question is not how task-relevant information enters the network, but whether the policy's internal state retains it. Guided by this perspective, we propose SleepWalking for Robot Locomotion (SWAQ), a one-stage end-to-end framework that uses next-step privileged physical reconstruction to shape what a recurrent history representation retains during policy learning, while the deployed actor uses only a direct history-to-action pathway. Under aligned training settings, SWAQ achieves a 15.0\% higher peak mean terrain level than DWAQ, the strongest non-exteroceptive baseline, while using 44.4\% fewer inference MACs per control step. Layerwise probes further show that information associated with the reconstructed physical variables remains linearly decodable through the policy head up to the layer preceding the action output. Complementary theoretical analysis relates privileged-variable recoverability to the achievable-return gap between history-based and privileged-information policy classes. These results suggest that semantic objectives can structure learning without requiring a corresponding architectural decomposition of the deployed controller.

AI.tldr: SWAQ is a one-stage end-to-end framework for partially observable robot locomotion that treats partial observability as an information-retention problem, using next-step privileged physical reconstruction to shape what a recurrent history representation retains during policy learning. It achieves 15.0% higher peak mean terrain level than the strongest non-exteroceptive baseline (DWAQ) while using 44.4% fewer inference MACs per control step.
AI.motivation: Partially observable locomotion requires policies to act when task-relevant robot-environment state properties are not fully specified by instantaneous observations. Existing approaches either explicitly estimate missing physical variables or process extended observation histories through structured architectures. The authors argue that partial observability is fundamentally an information-retention problem: the decisive question is whether the policy's internal state retains task-relevant information, not how it enters the network.
AI.method: SWAQ is a one-stage end-to-end framework that employs next-step privileged physical reconstruction as an auxiliary objective to shape what a recurrent history representation retains during policy learning. The deployed actor uses only a direct history-to-action pathway, without requiring architectural decomposition or explicit privileged inputs at inference time. The approach is complemented by layerwise probes to analyze information retention and theoretical analysis relating privileged-variable recoverability to the achievable-return gap between history-based and privileged-information policy classes.
AI.result: SWAQ achieves a 15.0% higher peak mean terrain level than DWAQ (the strongest non-exteroceptive baseline) while using 44.4% fewer inference MACs per control step. Layerwise probes show that information associated with reconstructed physical variables remains linearly decodable through the policy head up to the layer preceding the action output.
AI.conclusion: Semantic objectives can structure learning without requiring a corresponding architectural decomposition of the deployed controller. This suggests that shaping the learning objective to encourage information retention can effectively address partial observability in locomotion without explicit estimation modules or structured architecture designs.

title: APIFlow-Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Survive Long, Dependent API Workflows
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Under review at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Evaluation of Interactive Agents (IAEval). Harness, frozen task bank, and 44,362 execution transcripts: https://github.com/postmanlabs/APIFlow-Bench
summary: Tool-using agents are commonly evaluated by a single bit: whether an end-to-end workflow completed. This metric fails to distinguish failures that matter in production, such as expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution followed by incorrect final delivery. We introduce APIFlow-Bench, a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes performance into seven engineering capabilities and requires agents to produce answers supported by the actual call path. We generate synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask; each subtask is admitted only after a zero-LLM self-test triad verifies its grader and an oracle establishes solvability, and an adversarial audit identified and fixed six grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive: a state check traces a mock-minted canary through the API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, and a typed answer card is verified field by field. We release all answer keys and 44,362 unredacted execution transcripts. Across 19 frontier and open-weight models under one neutral scaffold, we find: (1) longer dependency chains degrade success, from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains and 61% when including the 8% of chain trials that a model-consensus screen flags as passed by no model; (2) reliability separates models more than best-case capability, with best-of-five spanning seven points but all-five-of-five reliability spanning 44 points; (3) the independent-error account of compounding failure does not fit the data: pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and on the clean slice 77% of failing runs reached the correct final state and failed only at delivery.

AI.tldr: APIFlow-Bench is a fully auditable benchmark for long-horizon, dependent REST-API workflows that decomposes agent performance into seven engineering capabilities and uses deterministic, provenance-sensitive grading. Testing 19 frontier and open-weight models, it reveals that longer dependency chains degrade success, reliability separates models more than best-case capability, and compounding failure is not explained by independent errors—most failures occur at final delivery despite correct execution.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of tool-using agents uses a single binary outcome (workflow completed or not), which fails to distinguish production-relevant failures such as expired credentials, malformed payloads, or correct execution followed by incorrect final delivery. This coarse metric obscures where agents actually fail.
AI.method: APIFlow-Bench generates synthetic API worlds forward, subtask by subtask. Each subtask is admitted only after a zero-LLM self-test triad verifies its grader and an oracle establishes solvability; an adversarial audit fixes six grader exploits. Grading is deterministic and provenance-sensitive: a state check traces a mock-minted canary through API data flow to the response the answer must originate from, and a typed answer card is verified field by field. 44,362 unredacted execution transcripts are released.
AI.result: Across 19 frontier and open-weight models under one neutral scaffold: (1) longer dependency chains degrade success from 93% on individual subtasks to 74% on clean 20-subtask chains, dropping to 61% when including the 8% of chain trials flagged by a model-consensus screen as passed by no model; (2) reliability separates models more than best-case capability—best-of-five spans 7 points while all-five-of-five reliability spans 44 points; (3) pass rates on 20-subtask chains are 33 percentage points above the product of subtask-level rates, and on the clean slice 77% of failing runs reached the correct final state and failed only at delivery.
AI.conclusion: Independent-error models do not explain compounding failure in long-horizon tool-use workflows. The dominant source of failure is incorrect final delivery despite correct execution, highlighting that deployment-grade evaluation must measure reliability and provenance-sensitive delivery, not just end-to-end completion.

title: LightNav-0: Eliciting VLM Spatial Intelligence for Generalist Embodied Navigation
summary: Embodied navigation requires agents to translate heterogeneous goals and visual observations into actions across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments. Modern vision-language models (VLMs) already encode spatial priors for visual grounding, spatial reasoning, and pointing, but these capabilities are rarely elicited directly for robot control. Existing navigation systems instead rely on task- or embodiment-specific components, fragmenting perception, reasoning, and action while offering limited generalization. Here we present LightNav-0, a compact generalist embodied navigation model that elicits the spatial intelligence of a pretrained VLM and aligns it with navigation, without task-specific prediction heads. LightNav-0 represents diverse navigation tasks through a unified token interface: dual-channel pointing expresses task-, scene-, and embodiment-agnostic spatial intent, while a residual vector-quantized action tokenizer maps this intent to precise, embodiment-specific trajectories. Together with temporally aware visual history compression, ER mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, this formulation supports instruction following, open-vocabulary object navigation, and visual tracking within a single model. The navigation training corpus spans 2K+ scenes and 4K+ hours of embodied navigation data. LightNav-ER, the embodied-reasoning checkpoint used to initialize LightNav-0, attains the highest complete-set average across 8 embodied-reasoning benchmarks, while LightNav-0 achieves state-of-the-art monocular success rates across all 10 public navigation simulation settings. Real-world evaluations further demonstrate zero-shot generalization across robot embodiments, diverse scenes, and static and dynamic targets. These results establish compact VLMs as a unified and transferable backbone for generalist embodied navigation.

AI.tldr: LightNav-0 is a compact generalist embodied navigation model that elicits spatial intelligence from a pretrained VLM and aligns it with navigation via a unified token interface (dual-channel pointing for spatial intent + residual VQ action tokenizer for trajectories), achieving SOTA performance across 10 navigation benchmarks and zero-shot real-world generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied navigation systems fragment perception, reasoning, and action into task- or embodiment-specific components, limiting generalization. While modern VLMs already encode spatial priors for visual grounding and spatial reasoning, these capabilities are rarely elicited directly for robot control.
AI.method: LightNav-0 uses: (1) a unified token interface with dual-channel pointing for task-, scene-, and embodiment-agnostic spatial intent, and a residual vector-quantized action tokenizer mapping intent to embodiment-specific trajectories; (2) temporally aware visual history compression; (3) ER mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning; (4) a navigation training corpus of 2K+ scenes and 4K+ hours of embodied navigation data.
AI.result: LightNav-ER (the initialization checkpoint) achieves the highest complete-set average across 8 embodied-reasoning benchmarks. LightNav-0 achieves state-of-the-art monocular success rates across all 10 public navigation simulation settings, and demonstrates zero-shot generalization across robot embodiments, scenes, and static/dynamic targets in real-world evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Compact VLMs can serve as a unified and transferable backbone for generalist embodied navigation, eliminating the need for task-specific prediction heads while maintaining strong performance across diverse tasks and embodiments.

title: More Perspectives, Stronger Signals: Multi-Perspective Enhancement and Progressive Fusion for Multimodal Entity Representation Learning
summary: Learning effective multimodal entity representations is fundamental for reasoning tasks such as multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC). However, existing methods often suffer from semantic over-smoothing within modalities and ineffective noise filtration across modalities, particularly under sparse or ambiguous conditions. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrismF, a unified framework that synergizes multi-perspective enhancement with progressive fusion to extract stronger signals from diverse inputs. PrismF enhances fine-grained intra-modal semantics through a multi-perspective mechanism that decomposes each modality into complementary views and constrains them with a decoupling loss to reduce representation collapse. Furthermore, it improves cross-modal integration through a progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates inter-modal interactions, enabling the model to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noisy or unreliable ones. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that PrismF achieves the strongest overall performance, including relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on KVC16K. Our code can be found at https://github.com/HubuKG/PrismF.

AI.tldr: PrismF is a unified framework for multimodal knowledge graph completion that combines multi-perspective enhancement (decomposing each modality into complementary views with a decoupling loss to prevent representation collapse) and progressive fusion (dynamic cross-modal calibration to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noise). It achieves state-of-the-art results, with relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on the KVC16K benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal entity representation methods suffer from semantic over-smoothing within modalities and ineffective noise filtration across modalities, particularly under sparse or ambiguous data conditions, limiting their performance on tasks like multimodal knowledge graph completion.
AI.method: PrismF proposes two key components: (1) a multi-perspective enhancement mechanism that decomposes each modality into complementary views and applies a decoupling loss to constrain representations and reduce collapse; (2) a progressive fusion strategy that dynamically calibrates inter-modal interactions to emphasize informative signals while suppressing noisy or unreliable ones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show PrismF achieves the strongest overall performance, including relative improvements of 4.04% in MRR and 11.17% in Hits@1 on KVC16K.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses intra-modal over-smoothing and cross-modal noise issues, delivering robust multimodal entity representations with state-of-the-art performance on MMKGC benchmarks.

title: Autonomously Acquiring Robot Manipulation Skills with Language-Driven Quality-Diversity
summary: Quality-diversity (QD) algorithms have been gaining traction in robot learning, where diverse motion primitive libraries allow robots to adapt zero-shot to constraints at deployment time. However, such methods typically require expert designers to write the success condition, fitness and diversity metrics, and this strongly limits the robot's autonomy. On the other hand, existing LLM-based reward-shaping techniques allow robots to learn autonomously but only output single high-performing solutions, limiting the robot's adaptability. In this paper, we propose an approach designed to output diverse motion primitive archives by autonomously leveraging quality-diversity algorithms, only requiring a free-form description of the task in common language. To address the difficulty of designing relevant fitness and diversity metrics, we propose an autonomous exploration mechanism able to reliably output sets of functionals covering the fitness and behavior descriptor (BD) space. First, we pose policy exploration as a functional design problem, where the functional spaces are lower-dimensional than the full BD and fitness spaces, and propose an LLM-based exploration scheme to sample from these low-dimensional spaces without any task-specific prompts, fine-tuning or expert intervention. We adapt a multi-BD variant of the MAP-Elites success (MES) algorithm, designed to leverage the heterogeneous BD samples. Finally, through experiments based on the genesis simulator, we show that our method effectively generates archives of diverse motion primitives, outperforming classical QD algorithms with inferred and hand-written parametrizations on a set of $4$ robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an autonomous LLM-driven Quality-Diversity (QD) approach that generates diverse motion primitive archives for robot learning from a free-form task description, without requiring expert-designed fitness/diversity metrics. It poses policy exploration as a functional design problem using LLM-based sampling in lower-dimensional spaces, adapts a multi-BD MAP-Elites Success algorithm, and demonstrates superior performance over classical QD methods on 4 robotic manipulation tasks in the Genesis simulator.
AI.motivation: Existing QD algorithms require expert designers to hand-craft success conditions, fitness metrics, and diversity metrics, limiting robot autonomy. Meanwhile, LLM-based reward-shaping produces only single high-performing solutions, which limits adaptability. The paper aims to combine the strengths of both—autonomy from LLMs and diversity from QD—to output diverse motion primitive archives from just a common-language task description.
AI.method: The approach treats policy exploration as a functional design problem where functional spaces are lower-dimensional than full BD and fitness spaces. It proposes an LLM-based exploration scheme to sample from these low-dimensional functional spaces without task-specific prompts, fine-tuning, or expert intervention. The method adapts a multi-BD variant of the MAP-Elites Success (MES) algorithm to leverage heterogeneous BD samples, enabling autonomous generation of fitness and behavior descriptor functionals.
AI.result: Experiments on the Genesis simulator across 4 robotic manipulation tasks show the proposed method effectively generates archives of diverse motion primitives, outperforming classical QD algorithms with both inferred and hand-written parametrizations.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that combining LLM-based autonomous metric design with QD archive generation enables robots to produce diverse, adaptable motion primitives from only a natural language task description, removing the need for expert intervention while preserving diversity for zero-shot adaptation at deployment.

title: JudgePanel: A Compact Judge with Panel Deliberation via Adaptive Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation. However, single-model judges are limited by their inherent model biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that mitigate this through diverse deliberation are prohibitively expensive at inference time. To this end, we propose \textbf{\modelname}, which equips a compact \underline{Judge} model with multi-agent \underline{Panel} deliberation capability. Specifically, we first train on panel deliberation traces from an ensemble of strong evaluators, capturing structured patterns of discussion, disagreement, and resolution. To further improve judgment quality beyond SFT, we introduce \textit{AdaReward}, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as different objectives saturate at different rates during RL training. For practical deployment, we further design a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains with few hundred labeled samples. As a result, (i) \textit{Novel}: the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost; (ii) \textit{Effective \& Reliable}: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and rapidly specializes to new domains with few hundred samples.

AI.tldr: JudgePanel is a framework that equips a compact 14B judge model with multi-agent panel deliberation capabilities at single-model inference cost, using SFT on panel deliberation traces from strong evaluator ensembles and an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm (AdaReward) for enhanced judgment quality, plus a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation.
AI.motivation: Single-model LLM judges are limited by inherent model biases, while multi-agent evaluation protocols that mitigate bias through diverse deliberation are prohibitively expensive at inference time. There is a need for a scalable approach that combines the quality of multi-agent deliberation with the efficiency of single-model evaluation.
AI.method: The paper proposes JudgePanel with three key components: (1) training a compact judge model via SFT on panel deliberation traces collected from an ensemble of strong evaluators to learn structured deliberation patterns (discussion, disagreement, resolution); (2) AdaReward, an adaptive multi-reward RL algorithm that dynamically rebalances reward component weights as different objectives saturate at different rates during RL training; (3) a lightweight domain specialization module for rapid adaptation to new evaluation domains using few hundred labeled samples.
AI.result: JudgePanel with a 14B backbone outperforms judge-specialized models up to 70B across four evaluation benchmarks, demonstrates strong position consistency, and rapidly specializes to new domains with only a few hundred labeled samples, all at single-model inference cost.
AI.conclusion: JudgePanel is the first framework to equip a single compact judge with multi-agent panel deliberation capability at single-model inference cost, achieving both effectiveness and practical deployability for LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation tasks.

title: DARP: A Calibrated Dual-Arm RGB-D-IR Dataset for Multi-View Robotic Perception
summary: Robotic perception from a single viewpoint is often limited by self-occlusion and incomplete surface visibility. This paper presents DARP(Dual-Arm Robotic Perception) https://doi.org/10.21227/rmv3-be47, a calibrated dual-arm RGB-D-IR dataset for object-centered robotic perception using two independently moving eye-in-hand manipulators positioned on opposite sides of a shared tabletop workspace. Each arm carries an Intel RealSense sensor that continuously records RGB, depth, and stereo infrared data while synchronized robot joint states are logged for pose recovery. Objects are placed without fixed poses or marked locations, and the acquisition procedure performs automatic localization, cross-arm confirmation, adaptive viewpoint generation, and continuous multimodal recording. DARP contains ten unique tabletop objects and preserves the original sensor recordings, robot-state logs, object-level metadata, and calibration information required to reconstruct camera trajectories in a shared metric frame. To evaluate the geometric consistency of the acquisition, we implement a deterministic multi-view fusion pipeline that converts calibrated RGB-D observations into complementary partial point clouds and measured surface meshes without using learned or generative completion methods. Evaluation on 224 held-out RGB-D keyframes comprising 1,563,466 three-dimensional query points yields a median point-to-mesh distance of 2.13~mm and an RMSE of 4.04~mm, with 96.56\% of points within 10~mm of the measured-surface mesh. DARP is intended as a reusable resource for multi-view reconstruction, collaborative robotic perception, multimodal fusion, active perception, and future learning-based reasoning over partial object observations.

AI.tldr: DARP is a calibrated dual-arm RGB-D-IR dataset for object-centered robotic perception, featuring two independently moving eye-in-hand manipulators with Intel RealSense sensors on opposite sides of a shared workspace. It includes ten tabletop objects with multimodal recordings, robot-state logs, and calibration data, validated via a deterministic multi-view fusion pipeline achieving 2.13 mm median point-to-mesh distance and 96.56% of points within 10 mm of measured surfaces.
AI.motivation: Single-viewpoint robotic perception suffers from self-occlusion and incomplete surface visibility, limiting downstream tasks like reconstruction and reasoning. A multi-view, multimodal dataset with precise calibration is needed to enable robust object-centered perception.
AI.method: The acquisition system uses two eye-in-hand manipulators positioned on opposite sides of a shared tabletop, each equipped with an Intel RealSense sensor capturing RGB, depth, and stereo infrared data alongside synchronized robot joint states. The pipeline performs automatic localization, cross-arm confirmation, adaptive viewpoint generation, and continuous multimodal recording without fixed object poses or marked locations. All sensor recordings, robot-state logs, object metadata, and calibration data are preserved for trajectory reconstruction in a shared metric frame.
AI.result: On 224 held-out RGB-D keyframes with 1,563,466 3D query points, the multi-view fusion evaluation achieved a median point-to-mesh distance of 2.13 mm, RMSE of 4.04 mm, and 96.56% of points within 10 mm of the measured-surface mesh.
AI.conclusion: DARP provides a reusable, geometrically validated resource for multi-view reconstruction, collaborative robotic perception, multimodal fusion, active perception, and learning-based reasoning over partial object observations, with geometric consistency confirmed by deterministic fusion without learned completion.

title: An Explainable Coherence Score for Detecting Temporal Inconsistencies in Political News
summary: Temporal inconsistencies, such as mandates attributed outside their real interval, events presented as past before they occurred, or inverted causal sequences, are a form of political disinformation that evades style-based fake news detectors: a well-written article with a single wrong date carries no lexical signal of falsehood.
