This paper introduces the Temporal Coherence Score (TCS), a continuous, intrinsically interpretable metric that quantifies the temporal coherence of a news article, computed by a four-stage pipeline: extraction of temporal facts, construction of a temporal knowledge graph, hierarchical verification against internal consistency rules and external reference sources, and score aggregation with automatically generated explanations. Verification combines eight internal checkers derived from Allen's interval algebra with a five-level external hierarchy ranging from a locally stored reference knowledge base of 1{,}256 curated political facts to live Wikidata SPARQL queries. On a benchmark of 100 political news articles with injected temporal errors, the system reaches a precision of 0.909 at the selected operating threshold, with a single residual false positive, a profile deliberately tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking assistance, where false alarms are costlier than missed detections. Unlike lexical baselines that output only a binary label, every flagged article is accompanied by the inconsistency type, the entities involved, and the reference source that contradicts the claim.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Temporal Coherence Score (TCS), a continuous, interpretable metric for quantifying temporal coherence in news articles via a four-stage pipeline—temporal fact extraction, temporal knowledge graph construction, hierarchical verification (eight Allen's interval algebra-based internal checkers plus a five-level external reference hierarchy), and score aggregation with explanations. On 100 political news articles with injected temporal errors, it achieves 0.909 precision, tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking where false alarms are costlier than misses.
AI.motivation: Temporal inconsistencies (wrong dates, misordered events, inverted causal sequences) are a form of political disinformation that elude style-based fake news detectors—a well-written article with a single wrong date carries no lexical falsehood signal.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline: (1) extraction of temporal facts, (2) construction of a temporal knowledge graph, (3) hierarchical verification combining eight internal checkers derived from Allen's interval algebra with a five-level external hierarchy (from a locally stored reference KB of 1,256 curated political facts to live Wikidata SPARQL queries), and (4) score aggregation with automatically generated explanations.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 100 political articles with injected temporal errors, TCS achieves a precision of 0.909 at the selected operating threshold with a single residual false positive, deliberately tuned for human-in-the-loop fact-checking.
AI.conclusion: TCS outperforms lexical baselines (which output only binary labels) by providing continuous, interpretable scores with per-flag explanations including inconsistency type, involved entities, and the contradicting reference source.

title: SUN: Persistent Programs For Language-Grounded Control-to-Learning-to-Real Policies
summary: Bridging model-based control and learned policies in long-horizon manipulation has harbored a silent disagreement: control executes specified objectives, learning amortizes that behavior into a reactive policy, yet existing protocols discard task semantics, leaving rewards hand-crafted and behavior drifting from what control verified.We introduce Semantically UNified (SUN) Programs, typed executables where geometric and contact relations are defined once and compiled into aligned Model Predictive Control (MPC) costs, satisfaction predicates, RL rewards, transition guards, and diagnostics. Our system, Kuafu, driven by large vision language systems, automatically synthesizes SUN Programs from language and scene semantics, screens feasibility via MPC, and retains semantics while training stage-conditioned policies. Across nine tasks, Kuafu achieves 82.03% macro-success, outperforming sparse-reward (35.67%) and Stage-BC (24.75%) baselines. At 8192-way scale, it generates 10.57x the successful trajectory time per hour of human teleoperation. With 500 trajectories per task, Kuafu data trains DP3 policies to 46.0% simulation success (vs. 22.4% for alternatives) and 34.7% on physical Franka and Kinova robots. These results establish that simulation-screened task semantics can effectively amortize control into robust policies, without demonstrations or manual dense rewards, unifying symbolic planning and data-driven execution.

AI.tldr: SUN Programs unify geometric/contact relations into typed executables compiled to MPC costs, RL rewards, and policy training. Kuafu, powered by large vision-language systems, auto-synthesizes these programs and trains stage-conditioned policies, achieving 82.03% macro-success across nine tasks and scaling data generation 10.57x over human teleoperation.
AI.motivation: Existing protocols for bridging model-based control and learned policies discard task semantics, leaving rewards hand-crafted and learned behavior drifting from what control verified. This creates a disconnect between what control optimizes for and what policies learn.
AI.method: Kuafu uses large vision-language systems to automatically synthesize SUN Programs from language and scene semantics. These typed executables define geometric and contact relations once, which are compiled into MPC costs, satisfaction predicates, RL rewards, transition guards, and diagnostics. Feasibility is screened via MPC, and semantics are retained during stage-conditioned policy training.
AI.result: Across nine tasks, Kuafu achieves 82.03% macro-success, outperforming sparse-reward (35.67%) and Stage-BC (24.75%) baselines. At 8192-way scale it generates 10.57x successful trajectory time per hour of human teleoperation. With 500 trajectories per task, DP3 policies trained on Kuafu data reach 46.0% simulation success (vs. 22.4% for alternatives) and 34.7% on physical Franka and Kinova robots.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-screened task semantics can effectively amortize control into robust policies without demonstrations or manual dense rewards, unifying symbolic planning and data-driven execution.

title: How Identity and Opinion Shape Political Sycophancy in LLMs
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles for tailored assistance, measuring their political alignment becomes increasingly important. However, many existing benchmarks for assessing political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and do not fully capture how a model's stance may adapt to user-provided context during interaction. We introduce a framework that disentangles two distinct triggers of political sycophancy: opinion (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity (stereotyping based on demographic labels). Using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes, we evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs. We uncover a dissociation: a model's susceptibility to explicit opinions does not necessarily predict its susceptibility to identity cues, and vice versa. When both signals are present, their effects are generally sub-additive rather than simply additive. Additionally, system-level personas primarily shift a model's baseline stance while having limited effect on the stance shift caused by user opinion or identity. Ultimately, our results suggest that LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than being a fixed trait, highlighting how personalization may amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in the model's behaviors.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework to disentangle two triggers of political sycophancy in LLMs—opinion (explicit narrative alignment) and identity (demographic stereotyping)—and evaluates 13 instruction-tuned LLMs using 450 manually-checked political dilemmas, finding that these two triggers are dissociable, their effects are sub-additive when combined, and system personas shift baselines without altering user-driven stance shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for assessing LLM political behavior rely on closed-ended questions and fail to capture how model stances adapt to user-provided context during interaction. As LLMs increasingly encourage users to disclose personal profiles, understanding how their political alignment shifts under different triggers becomes critical.
AI.method: The authors construct a framework that separates two triggers of political sycophancy: opinion-based (aligning with explicit narratives) and identity-based (stereotyping based on demographic labels). They create 450 manually-checked political dilemmas as controlled probes and evaluate 13 instruction-tuned LLMs under various conditions including individual triggers, combined triggers, and system-level personas.
AI.result: The study finds a dissociation between opinion and identity susceptibility—a model prone to one is not necessarily prone to the other. When both signals are present, their combined effects are sub-additive rather than additive. System personas shift a model's baseline stance but do not significantly change how user opinion or identity cues influence stance shifts.
AI.conclusion: LLM political stance is interactively and steerably vulnerable rather than a fixed trait. Personalization can amplify identity- or opinion-conditioned shifts in model behavior, highlighting important implications for how LLMs handle user-provided personal information during political discussions.

title: Scaffolding Foundation Models into Physical-World Agents Pushes the Frontier of Long-Horizon Navigation
summary: Long-horizon physical-world agents must reason over distant goals while grounding decisions in reliable closed-loop behavior. Today's foundation models split these capabilities: vision-language models (VLMs) infer missing information and adapt high-level plans but remain brittle and inefficient at repeated navigation grounding, while navigation foundation models (NFMs) robustly execute semantic goals but operate as bounded episodes without persistent task-level reasoning. We introduce NavMCP, an agentic scaffolding framework that couples a VLM reasoning agent with an NFM executor for long-horizon exploration. The VLM decides what evidence to seek, where to search, and when to stop, while the NFM grounds each semantic sub-goal into closed-loop navigation. Three channels structure their collaboration: intent translates evidence needs into navigation calls, observation converts rollouts into source-grounded trajectory evidence, and memory accumulates findings, negative evidence, and unresolved goals across calls. This design turns isolated navigation rollouts into persistent embodied interaction without retraining either model. On Embodied Question Answering, NavMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on HM-EQA, MT-HM3D, and EXPRESS-Bench. Under matched agent and executor backbones, it outperforms an episodic interface by 14.9 percentage points on HM-EQA. On a Unitree Go2, NavMCP reaches 78.3% success, with its margin over the strongest baseline growing from 10 to 45 points as the task horizon increases. These results demonstrate the potential of scaffolding complementary foundation models into long-horizon physical-world agents.

AI.tldr: NavMCP is an agentic scaffolding framework that couples a VLM reasoning agent with a navigation foundation model (NFM) executor for long-horizon exploration, using three channels (intent, observation, memory) to structure collaboration. It achieves state-of-the-art results on HM-EQA, MT-HM3D, and EXPRESS-Bench, outperforming episodic interfaces by 14.9 percentage points on HM-EQA and reaching 78.3% success on a Unitree Go2 robot.
AI.motivation: Today's foundation models exhibit a capability split: VLMs can reason over high-level plans and infer missing information but are brittle and inefficient at repeated navigation grounding, while NFMs execute semantic goals robustly but operate as bounded episodes without persistent task-level reasoning. No single model handles both long-horizon reasoning and reliable closed-loop execution.
AI.method: NavMCP scaffolds a VLM reasoning agent with an NFM executor via three structured collaboration channels: (1) intent translates evidence needs into navigation calls, (2) observation converts NFM rollouts into source-grounded trajectory evidence, and (3) memory accumulates findings, negative evidence, and unresolved goals across navigation calls. This creates persistent embodied interaction without retraining either model.
AI.result: NavMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on HM-EQA, MT-HM3D, and EXPRESS-Bench. Under matched backbones it outperforms an episodic interface by 14.9 percentage points on HM-EQA. On a Unitree Go2 robot it reaches 78.3% success, with the margin over the strongest baseline growing from 10 to 45 points as task horizon increases.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding complementary foundation models—a VLM for reasoning and an NFM for grounded execution—is a viable and effective approach for building long-horizon physical-world agents, with performance gains that scale with task horizon.

title: Benevolent Bias in Multi-Turn Human-Agent Dialogue
summary: Bias in human-agent interaction can manifest not only through hostile language but also as benevolent bias, whereby unequal treatment hides behind a warm, positive tone. To make it detectable, we operationalise benevolent bias along two dimensions, tone and treatment, yielding three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. Building on these definitions, we construct BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues spanning user and agent demographics, roles, and generators, to support controlled evaluation. We then test two detector families on it: off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted large language model (LLM) judges. Our results reveal a detection gap: off-the-shelf detectors reliably flag overt bias yet largely miss benevolent bias, while LLM judges catch more under more explicit detection criteria but increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias, and demographic context amplifies the false alarms. These findings suggest that fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must look beyond surface cues to whether the agent's treatment is disparate.

AI.tldr: This paper studies benevolent bias in human-agent interaction, operationalizing it along tone and treatment dimensions into three classes (neutral support, overt bias, benevolent bias). The authors construct BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues, and test two detector families—off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted LLM judges—revealing a detection gap where detectors reliably flag overt bias but miss benevolent bias, while LLM judges over-detect and misclassify neutral support, especially with demographic context.
AI.motivation: Bias in human-agent interaction is not limited to hostile language; it can hide in warm, positive tones as benevolent bias. Existing detection approaches focus on surface-level hostile language, leaving subtle yet consequential unequal treatment undetected in increasingly deployed conversational agents.
AI.method: The authors operationalize benevolent bias along two dimensions (tone and treatment), defining three classes: neutral support, overt bias, and benevolent bias. They build BENEVDIAL, a class-balanced corpus of 362,880 multi-turn support dialogues varying user/agent demographics, roles, and generators. They evaluate two detector families: off-the-shelf safety detectors and prompted LLM judges.
AI.result: Off-the-shelf detectors reliably flag overt bias but largely miss benevolent bias. LLM judges catch more under explicit detection criteria but increasingly misclassify neutral support as benevolent bias, and demographic context amplifies false alarms.
AI.conclusion: Fair monitoring of human-agent dialogue must go beyond surface cues to evaluate whether the agent's treatment is truly disparate, suggesting that current detection approaches are insufficient for capturing benevolent bias.

title: Hyper-Fold: Exploring the Expressive Limit of Sequence-Geometry Learning for Proteins via Hypergraph Modeling
summary: Protein structure modeling rests on a single computational primitive: the interaction between what a residue is (sequence content) and where it sits (three-dimensional geometry). What is the expressive limit of this layer class? We show that the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products--the sufficient statistic of all second-order interactions--is the expressive ceiling, while the additive message passing of mainstream geometric GNNs is provably blind to content-geometry binding. We then introduce Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone approaching this ceiling at message-passing cost: each radius neighborhood is organized into a sequence hyperedge and a contact hyperedge, modulated by an edge-conditioned matrix-valued operator factorized into K learned basis operators with geometry-generated coefficients. Across enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection, Hyper-Fold and its hierarchical variant Hyper-Fold-Deep achieve the best results among protein-specific structure encoders; Hyper-Fold-Pocket, an anchored set-prediction head, surpasses UniSite-3D on UniSite-DS and two zero-shot benchmarks with no sequence language model features, 68x fewer parameters, and 4.8x lower latency--suggesting that a sufficiently expressive 3D backbone recovers information that fusion architectures previously borrowed from evolution-scale pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products is the expressive ceiling for residue-geometry interactions in protein structure modeling, shows additive message passing in geometric GNNs cannot capture content-geometry binding, and introduces Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone that approaches this ceiling at message-passing cost. Hyper-Fold variants achieve state-of-the-art results in enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection, with Hyper-Fold-Pocket surpassing UniSite-3D using 68x fewer parameters and 4.8x lower latency without sequence language model features.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental expressive limits of the computational layer underlying protein structure modeling—the interaction between residue sequence content and 3D geometric position—and to determine whether mainstream geometric GNN message-passing schemes are sufficiently expressive to capture content-geometry binding relationships.
AI.method: The paper first provides a theoretical analysis establishing the complete bilinear operator over content-geometry outer products as the expressive ceiling for second-order interactions, while proving additive message passing is blind to content-geometry binding. It then proposes Hyper-Fold, a rank-K separable convolutional backbone that organizes each radius neighborhood into sequence and contact hyperedges, modulated by edge-conditioned matrix operators factorized into K learned basis operators with geometry-generated coefficients. A hierarchical variant (Hyper-Fold-Deep) and an anchored set-prediction head (Hyper-Fold-Pocket) are also introduced.
AI.result: Hyper-Fold and Hyper-Fold-Deep achieve the best results among protein-specific structure encoders across enzyme function prediction, fold classification, and ligand binding site detection. Hyper-Fold-Pocket surpasses UniSite-3D on UniSite-DS and two zero-shot benchmarks, achieving this without sequence language model features while using 68x fewer parameters and 4.8x lower latency.
AI.conclusion: A sufficiently expressive 3D backbone can recover information that fusion architectures previously borrowed from evolution-scale pretraining, suggesting that the expressive ceiling of content-geometry bilinear interactions is both achievable and practically beneficial for protein structure modeling tasks.

title: Imag-Eval: a language-grounded framework for interpretable Text-to-Image instruction following evaluation
comment: Accepted to the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have recently achieved impressive visual fidelity, yet their evaluation remains constrained by benchmarks that are often difficult to interpret and insufficiently diagnostic. Existing skill-based evaluations tend to overlook critical failure modes that strongly impact usability but fall outside standard taxonomies, such as global incoherence arising from missing parts or physically implausible configurations (e.g., floating objects). In addition, prompt difficulty is typically controlled along a single dimension; either prompt length or the number of elements to generate. To address these limitations, we introduce Imag-Eval, a controlled benchmark designed to assess how T2I models ground compositional natural-language instructions into visual outputs. Unlike prior work that conflates surface linguistic complexity with compositional difficulty, Imag-Eval explicitly seeks to disentangles these factors by independently varying both the number of instances and the combination of constraints (rules), while avoiding error propagation. This design enables fine-grained and interpretable analysis of where cross-modal instruction following fails. Our benchmark comprises 1,140 prompts and 8,842 combined rules, and we evaluate it on several state-of-the-art models. Complementing this analysis with an additional study of over 2,000 prompts from a concurrent benchmark, our results suggest that, for structured skills, compositional difficulty is primarily governed by the number of grounded rules and their binding to instances,, rather than by prompt length alone.

AI.tldr: Imag-Eval is a controlled benchmark for evaluating text-to-image (T2I) models on compositional instruction grounding. It independently varies the number of instances and constraint rules to disentangle surface linguistic complexity from compositional difficulty, comprising 1,140 prompts and 8,842 rules tested on state-of-the-art models. Results from an additional 2,000+ prompt study show compositional difficulty is primarily driven by the number of grounded rules and their instance-binding, not prompt length.
AI.motivation: Existing T2I evaluation benchmarks are hard to interpret and insufficiently diagnostic, overlooking critical failure modes such as global incoherence (missing parts, physically implausible configurations like floating objects). Additionally, prompt difficulty is typically controlled along a single dimension (length or number of elements), conflating linguistic complexity with compositional difficulty.
AI.method: Imag-Eval independently varies the number of instances and the combination of constraints (rules) to disentangle linguistic complexity from compositional difficulty while avoiding error propagation. The benchmark includes 1,140 prompts and 8,842 rules evaluated across several state-of-the-art T2I models, complemented by an additional analysis of over 2,000 prompts from a concurrent benchmark.
AI.result: For structured skills, compositional difficulty is primarily governed by the number of grounded rules and their binding to instances, rather than by prompt length alone. The design enables fine-grained, interpretable analysis of where cross-modal instruction following fails.
AI.conclusion: Imag-Eval provides a more controlled and diagnostic benchmark for T2I evaluation, demonstrating that rule count and instance-binding, rather than surface prompt length, are the dominant factors in compositional instruction-following difficulty.

title: Computational Depth Measurement in Thermographic Video: Overcoming Spatial Overfitting via Spatio-Temporal Decoupling
summary: Accurate through-thickness measurement of subsurface delamination depth in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) is important for structural assessment because defect location determines affected load-bearing layers. Optical pulsed thermography (OPT) provides a two-dimensional thermal video rather than volumetric measurements, so depth must be inferred from temporal heat-diffusion responses. A challenge is spatial dataset bias: when calibration defects follow regular grids, regression models may memorize their geometry instead of learning physical relationship between thermal decay and depth. This work introduces a spatio-temporal decoupling architecture that separates spatial defect localization from temporal depth measurement. Defect regions are first localized using segmentation methods, after which thermal responses are spatially averaged and converted into sixteen physics-informed temporal, energy, statistical, and geometric features. These features expose the one-dimensional heat-conduction relationship while withholding pixel coordinates from the depth model. Four regression models are evaluated using specimen-level cross-validation: Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Advanced Multi-Layer Perceptron (Adv-MLP), and XGBoost. Unregularized trees and over-parameterized Adv-MLP exhibit calibration collapse under geometric shifts, with errors exceeding 0.5 mm. In contrast, regularized XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains cross-specimen calibration, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.056 mm and root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.085 mm. Predicted depths are merged with masks to generate Delaunay-triangulated three-dimensional defect models in three to five seconds per specimen. Results show that mathematical regularization and spatio-temporal decoupling reduce spatial memorization in thermal-video depth regression.

AI.tldr: A spatio-temporal decoupling architecture for CFRP subsurface delamination depth measurement using optical pulsed thermography, which separates spatial defect localization from temporal depth regression using physics-informed thermal features. Regularized XGBoost achieves MAE of 0.056 mm and RMSE of 0.085 mm, avoiding calibration collapse caused by spatial memorization in unregularized models.
AI.motivation: Accurate through-thickness measurement of subsurface delamination depth in CFRP is critical for structural assessment, as defect location determines which load-bearing layers are affected. While OPT provides thermal video, depth must be inferred from temporal heat diffusion responses. A key challenge is that spatial dataset bias causes regression models to memorize defect geometry rather than learn the physical heat-diffusion relationship, leading to calibration collapse under geometric shifts.
AI.method: A spatio-temporal decoupling architecture is proposed that first localizes defect regions via segmentation methods, then spatially averages thermal responses and converts them into sixteen physics-informed temporal, energy, statistical, and geometric features. These features reveal the one-dimensional heat-conduction relationship while withholding pixel coordinates from the depth model. Four regression models (RF, GBM, Adv-MLP, XGBoost) are evaluated using specimen-level cross-validation.
AI.result: Unregularized trees and over-parameterized Adv-MLP exhibit calibration collapse under geometric shifts with errors exceeding 0.5 mm. Regularized XGBoost with L1/L2 penalties and column sampling maintains cross-specimen calibration, achieving MAE of 0.056 mm and RMSE of 0.085 mm. Predicted depths are merged with masks to generate Delaunay-triangulated 3D defect models in 3-5 seconds per specimen.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical regularization and spatio-temporal decoupling reduce spatial memorization in thermal-video depth regression, providing reliable cross-specimen depth measurements and enabling rapid 3D defect visualization for CFRP structural assessment.

title: Localizing Emergent Failures in Agentic AI: Recovering Minimal Repair Families via Counterfactual Replay
summary: Failures in agentic AI systems can arise from interactions among messages exchanged by multiple large language model (LLM) agents. Pointwise attribution cannot distinguish a jointly necessary repair from alternative singleton repairs. We formulate Minimal Repair Family Recovery (MRFR): recovering all inclusion-minimal event sets whose counterfactual replay restores task success within a declared size bound. We propose Graph-Constrained Joint Replay (GCJR), which slices failure-relevant events from an execution dependency graph, constructs graph-feasible singleton and pair candidates, and verifies them by replay with paired clean counterparts. For fixed replay outcomes, GCJR is exact within its declared graph domain. On 90 in-scope cases from a 120-DAG controlled benchmark, GCJR achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match while reducing mean replay calls from 56.3 to 25.3 (55.1%) relative to exhaustive search. On a 24-case, four-agent LLM pilot, it again achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match and reduces mean model calls from 21.0 to 10.0 (52.4%); single-event replay misses jointly necessary repairs.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses failures in multi-agent LLM systems caused by interacting messages. It formulates Minimal Repair Family Recovery (MRFR)—finding all inclusion-minimal event sets whose causal replay restores task success within a size bound—and proposes Graph-Constrained Joint Replay (GCJR), which prunes the search space using an execution dependency graph. GCJR achieves exact results with ~55% fewer replay calls on both a controlled benchmark (1.000 Family Exact Match on 90/120 cases) and a real four-agent LLM pilot.
AI.motivation: Failures in agentic AI systems can stem from interactions among multiple LLM agent messages. Pointwise (single-event) attribution cannot distinguish a jointly necessary repair from alternative singleton repairs, meaning that identifying only individual faulty events is insufficient—some failures require repairing multiple events together.
AI.method: The paper formulates MRFR (Minimal Repair Family Recovery) and proposes GCJR, which: (1) slices failure-relevant events from an execution dependency graph, (2) constructs graph-feasible singleton and pair candidates, and (3) verifies them via counterfactual replay with paired clean counterparts. GCJR is exact within its declared graph domain for fixed replay outcomes.
AI.result: On 90 in-scope cases from a 120-DAG controlled benchmark, GCJR achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match while reducing mean replay calls from 56.3 to 25.3 (a 55.1% reduction). On a 24-case, four-agent LLM pilot, it again achieves 1.000 Family Exact Match and reduces mean model calls from 21.0 to 10.0 (a 52.4% reduction). Single-event replay is shown to miss jointly necessary repairs.
AI.conclusion: GCJR provides an exact and efficient mechanism for recovering all inclusion-minimal repair families in multi-agent LLM systems, demonstrating that jointly necessary repairs can be identified with substantial computational savings over exhaustive search.

title: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge
summary: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by Large Language Models (LLMs). While often plausible, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted and augmented by LLMs from informal culinary sources. Developed as part of FKG.in, a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic framework for validating LLM-augmented recipe data, thereby strengthening the foundations of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted and augmented by LLMs from informal culinary sources, developed as part of FKG.in, a knowledge graph of Indian food. The pipeline combines formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification to identify and address failure modes such as structural inconsistencies, semantic/logical incoherence, and source-text deviations.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated recipe content often contains hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting its suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. There is a need for a systematic validation framework to ensure the soundness of LLM-augmented structured recipe data.
AI.method: A multi-stage semi-automated pipeline combining: (1) formal grammars for structural consistency checks, (2) vocabulary-based validation, (3) statistical heuristics, (4) Set Transformer-based coherence modeling for semantic/logical assessment, and (5) retrieval-based verification against source texts to detect deviations.
AI.result: The framework successfully identifies and addresses common failure modes in LLM-extracted recipe data, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from source text. Although evaluated on Indian recipes within FKG.in, the methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic framework for validating LLM-augmented recipe data, strengthening the foundations of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

title: GuardianAgent: Policy-Conditioned Risk-Adaptive Anonymization with Verified Adversarial Escalation
summary: Privacy protection for live web traffic requires more than detecting private spans. Agent-based privacy protection systems must determine whether an outgoing action complies with the destination site's privacy policy, then apply only the level of rewriting or sanitisation justified by the residual disclosure risk. We present GuardianAgent, a policy-conditioned anonymization framework that couples structured risk assessment with verified adaptive rewriting. GuardianAgent computes risk through AMRSF (Adaptive Multi-factor Risk Scoring Formula), an explicit controller that combines policy-violation likelihood with data sensitivity, recipient transmission, purpose legitimacy, contextual basis, and policy transparency, rather than relying on an LLM to assign risk directly. This risk score determines both the allow/transform/deny decision and the initial anonymization level. For efficiency, GuardianAgent uses an evidential fast path for low-uncertainty policy matches and invokes an LLM slow path only for uncertain cases. For rewriting, it applies a five-level hierarchy driven by a verified adversarial guesser: guesses trigger escalation only when supported by the original text, preventing hallucinated attacker confidence from causing unnecessary over-anonymization. Experiments across three benchmarks spanning legal text (TAB), Reddit posts (SynthPAI), and multi-format synthetic PII records (PII-Masking-300k) show that GuardianAgent achieves the strongest privacy-utility trade-off among published baselines and is the only method to reach more than 0.90 privacy in all three domains, remaining robust under a backbone switch. Action-context stress tests further show that the same outgoing text receives different decisions and anonymization strengths under different recipients, purposes, action bases, and policy-transparency conditions.

AI.tldr: GuardianAgent is a policy-conditioned anonymization framework for agent-based privacy protection that couples structured risk assessment via AMRSF (Adaptive Multi-factor Risk Scoring Formula) with verified adaptive rewriting, achieving the strongest privacy-utility trade-off across three benchmarks and being the only method to exceed 0.90 privacy in all domains tested.
AI.motivation: Privacy protection for live web traffic requires more than detecting private spans—agent-based systems must determine whether an outgoing action complies with a destination site's privacy policy and apply only the level of sanitization justified by residual disclosure risk, rather than relying on LLMs to directly assign risk.
AI.method: GuardianAgent computes privacy risk through AMRSF, an explicit controller combining policy-violation likelihood with data sensitivity, recipient transmission, purpose legitimacy, contextual basis, and policy transparency. The risk score determines both decision (allow/transform/deny) and initial anonymization level. It uses an evidential fast path for low-uncertainty policy matches and an LLM slow path for uncertain cases. Rewriting employs a five-level hierarchy driven by a verified adversarial guesser that only escalates when guesses are supported by original text, preventing hallucinated over-anonymization.
AI.result: Experiments across three benchmarks (TAB for legal text, SynthPAI for Reddit posts, PII-Masking-300k for multi-format synthetic PII) show GuardianAgent achieves the strongest privacy-utility trade-off among published baselines, is the only method to exceed 0.90 privacy across all three domains, remains robust under backbone switching, and demonstrates action-context sensitivity where the same text receives different decisions and anonymization strengths under different recipients, purposes, action bases, and policy-transparency conditions.
AI.conclusion: A verified, policy-conditioned risk-scoring approach with adaptive rewriting hierarchy provides superior privacy-utility trade-offs and contextually responsive anonymization for agent-based web privacy protection.

title: Dynamic Important Example Mining for Reinforcement Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is increasingly used to strengthen the reasoning abilities of large models, yet its effectiveness is bound by how training data are selected and used. Most data-centric RFT methods rely on static or heuristic sample selection, implicitly assuming a sample's value is fixed over training. This overlooks the non-stationary dynamics of policy learning and can lead to suboptimal updates. We propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), a principled and fully automated framework that makes data utilization adaptive throughout RFT. DIEM integrates two components into each optimization step: (i) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement; and (ii) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving the update's gradient magnitude to stabilize optimization. Across several reasoning benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines. The code will be released via https://github.com/hrtan/DIEM.

AI.tldr: DIEM is a fully automated framework for adaptive data utilization in reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) of large models, using gradient-alignment importance estimation and constrained batch reweighting to dynamically select the most valuable training samples at each optimization step, consistently outperforming static and dynamic baselines across reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing data-centric RFT methods rely on static or heuristic sample selection that assumes a sample's value is fixed over training, overlooking the non-stationary dynamics of policy learning and leading to suboptimal updates.
AI.method: DIEM integrates two components per optimization step: (i) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement; and (ii) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving the update's gradient magnitude for optimization stability.
AI.result: Across several reasoning benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines. Code will be released at https://github.com/hrtan/DIEM.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, gradient-informed sample importance estimation and reweighting during RFT improves reasoning performance over static/heuristic selection methods.

title: RACER: Reinforced Agent Collaboration for Explainable Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
comment: 15 pages, 1 figures, This paper has been accepted by ICONIP 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffer from hallucination and struggle with complex reasoning tasks requiring multi-hop domain knowledge. While integrating Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provides a structured and verifiable information source, current KG-enhanced LLM paradigms usually rely on single-agent path extraction and fixed prompting, lacking adaptability and facing huge search spaces. To address these challenges, we propose RACER, a Reinforced Agent Collaboration framework for Explainable Reasoning on knowledge graphs. RACER employs a semantic-aware action pruning and teacher-guided reinforcement learning mechanism to efficiently extract high-quality reasoning pathways from large-scale KGs. Furthermore, to mitigate single-path generation pitfalls, we introduce a cross-task accumulated shared memory graph paired with an attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement module. Finally, RACER orchestrates these components through a four-role multi-agent collaboration system (GraphAgent, TemplateAgent, AnswerAgent, and CriticAgent) to dynamically refine prompts and evaluate answers. Extensive experiments on CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA datasets demonstrate that RACER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines with an average improvement of 5\%, offering robust and highly interpretable reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: RACER is a reinforced multi-agent collaboration framework that enhances LLM reasoning on knowledge graphs by combining semantic-aware action pruning, teacher-guided reinforcement learning, a cross-task shared memory graph, attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement, and a four-role agent system, achieving a 5% average improvement over SOTA KG-enhanced LLM baselines on CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucination and struggle with multi-hop domain reasoning. Current KG-enhanced paradigms rely on single-agent path extraction and fixed prompting, lacking adaptability and facing large search spaces that scale poorly with knowledge graph size.
AI.method: RACER employs (1) semantic-aware action pruning and teacher-guided reinforcement learning for efficient high-quality path extraction from large KGs, (2) a cross-task accumulated shared memory graph with an attention-driven multi-path knowledge refinement module to mitigate single-path pitfalls, and (3) a four-role multi-agent collaboration system (GraphAgent, TemplateAgent, AnswerAgent, CriticAgent) for dynamic prompt refinement and answer evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA show RACER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines with an average improvement of 5%, delivering robust and highly interpretable reasoning.
AI.conclusion: RACER demonstrates that combining reinforcement learning with multi-agent collaboration and shared memory can effectively address hallucination and complex multi-hop reasoning challenges when integrating KGs with LLMs, offering a more adaptable and interpretable reasoning paradigm.

title: EpaCache: Error-Propagation-Aware Caching for Accelerating Diffusion-Based Visual Generation
comment: This is a preview version of EpaCache, which is still under review
summary: Diffusion-based visual generative models deliver strong image and video synthesis quality but incur high inference costs because sequential samplers repeatedly evaluate large networks. Caching-based methods reduce inference latency by reusing intermediate computations across adjacent timesteps. However, existing cache controllers rely primarily on local temporal variation and overlook the trajectory-level consequences of cache reuse. We introduce Error-Propagation-Aware Cache (EpaCache), a training-free caching policy that adaptively allocates the reuse budget on timesteps with lower downstream impact. Experiments on image and video synthesis models demonstrate that EpaCache consistently improves the latency--fidelity trade-off over existing caching methods. On FLUX.1-dev, EpaCache outperforms the prior state-of-the-art caching method in both latency and fidelity, reducing inference time from $11.7$ s to $11.3$ s while improving PSNR from $21.4$ to $22.8$. On HunyuanVideo, EpaCache achieves a $2.63\times$ speedup over uncached inference and improves SSIM from $0.891$ to $0.905$ over the prior state-of-the-art method at matched latency.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EpaCache, a training-free caching policy for diffusion-based visual generative models that adaptively allocates the cache reuse budget on timesteps with lower downstream error propagation impact, improving latency-fidelity trade-offs over existing caching methods on image and video synthesis.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based visual generative models suffer from high inference costs due to sequential sampling with repeated large network evaluations. While caching-based methods reduce latency by reusing intermediate computations across adjacent timesteps, existing cache controllers rely primarily on local temporal variation and overlook the trajectory-level consequences of cache reuse, leading to suboptimal fidelity.
AI.method: EpaCache is a training-free caching policy that adaptively allocates the reuse budget on timesteps with lower downstream impact, explicitly modeling error propagation along the sampling trajectory to decide where caching is most beneficial without degrading quality.
AI.result: On FLUX.1-dev, EpaCache outperforms the prior state-of-the-art caching method in both latency and fidelity, reducing inference time from 11.7s to 11.3s while improving PSNR from 21.4 to 22.8. On HunyuanVideo, EpaCache achieves a 2.63x speedup over uncached inference and improves SSIM from 0.891 to 0.905 over the prior state-of-the-art at matched latency.
AI.conclusion: EpaCache consistently improves the latency-fidelity trade-off over existing caching methods on both image and video synthesis models, demonstrating that trajectory-level error propagation awareness is key to effective caching in diffusion-based generative models.

title: Understanding Deep Learning via Entropy Space Theory
summary: Deep learning is often criticized for its theoretical research lagging behind practice. To make deep learning easier to understand, the entropy space theory is first introduced here. The entropy space can cover all the possibilities of any deep learning model by topological structure. It is independent of network parameters. Through the designed fundamental operations and norm, entropy space is proven to be a normed space within the formal axiomatic framework. Based on the theory, a unified coordinate system is proposed. It can coordinatize every state of a model and rank them by compression of the maximal value of information entropy. The theory offers a novel priori framework for mathematical fundamentals of deep learning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces entropy space theory as a novel mathematical framework for deep learning, providing a topological structure that covers all possible states of any deep learning model, independent of network parameters. The theory proves entropy space is a normed space and proposes a unified coordinate system that coordinatizes and ranks model states by maximal information entropy compression.
AI.motivation: Deep learning's theoretical research lags significantly behind its practical applications. The authors aim to address this gap by introducing a formal theoretical framework that makes deep learning more understandable and mathematically rigorous.
AI.method: The paper introduces entropy space theory, which uses topological structures to cover all possibilities of any deep learning model independent of network parameters. It designs fundamental operations and a norm to prove entropy space is a normed space within a formal axiomatic framework, and proposes a unified coordinate system to coordinatize and rank model states based on maximal information entropy compression.
AI.result: The entropy space is formally proven to be a normed space. A unified coordinate system is established that can coordinatize every state of a model and rank them by compression of the maximal value of information entropy.
AI.conclusion: The theory offers a novel prior framework for the mathematical foundations of deep learning, potentially helping bridge the gap between theoretical understanding and practical applications.

title: MMPCBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models on Proactive Critique of Flawed Inputs
summary: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) evolve into sophisticated interactive assistants, their reliability depends not only on following instructions but also on validating them. We define Proactive Critique as the model's autonomous ability to identify, analyze and fix faulty user inputs without extra prompts. However, evaluations mainly test models under ideal circumstances or simple refusal behaviors, largely ignoring active error processing. To fill this gap, we propose MMPCBench, a comprehensive framework for evaluating MLLMs' proactive critique competence. It features a fine-grained taxonomy of 4 primary error types spanning 12 subcategories, ranging from cross-modal contradictions to missing visual premises. We adopt a hierarchical evaluation protocol to measure models' error detection, diagnosis and resolution performance, and apply alignment-aware metrics to assess the coherence between internal reasoning and final responses. Tests on 14 mainstream MLLMs show obvious weaknesses in proactive critique, especially in dealing with subtle visual anomalies. Notably, we identify a pervasive "consistency gap": reasoning models can often correctly identify and analyze errors during internal reasoning yet suppress these valid insights in final outputs to prioritize response compliance. The code and data is available at https://github.com/ALIENS32/MMPCBench.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MMPCBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) proactive critique ability—the capacity to autonomously identify, analyze, and fix faulty user inputs without prompting. The benchmark covers 4 primary error types across 12 subcategories and uses a hierarchical evaluation protocol measuring detection, diagnosis, and resolution, plus alignment-aware metrics. Testing on 14 mainstream MLLMs reveals widespread weaknesses, particularly with subtle visual anomalies, and uncovers a "consistency gap" where reasoning models correctly identify errors internally but suppress these insights in final outputs to prioritize compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM evaluations focus on ideal scenarios or simple refusal behaviors, largely ignoring the active error processing required for reliable interactive assistants. This gap means models' ability to proactively critique faulty instructions remains unassessed.
AI.method: The authors propose MMPCBench, featuring a fine-grained taxonomy of 4 primary error types spanning 12 subcategories (from cross-modal contradictions to missing visual premises), a hierarchical evaluation protocol measuring error detection, diagnosis, and resolution, and alignment-aware metrics to assess coherence between internal reasoning and final responses.
AI.result: Testing on 14 mainstream MLLMs reveals obvious weaknesses in proactive critique, especially regarding subtle visual anomalies. A pervasive "consistency gap" is identified: reasoning models often correctly identify and analyze errors during internal reasoning yet suppress valid insights in final outputs to prioritize response compliance.
AI.conclusion: Proactive critique is a significant, underaddressed capability gap in current MLLMs. The identified consistency gap suggests that current models' tendency toward response compliance undermines their reliability when user inputs are faulty, highlighting the need for alignment strategies that balance helpfulness with critical validation.

title: Accelerating Unified Multimodal Models with Core-Expansion Routing and Unified Computation Scheduling
summary: Unified multimodal models jointly support understanding and generation, but incur substantial redundant computation across tokens, layers, and generation timesteps. Through token-importance probing, we identify an asymmetric core-expansion structure: understanding exhibits a stable importance component, while generation largely shares this component but requires progress-dependent corrections. We therefore propose CE-Router, which uses a task-shared core scorer and progress-conditioned generation expansions, optimized through generation decomposition and cross-task core alignment. At inference, CE-Router compacts token computation and supplies a learned routing signal to Unified Computation Scheduling, which coordinates layer skipping, FFN pruning, diffusion-head cache reuse, and denoising-step early exit. Experiments on two representative UMM architectures demonstrate consistent quality--efficiency improvements across both tasks, retaining 98.03\% of dense understanding performance with a 1.93$\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.

AI.tldr: CE-Router introduces a task-shared core scorer with progress-conditioned generation expansions to identify and route only important tokens in unified multimodal models, combined with Unified Computation Scheduling for coordinated layer skipping, FFN pruning, diffusion-head cache reuse, and denoising-step early exit. It achieves 98.03% of dense understanding performance with a 1.93× end-to-end inference speedup across two UMM architectures.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models supporting both understanding and generation incur substantial redundant computation across tokens, layers, and generation timesteps. The authors identify via token-importance probing an asymmetric core-expansion structure: understanding has a stable importance component, while generation shares this component but requires progress-dependent corrections.
AI.method: CE-Router employs a task-shared core scorer and progress-conditioned generation expansions, optimized through generation decomposition and cross-task core alignment. At inference, it compacts token computation and provides a learned routing signal to Unified Computation Scheduling, which coordinates layer skipping, FFN pruning, diffusion-head cache reuse, and denoising-step early exit.
AI.result: Experiments on two representative UMM architectures demonstrate consistent quality-efficiency improvements across both tasks, retaining 98.03% of dense understanding performance with a 1.93× end-to-end inference speedup.
AI.conclusion: CE-Router effectively exploits the asymmetric core-expansion structure in unified multimodal models to achieve substantial inference speedups with minimal quality loss, validated across multiple architectures and tasks.

title: Predicting Future Organ Dysfunction in ICU Patients Using Temporal Convolutional Networks on MIMIC-IV Data
summary: Predicting future organ dysfunction in Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine learning approaches have largely treated the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score as an input to binary mortality prediction rather than as a continuous clinical outcome in its own right. We investigate the extent to which a Temporal Convolutional Net work (TCN) can predict next-day SOFA scores from multivariate ICU time-series data extracted from MIMIC-IV, characterise the relative contribution of each organ system to total SOFA variance and deterioration, and identify distinct trajectory patterns across ICU stays. A residual TCN trained on three-day sliding windows achieved a five-fold cross-validation R2 of 0.740 +- 0.013 and MAE of 1.431 +- 0.022, outperforming a naive persistence baseline on RMSE and R2. SHAP interpretability analysis revealed that the model functions primarily as a severity-anchoring mechanism rather than a true sequence model, with predictions dominated almost entirely by the most recent observation day. Cardiovascular dysfunction emerged as the strongest discriminator of both cross-sectional severity and acute deterioration, and unsupervised trajectory clustering identified two clinically meaningful phenotypes, an improving group (58.9%) and a persistently severe group (41.1%), differentiated by cardiovascular, hepatic, coagulation, and renal involvement. We conclude that TCNs can extract meaningful predictive signal from ICU physiological data, but that short input windows and complete-case selection bias currently limit their clinical utility, motivating future work on longer input horizons, alternative missing-data strategies, and external validation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) to predict next-day SOFA scores as a continuous clinical outcome in ICU patients from MIMIC-IV data. The model achieves R2 of 0.740 and MAE of 1.431, but SHAP analysis reveals it functions primarily as a severity-anchoring mechanism dominated by the most recent observation day rather than a true sequence model. Cardiovascular dysfunction is the strongest discriminator of severity and deterioration, and trajectory clustering identifies two phenotypes: an improving group (58.9%) and a persistently severe group (41.1%).
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning approaches in ICU treat SOFA score as an input to binary mortality prediction rather than as a continuous clinical outcome itself. Predicting future organ dysfunction is critical for early intervention but has been under-explored as a standalone predictive target.
AI.method: A residual Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) was trained on three-day sliding windows of multivariate ICU time-series data from MIMIC-IV to predict next-day SOFA scores. Five-fold cross-validation was used, with SHAP interpretability analysis and unsupervised trajectory clustering applied to characterize model behavior and patient phenotypes.
AI.result: The TCN achieved five-fold cross-validation R2 of 0.740 ± 0.013 and MAE of 1.431 ± 0.022, outperforming a naive persistence baseline on RMSE and R2. SHAP analysis showed predictions were dominated almost entirely by the most recent observation day, revealing a severity-anchoring mechanism. Cardiovascular dysfunction was the strongest discriminator of both cross-sectional severity and acute deterioration. Trajectory clustering identified two phenotypes: improving (58.9%) and persistently severe (41.1%), differentiated by cardiovascular, hepatic, coagulation, and renal involvement.
AI.conclusion: TCNs can extract meaningful predictive signal from ICU physiological data for continuous SOFA prediction, but short input windows and complete-case selection bias currently limit clinical utility. Future work should explore longer input horizons, alternative missing-data strategies, and external validation.

title: Formal Concept Analysis with Three Types of Negation
summary: Classic Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) primarily focuses on the positive relationships between objects and attributes and does not have mechanisms for handling negation.To overcome this limitation, we introduce three types of negation concepts (contradictory negation, opposite negation, intermediary negation) into FCA.Based on the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI with these three types negation, we define formal context, Galois connection operators, formal concept and concept lattice with three types of negation,this leads to the proposal of a FCACOI: Formal Concept Analysis with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation.For the reasoning in FCACOI, this paper focuses on attribute implication reasoning. Based on the logic LCOI+PLCOI and its semantics, we introduce the notion of ICOI-entailment as the semantic implication for attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI. Through ICOI-entailment, a connection is established between attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI and inference in the logic LCOI+PLCOI, it indicate that formally proven inference rules (theorems) in LCOI+PLCOI are valid in the attribute implication reasoning of FCACOI, LCOI+PLCOI provides a logical foundation for attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI. To illustrate the capability of attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI, we discuss its application in a concrete example. Moreover, we explore attribute reduction of the formal context in FCACOI, propose two research frameworks for attribute reduction from different perspectives, and compare their characteristics.We believe that, based on richer logic and semantics, FCACOI elevates FCA from a theory that describes affirmations to one that can describe affirmations and its contradiction(either this or that), opposition(extreme negation) and intermediary (transitional states between oppositions).

AI.tldr: This paper extends classic Formal Concept Analysis (FCA), which only handles positive relations between objects and attributes, by introducing three types of negation—contradictory, opposite, and intermediary negation—grounded in a logical system LCOI+PLCOI. This yields a new framework called FCACOI (Formal Concept Analysis with contradictory, opposite, and intermediary negation), including formal contexts, Galois connection operators, formal concepts, and concept lattices. The paper focuses on attribute implication reasoning via ICOI-entailment, linking it to logical inference in LCOI+PLCOI, and explores attribute reduction through two research frameworks.
AI.motivation: Classic FCA lacks mechanisms for handling negation, limiting its expressive power to only positive relationships. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by introducing multiple types of negation—contradictory, opposite, and intermediary—to capture richer semantics involving affirmation, contradiction, opposition, and transitional states.
AI.method: The authors define formal contexts, Galois connection operators, formal concepts, and concept lattices within FCACOI using the set SCOI and logic LCOI+PLCOI, which incorporates the three types of negation. They introduce ICOI-entailment as the semantic implication for attribute implication reasoning, and propose two research frameworks for attribute reduction from different perspectives.
AI.result: The paper establishes a formal connection between attribute implication reasoning in FCACOI and inference in the logic LCOI+PLCOI, showing that proven inference rules in LCOI+PLCOI are valid in FCACOI's attribute implication reasoning. It demonstrates the capability of this reasoning on a concrete example and compares the characteristics of the two proposed attribute reduction frameworks.
AI.conclusion: FCACOI elevates classic FCA from a theory describing affirmations to one that can describe affirmations and their contradictions (either/or), oppositions (extreme negation), and intermediary states (transitional states between oppositions), built on a richer logical and semantic foundation.

title: BIRD-History: A Benchmark for History-Driven Text-to-SQL with Fine-Grained Knowledge Annotations
comment: Accepted at Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP, 2026
summary: While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based text-to-SQL systems achieve impressive performance on standard benchmarks, they struggle when user queries implicitly rely on domain-specific knowledge, such as business logic, data conventions, and analytical practices, that is neither captured by the schema nor explicitly stated in the natural language question. Historical SQL query logs offer a valuable source of such knowledge, yet existing benchmarks do not adequately support evaluation of history-driven approaches. To address this gap, we introduce BIRD-History, a benchmark consisting of 1,393 tasks across 11 databases, designed to evaluate text-to-SQL systems' ability to ground underspecified natural language questions using historical SQL scripts. Each task is annotated with ground-truth labels specifying which historical queries contain relevant knowledge and which SQL clauses encode it, enabling systematic evaluation of both retrieval effectiveness and knowledge utilization. Alongside the benchmark, we propose a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts, then retrieves and reranks relevant fragments for query generation. The retriever integrates seamlessly into existing few-shot text-to-SQL pipelines without requiring prompt modifications. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across four text-to-SQL systems, highlighting the value of leveraging historical query logs for handling underspecified queries. Dataset and code are open-sourced on https://github.com/zjuidg/BIRD-History.

AI.tldr: Introduces BIRD-History, a benchmark of 1,393 tasks across 11 databases for evaluating text-to-SQL systems' ability to use historical SQL query logs to ground underspecified natural language questions. Also proposes a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts and integrates into existing few-shot text-to-SQL pipelines, yielding consistent improvements across four systems.
AI.motivation: LLM-based text-to-SQL systems perform well on standard benchmarks but fail when user queries implicitly depend on domain-specific knowledge (business logic, data conventions, analytical practices) not present in the schema or question. Historical SQL query logs capture such knowledge, yet no existing benchmark adequately supports evaluating history-driven approaches.
AI.method: Constructs BIRD-History benchmark with 1,393 tasks across 11 databases, annotated with ground-truth labels for which historical queries contain relevant knowledge and which SQL clauses encode it. Proposes a plug-in retriever that extracts five types of external knowledge from historical SQL scripts and retrieves/reranks relevant fragments for query generation, integrating into existing few-shot text-to-SQL pipelines without prompt modifications.
AI.result: Experiments show consistent improvements across four text-to-SQL systems when using the proposed retriever, demonstrating the value of leveraging historical query logs for handling underspecified queries.
AI.conclusion: Historical SQL query logs are a valuable resource for grounding underspecified natural language questions in text-to-SQL systems, and the proposed benchmark and retriever enable systematic evaluation and utilization of this knowledge source.

title: Extending TotalSegmentator: Predicting Patient and Acquisition Characteristics from CT and MR Images
summary:
Background: Patient details and acquisition metadata are important for clinical decisions, image quality control, and automated research pipelines, but may be missing or unreliable in imaging archives.
  Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fast open-source model that predicts patient and acquisition characteristics directly from CT and MR images.
  Materials and Methods: Separate 3D ResNet-10 ensembles for CT and MR were trained on 57,291 and 43,200 clinical examinations acquired from 2011 to 2025. Both predicted weight, height, age, sex, contrast presence, vertebral coverage, and image noise. The CT model additionally predicted scanner manufacturer, tube voltage, tube current, convolution kernel, and post-injection time; the MR model predicted sequence class. Performance was evaluated on internal CT (n=501) and MR (n=636) test sets and an external CT dataset (n=54).
  Results: Internal CT MAEs were 3.90 kg, 3.68 cm, and 4.42 years for weight, height, and age, with sex F1=0.990; corresponding MR results were 4.34 kg, 4.62 cm, 7.13 years, and F1=0.970. The CNN outperformed a segmentation-derived XGBoost baseline for all four core targets in both modalities (adjusted P<=.042). F1 scores were 0.963 for CT contrast, 0.953 for MR sequence, and 0.823 for MR contrast. External CT MAEs were 4.45 kg, 4.05 cm, and 5.17 years, with sex F1=0.971. CPU inference required 20 seconds for CT and 12 seconds for MR.
  Conclusion: One 3D multitask model per modality can rapidly recover patient and acquisition characteristics from heterogeneous CT and MR examinations. Models are available in TotalSegmentator: https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fast open-source 3D ResNet-10 ensemble that predicts patient demographics (weight, height, age, sex) and acquisition characteristics (contrast presence, vertebral coverage, image noise, and modality-specific parameters) directly from CT and MR images, achieving strong accuracy with inference times of ~20 seconds (CT) and ~12 seconds (MR) on CPU, and is made available in TotalSegmentator.
AI.motivation: Patient details and acquisition metadata are critical for clinical decisions, image quality control, and automated research pipelines, but are frequently missing or unreliable in imaging archives. There is a need for a fast method to recover these characteristics directly from the images themselves.
AI.method: Separate 3D ResNet-10 ensembles were trained for CT (n=57,291) and MR (n=43,200) clinical examinations. Both models predict weight, height, age, sex, contrast presence, vertebral coverage, and image noise; the CT model additionally predicts scanner manufacturer, tube voltage, tube current, convolution kernel, and post-injection time, while the MR model predicts sequence class. Performance was evaluated on internal CT (n=501) and MR (n=636) test sets and an external CT dataset (n=54), benchmarked against a segmentation-derived XGBoost baseline.
AI.result: Internal CT MAEs were 3.90 kg, 3.68 cm, and 4.42 years for weight, height, and age with sex F1=0.990; MR results were 4.34 kg, 4.62 cm, 7.13 years, and F1=0.970. The CNN outperformed the XGBoost baseline for all four core targets in both modalities (adjusted P<=.042). F1 scores were 0.963 (CT contrast), 0.953 (MR sequence), and 0.823 (MR contrast). External CT MAEs were 4.45 kg, 4.05 cm, 5.17 years with sex F1=0.971. CPU inference required 20 seconds for CT and 12 seconds for MR.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D multitask model per modality can rapidly and accurately recover patient and acquisition characteristics from heterogeneous CT and MR examinations, with models publicly available in TotalSegmentator.

title: Cross-Relational Preference Learning for Better LLM Instruction Following
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) still exhibit limited capability in following complex instructions. While existing approaches often rely on preference learning to enhance this ability, they typically overlook the relationships between the permissible response spaces of different instructions, which restricts a model to align with subtle and diverse constraint variations. To address this, we propose Cross-Relational Preference Learning (CRPL), a novel framework for constructing preference data that explicitly models inter-instruction relationships through two key techniques: Cross-Relationship Perturbation and Cross-Region Pair Sampling. This enables the generation of more diverse preference data that captures a wide spectrum of constraint variations. Additionally, we introduce an atomic constraint-based verification mechanism to rigorously assess response satisfaction, ensuring high-quality preference pair construction. Extensive experiments across multiple preference learning methods (e.g., DPO, KTO), LLM backbones and four instruction-following benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves substantial improvements over prior baselines and exhibits strong generalization.

AI.tldr: Proposes Cross-Relational Preference Learning (CRPL), a framework that constructs preference data by explicitly modeling inter-instruction relationships via Cross-Relationship Perturbation and Cross-Region Pair Sampling, with an atomic constraint-based verification mechanism, improving LLM instruction-following across multiple methods and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with complex instruction following, and existing preference learning approaches typically disregard the relationships between permissible response spaces of different instructions, limiting models from aligning with subtle and diverse constraint variations.
AI.method: CRPL introduces two key techniques: (1) Cross-Relationship Perturbation to create diverse preference data capturing constraint variations, and (2) Cross-Region Pair Sampling to sample preference pairs across the response spaces of different instructions. Additionally, an atomic constraint-based verification mechanism is used to rigorously assess response satisfaction for high-quality preference pair construction.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple preference learning methods (e.g., DPO, KTO), different LLM backbones, and four instruction-following benchmarks show substantial improvements over prior baselines with strong generalization.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling inter-instruction relationships in preference data construction significantly enhances LLMs' complex instruction-following capability, and CRPL provides a generalizable framework applicable across preference learning methods and model architectures.

title: APPSolver: Adaptive Patch Partitioning for Point-Wise Ship Flow Prediction on Unstructured Meshes
summary: Large non-uniform point sets make direct attention-based surrogate modeling costly for ship hydrodynamics. We introduce APPSolver, a point-wise flow-prediction framework built around Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP), a deterministic quadtree representation for fixed two-dimensional horizontal slices extracted from ship CFD simulations. APP assigns finer patches near the hull and coarser patches farther away, downsamples patch contents, and recovers predictions to the full reference point set. Under a corrected protocol that constructs natural $(t,t+1)$ pairs before splitting, reuses training-set normalization statistics, and reports three model seeds, learned tokenizers are more accurate than APP-Transformer, and a persistence baseline has lower one-step MAE on all three ShipBench hulls. The supported benefit of APP is therefore computational rather than universal predictive superiority: on a representative DTC input, APP-Transformer requires 1.815 GFLOPs and 1.309 ms per model forward, while a matched ablation shows that adaptive partitioning reduces MAE by 16.4-24.9\% relative to a uniform partition augmented with learned slicing. Condition encoders provide setting-dependent gains in leave-one-hull-out evaluation, but the current absolute next-state objective does not establish accurate long-horizon dynamics. These results characterize APP as a compact spatial representation with an explicit accuracy--efficiency trade-off. Code is available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/APPSolver .

AI.tldr: APPSolver is a point-wise flow-prediction framework for ship hydrodynamics that uses Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP), a quadtree-based representation that assigns finer patches near the hull and coarser patches farther away. Due to computational efficiency gains, the paper provides a corrected benchmarking protocol. However, a persistence baseline achieves lower one-step MAE on all ShipBench hulls, and learned tokenizers outperform APP-Transformer. APP's benefit is computational (1.815 GFLOPs, 1.309 ms per forward pass, 16.4-24.9% MAE reduction over uniform partitioning) rather than universal predictive superiority.
AI.motivation: Direct attention-based surrogate modeling is computationally prohibitive for large non-uniform point sets in ship hydrodynamic CFD simulations, motivating a more efficient spatial representation for point-wise flow prediction.
AI.method: APPSolver uses Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP): a deterministic quadtree applied to fixed 2D horizontal slices of ship CFD data. APP refines patches near the hull, coarsens them farther away, downsamples patch contents, and recovers predictions to the full resolution. A corrected experimental protocol constructs natural (t,t+1) pairs before splitting, reuses training-set normalization statistics, and reports three model seeds.
AI.result: On three ShipBench hulls, a persistence baseline has lower one-step MAE than APP-Transformer, and learned tokenizers outperform APP-Transformer. APP provides computational gains—on DTC input, 1.815 GFLOPs and 1.309 ms per forward pass—and reduces MAE by 16.4-24.9% over a uniform partition with learned slicing. Condition encoders help in leave-one-hull-out evaluation, but the next-state objective does not establish accurate long-horizon dynamics.
AI.conclusion: APP is characterized as a compact spatial representation offering an explicit accuracy-efficiency trade-off: its value is computational rather than universal predictive superiority. The framework is open-sourced at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/APPSolver.

title: Plant-Inspired AI: Plants as Inspiration for Novel Problem Formulations, and Two Case Studies
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has long been inspired by studies of biological intelligence. Reinforcement learning, for instance, drew inspiration from studies involving animal learning and is now a powerful paradigm for solving many real-world problems. Recently, plant biologists have uncovered a wide range of complex behaviors in plants that enable them to flexibly adapt to variable environments. Here, we argue that such behavior can motivate new AI frameworks encompassing a range of problems overlooked by existing problem-solving frameworks such as supervised learning, tree search, and constraint satisfaction. We illustrate this idea with two examples of intelligent problem-solving in plants: (1) leaf mimicry in Boquila trifoliolata, a vine capable of altering its leaves' morphology to resemble those of multiple host trees simultaneously; and (2) coordinated root-shoot growth, wherein plants allocate resources across organ systems exploring distinct environments. While leaf mimicry is highly specific to Boquila, coordination of root-shoot growth is shared across most plants. For both examples, we capture underlying computational principles and identify problems fitting these frameworks that are currently unaddressed by AI. Finally, we outline preliminary task formulations and discuss how these formulations may be applied to non-plant problems.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that plant intelligence—specifically behaviors like leaf mimicry in Boquila trifoliolata and coordinated root-shoot growth—can inspire new AI problem-solving frameworks that address challenges not covered by existing paradigms such as supervised learning, tree search, and constraint satisfaction.
