From the user's perspective, we decompose ASR into the Covert Success Rate (CSR), counting successes leaving no trace in the final response, and the Overt Success Rate (OSR), counting successes the user can detect. To understand what drives the gap, we analyze successful trajectories and find that the agent's behavior after the injection separates covert from overt: covert traces hand control back to the user task before ending, while overt traces end at the attack itself. This split follows from the ReAct format, where the final response summarizes the most recent action. Building on this observation, we propose ICoA (Induced Covert Attack), an IPI attack designed to induce covert outcomes by steering the agent back to the user task after executing the injection. Across four target models on AgentDojo, ICoA achieves the highest CSR, with gains of 3.79-12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a refined metric for evaluating indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on LLM agents, distinguishing between covert successes (CSR) and overt successes (OSR) within the traditional Attack Success Rate (ASR). It proposes ICoA, an attack designed to induce covert outcomes by steering the agent back to the user task after executing the injection, achieving the highest CSR gains of 3.79-12.01 percentage points across four target models on AgentDojo.
AI.motivation: The standard Attack Success Rate (ASR) metric is insufficient for evaluating IPI threats because it treats all successful injections equally, ignoring whether the user can detect the injected action in the agent's final response. This distinction matters significantly from the user's perspective and needs a more granular evaluation framework.
AI.method: The paper decomposes ASR into Covert Success Rate (CSR) and Overt Success Rate (OSR). By analyzing successful attack traces, it identifies that the agent's behavior after injection determines covertness: covert traces return control to the user task before ending, while overt traces end at the attack itself, a pattern arising from the ReAct format where the final response summarizes the most recent action. Based on this, the authors propose ICoA (Induced Covert Attack), an IPI attack that guides the agent back to the user task after executing the injection to produce covert outcomes.
AI.result: Across four target models on AgentDojo, ICoA achieves the highest Covert Success Rate, with improvements of 3.79-12.01 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Covert and overt successes represent meaningfully distinct outcomes in IPI attacks, and attacks can be designed to deliberately induce covert outcomes by steering the agent's post-injection behavior back to the user task, highlighting a gap in current security evaluations.

title: Augmenting Human Performance with an XR Agent Learning from Online Behavior and BCI Evidence
comment: To appear in ACM UIST 2026. 30 pages, 23 figures
summary: We present OLIVE, a framework for adapting a foundation model to provide real-time assistance in temporally demanding, high-stakes, and dynamic tasks. We show that passive EEG, fused online with behavioral evidence, can meaningfully extend the number of targets users detect and engage beyond their unaided action bandwidth. OLIVE learns from both explicit behavioral signals (the targets the user shoots down in an XR first-person shooter game) and implicit physiological signals (fixation-locked EEG) to provide timely guidance, continuously adapting a frozen vision-language model's inference on which items are task-relevant by jointly estimating per-source reliability without manual labels or offline training. Through three user studies, including two live deployments of an assistive agent driven by OLIVE in XR, we show that OLIVE Pareto-dominates prior test-time adaptation frameworks, achieving the highest convergence rate at comparable convergence speed. Combining implicit physiological and explicit behavioral signals, the OLIVE agent produces the largest and most reliable within-session improvement to a user's ability to detect and engage targets, largely independent of the individual's skill. When the target switches silently, the agent that uses both behavioral and physiological signals reconverges significantly faster than the behavior-only agent (1.27 times faster on average, p = .008), restoring trustworthy guidance at the moment the task changes, precisely when reliable assistance matters most.

AI.tldr: OLIVE is a test-time adaptation framework that fuses passive EEG with behavioral signals to extend human detection and engagement capabilities in real-time, high-stakes tasks. It jointly estimates per-source reliability to adapt a frozen vision-language model without labels or offline training, and demonstrates Pareto-dominant performance over prior frameworks—achieving 1.27× faster reconvergence when targets switch, verified through three user studies including live XR deployments.
AI.motivation: People have limited action bandwidth in temporally demanding, high-stakes dynamic tasks, and existing assistive systems rely on explicit behavioral signals alone or require manual labels/offline training. The paper motivates the need for a framework that can leverage both implicit physiological and explicit behavioral evidence in real time to extend what users can detect and engage beyond their unaided capabilities.
AI.method: OLIVE adapts a frozen vision-language model at test time by fusing fixation-locked EEG (implicit physiological) with target engagement behavior (explicit actions) from an XR first-person shooter game. It jointly estimates per-source reliability to weight each modality's contribution and provides timely guidance without manual labels or offline training. The framework was evaluated across three user studies including two live XR deployments.
AI.result: OLIVE Pareto-dominates prior test-time adaptation frameworks, achieving the highest convergence rate at comparable convergence speed. The combined behavioral+physiological agent produced the largest and most reliable within-session improvements in target detection and engagement, largely independent of individual skill. When the target switched silently, the multimodal agent reconverged 1.27× faster than behavior-only (p = .008).
AI.conclusion: Passive EEG fused with behavioral evidence meaningfully extends user capability beyond unaided action bandwidth. Combining implicit physiological and explicit behavioral signals in a reliability-weighted test-time adaptation framework provides trustworthy, timely assistance that adapts rapidly to changing task demands—precisely when reliable support matters most.

title: Dense Clinical Contrasts Enhance Medical Knowledge Updating in Large Language Models
summary: Medical knowledge changes continually, making large language models vulnerable to relying on outdated yet clinically plausible information. We study whether the format of supervision affects medical knowledge updating under a matched training-budget setting. We introduce SEER-Bench, a temporally anchored oncology-staging benchmark curated from the latest versioned SEER Research Data release, and render identical medical update events from NCCN oncology guidelines into four supervision formats: EMQ, MSQ, FITB, and SAQ. Across SEER-Bench and HealthBench Professional, EMQ gives the most stable external transfer and retention among same-budget SFT variants. With EMQ supervision, the updated 4B model produces competitive results on temporally anchored oncology staging, reaching 64.8% answer accuracy and 59.6% rationale accuracy on SEER-Bench. Diagnostic analyses suggest that EMQ exposes denser clinical contrast signals while preserving discriminative representations with smaller movement from the base model. These results show that medical knowledge updating depends not only on the update algorithm, but also on how knowledge is structured as supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how supervision format affects medical knowledge updating in LLMs under matched training budgets, introducing SEER-Bench and showing that EMQ (Extended Multiple-choice Questions) format yields the best external transfer, retention, and accuracy on temporally anchored oncology staging tasks.
AI.motivation: Medical knowledge evolves continuously, yet LLMs are prone to relying on outdated but clinically plausible information. Prior work focuses on update algorithms but overlooks how the format of supervision itself influences knowledge updating effectiveness.
AI.method: The authors introduce SEER-Bench, a temporally anchored oncology-staging benchmark based on the latest SEER Research Data release. Identical medical update events from NCCN oncology guidelines are rendered into four supervision formats: EMQ (extended multiple-choice), MSQ (multi-select questions), FITB (fill-in-the-blank), and SAQ (short-answer questions). Models are fine-tuned under a matched training-budget setting, then evaluated on SEER-Bench and HealthBench Professional for external transfer and retention.
AI.result: EMQ gives the most stable external transfer and retention among same-budget SFT variants. The EMQ-supervised 4B model achieves 64.8% answer accuracy and 59.6% rationale accuracy on SEER-Bench. Diagnostic analyses show EMQ exposes denser clinical contrast signals and preserves discriminative representations with smaller deviation from the base model.
AI.conclusion: Medical knowledge updating depends not only on the update algorithm but also on how knowledge is structurally formatted as supervision. EMQ is a superior supervision format for temporally anchored medical knowledge updates.

title: DERELAB: Probing Defeasible Reasoning and Confirmation Bias in LLMs with a Generative Benchmark
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Defeasible reasoning is a type of reasoning where inferences are drawn from plausible current evidence, but can be retracted upon the introduction of newer evidence. Although recent studies have examined language-model behaviors in defeasible reasoning, the datasets have been static and lack wide coverage of non-monotonic reasoning categories. We introduce DeReLab, a generative framework that produces multi-turn belief-updating conversations from parameterized graph structures across default and inheritance reasoning, with formally verified ground truth at every turn, enabling controlled measurement of how models respond to confirming and disconfirming evidence. This controlled generation process creates a testbed for experimental designs that isolate specific reasoning demands. Applying this capability to the study of confirmation bias, we evaluate nine open and proprietary large language models and find that nearly all exhibit a systematic tendency to accept congruent evidence while resisting incongruent updates, with several models correctly identifying a weakening update yet failing to revise their conclusion. We believe our work and findings will facilitate future research on evaluating language models in defeasible reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DeReLab, a generative framework that creates multi-turn belief-updating conversations with formally verified ground truth across default and inheritance reasoning categories, enabling controlled measurement of how language models respond to confirming/disconfirming evidence. Evaluating nine LLMs, the authors find nearly all exhibit confirmation bias—accepting congruent evidence while resisting incongruent updates.
AI.motivation: Existing datasets for studying defeasible reasoning in language models are static and lack broad coverage of non-monotonic reasoning categories, limiting controlled investigation of how models handle evidence that may retract previous inferences.
AI.method: DeReLab is a generative framework that produces multi-turn belief-updating conversations from parameterized graph structures spanning default and inheritance reasoning, with formally verified ground truth at each turn. The controlled generation enables experimental designs that isolate specific reasoning demands, which is applied to study confirmation bias in nine open and proprietary LLMs.
AI.result: Nearly all evaluated LLMs exhibit a systematic tendency to accept congruent evidence while resisting incongruent updates; several models correctly identify that a piece of evidence weakens a conclusion yet fail to revise their original belief accordingly.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a controlled testbed for evaluating defeasible reasoning in LLMs and reveals widespread confirmation bias in current models, facilitating future research on this important reasoning capability.

title: From Metaheuristics to Exact Methods: A CP-SAT Approach for Multi-Objective Healthcare Workforce Scheduling
comment: 13 pages, 10 tables. Accepted at MODeM Workshop, IJCAI-ECAI 2026. Extends arXiv:2607.05177
summary:
Healthcare workforce scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem requiring simultaneous satisfaction of labor regulations, coverage requirements, employee preferences and cost objectives. Existing approaches (genetic algorithms, integer programming, constraint programming) model 6-12 constraints at shift-level granularity and cannot guarantee regulatory compliance. They also lack support for multi-role, multi-skill heterogeneity, mandatory break scheduling with midpoint control, acuity-weighted workload equity, sub-shift granularity, inter-week stability, and cross-midnight shifts.
  This paper presents CP-SAT: a Constraint Programming formulation for multi-role, multi-skill healthcare scheduling. CP-SAT enforces 14 hard constraints guaranteeing zero regulatory violations, while optimizing 15 soft objectives via a unified weighted penalty function. Contributions include a shift-window decomposition enabling break scheduling with centrality control, acuity-weighted workload equity, multi-granularity resolution from 15 minutes to 1 day, inter-week stability, and grid-offset preprocessing mapping cross-midnight shifts into a single scheduling day without solver changes.
  CP-SAT is evaluated on 18 instances: five synthetic hospital units (10-33 nurses), 10 INRC-II benchmarks (5-80 nurses, up to 8-week horizons) and 3 NRP-23 compatible instances (10-25 nurses) with cross-midnight Night shifts. Results: zero hard-constraint violations across all 18 instances by construction; proven optimality on INRC-II n005w4 (objective 118, gap 0.0%, 104s); feasible schedules scaling to 179,800 variables and 351,425 constraints (80 nurses); service quality improved 50-67% over MOGA; and model size scaling near-linearly at approximately 4,400 variables per employee. The formulation enforces 29 total constraints (14 hard, 15 soft), nearly three times the industry average.

AI.tldr: CP-SAT is a Constraint Programming formulation for multi-role, multi-skill healthcare workforce scheduling that enforces 14 hard constraints (guaranteeing zero regulatory violations) and optimizes 15 soft objectives via a unified weighted penalty function. It introduces shift-window decomposition for break scheduling, acuity-weighted workload equity, multi-granularity resolution, inter-week stability, and grid-offset preprocessing for cross-midnight shifts. Evaluated on 18 instances (synthetic, INRC-II, NRP-23), it achieves zero hard-constraint violations, proven optimality on one INRC-II benchmark, scales to 80 nurses and 179,800 variables, and improves service quality 50-67% over MOGA.
AI.motivation: Existing healthcare scheduling approaches model only 6-12 constraints at shift-level granularity and cannot guarantee regulatory compliance. They lack support for multi-role/multi-skill heterogeneity, mandatory break scheduling with midpoint control, acuity-weighted workload equity, sub-shift granularity, inter-week stability, and cross-midnight shifts—all critical in real-world hospital operations.
AI.method: A Constraint Programming (CP-SAT) formulation enforcing 14 hard constraints and 15 soft objectives via a single weighted penalty function. Key innovations include: (1) shift-window decomposition for break scheduling with centrality control, (2) acuity-weighted workload equity, (3) multi-granularity resolution (15 min to 1 day), (4) inter-week stability modeling, and (5) grid-offset preprocessing mapping cross-midnight shifts into a single scheduling day without modifying the solver.
AI.result: On 18 instances (5 synthetic hospital units, 10 INRC-II benchmarks, 3 NRP-23 instances), CP-SAT achieved: zero hard-constraint violations across all instances by construction; proven optimality on INRC-II n005w4 (objective 118, 0% gap, 104s); scalability to 179,800 variables and 351,425 constraints (80 nurses); 50-67% service quality improvement over MOGA; near-linear model scaling at ~4,400 variables per employee; and 29 total constraints (nearly 3x the industry average of 6-12).
AI.conclusion: CP-SAT demonstrates that a comprehensive Constraint Programming formulation can simultaneously deliver regulatory compliance guarantees, rich real-world feature coverage (breaks, acuity, multi-skill, cross-midnight shifts), proven optimality on benchmark instances, and scalable performance—significantly advancing beyond prior approaches in both constraint richness and solution quality.

title: EvoSkill Injection: Red-Teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in Self-Evolving Agents
summary: LLM-based agent systems increasingly adopt skill-based architectures to reduce repetitive reasoning costs and improve stable, efficient task execution. Recent studies propose self-evolving agents that autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills from past experiences to enable continuous capability evolution. However, autonomous skill evolution introduces a new attack surface in which malicious capabilities are generated, stored, and reused as legitimate skills. In this paper, we define EvoSkill Injection as a threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents. We further propose SARGE (Red-teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in self-evolving agents), a red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model through iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. To support our framework, we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a post-attack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors. Our evaluation shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EvoSkill Injection, a new threat model targeting autonomous skill generation and evolution pipelines in self-evolving LLM-based agents. The authors propose SARGE, a red-teaming framework with a benchmark (EvoSkillBench and EvoSkillSafetyBench) to evaluate and demonstrate that malicious skills can be injected, persistently stored, and repeatedly activated in such systems.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills, which introduces a new attack surface where malicious capabilities can be injected, stored, and reused as legitimate skills—a security risk not previously addressed.
AI.method: The paper defines EvoSkill Injection as a threat model, proposes the SARGE red-teaming framework (iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement), and constructs two benchmarks: EvoSkillBench for malicious interaction trajectories and EvoSkillSafetyBench for post-attack evaluation of skill retrieval and activation.
AI.result: Evaluation shows SARGE induces malicious skill formation, and injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, demonstrating the risk of persistent capability corruption in self-evolving agents.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous skill evolution introduces critical security vulnerabilities that enable persistent capability corruption, requiring attention to defense mechanisms for skill-based agent architectures.

title: CHASE: How Content Ecosystems Are Reshaped When Ranking Is the Only Target
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026
summary: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is increasingly used to improve content visibility in LLM-based retrieval systems, yet its population-level effects under repeated optimization remain poorly understood. We introduce Content Homogenization under rAnking Signal Exploitation (CHASE), a controlled simulation framework for studying how content ecosystems are reshaped when creators repeatedly adapt documents to an LLM ranking signal. We use ranking as a proxy for source visibility and validate this abstraction against citations in grounded generated responses, obtaining a rank-citation AUC of 0.853 $\pm$ 0.093 across six domains. CHASE then iterates ranking, feature discrimination, rewriting, and evaluation over 20 rounds across different domains. Quality-ranking alignment decreases in all six domains: from R0 to R20, the change in Spearman's rho ranges from -0.107 to -0.018, with a mean change of -0.068, which means documents closer to the ranking feature profile become less aligned with independently judged document quality over the simulation horizon. A random-target control has shown that it is associated with adaptation toward ranking-derived incentives rather than iterative rewriting alone. The resulting ecosystem dynamics are strongly domain-dependent. Together, these findings show how repeated optimization against a fixed LLM ranking signal can reshape both content populations and the incentives faced by content creators.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CHASE, a controlled simulation framework to study how repeated content optimization against LLM-based ranking signals reshapes content ecosystems. Over 20 rounds across six domains, quality-ranking alignment consistently decreases (mean Spearman's rho change of -0.068), showing that documents adapted to ranking features become less aligned with independently judged quality. A random-target control confirms this stems from adaptation to ranking incentives rather than rewriting alone, with domain-dependent ecosystem dynamics.
AI.motivation: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is increasingly used to improve content visibility in LLM-based retrieval systems, yet its population-level effects under repeated optimization remain poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap by studying how content ecosystems are reshaped when creators repeatedly adapt documents to an LLM ranking signal.
AI.method: CHASE (Content Homogenization under rAnking Signal Exploitation) is a controlled simulation framework that iterates ranking, feature discrimination, rewriting, and evaluation over 20 rounds across six domains. The framework uses ranking as a proxy for source visibility, validated by a rank-citation AUC of 0.853 ± 0.093 against citations in grounded generated responses. A random-target control isolates the effect of adaptation toward ranking-derived incentives versus iterative rewriting alone.
AI.result: Quality-ranking alignment decreases in all six domains from R0 to R20, with Spearman's rho changes ranging from -0.107 to -0.018 (mean -0.068). Documents closer to the ranking feature profile become less aligned with independently judged document quality over the simulation horizon. The random-target control shows this is associated with adaptation toward ranking-derived incentives. Ecosystem dynamics are strongly domain-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Repeated optimization against a fixed LLM ranking signal can reshape both content populations and the incentives faced by content creators, leading to quality-ranking misalignment. The findings highlight the need to consider population-level consequences of GEO beyond individual content visibility improvements.

title: CM2: Multimodal Cultural Reasoning via an Integrated Multi-Agent Framework
comment: Accepted to the 23rd Pacific Rim International Conference on Artificial Intelligence (PRICAI 2026) as a short paper. 11 pages, 4 figures. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/GitHub-12138/CM2-Multimodal-Cultural-Reasoning-via-an-Integrated-Multi-Agent-Framework
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown remarkable success in STEM domains, where progress is often driven by vertical, step-by-step deduction under relatively stable symbol systems. Their horizontal, interdisciplinary cultural reasoning, however, remains underexplored.We propose CM2, a multi-agent framework grounded in the cognitive pathway of human cultural interpretation. CM2 integrates multimodal perception, retrieval-augmented generation, networked reasoning, gated fusion, and reward-driven feedback.Experiments on CM2D across multiple MLLM backbones show consistent gains over CoT and typical reasoning paradigms; ablations validate each module's contribution, and conflict analyses confirm genuine cross-modal arbitration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CM2, a multi-agent framework for horizontal interdisciplinary cultural reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). It integrates multimodal perception, retrieval-augmented generation, networked reasoning, gated fusion, and reward-driven feedback, modeled on human cultural interpretation pathways. Experiments on the CM2D benchmark show consistent improvements over chain-of-thought and standard reasoning paradigms across multiple MLLM backbones, with ablations and conflict analyses confirming module contributions and genuine cross-modal arbitration.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs excel at vertical, step-by-step STEM reasoning with stable symbol systems, their horizontal, interdisciplinary cultural reasoning remains underexplored. The authors aim to address this gap by proposing a framework that mimics the cognitive pathway of human cultural interpretation.
AI.method: CM2 is a multi-agent framework incorporating five components: multimodal perception, retrieval-augmented generation, networked reasoning, gated fusion, and reward-driven feedback, collectively designed to emulate human cultural interpretation processes.
AI.result: Experiments on the CM2D benchmark across multiple MLLM backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains over CoT and typical reasoning paradigms. Ablation studies validate each module's contribution, and conflict analyses confirm genuine cross-modal arbitration behavior.
AI.conclusion: CM2 effectively advances MLLMs' cultural reasoning capabilities by integrating a human-inspired cognitive pathway into a multi-agent framework, with validated modular contributions and genuine cross-modal decision-making.

title: ScienceArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Latest Scientific Olympiad Competitions
summary: Benchmark saturation and data contamination increasingly obscure genuine scientific reasoning in frontier LLMs. We introduce \textsc{ScienceArena}, an olympiad-style benchmark from thirteen public science competitions in physics, chemistry, and biology, including IPhO and IChO 2025--2026, IBO 2023, USAPhO 2026, and USNCO 2025. Its open-ended, multi-step problems use process-credit rubrics, making faithful scoring difficult. We build ScienceArena through an expert-audited digitization pipeline that converts official exams, figures, solutions, and rubrics into structured items verified by olympiad medalists. To scale evaluation beyond costly human grading, we calibrate LLM-as-judge against medalist ground truth on archived answers from five models across IPhO and IChO; two strong judges stay within one point of expert total scores. Medalist notes show that failures often stem from visual grounding, structure fidelity, and global problem control rather than missing terminology. Evaluating fourteen recent LLMs with interleaved solving, we find that top models obtain medal-equivalent rubric scores on several public international exams, while chemistry and long-horizon consistency remain key bottlenecks. We provide an interactive \href{https://science-arena.onrender.com/}{demo}.

AI.tldr: ScienceArena is an olympiad-style benchmark built from thirteen public science competitions (physics, chemistry, biology) with open-ended, multi-step problems scored via process-credit rubrics. It uses an expert-audited digitization pipeline verified by olympiad medalists, calibrates LLM-as-judge against medalist ground truth, and evaluates fourteen recent LLMs, finding top models achieve medal-equivalent rubric scores on international exams while chemistry and long-horizon consistency remain bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Benchmark saturation and data contamination obscure genuine scientific reasoning in frontier LLMs, necessitating a fresh, difficult benchmark that resists memorization and tests true multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: Built via an expert-audited digitization pipeline converting official exams, figures, solutions, and rubrics into structured items verified by olympiad medalists. Calibrates LLM-as-judge against medalist ground truth on archived answers from five models across IPhO and IChO. Evaluates fourteen LLMs with interleaved solving.
AI.result: Two strong judges stay within one point of expert total scores. Top models obtain medal-equivalent rubric scores on several public international exams; chemistry and long-horizon consistency remain key bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: ScienceArena provides a credible, contamination-resistant benchmark for assessing scientific reasoning, with failure analysis indicating bottlenecks in visual grounding, structure fidelity, and global problem control rather than missing terminology.

title: Learning-Assisted Congestion-Aware Route Scheduling for Semiconductor Fab Material Control Systems
summary: Automated material handling systems in semiconductor fabs are operated by a material control system (MCS) that must schedule a relay route for every transport command online, before execution. This is a data-driven scheduling problem in which route cost is dominated in the upper tail by queueing at heterogeneous, partially observable relay equipment, so route selection requires estimating both delivery time and congestion risk at the decision moment. This paper proposes a transport-network-aware dynamic congestion representation (TN-DCR). Built on a static directed transport graph induced by historically observed relay segments, TN-DCR combines structural route priors, multi-window network-wide congestion context, route-level bottleneck exposure, and an inductive graph-aware route embedding, all constructed under a prediction-time-safety invariant that admits only information observed strictly before the prediction moment. The representation feeds separate queue- and transfer-time regressors and an ordinal multi-label classifier producing calibrated multi-threshold exceedance scores, with an empirical-Bayes stock-key residual correction reducing systematic queue-time underprediction. The predictions serve as costs in a risk-constrained route-scheduling rule that minimizes predicted delivery time subject to a bound on extreme-congestion probability, embedding the learned predictors within a lightweight operations-research decision model. In a controlled closed-loop evaluation, mean delivery time falls by 16.4\% and internal resource waiting time by 22.6\% while throughput remains essentially unchanged.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TN-DCR, a transport-network-aware dynamic congestion representation for online route scheduling in semiconductor fab automated material handling systems. The approach combines structural route priors, multi-window congestion context, bottleneck exposure, and graph-aware route embeddings to predict queue and transfer times, feeds these into a risk-constrained route-scheduling rule, and achieves 16.4% mean delivery time and 22.6% internal resource waiting time reductions without throughput loss.
AI.motivation: Route cost in semiconductor fab material handling is dominated by queueing at heterogeneous, partially observable relay equipment. Since scheduling decisions must be made online before execution, there is a need to estimate both delivery time and congestion risk at the decision moment, which current approaches do not adequately address.
AI.method: TN-DCR builds on a static directed transport graph from historically observed relay segments, combining structural route priors, multi-window network-wide congestion context, route-level bottleneck exposure, and an inductive graph-aware route embedding under a prediction-time-safety invariant. Separate regressors predict queue and transfer times, an ordinal multi-label classifier produces calibrated multi-threshold exceedance scores, and an empirical-Bayes stock-key residual correction reduces systematic queue-time underprediction. Predictions serve as costs in a risk-constrained scheduling rule that minimizes predicted delivery time subject to extreme-congestion probability bounds.
AI.result: In a controlled closed-loop evaluation, mean delivery time decreased by 16.4%, internal resource waiting time by 22.6%, while throughput remained essentially unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The proposed representation and prediction-driven risk-constrained scheduling approach effectively reduces delivery times and internal waiting times in semiconductor fab material handling without sacrificing throughput, demonstrating the value of combining data-driven congestion prediction with lightweight operations-research scheduling.

title: DiffPDE: Masked Diffusion Language Models as PDE Solver
summary: Existing approaches for synthesizing Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solvers predominantly rely on autoregressive models, yet their global left-to-right decoding incurs substantial redundancy when addressing inherently localized bugs. In this work, we challenge this inefficient paradigm and propose DiffPDE, a framework leveraging discrete diffusion language models for targeted code repair. By introducing a localized re-masking and infilling strategy, DiffPDE regenerates only erroneous regions while preserving correct context, naturally aligning generation with the sparse nature of PDE errors. Furthermore, to handle coupled bugs requiring sequential interventions, we present Iterative Debugging GRPO (ID-GRPO), a reinforcement learning scheme that enables multi-round debugging within single trajectories via intermediate rewards. Experiments on PDEBench show that DiffPDE achieves competitive accuracy, outperforms same-scale AR models, and significantly accelerates repair.

AI.tldr: DiffPDE is a framework using discrete diffusion language models for targeted PDE solver code repair, featuring localized re-masking/infilling and iterative reinforcement learning for multi-round debugging.
AI.motivation: Existing autoregressive PDE solver synthesis approaches use global left-to-right decoding, which is inefficient when bugs are inherently localized and sparse. This paradigm creates substantial redundancy in the repair process.
AI.method: DiffPDE employs a discrete diffusion language model with a localized re-masking and infilling strategy that regenerates only erroneous regions while preserving correct context. It also introduces ID-GRPO, an iterative reinforcement learning scheme providing intermediate rewards for multi-round debugging within single trajectories to handle coupled bugs.
AI.result: Experiments on PDEBench show DiffPDE achieves competitive accuracy, outperforms same-scale autoregressive models, and significantly accelerates the repair process.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based targeted repair is a more efficient and effective paradigm for PDE solver synthesis than autoregressive approaches, particularly given the localized nature of PDE code bugs.

title: Designing an Auditable LLM-Supported Workflow for Qualitative Thematic Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for scaling qualitative analysis, but existing applications often provide limited methodological transparency regarding how qualitative methods are translated into computational procedures. This paper presents an auditable and privacy-preserving computational operationalization of inductive and latent Thematic Analysis (TA). This paper first derives five design principles from the methodological requirements of TA and the conditions introduced by LLM-based inference: preserving interpretative context, maintaining traceable relationships between empirical material and analytical outputs, representing analytical constructs and reasoning explicitly, constraining LLM inference to interpretative tasks, and enabling privacy-preserving local deployment. Second, it presents a proof-of-concept for a two-phase workflow that operationalizes these principles by combining interpretative LLM inference with deterministic procedural control to generate codes, analytical justifications, themes, and theme descriptions while preserving explicit links to the source material. Third, it proposes an evaluation framework combining structural comparison with human-led TA and independent expert assessment of analytical quality. The evaluation is conducted on semi-structured Danish interview transcripts. and the results shows that the workflow produces code-level outputs with coverage broadly comparable to human annotations and highly rated analytical justifications, while generating a more compressed thematic structure characterized by fewer and broader themes. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of auditable LLM-supported TA through a modular workflow designed to scale to larger datasets, accommodate different LLMs, and support transfer across research domains, with domain adaptation primarily requiring adjustments to the prompting strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an auditable and privacy-preserving computational operationalization of inductive latent Thematic Analysis using LLMs, deriving five design principles, implementing a two-phase workflow combining interpretative LLM inference with deterministic procedural control, and evaluating it on Danish interview transcripts with results showing comparable code coverage to human annotations but more compressed thematic structures.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM applications for qualitative analysis lack methodological transparency regarding how qualitative methods are translated into computational procedures. There is a need for auditable and privacy-preserving approaches that faithfully operationalize qualitative methods like Thematic Analysis.
AI.method: The paper derives five design principles from TA methodological requirements and LLM inference constraints (preserving interpretative context, traceable empirical-analytical relationships, explicit analytical constructs, constrained LLM inference to interpretative tasks, privacy-preserving local deployment). It then implements a two-phase proof-of-concept workflow combining LLM interpretative inference with deterministic procedural control, and proposes an evaluation framework using structural comparison with human TA and independent expert assessment.
AI.result: Evaluation on semi-structured Danish interview transcripts shows code-level outputs with coverage broadly comparable to human annotations and highly rated analytical justifications, but with a more compressed thematic structure characterized by fewer and broader themes.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of auditable LLM-supported TA through a modular workflow that scales to larger datasets, accommodates different LLMs, and transfers across research domains with domain adaptation primarily requiring adjustments to prompting strategy.

title: GarmentWeaver: Schema-Aware Structured Synthesis for Multimodal Sewing Patterns
summary: Multimodal Sewing pattern generation aims to infer executable sewing patterns from design cues such as sketches and textual descriptions. As an interpretable and simulation-compatible representation, sewing patterns are particularly valuable for digital garment creation. However, existing methods often model garment specifications as flat long sequences, which entangles garment structure with detailed parameters and leads to redundant components, inaccurate local details, and poor simulation compatibility. In this paper, we present GarmentWeaver, a schema-aware framework for multimodal Sewing pattern generation. GarmentWeaver constructs compact hierarchical targets by activating garment-relevant structural branches and predicts executable Sewing patterns in a structured manner. Specifically, we introduce a schema-aware target construction strategy, build the generator on top of a pretrained vision-language model for multimodal garment understanding, and impose feasibility-aware regularization to encourage structurally valid and simulation-compatible outputs. Extensive experiments show that GarmentWeaver produces more accurate and more executable sewing patterns than strong baselines, while also yielding better simulation results. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of schema-aware structured generation for reliable multimodal Sewing pattern prediction.

AI.tldr: GarmentWeaver is a schema-aware framework for multimodal sewing pattern generation that constructs compact hierarchical targets and predicts executable sewing patterns in a structured manner, outperforming strong baselines in accuracy, executability, and simulation compatibility.
AI.motivation: Existing methods model garment specifications as flat long sequences, which entangle garment structure with detailed parameters, leading to redundant components, inaccurate local details, and poor simulation compatibility in multimodal sewing pattern generation.
AI.method: GarmentWeaver introduces a schema-aware target construction strategy that activates garment-relevant structural branches to build compact hierarchical targets, builds the generator on a pretrained vision-language model for multimodal garment understanding, and imposes feasibility-aware regularization to encourage structurally valid and simulation-compatible outputs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show GarmentWeaver produces more accurate and more executable sewing patterns than strong baselines, while also yielding better simulation results.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of schema-aware structured generation for reliable multimodal sewing pattern prediction.

title: AdaPath: Query-Adaptive Path-Finding via Path-Bank for Multi-Hop Implicit Biomedical KGQA
summary: Path-finding over knowledge graphs has become an effective way to ground LLM reasoning on multi-hop questions. However, biomedical QA introduces two distinct challenges that general-domain methods are not designed for: (i) queries do not expose intermediate reasoning and can be answered through multiple valid pathways, and (ii) biomedical knowledge graphs are densely connected, so path-finding methods easily take wrong turns. To address these challenges, we propose AdaPath, a path-finding framework that retrieves query-adaptive meta-paths from Path-Bank, which captures both query semantics and biomedical knowledge graph structure. AdaPath provides the missing cues in biomedical queries while effectively pruning dense knowledge graph neighborhoods during multi-hop reasoning. We further release BioStrat-QA, a biomedical KGQA benchmark that stratifies multi-hop queries by how much intermediate reasoning they expose. Across biomedical KGQA benchmarks, AdaPath consistently outperforms baselines, sustaining meaningful path-finding even when multi-hop queries expose less surface information. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jun-Hyeong-Kim/AdaPath.

AI.tldr: AdaPath is a path-finding framework for biomedical knowledge graph QA that retrieves query-adaptive meta-paths from a Path-Bank to address challenges of hidden intermediate reasoning in queries and dense KG connectivity. The authors also release BioStrat-QA, a benchmark stratifying multi-hop queries by how much intermediate reasoning they expose.
AI.motivation: Biomedical QA poses two challenges not addressed by general-domain path-finding methods: (i) queries lack exposed intermediate reasoning and can be answered via multiple valid pathways, and (ii) biomedical knowledge graphs are densely connected, making path-finding prone to wrong turns.
AI.method: AdaPath retrieves query-adaptive meta-paths from a Path-Bank that jointly captures query semantics and biomedical knowledge graph structure. This provides missing contextual cues in queries while pruning dense KG neighborhoods during multi-hop reasoning. A new benchmark, BioStrat-QA, stratifies multi-hop queries by the amount of intermediate reasoning they expose.
AI.result: AdaPath consistently outperforms baselines across biomedical KGQA benchmarks, maintaining meaningful path-finding even when multi-hop queries expose less surface information.
AI.conclusion: Query-adaptive meta-path retrieval from a structured Path-Bank effectively grounds LLM multi-hop reasoning on biomedical knowledge graphs, particularly benefiting queries with less exposed intermediate reasoning. The code and benchmark are publicly released.

title: TuringLLM: Efficiently Scaling Foundation Models Toward Physical AI
summary: We present Turing-20B-A2B, a 20B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model that activates approximately 2B parameters per token, designed for long-context and latency-sensitive physical AI applications. The model adopts Quantile Routing in a dynamic top-k configuration, enabling token-adaptive expert allocation while maintaining balanced expert utilization and a controlled average compute budget. During deployment, we further apply capacity-constrained routing to prompt prefill for more regular and efficient expert execution, while retaining dropless routing during pretraining. Turing-20B-A2B also employs a hybrid attention architecture that combines Lightning Attention with a small number of full-attention layers for efficient long-context modeling. The model is pretrained with a progressive three-stage curriculum and extended to a native context length of 128K through continued pretraining, with further inference-time extension to 512K using YaRN. Despite its compact active-parameter budget, Turing-20B-A2B achieves, at the base-model stage, overall general capability exceeding Qwen3-8B Base and approaching Qwen3.5-9B Base, while maintaining strong long-context performance and favorable prefill-latency scaling. These results demonstrate an effective balance among model capability, long-context scalability, and practical inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Turing-20B-A2B is a 20B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model activating ~2B parameters per token, combining Quantile Routing with dynamic top-k expert allocation, hybrid Lightning/full attention, and a progressive three-stage curriculum to achieve native 128K context (extendable to 512K via YaRN). It outperforms Qwen3-8B Base and approaches Qwen3.5-9B Base on general capabilities while maintaining strong long-context performance and efficient prefill latency.
AI.motivation: To address the need for large language models that balance high capability, long-context handling, and low inference latency for physical AI applications that require real-time responsiveness and efficient compute.
AI.method: The model employs (1) Quantile Routing with dynamic top-k expert selection for token-adaptive expert allocation with balanced utilization, (2) capacity-constrained routing during prefill for regular execution while using dropless routing in pretraining, (3) hybrid attention combining Lightning Attention with a few full-attention layers for long contexts, and (4) a progressive three-stage pretraining curriculum with continued pretraining to 128K and inference-time YaRN extension to 512K.
AI.result: Turing-20B-A2B exceeds Qwen3-8B Base and approaches Qwen3.5-9B Base on general capability at the base-model stage, while maintaining strong long-context performance and favorable prefill-latency scaling with only ~2B active parameters per token.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that a well-designed MoE architecture with dynamic routing and hybrid attention can effectively balance model capability, long-context scalability, and practical inference efficiency, making it suitable for latency-sensitive physical AI deployments.

title: Automated Testing of LLM-Based Post Hoc Explainers Using Model Checking as an Oracle
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used as post hoc explainers of sequential decision-making policies, producing natural-language explanations of why an action was chosen. However, LLMs often generate plausible but incorrect statements, and no existing approach systematically tests whether such explanations are faithful to the underlying environment. Two classic software testing challenges stand in the way: there is no oracle for the correctness of an explanation, and the test inputs, natural language queries about a policy's behavior, lack the structure needed for systematic test case generation. We address both. Probabilistic model checking provides the test oracle, computing exact reference results against which LLM answers are graded automatically. A taxonomy of post hoc query categories structures the input space around the environment-level facts from which policy explanations are composed; test cases generated from it are prioritized by question-specific diagnostic difficulty scores. Across seven MDP environments, the testing separates three open-weight LLMs: a reasoning model passes 85% of test cases, a mid-size model 70%, and a 1B model falls below the random baseline, while prioritization surfaces significantly harder cases than random selection. Our results indicate how trustworthy LLM-generated explanations are in model-free settings, where the same LLMs are used but no oracle exists to verify them.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a systematic framework for testing whether LLM-generated natural-language explanations of sequential decision-making policies are faithful to the underlying environment. It uses probabilistic model checking as a test oracle and a taxonomy of post hoc query categories with diagnostic difficulty scores to structure test case generation. Evaluated across seven MDP environments, the approach separates reasoning (85% pass), mid-size (70%), and 1B models (below random baseline), with prioritized test cases being significantly harder than random selection.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as post hoc explainers of sequential decision-making policies, but they often produce plausible yet incorrect explanations. No existing approach systematically tests faithfulness of such explanations due to two software testing challenges: the absence of an oracle for explanation correctness, and the lack of structure in natural-language test inputs needed for systematic test generation.
AI.method: The authors address the oracle problem using probabilistic model checking to compute exact reference results for grading LLM answers automatically. They structure the input space using a taxonomy of post hoc query categories based on environment-level facts from which explanations are composed, generating test cases prioritized by question-specific diagnostic difficulty scores.
AI.result: Across seven MDP environments, the testing framework separates three open-weight LLMs: a reasoning model passes 85% of test cases, a mid-size model passes 70%, and a 1B parameter model falls below the random baseline. Prioritization surfaces significantly harder test cases compared to random selection.
AI.conclusion: The results quantify how trustworthy LLM-generated explanations are in model-free settings where no oracle exists to verify them, suggesting that reasoning-capable models may produce more faithful explanations but that model capability strongly correlates with explanation faithfulness.

title: Geometry of Divergence: Tracking Hidden-State Trajectories for Adaptive Multi-Turn Reasoning
summary: LLM agents need to sustain goal-consistent reasoning across long multi-turn interactions under strict resource constraints. However, as the multi-turn context accumulates, it can destabilize the underlying LLM's internal representation of task-relevant information from earlier turns, blurring the boundary between constructive reasoning and representation drift. We formulate multi-turn reasoning as a hidden-state trajectory of the underlying LLM that is characterized via two complementary signals: temporal curvature that captures the directional consistency of turn-to-turn updates, and variance slope which measures the expansion or contraction of the exploration space. Across four tasks and three underlying LLMs, we observed that these geometric signals distinguish between correct and incorrect episodes prior to completion. We further decompose each episode into three-action chains formed from four actions (Read, Write, Respond, Transfer) and show that separability is action-dependent, with different signals distinguishing various chain patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that trajectory geometry can identify critical turns in the reasoning process, increasing task success rates on $τ$-Bench from 24.1% to 39.6% while reducing token cost by 11.2%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes characterizing LLM agents' multi-turn reasoning as hidden-state trajectories, using two geometric signals—temporal curvature (directional consistency of turn-to-turn updates) and variance slope (expansion/contraction of exploration space)—to detect reasoning quality prior to task completion. Action-dependent separability across different action chains improves task success and reduces token cost.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to maintain goal-consistent reasoning across long multi-turn interactions under resource constraints, as accumulating context destabilizes the model's internal representation of earlier task-relevant information, blurring the line between constructive reasoning and representation drift.
AI.method: The authors formulate multi-turn reasoning as a hidden-state trajectory characterized by two geometric signals: temporal curvature (measuring directional consistency of turn-to-turn updates) and variance slope (measuring expansion/contraction of the exploration space). They decompose episodes into three-action chains formed from four action types (Read, Write, Respond, Transfer) and analyze action-dependent separability of these signals.
AI.result: Across four tasks and three underlying LLMs, the geometric signals distinguish correct from incorrect episodes prior to completion. Separability is action-dependent, with different signals distinguishing various action chain patterns. The trajectory geometry approach improves τ-Bench task success from 24.1% to 39.6% while reducing token cost by 11.2%.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory geometry of hidden LLM states provides an effective, resource-efficient mechanism for identifying critical reasoning turns and intervening to improve agent performance, striking a favorable balance between accuracy gains and token savings.

title: PyKEEN-NSX: A Modular Framework for Static, Dynamic and Schema-Aware Negative Sampling in PyKEEN
summary: Embedding methods have become popular due to their scalability on link prediction and/or triple classification tasks on Knowledge Graphs (KGs). Embedding models are trained relying on both positive and negative samples of triples. However, since KGs generally contain only positive assertions, negative samples are artificially generated through negative sampling strategies, ranging from simple random corruption to more sophisticated approaches that exploit structural, semantic, or embedding information. The design and implementation of advanced negative samplers remains challenging, as most popular Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) libraries provide support only for basic strategies and lack a unified framework for developing more advanced and customized solutions. To address this gap, we introduce PyKEEN-NSX, an extension of PyKEEN, the popular KGE framework, that provides a modular engineered abstraction for negative sampling. The proposed architecture separates the generation of candidate negative pools, conditioned on an explicit context, from the selection strategy, enabling the development and integration of static, schema-aware and dynamic approaches within a consistent framework. Based on this abstraction, we implement six negative samplers, while remaining fully compatible with existing PyKEEN workflows and pipelines. As a proof of concept, we study negative availability across four datasets, showing that constrained pools frequently fall below the requested number of negatives, so that the encoded criterion is to a large extent replaced by the random fallback that supplements them.

AI.tldr: PyKEEN-NSX is an extension of the PyKEEN Knowledge Graph Embedding framework that provides a modular, unified abstraction for negative sampling. It separates candidate negative pool generation from selection strategies, enabling static, schema-aware, and dynamic negative samplers within a consistent framework. The paper also reveals via empirical analysis that constrained negative pools often fall short of requested sample sizes, relying heavily on random fallbacks.
AI.motivation: Knowledge Graph Embedding models require negative samples for training, but KGs only contain positive triples. Advanced negative sampling strategies are difficult to implement because popular KGE libraries only support basic strategies and lack a unified framework for developing customized solutions.
AI.method: The paper introduces a modular architecture for PyKEEN that separates negative candidate pool generation (conditioned on an explicit context) from the selection strategy. This abstraction enables the implementation of six negative samplers, including static, schema-aware, and dynamic approaches, while remaining fully compatible with existing PyKEEN workflows.
AI.result: Six negative samplers were implemented on top of the proposed abstraction. A proof-of-concept study across four datasets shows that constrained negative pools frequently fall below the requested number of negatives, meaning the encoded sampling criterion is largely replaced by random fallback supplementation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a reusable and extensible foundation for developing advanced negative samplers in KGE, but also highlights a critical practical issue: constrained negative pools are often insufficient, undermining the intended sampling criteria and relying heavily on random fallback, which should be addressed in future negative sampling designs.

title: HiRS-Agent: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent System for Reliable Long-Horizon Remote Sensing Task Solving
summary: Recent advances in large language models and multimodal models have pushed remote sensing (RS) processing from simple perception models to agentic systems designed to tackle complex, long-horizon RS tasks. However, existing systems often rely on monolithic decision-making frameworks, which fail to accommodate the multi-stage, interdependent nature of RS tasks. This centralized approach leads to challenges such as unstable task execution, incorrect tool usage, and error propagation across stages. To address these issues, we propose HiRS-Agent, a hierarchical multi-agent system for long-horizon RS task solving. HiRS-Agent adopts a two-level collaborative architecture: the Manager Layer handles dynamic routing, step-level verification, replanning, and termination control, while the Specialist Layer organizes domain-specific tools according to the RS workflow and is responsible for subtask reasoning and tool execution. To further enhance the system's capability, we introduce a two-stage supervised tuning strategy and a verification-guided hierarchical reinforcement learning stage to jointly optimize coordination and tool-use policies. Experiments on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo show that HiRS-Agent substantially improves long-horizon tool-use capability and final-task correctness, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured multi-agent collaboration for reliable RS agents. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/IntelliSensing/HiRS-Agent.

AI.tldr: HiRS-Agent is a hierarchical multi-agent system for long-horizon remote sensing tasks, featuring a two-level architecture (Manager Layer for routing/verification/replanning, Specialist Layer for domain-specific tool use) combined with a two-stage supervised tuning and verification-guided reinforcement learning strategy, achieving substantial improvements on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing agentic systems rely on monolithic decision-making frameworks that fail to handle the multi-stage, interdependent nature of RS tasks, leading to unstable task execution, incorrect tool usage, and error propagation across stages.
AI.method: HiRS-Agent employs a hierarchical multi-agent architecture with two collaborative layers: the Manager Layer handles dynamic routing, step-level verification, replanning, and termination control; the Specialist Layer organizes domain-specific tools according to the RS workflow for subtask reasoning and tool execution. Training involves a two-stage supervised tuning strategy followed by verification-guided hierarchical reinforcement learning to jointly optimize coordination and tool-use policies.
AI.result: Experiments on Earth-Agent Benchmark and ThinkGeo demonstrate that HiRS-Agent substantially improves long-horizon tool-use capability and final-task correctness compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-agent collaboration is effective for building reliable remote sensing agents, and HiRS-Agent validates that hierarchical coordination with verification mechanisms mitigates error propagation and improves task completion in long-horizon RS scenarios.

title: MedAgent-R1: Faithfulness-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Medical Reasoning
summary: When medical AI systems hallucinate clinical reasoning, the consequences extend beyond incorrect answers: fabricated justifications that superficially reference retrieved evidence can mislead clinicians into unsafe treatment decisions. Medical reasoning agents must therefore produce not only correct answers but also faithful justifications that clinicians can verify against cited evidence. We identify a systematic failure mode in RL-trained retrieval agents: outcome-only rewards improve accuracy while degrading faithfulness, a phenomenon we term confident hallucination. The agent learns to answer from parametric memory and backfill plausible but unsupported justifications; citation fabrication rates rise from 16.5% to 31.8% even as accuracy improves by 5 points over the supervised baseline. We address this with a faithfulness-gated reward design: accuracy credit is conditioned on evidence grounding via a hard gate, complemented by retrieval validity and conciseness signals that close exploitation paths unique to agentic retrieval. The resulting system, MedAgent-R1, reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7% and raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6 while maintaining 75.1% accuracy, with 13.2-point gains on HealthBench Safety. Under the same agentic retrieval setup, MedAgent-R1 outscores GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15) while remaining below GPT-4o in overall accuracy, suggesting that explicit faithfulness training yields evidence-grounding gains not achieved by scaling alone.

AI.tldr: MedAgent-R1 addresses "confident hallucination" in RL-trained medical retrieval agents—where outcome-only rewards improve accuracy but degrade faithfulness, causing fabricated justifications that reference evidence superficially—via a faithfulness-gated reward that conditions accuracy credit on evidence grounding. This reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7%, raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6, maintains 75.1% accuracy, and outscores GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15).
AI.motivation: Medical AI systems must produce not only correct answers but also faithful justifications verifiable against cited evidence, because fabricated reasoning that superficially references retrieved evidence can mislead clinicians into unsafe treatment decisions. The paper identifies a systematic failure in RL-trained retrieval agents where outcome-only rewards improve accuracy while degrading faithfulness—a phenomenon called confident hallucination—where agents answer from parametric memory and backfill plausible but unsupported justifications.
AI.method: The paper proposes a faithfulness-gated reward design where accuracy credit is conditioned on evidence grounding via a hard gate, complemented by retrieval validity and conciseness signals that close exploitation paths unique to agentic retrieval. This forms the MedAgent-R1 system.
AI.result: MedAgent-R1 reduces citation fabrication from 31.8% to 4.7%, raises evidence completeness from 58.7 to 82.6, maintains 75.1% accuracy, and gains 13.2 points on HealthBench Safety. Under identical agentic retrieval setup, MedAgent-R1 outscores GPT-4o on faithfulness dimensions (Factual Support 4.55 vs. 4.25; Overclaiming 4.40 vs. 4.15) while remaining below GPT-4o in overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Explicit faithfulness training yields evidence-grounding gains not achieved by scaling alone, as demonstrated by MedAgent-R1 outperforming GPT-4o on faithfulness-specific dimensions under the same retrieval setup despite lower overall accuracy.

title: ATLAS: Dual-Horizon Diagnostic Evaluation for Industrial Tool-Use Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in user-facing services that require iterative tool use under dynamic business conditions. Reliable evaluation is essential for sustained improvement: it must reveal capability deficiencies, inform priorities, and assess interventions. Yet industrial agent service unfolds both through the iterative trajectory of a current request and through continued user interaction. Final-outcome assessment can therefore obscure where deficiencies arise and whether later service remains aligned with context from earlier exchanges. We propose ATLAS, a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial tool-use agents. At the request horizon, trajectory-wise diagnostic signals relate deficiencies to execution locations and capability concerns. At the interaction horizon, user-wise signals assess whether service remains responsive across continued interaction. Together, these views provide structured diagnostic evidence for analyzing execution deficiencies and sustained service behavior. ATLAS instantiates them as executable signals with explicit evidence scopes and decision boundaries. LLM judge interfaces are calibrated against high-confidence references from real business logs; when needed, their decision behavior is distilled into efficient diagnostic models for lower-latency, lower-cost evaluation. The resulting feedback supports policy optimization. We evaluate ATLAS on Meituan Xiaotuan production traffic. Offline experiments assess diagnostic-signal fidelity and replay-based policy improvement, while online A/B experiments show concurrent gains in user engagement, downstream business outcomes, and sampled human-audit quality.

AI.tldr: ATLAS is a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework for industrial tool-use LLM agents, providing trajectory-wise signals at the request horizon and user-wise signals at the interaction horizon to identify execution deficiencies and assess sustained service alignment.
AI.motivation: Industrial LLM agent services unfold through both iterative tool-use trajectories and continued user interactions, but final-outcome assessment obscures where deficiencies arise and whether later service remains aligned with earlier context. This motivates a diagnostic framework that distinguishes between request-level and interaction-level evaluation.
AI.method: ATLAS instantiates dual-horizon diagnostic signals with explicit evidence scopes and decision boundaries. At the request horizon, trajectory-wise signals localize deficiencies to execution steps and capability concerns. At the interaction horizon, user-wise signals assess continued service alignment. LLM judge interfaces are calibrated against high-confidence references from production logs, with optional distillation into efficient diagnostic models for lower latency/cost.
AI.result: Offline experiments on Meituan Xiaotuan production traffic validate diagnostic-signal fidelity and demonstrate replay-based policy improvement. Online A/B tests show concurrent gains in user engagement, downstream business outcomes, and sampled human-audit quality.
AI.conclusion: Dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation provides structured feedback that supports policy optimization and yields measurable improvements in both service quality and business outcomes for industrial tool-use agents.

title: Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal Prototype Optimization for Sentiment Analysis
summary: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) is a fundamental component of affective computing that aims to decipher complex emotional states by integrating verbal content with non-verbal cues including vocal intonation and facial micro-expressions. While recent disentanglement-based approaches have advanced the field, their potential is hindered by two methodological challenges. First, static computation graphs process all samples indiscriminately regardless of semantic complexity, which leads to suboptimal representation for diverse emotional expressions and contextual scenarios. Second, generic contrastive objectives often neglect the intrinsic ordinal hierarchy of sentiment intensities. To systematically address these limitations, we introduce Multimodal Adaptive Expert Selection with Text Routing and Ordinal prototype optimization (MAESTRO), a novel framework designed to dynamically orchestrate and refine multimodal representations. Drawing inspiration from an orchestra conductor, we design a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism. Unlike static fusion, this module utilizes linguistic context as a routing signal to dynamically activate specific audio-visual experts, thereby resolving cross-modal ambiguity through adaptive feature enhancement. Furthermore, to capture fine-grained sentiment gradations, we propose an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (O-PCL). By incorporating distance-based penalties into the prototype learning objective, O-PCL enforces a structured latent space that preserves the natural order of emotion. Extensive experiments on the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that MAESTRO achieves state-of-the-art performance, and qualitative analysis further confirms the interpretability of our dynamic routing paradigm.

AI.tldr: MAESTRO is a novel multimodal sentiment analysis framework that combines a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts mechanism for adaptive audio-visual expert selection and an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning method to preserve sentiment intensity ordering, achieving state-of-the-art results on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing disentanglement-based multimodal sentiment analysis approaches face two critical limitations: (1) static computation graphs process all samples uniformly regardless of semantic complexity, leading to suboptimal representations across diverse emotional contexts, and (2) generic contrastive objectives ignore the inherent ordinal hierarchy of sentiment intensities, failing to capture fine-grained emotional gradations.
AI.method: MAESTRO introduces two key components: (1) a Text-Guided Hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism that uses linguistic context as a routing signal to dynamically activate specific audio-visual experts, enabling adaptive feature enhancement and resolving cross-modal ambiguity; (2) an Ordinal-aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (O-PCL) method that incorporates distance-based penalties into prototype learning to enforce a structured latent space preserving the natural order of emotion intensities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that MAESTRO achieves state-of-the-art performance, and qualitative analysis confirms the interpretability of the dynamic routing paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that dynamic, context-aware expert selection combined with ordinal-aware representation learning effectively addresses the limitations of static fusion and generic contrastive learning in multimodal sentiment analysis, offering both superior performance and interpretability.

title: Autoregressive Mosaics: Probing 2D Spatial Reasoning in Text-Only Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained only on text and code can sometimes generate programs that draw recognizable images. However, it is unclear whether this reflects an internal representation of 2D spatial layout or simply the ability to translate spatial descriptions into code. We introduce Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench), a benchmark that separates these factors: First, a translation task gives a model a fully specified geometry of a picture in words as a prompt and asks for the code that produces it. Second, a layout task requires the model to compose an image from an underspecified prompt. Across eight open-weight text-and-code-only models, all models reliably translate specified geometry into code, but their open-ended layout performance differs substantially, indicating that these differences are not explained by code-generation ability alone. An output-medium ablation further shows that the interface or medium of expression that the model uses matters: replacing procedural code with raw SVG improves layout scores across all models. Finally, probing model activations shows that a coarse layout plan is present before generation, but reflects only the layout implied by the prompt. During generation, models track the evolving geometric state instead of executing an initially fixed plan. Overall, these results show that 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both the model and the output medium, and is not explained by code-generation ability alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AM-Bench, a benchmark that separates code generation ability from genuine 2D spatial reasoning in text-only LLMs. It consists of a translation task (fully specified geometry to code) and a layout task (underspecified prompt to image composition). Across eight open-weight models, all translate geometry well, but layout performance varies substantially—not explained by code ability alone. Switching output medium from code to SVG improves all models, and activation probing shows models track evolving geometric state during generation rather than executing a fixed plan.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows LLMs trained only on text/code can generate code that draws images, but it is unclear whether this reflects genuine internal 2D spatial representations or merely the ability to translate spatial descriptions into programming code. The authors aim to disentangle these possibilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce AM-Bench with two tasks: (1) a translation task where a model is given a fully specified geometry in words and asked to produce code that renders it, and (2) a layout task requiring the model to compose an image from an underspecified prompt. They evaluate eight open-weight text-and-code-only models, perform an output-medium ablation (code vs. raw SVG), and probe model activations to analyze internal spatial plan representation and generation dynamics.
AI.result: All models reliably translate fully specified geometry into code, but open-ended layout performance varies substantially across models. These differences are not explained by code-generation ability alone. Using raw SVG instead of procedural code improves layout scores for all models. Activation probing reveals a coarse layout plan is present before generation that reflects the prompt's implied layout, but during generation models track evolving geometric state rather than executing an initially fixed plan.
AI.conclusion: 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both the specific model and the output medium, and is not reducible to code-generation ability alone. The output medium significantly affects spatial reasoning performance, suggesting the interface of expression matters for how well LLMs can manifest spatial understanding.

title: Which Rules Matter Now? Policy-Centroid Routing Before an Intelligent System Acts
comment: Theory and research-program paper; 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Includes a synthetic worked example; reports no empirical efficacy result
summary:
Before an intelligent system can decide whether an action is allowed, it must first know which rules the action has approached. A single proposed action can implicate several policy regimes at once. Their requirements may stack, overlap, or qualify one another, yet many remain written in natural language while the action itself arrives as an incomplete description of intent. The first problem is not judgment. It is attention.
  Policy-centroid routing creates a layer before adjudication. It compresses expressions within each policy regime into one or more representative centroids, places the proposed action in the same semantic space, applies a declared measure, and routes every regime crossing a declared threshold to authoritative review. Several regimes may trigger at once. The output is a review agenda, not permission, prohibition, legality, breach, compliance, certification, or enforcement.
  The paper develops six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on studies comparing the hypothesis with structured workflows, lexical and semantic retrieval, hierarchical and direct classification, and selective prediction under matched review burden. The studies are designed to identify where policy geometry recovers applicable regimes, where compression loses rare or overlapping obligations, and where the mechanism should abstain. The paper includes a synthetic worked example and reports no empirical efficacy result.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces policy-centroid routing, a pre-adjudication layer that compresses policy regimes into semantic centroids and routes proposed actions to relevant regimes for review, outputting a review agenda rather than compliance judgments. It proposes six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on studies for empirical validation, and includes a synthetic worked example without reporting empirical efficacy results.
AI.motivation: The fundamental challenge before rule-based decision-making is attention: a single proposed action can implicate multiple policy regimes whose requirements stack, overlap, or qualify each other. Many policies remain in natural language while actions arrive as incomplete intent descriptions. The first problem is determining which rules apply—not adjudicating them—and existing approaches lack a systematic mechanism for this routing task.
