AI.method: The method is policy-centroid routing: (1) compress expressions within each policy regime into representative centroids in a shared semantic space, (2) place the proposed action in the same space, (3) apply a declared similarity measure, and (4) route all regimes crossing a declared threshold to review. The paper develops six falsifiable propositions and seven follow-on study designs comparing the approach against structured workflows, lexical/semantic retrieval, hierarchical/direct classification, and selective prediction under matched review burden.
AI.result: The paper reports no empirical efficacy result. It includes a synthetic worked example and presents the study designs intended to identify where policy geometry recovers applicable regimes, where compression loses rare or overlapping obligations, and where the mechanism should abstain from routing.
AI.conclusion: The paper positions policy-centroid routing as an attention-layer mechanism that generates a review agenda rather than permissions, prohibitions, or compliance verdicts. The research program aims to empirically test where this approach succeeds and fails, particularly regarding rare or overlapping obligations, with subsequent studies designed to rigorously compare against alternative retrieval and classification baselines.

title: SkillZip Pro: Execution-Aware Dynamic Compression of Progressively Loaded Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
summary:
Production agent skills are directory bundles, not isolated prompts. The root is loaded at activation; references, schemas, scripts, assets, and nested subskills are loaded only when an execution path needs them. Compressing only the root misses most deployment cost and may move branch-specific details into the always-loaded context. Flattening instead destroys progressive-loading boundaries.
  We introduce \method, an evaluation-free compressor for complete, progressively loaded skill bundles. It leaves the agent harness unchanged and emits an ordinary directory. The method combines two safeguards. First, it compresses \emph{across files}, removing content from a reference or subskill when the root or a declared environment contract already provides it. Second, it preserves routing, so every required file and directly callable entry remains reachable after rewriting. Users can configure \method along two independent axes. \emph{One-Shot} mode rebuilds the full bundle; \emph{Continual} mode reuses state and applies Zip-on-Write after each evolution patch. \emph{Persistent} compression rewrites the shipped bundle to reduce storage and runtime context. \emph{Transient} compression keeps that bundle byte-identical and builds a task-specific view, reducing only per-run context after build cost. Entry contracts mark private, public, and conditional resources; a multi-entry audit preserves standalone public subskills.
  On a production content-moderation skill evaluated by our industrial multi-round harness, \method removes \hl{38\%} of skill bundle tokens and \hl{10.4\%} of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss, while an unprotected 71\% configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points to one-sided false positives. On a multi-entry bundle, \method effeciently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a method for compressing complete, progressively-loaded agent skill bundles (directory structures) rather than isolated prompts. The method compresses across files, preserves routing, and offers two axes of configuration (One-Shot/Continual and Persistent/Transient). Evaluation on a production content-moderation skill shows 38% bundle token reduction and 10.4% end-to-end per-run token reduction with no quality loss.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are directory bundles with progressive loading—only the root is loaded at activation, while references, schemas, scripts, assets, and nested subskills load on demand. Compressing only the root misses most deployment cost and can move branch-specific details into always-loaded context; flattening destroys progressive-loading boundaries. Existing approaches fail to account for this structure.
AI.method: The method is an evaluation-free compressor for complete, progressively loaded skill bundles. It compresses across files, removing content from references/subskills when the root or a declared environment contract already provides it. It preserves routing so every required file and directly callable entry remains reachable. It offers two independent configuration axes: One-Shot vs. Continual (rebuild full bundle vs. reuse state with Zip-on-Write after patches) and Persistent vs. Transient (rewrite shipped bundle vs. keep byte-identical with task-specific view). Entry contracts mark private, public, and conditional resources; a multi-entry audit preserves standalone public subskills.
AI.result: On a production content-moderation skill evaluated via an industrial multi-round harness, the method removes 38% of skill bundle tokens and 10.4% of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss. An unprotected 71% compression configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points to one-sided false positives. On a multi-entry bundle, the method efficiently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.
AI.conclusion: Compressing agent skill bundles requires a structure-aware, evaluation-free approach that compresses across files while preserving progressive-loading boundaries and routing. The proposed method achieves significant token reduction without quality degradation, and its configuration axes allow flexibility between one-shot/continual and persistent/transient compression strategies.

title: HSRM: Hidden-State Reward Models for Test-Time Verification
summary: Large language models can often generate plausible mathematical reasoning traces, but reliably identifying the correct solution among multiple candidates remains a key challenge. Existing test-time reasoning pipelines typically rely on text-based verifiers that re-read each generated solution, making verification an expensive component of inference. Prior work has shown, however, that LLMs often encode correctness-related signals in their internal representations, including awareness of when their own answers are likely to be wrong. Building on this observation, we introduce HSRM, a lightweight hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate solutions by directly reading the generator's internal representations rather than re-processing its text. HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries and uses a small Transformer encoder to rank candidates. It is trained from self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring neither human-written process supervision nor a large pretrained verifier. Across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator--dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters, providing an efficient alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation.

AI.tldr: HSRM is a lightweight (~2M parameter) hidden-state reward model that verifies candidate math solutions by reading a frozen generator's internal representations at reasoning-step boundaries, matching or outperforming a 55M-parameter text-only verifier in 15 of 16 settings across four math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time reasoning verification relies on text-based verifiers that re-read solutions, making verification expensive. Prior work shows LLMs encode correctness signals internally, suggesting hidden states could enable cheaper verification.
AI.method: HSRM extracts hidden states from a frozen generator at reasoning-step boundaries, feeds them into a small Transformer encoder to rank candidate solutions. It is trained on self-generated trajectories with outcome labels, requiring no human-written process supervision or large pretrained verifier.
AI.result: Across four math reasoning benchmarks, HSRM matches or outperforms a 55M-parameter text-only energy verifier in 15 of 16 generator-dataset settings while using only about 2M parameters.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-state-based verification is an efficient and effective alternative to text-only verification by reusing representations already computed during generation, significantly reducing verification cost without sacrificing accuracy.

title: VFR-Audit: Verdict-Level Reliability for Fairness Audits in Hospital Length-of-Stay Prediction
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Fairness audits in clinical Artificial Intelligence convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass-or-fail verdicts against operational thresholds, where hospital governance boards, payers, and regulators act on the resulting verdicts. Such audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, thus the same verdict can flip between pass and fail across audits. Existing uncertainty methods such as Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests address verdict instability only at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into a verdict-stability claim remains a manual step that scales poorly across the (model, metric, attribute) cells an audit covers. Existing uncertainty methods also leave open whether bias-mitigation steps, such as reweighing or per-group threshold shifts, yield a stable passing verdict at the cost of model discrimination measured as AUROC or AUPRC.To address this verdict-stability gap, we propose VFR-Audit, a framework built around the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar bounded between 0 and 0.5 that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. VFR-Audit reports VFR alongside three reliability axes, namely within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes VFR-Audit, a framework that addresses the gap between metric-level uncertainty and verdict-level stability in clinical AI fairness audits. It introduces the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar between 0 and 0.5 measuring the probability of pass/fail verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling, alongside three reliability axes (within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa).
AI.motivation: Fairness audits in clinical AI convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass/fail verdicts against operational thresholds, but existing uncertainty methods (Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests) only address instability at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into verdict-stability claims remains manual and scales poorly across (model, metric, attribute) cells. Additionally, existing methods do not clarify whether bias-mitigation steps yield stable passing verdicts at the cost of model discrimination.
AI.method: VFR-Audit introduces the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a bounded scalar (0 to 0.5) that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. The framework reports VFR alongside three reliability axes: (1) within-cohort resampling stability, (2) audit-size sensitivity, and (3) cross-hospital verdict agreement computed via Fleiss' kappa.
AI.result: The paper presents a framework design (VFR-Audit) that quantifies verdict flip probability under bootstrap resampling and provides multi-axis reliability assessment for verdict stability across cohorts, audit sizes, and hospital sites.
AI.conclusion: VFR-Audit bridges the gap between metric-level uncertainty and verdict-level stability in clinical AI fairness audits, offering a scalable and comprehensive approach to assessing whether pass/fail verdicts are trustworthy and whether bias-mitigation strategies achieve stable passing outcomes without excessive discrimination cost.

title: Predicting Residential Rents in Dakar Using Machine Learning
summary: Dakar's residential rental market remains poorly documented despite its economic and social importance: 54.4% of households are renters, compared to 23.3% nationally. This study develops a complete machine learning pipeline to predict residential rents in Dakar, from data collection to model interpretation. An original dataset of 1,507 rental listings was built through systematic web scraping and a documented cleaning pipeline, then enriched with four purpose-built features, including a luxury score and a keyword-based quality score. Five models were compared: linear regression, Random Forest (baseline), XGBoost, and LightGBM optimized through Bayesian optimization with Optuna, using leakage-free KFold target encoding for location. The optimized XGBoost model achieved the best performance with an $R^2$ of 0.847, an MAE of 210,902 XOF, and an RMSE of 324,195 XOF. Feature importance was assessed using native XGBoost gain and SHAP values, revealing a substantial difference in the ranking of location, which appears as a minor predictor by gain but as the second most influential variable by SHAP. This result carries methodological implications for hedonic studies using target-encoded categorical variables. This study provides an interpretable benchmark for Dakar's rental market and highlights several avenues for improvement, including the integration of geospatial features and conformal prediction.

AI.tldr: This study builds a complete ML pipeline to predict residential rental prices in Dakar, Senegal, using a scraped dataset of 1,507 listings enriched with purpose-built features (luxury and quality scores). An Optuna-optimized XGBoost model achieved the best performance (R²=0.847, MAE=210,902 XOF), and the analysis reveals that SHAP and native gain-based feature importance rankings diverge, particularly for location, carrying methodological implications for hedonic studies using target-encoded categorical variables.
AI.motivation: Dakar's rental market is a critical economic and social sector (54.4% of households are renters, more than double the national average), yet it remains poorly documented, motivating the need for a data-driven, interpretable benchmark to understand and predict residential rents.
AI.method: The study develops a full ML pipeline: (1) systematic web scraping to build a dataset of 1,507 rental listings; (2) a documented cleaning pipeline; (3) enrichment with four purpose-built features including a luxury score and keyword-based quality score; (4) comparison of five models (linear regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) with Bayesian optimization via Optuna; (5) leakage-free KFold target encoding for location; and (6) feature importance assessment using both native XGBoost gain and SHAP values.
AI.result: The optimized XGBoost model achieved the best performance with R²=0.847, MAE=210,902 XOF, and RMSE=324,195 XOF. Feature importance analysis revealed a substantial discrepancy: location ranks as a minor predictor by native XGBoost gain but as the second most influential variable by SHAP values.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an interpretable benchmark for Dakar's rental market while highlighting an important methodological caveat regarding how target-encoded categorical variables are ranked by different feature importance techniques. Future work should integrate geospatial features and conformal prediction to further improve the model.

title: CAER: Causal Action Effect Reweighting for World Model Training
summary: World models are becoming core infrastructure for embodied intelligence, with action-conditioned video generation providing controllable predictions of how scenes evolve after agent interventions. Yet existing models are commonly trained with space-time-uniform mean squared error, allowing abundant background tokens to dominate the gradient while sparse interaction dynamics remain under-optimized; such uniform fitting rewards reconstructing appearance rather than learning how actions change the world. We introduce Causal Action Effect Reweighting (CAER), a general training paradigm that redistributes supervision toward the tokens whose predicted future is causally affected by the action. CAER contrasts the model's own predictions with and without action conditioning to localize these tokens online, then normalizes the resulting effect map into a weight that preserves the total coefficient mass and changes only where it is spent. This online signal requires no external annotations or offline preprocessing, avoids additional data-processing time, and scales naturally with model and dataset size. Experiments across heterogeneous action-conditioned world-model tasks show that CAER converges to better solutions than uniform MSE training, with consistent improvements in the physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality of generated videos.

AI.tldr: CAER is a training paradigm for action-conditioned world models that reweights supervision toward tokens causally affected by actions instead of uniform MSE, improving physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality in video generation.
AI.motivation: Existing action-conditioned world models are trained with space-time-uniform MSE loss, which allows abundant background tokens to dominate gradients while sparse interaction dynamics remain under-optimized. This uniform fitting emphasizes reconstructing appearance rather than learning how actions change the world.
AI.method: CAER redistributes supervision toward tokens whose predicted future is causally affected by the action. It contrasts the model's own predictions with and without action conditioning to localize causal effect tokens online, then normalizes the resulting effect map into weights that preserve total coefficient mass. No external annotations or offline preprocessing are required.
AI.result: Experiments across heterogeneous action-conditioned world-model tasks show CAER converges to better solutions than uniform MSE training, with consistent improvements in physical consistency, controllability, and visual quality of generated videos.
AI.conclusion: CAER provides a scalable, annotation-free training paradigm that improves action-conditioned world models by focusing learning on causally action-affected tokens, making it a general improvement over uniform MSE training.

title: Responsible Integration of AI in Cancer Genomics: Barriers, Risks, and Pathways to Trustworthy Clinical Translation
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly used to extract, integrate, and interpret biomedical knowledge relevant to cancer genomics, yet their translation into routine clinical oncology has been comparatively slow. The central challenge is not computational capability alone, but trustworthy integration into clinical workflows. This review examines how NLP and AI support the cancer genomics pipeline, from literature mining and automated variant interpretation to clinical trial matching, knowledge graph construction, and multimodal data integration. We identify four interrelated translational failure domains: evidence inconsistency, explainability and uncertainty, data governance and reproducibility, and interoperability. Rather than considering these challenges in isolation, we take a systems-level view, focusing on their interaction across the translational pathway. We propose a conceptual framework and roadmap for addressing these domains through rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle. Progress toward routine clinical use will depend less on further improving model capability than on systematically addressing these interacting failure domains from development through deployment and post-deployment monitoring.

AI.tldr: This review examines how NLP and AI support the cancer genomics pipeline (from literature mining to clinical trial matching and multimodal data integration) and identifies four interrelated translational failure domains — evidence inconsistency, explainability/uncertainty, data governance/reproducibility, and interoperability — proposing a systems-level conceptual framework and roadmap for trustworthy integration into routine clinical oncology.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in AI/NLP for cancer genomics, translation into routine clinical practice has been slow. The central challenge is trustworthy integration into clinical workflows, not computational capability. The authors aim to identify and address the interacting failure domains that hinder clinical adoption.
AI.method: A systematic review of NLP and AI applications across the cancer genomics pipeline, including literature mining, variant interpretation, trial matching, knowledge graph construction, and multimodal integration. The authors adopt a systems-level perspective to analyze four translational failure domains and their interactions, then propose a conceptual framework and roadmap addressing validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructures, regulatory alignment, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle.
AI.result: Four interrelated translational failure domains were identified: evidence inconsistency, explainability and uncertainty, data governance and reproducibility, and interoperability. These domains interact across the translational pathway rather than existing in isolation, requiring a systems-level approach.
AI.conclusion: Progress toward routine clinical use of AI/NLP in cancer genomics will depend less on further improving model capability than on systematically addressing these interacting failure domains from development through deployment and post-deployment monitoring, guided by rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware methods, interoperable infrastructure, regulatory alignment, and human oversight.

title: CARVE: Verified Expansion for Variable-Length Generation in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models predict tokens from a partially observed response canvas, enabling bidirectional conditioning and parallel token refinement. Yet standard masked-diffusion decoders use a rigid inference interface: the number of masked positions allocated to the answer is fixed before generation begins. Choosing this length is difficult. A short canvas can truncate reasoning or code, while a long canvas wastes computation and can perturb denoising. We introduce CARVE (Counterfactual-Aware Reveal with Verified Expansion), a training-free variable-length algorithm for masked diffusion LMs. Starting from a shorter canvas, CARVE can grow the response during decoding by inserting additional [MASK] positions. Rather than keeping every insertion, CARVE tests a candidate expanded canvas and asks a counterfactual question: would the model make similar predictions for the unresolved positions in the original canvas if the extra masked space were present? The inserted masks are kept only when they induce low Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence on aligned unresolved positions. This makes length growth a verified stability decision rather than a pure confidence heuristic. CARVE applies without retraining to both full-canvas and blockwise diffusion decoders. Across code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CARVE consistently improves average performance over fixed-length baselines across all evaluated model families. Crucially, CARVE achieves these accuracy gains while reducing inference cost, reaching half the FLOPs of fixed-length decoding in some settings.

AI.tldr: CARVE is a training-free, variable-length decoding algorithm for masked diffusion language models that dynamically grows the response canvas during generation by inserting masked positions only when a counterfactual stability check (based on JS divergence) confirms they won't perturb existing predictions. It improves accuracy across code generation and math reasoning benchmarks while reducing FLOPs by up to half compared to fixed-length decoding.
AI.motivation: Standard masked-diffusion decoders require fixing the number of masked positions (canvas length) before generation. Choosing this length is difficult: too short truncates reasoning/code, too long wastes computation and can perturb denoising. This rigid inference interface is a fundamental limitation.
AI.method: CARVE starts with a shorter canvas and grows the response during decoding by inserting additional [MASK] positions. For each candidate expansion, it performs a counterfactual verification: computes whether the model's predictions for unresolved positions remain similar (low Jensen-Shannon divergence) with the extra masked space present. Insertions are kept only when they pass this stability check, making length growth a verified decision rather than a confidence heuristic. It applies to both full-canvas and blockwise diffusion decoders without retraining.
AI.result: Across code generation and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CARVE consistently improves average performance over fixed-length baselines across all evaluated model families. It also reduces inference cost, reaching half the FLOPs of fixed-length decoding in some settings.
AI.conclusion: CARVE demonstrates that variable-length decoding with counterfactual verification is both more accurate and more efficient than rigid fixed-length decoding for masked diffusion LMs, offering a practical, training-free improvement applicable across decoder architectures.

title: Learning Action Models with Conditional and Quantified Effects via Uncertainty-Guided Exploration
summary: Accurate action models are critical for effective planning. Existing action-model learning methods largely assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when learning conditional and quantified effects. We present Online Hypothesis-Driven Conditional Action Model Learning (OHCAM), an online approach for learning action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited interactions with the environment. OHCAM maintains a belief over hypothesized action models and actively selects informative actions to reduce uncertainty by maximizing disagreement among competing hypotheses, while being robust to noisy observations. To enable scalability, OHCAM begins with a small set of simple action model hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when the current hypotheses become inconsistent with the data. Experiments on six benchmark planning domains demonstrate that OHCAM is sample efficient in learning action models that solve substantially more tasks than baselines, even with observation noise. We validate OHCAM on two tasks using a Kinova Gen3 robot, demonstrating the real-world applicability of our approach.

AI.tldr: OHCAM is an online approach for learning action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited environment interactions, using hypothesis-driven active learning to maximize disagreement among competing hypotheses while remaining robust to noise, validated across six benchmark domains and on a Kinova Gen3 robot.
AI.motivation: Existing action-model learning methods either assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when handling conditional and quantified effects. There is a need for a scalable, sample-efficient approach that can learn these complex effects from limited interactions.
AI.method: OHCAM maintains a belief over hypothesized action models and actively selects informative actions by maximizing disagreement among competing hypotheses. It starts with simple hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when current hypotheses become inconsistent with data, enabling scalability and robustness to noisy observations.
AI.result: Experiments on six benchmark planning domains show OHCAM is sample efficient and solves substantially more tasks than baselines, even under observation noise. Validation on two real-world tasks using a Kinova Gen3 robot confirms practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: OHCAM provides an effective and scalable solution for learning action models with conditional and quantified effects online, demonstrating strong sample efficiency and real-world viability.

title: MNIST-PRO: MNIST is Back as a Partially Observable World for AI Agents
summary: AI agents in partially observable environments need to coordinate active sensing with working memory to maintain an evolving perceptual state. However, existing benchmarks struggle to isolate this perceptual-state construction and interpretation capability because they introduce physical and control complexities. We address this with MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that isolates agentic perception by converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. We evaluate ten multimodal models across four memory representations, including raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas. While models excel under full observability, partial observability exposes a clear performance gap. We identify three distinct bottlenecks. First, perceptual-state construction and interpretation present a challenge, as agents struggle to integrate fragmented glimpses. Second, agents often stop exploring before they see the full sequence. Third, models often fail to revise early, incorrect beliefs even when faced with subsequent contradictory evidence. These results show that simply acquiring visual evidence is not enough. Agents must also be able to build and update a reliable perceptual state.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MNIST-PRO, a benchmark that isolates agentic perception by reformulating MNIST digit recognition as a sequential, glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. Evaluating ten multimodal models across four memory representations reveals that partial observability exposes significant performance gaps, with three identified bottlenecks: difficulty integrating fragmented glimpses, premature exploration termination, and failure to revise incorrect early beliefs.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks cannot cleanly isolate the perceptual-state construction and interpretation capability of AI agents because they conflate it with physical and control complexities. A focused benchmark is needed to study how agents coordinate active sensing with working memory in partially observable environments.
AI.method: The authors create MNIST-PRO, converting MNIST digit recognition into a sequential glimpse-based search task with lookback constraints. They evaluate ten multimodal models across four memory representations: raw visual history, textual states, structured metric grid maps, and a consolidated visual canvas.
AI.result: Models perform well under full observability but show a clear performance gap under partial observability. Three distinct bottlenecks are identified: (1) perceptual-state construction and interpretation challenges when integrating fragmented glimpses, (2) premature stopping of exploration before the full sequence is seen, and (3) failure to revise incorrect early beliefs despite subsequent contradictory evidence.
AI.conclusion: Acquiring visual evidence alone is insufficient; agents must also be able to build and update a reliable perceptual state. The findings highlight perceptual-state construction and revision as a critical bottleneck for agentic perception in partially observable settings.

title: Measure Before You Manage: Evaluating Agent Working Memory in Coding Agents
summary: Agent working memory is heterogeneous. Objects such as instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, and agent-generated state play different semantic roles and exhibit different size, retention, and representation profiles. Recent work has begun to explore memory-management mechanisms that account for such heterogeneity. This work focuses on semantic heterogeneity and studies how it should shape the management and evaluation of working memory in coding agents. Across 55 archived coding-agent trajectories, we find that semantically different working-memory objects exhibit distinct retention and compression behavior. This heterogeneity motivates semantically informed memory management. We study two semantically informed strategies: an object-aware compression policy and a retrieval-based policy. Their evaluation shows that calibration gains may not transfer to held-out tasks, and that equal token budgets do not imply equal delivered context or management cost. A real-system replay further exposes serving limits that nominal budgets alone do not capture. Together, these results show why semantic structure matters for agent working memory and why evaluating memory-management strategies requires more than a nominal token budget. We organize these lessons into four levels: stored state, delivered context, management work, and task or process outcome.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates heterogeneous working memory in coding agents, showing that semantically different memory objects (instructions, artifacts, tool outputs, agent state) exhibit distinct retention and compression behaviors. It evaluates two semantically informed memory-management strategies (object-aware compression and retrieval-based policies) across 55 coding-agent trajectories, finding that calibration gains may not transfer to held-out tasks, that equal token budgets do not imply equal delivered context or management cost, and that real-system replay reveals serving limits beyond nominal budgets. The authors organize lessons into four levels: stored state, delivered context, management work, and task/process outcome.
AI.motivation: Agent working memory is inherently heterogeneous, yet existing memory-management mechanisms largely treat it as uniform. Understanding how semantic differences in memory objects should shape management and evaluation is critical for building effective coding agents, but prior work has not systematically characterized this heterogeneity nor its implications for memory policy design and evaluation.
AI.method: The study analyzes 55 archived coding-agent trajectories to characterize retention and compression patterns of semantically distinct working-memory objects. It then designs and evaluates two semantically informed memory-management strategies: an object-aware compression policy and a retrieval-based policy. Evaluation includes calibration on tasks, held-out transfer testing, token-budget comparison, and a real-system replay to expose serving constraints.
AI.result: Semantically different working-memory objects exhibit distinct retention and compression behaviors. Calibration gains from semantically informed strategies may not transfer to held-out tasks. Equal token budgets do not guarantee equal delivered context or management cost, and real-system replay reveals serving limitations not captured by nominal budgets alone.
AI.conclusion: Semantic structure matters for agent working memory management; evaluating such strategies requires a multi-level framework (stored state, delivered context, management work, and task/process outcome) rather than relying on nominal token budgets alone.

title: Wrong Prediction, Right Answer: Recovering Evidence from Collapsed LLM Sequence Scores
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, and 43 appendix tables. Research paper on language-model interpretability, reasoning evaluation, output-scoring bottlenecks, and label-free calibration. The paper evaluates controlled three-way logical reasoning tasks, ProofWriter, ANLI, and FOLIO using Qwen3.5, OLMo-2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Pythia checkpoints
summary: When a large language model fails a reasoning task, it is often assumed to lack the underlying capability. However, this conflates a genuine absence of reasoning with a late-stage output bottleneck. We observe a consistent readout gap across diverse reasoning benchmarks: hidden-state probes successfully decode correct answers even when native sequence scoring completely collapses due to structural biases. To test whether instance-specific logic survives this collapse, we introduce a diagnostic protocol using a minimal, target-label-free additive correction. Fitting just two parameters on as few as 25 unlabeled examples recovers 9--34 accuracy points for Qwen3.5 models, transferring successfully to OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. Crucially, these recovered decisions persist on hard instances unresolved by simple lexical overlap and significantly exceed count-preserving permutation baselines. Our results show that many apparent zero-shot reasoning deficits are expression failures masking intact internal logic, urging a narrower interpretation of benchmark evaluations.

AI.tldr: LLMs often fail reasoning benchmarks not because they lack capability but due to a late-stage output bottleneck (readout gap), where hidden-state probes can decode correct answers despite collapsed native sequence scoring. A two-parameter additive correction fitted on as few as 25 unlabeled examples recovers 9-34 accuracy points across multiple model families, and the recovered decisions persist on hard instances, indicating intact internal logic masked by expression failures.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption that LLM failures on reasoning tasks indicate a genuine absence of capability. It highlights a conflation between true reasoning deficits and late-stage output bottlenecks (readout gaps), where hidden states contain correct answers but sequence-level decoding fails due to structural biases. The authors aim to demonstrate that many apparent zero-shot reasoning failures are actually expression failures masking intact internal reasoning.
AI.method: The authors introduce a diagnostic protocol using a minimal, target-label-free additive correction. They fit just two parameters on as few as 25 unlabeled examples to bridge the readout gap between hidden-state probe accuracy and native sequence scoring. They evaluate across diverse reasoning benchmarks on Qwen3.5 models, and validate transfer to OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B. They also compare against count-preserving permutation baselines and test persistence on hard instances requiring complex reasoning beyond simple lexical overlap.
AI.result: The two-parameter correction recovers 9-34 accuracy points for Qwen3.5 models on diverse reasoning benchmarks. The approach transfers successfully to other model families (OLMo-2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B). Crucially, the recovered decisions persist on hard instances unresolved by simple lexical overlap and significantly exceed count-preserving permutation baselines, demonstrating the recovered reasoning is genuine and not attributable to superficial heuristics.
AI.conclusion: Many apparent zero-shot reasoning deficits in LLMs are actually expression failures that mask intact internal logic. The readout gap between hidden states and surface-level decoding represents a recoverable output bottleneck rather than a genuine capability deficit. The authors urge a narrower interpretation of benchmark evaluations, suggesting that hidden-state readouts should be considered when assessing model reasoning capabilities.

title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
summary: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can substantially improve reasoning in mathematics and code, where outcomes can be checked automatically. Extending this progress to open-ended and agentic tasks remains difficult because reliable rewards are harder to obtain and direct human supervision cannot keep pace with the scale and complexity of model-generated experience. This paper studies how LRMs can continue to improve as human supervision gradually recedes from the learning loop. We examine two connected dimensions of this problem. The reward axis traces the development from per-instance human judgments to reusable verifiers and rewards that operate even without human feedback. The experience axis examines how learning can progress from human-curated tasks and environments toward self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution. We connect these dimensions through a five-level ladder from L0 to L4 that identifies which parts of the learning process remain under continued human control. Our analysis further highlights the risks introduced by increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors. Consequently, we also provide the evaluation around three complementary objects: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality. This analysis provides a structured account of current approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision and the open problems involved in developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence. Furthermore, we maintain a continuously updated \href{https://github.com/visitworld123/Awesome-Scaling-LRM-Beyond-Human-Supervision}{GitHub repository} to track the latest advances.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how large reasoning models (LRMs) can continue improving as human supervision diminishes, introducing a five-level ladder (L0–L4) that categorizes the degree of human control across reward generation and experience acquisition, while also discussing associated risks and evaluation frameworks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has proven effective for LRMs in math and code where outcomes are automatically checkable, but extending this to open-ended agentic tasks is difficult because reliable rewards are hard to obtain and human supervision cannot scale with model-generated experience. The paper addresses how LRMs can keep improving as human involvement recedes from the learning loop.
AI.method: The paper examines two dimensions: the reward axis (from per-instance human judgments to reusable verifiers and human-free rewards) and the experience axis (from human-curated tasks to self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution). These dimensions are connected through a five-level ladder (L0–L4) identifying which parts of the learning process remain under human control. The paper also proposes evaluation across three objects: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality.
AI.result: The paper provides a structured taxonomy (L0–L4 ladder) of approaches for scaling LRMs beyond human supervision, identifies key risks including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors, and outlines a three-part evaluation framework. It also maintains a continuously updated GitHub repository tracking the latest advances.
AI.conclusion: The analysis offers a structured account of current approaches and open problems in developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence, highlighting the need to manage risks introduced by increasingly autonomous reward and experience generation.

title: Reconciling Process Supervision with Outcome-Based Credit in Agentic Policy Optimization
summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides verified feedback for language-model agents, but assigns trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all decisions, yielding coarse credit over long-horizon interactions. On-policy self-distillation offers finer supervision by re-evaluating sampled behavior with privileged information (PI) available only during training. However, fine-grained supervision is not necessarily fine-grained credit: PI-induced likelihood changes describe how additional information alters policy preference, but do not directly determine how an executable action should inherit the verified task outcome. This creates a supervision-credit gap. Privileged signals may be irrelevant to the current interaction state, operate at a token granularity misaligned with executable decisions, and lack the outcome semantics required for reinforcement. We introduce TASPO, which converts privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit. TASPO constructs decision-applicable PI from verified successful experience, aggregates PI-induced likelihood shifts at the executable-action level, and converts relative action support into positive, bounded, mean-preserving weights on the original trajectory advantage. Thus, the verified outcome determines the update direction and average scale, while PI only redistributes credit across actions. Across three agentic benchmarks, TASPO improves over GRPO by 10.6\% and generalizes better to unseen tasks. Further analysis indicates that TASPO reduces supervision mismatch and that action-level assignment stabilizes the policy optimization process. These findings offer the community another interesting perspective.

AI.tldr: TASPO converts privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit for RL-trained language-model agents, improving over GRPO by 10.6% across three agentic benchmarks by redistributing trajectory-level advantage across executable actions using decision-applicable privileged information.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based reinforcement learning assigns trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all decisions, which is too coarse for long-horizon interactions. On-policy self-distillation with privileged information offers finer supervision, but this does not necessarily translate into fine-grained credit: PI-induced likelihood shifts describe policy preference changes but lack outcome semantics and are misaligned with executable decisions, creating a supervision-credit gap.
AI.method: TASPO converts privileged supervision into outcome-grounded action credit via three steps: (1) constructing decision-applicable PI from verified successful experience, (2) aggregating PI-induced likelihood shifts at the executable-action level, and (3) converting relative action support into positive, bounded, mean-preserving weights on the original trajectory advantage. This ensures the verified outcome controls update direction and average scale while PI only redistributes credit across actions.
AI.result: Across three agentic benchmarks, TASPO outperforms GRPO by 10.6% and generalizes better to unseen tasks. Further analysis shows TASPO reduces supervision mismatch and action-level assignment stabilizes policy optimization.
AI.conclusion: Privileged information should redistribute rather than dictate credit; anchoring credit to verified outcomes while using PI only for relative redistribution improves performance and robustness. TASPO offers a promising perspective for bridging fine-grained supervision and fine-grained credit in RL-trained language agents.

title: Token-Efficient Data Reasoning Agents via Adaptive Structuring of Unstructured Data
summary: Valuable data remains embedded in unstructured sources: web pages, reports, contracts, filings, earnings calls, and PDFs. The big bet in enterprise AI is deploying LLM agents that reason over this data to answer complex questions for every knowledge worker. Agents can do this today, but at prohibitive cost. Each question repeatedly opens large documents to recover scattered evidence, consuming up to a million tokens. However, if the data were already structured, the same question would reduce to a cheap database lookup. For example, on FanOutQA benchmark, reasoning over an ideal pre-structured store is 28X cheaper, and the gap grows to orders of magnitude as questions fan out over more documents. Yet structuring everything in advance is not viable: documents hold vastly more possible structure than any workload will use, and the useful structure and documents are unknown until queries arrive. We propose agentic data cracking, a method that structures unstructured data adaptively and speculatively as a byproduct of reasoning itself. Structuring is adaptive because observed queries decide when it happens and what matters, and speculative because it goes beyond the current question. Whenever the agent opens a document to answer, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure likely to serve related future queries. Over time, an increasing share of queries is fully covered by structured data and answered without opening a document, keeping agentic accuracy at close to RAG cost. On FanOutQA, extended with merely one related question per test question, cracking cuts cost by 53% while preserving accuracy. Agentic data cracking is a first step toward next-generation data infrastructure for agentic reasoning over unstructured data: a shared substrate beneath the model where knowledge that reasoning already paid to uncover accumulates.

AI.tldr: Agentic data cracking is a method that automatically structures unstructured data adaptively and speculatively as a byproduct of LLM agent reasoning. When an agent opens a document to answer a query, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure for future queries. Over time, more queries are answered from structured data without opening documents, cutting costs by 53% on FanOutQA while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM agents reasoning over unstructured data (web pages, reports, contracts, PDFs) incur prohibitive costs—up to a million tokens per question due to repeatedly opening large documents to recover scattered evidence. Pre-structuring everything in advance is not viable because documents contain vastly more possible structure than any workload will use, and useful structure is unknown until queries arrive. The gap between agentic RAG and database lookups can be 28X on FanOutQA.
AI.method: The method, agentic data cracking, structures unstructured data adaptively and speculatively as a byproduct of agent reasoning. It is adaptive because observed queries decide when structuring happens and what matters; it is speculative because it extracts structure beyond the current question. Whenever the agent opens a document, a cracking sub-agent forks from the already-loaded context at marginal cost and extracts grounded structure likely to serve related future queries.
AI.result: On FanOutQA, extended with just one related question per test question, cracking cuts cost by 53% while preserving accuracy. Over time, an increasing share of queries is fully covered by structured data and answered without opening a document, achieving agentic accuracy at close to RAG cost. The gap between reasoning over an ideal pre-structured store and unstructured data is 28X cheaper on FanOutQA.
AI.conclusion: Agentic data cracking is a first step toward next-generation data infrastructure for agentic reasoning over unstructured data: a shared substrate beneath the model where knowledge that reasoning already paid to uncover accumulates, enabling progressively cheaper query answering without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Cross-Regional Grapevine Cold Hardiness Prediction via Learned Multimodal Latent Representations
summary: Accurate daily predictions of cold hardiness in woody plants are critical in regions where freezing temperatures can damage dormant buds and reduce seasonal yield. Existing biophysical, hybrid, and deep learning models have shown high predictive accuracy when trained on local data but remain largely site-specific. The limited availability of cold hardiness data, coupled with the lack of principled methods for transferring cold hardiness predictions to new regions and cultivars, has limited the broader adoption and practical utility of these approaches, particularly in data-scarce regions. To address these limitations, we propose a cold hardiness prediction framework that learns a transferable latent representation by capturing region-specific variation through learned embeddings. To enable prediction in previously unseen regions, we infer embeddings from (1) text descriptions of the cultivar and growing region, and (2) limited historical observations, supporting both zero-shot and few-shot transfer. Experiments on datasets from six regions across North America demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cold hardiness prediction methods, yielding more accurate predictions and substantially improving transfer to data-scarce regions.

AI.tldr: A transferable cold hardiness prediction framework using learned embeddings from text descriptions and limited observations, supporting zero-shot and few-shot transfer across regions and cultivars.
AI.motivation: Existing cold hardiness prediction models (biophysical, hybrid, deep learning) are site-specific and require local training data. Limited data availability and lack of principled transfer methods restrict practical adoption in data-scarce regions.
AI.method: Proposes a framework that learns transferable latent representations via region-specific learned embeddings. For unseen regions, embeddings are inferred from (1) text descriptions of cultivar and growing region, and (2) limited historical observations, enabling both zero-shot and few-shot transfer.
AI.result: Experiments across six North American regions show consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art cold hardiness prediction methods, with more accurate predictions and substantially improved transfer to data-scarce regions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed embedding-based transfer framework effectively generalizes cold hardiness predictions to new regions and cultivars, addressing the site-specificity limitation and broadening practical utility in data-scarce settings.

title: BLOOM-WILT: Logit Tilting for Behaviour Elicitation in Automated LLM Auditing
summary: Users of a deployed language model routinely encounter behaviours that testing almost never surfaces, since deployment puts the model through orders of magnitude more interactions than any evaluation can simulate. Automated auditors make testing cheap to scale and flexible enough to cover almost any specified behaviour, yet their lack of optimisation pressure makes them sample-inefficient. To address this shortcoming, we introduce BLOOM-WILT, a full auditing pipeline that elicits natural multi-turn instances of rare behaviours, without training cost or access beyond the target's next-token distribution. On the input side, WILT's auditor model revises its conversational strategy across rounds, learning from previous scored interactions. On the output side, WILT adaptively reweights the target's decoding using the model's own distribution conditioned on an elicitation prompt, so that behaviour-relevant generations are sampled ahead of others it finds equally probable when unprompted. We evaluate WILT across 4 target models and 8 behaviours, where it beats the baseline auditor in 30 of the 32 settings and overturns the previous model safety rankings. WILT raises average behaviour presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, beating every elicitation method we port into the same pipeline at matched compute, without pushing output probability below the baseline's.

AI.tldr: BLOOM-WILT is a full auditing pipeline that elicits rare multi-turn behaviors from deployed language models without training cost, using an adaptive auditor model for conversational strategy revision and adaptive decoding reweighting, beating a baseline auditor in 30 of 32 settings across 4 targets and 8 behaviors.
AI.motivation: Deployed language models encounter behaviors that standard testing rarely surfaces due to the massive scale of real-world interactions. While automated auditors make testing scalable and flexible, they are sample-inefficient due to a lack of optimization pressure.
AI.method: WILT works on two sides: on the input side, an auditor model revises its conversational strategy across rounds, learning from previously scored interactions; on the output side, it adaptively reweights the target model's decoding using its own distribution conditioned on an elicitation prompt, prioritizing behavior-relevant generations over equally-probable ones. The pipeline requires no training cost and only needs access to the target's next-token distribution.
AI.result: WILT beats the baseline auditor in 30 of 32 settings across 4 target models and 8 behaviors, overturning previous model safety rankings. It raises average behavior presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, surpassing every elicitation method ported into the same pipeline at matched compute without dropping output probability below baseline.
AI.conclusion: BLOOM-WILT demonstrates that efficient black-box auditing of rare behaviors in deployed language models is achievable through adaptive conversational strategies and distribution-aware decoding reweighting, requiring no training cost and providing more reliable safety assessments that can overturn prior rankings.

title: When Does Bigger Help? A Controlled Study of LLM Scale for Ontology Learning
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, and 5 tables. WOP 2026 workshop at ISWC 2026
summary: The effect of Large Language Model (LLM) scale on ontology learning (OL) performance remains insufficiently characterized. We present a controlled evaluation of 13 models spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants from the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 lineages, together with proprietary GPT release variants, using the OntoLearner retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. All models are evaluated with the same embedding model, retrieval configuration, prompt templates, decoding settings, datasets, and metrics on term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relationship extraction across four biomedical and materials science and engineering ontologies. Within the dense Qwen3.5 lineage, increasing parameter count primarily improves precision rather than recall, with the largest gains occurring between 9B and 27B parameters. However, the effect of scale is neither monotonic nor uniform across tasks and domains. Dense 27B models outperform substantially larger sparse models on term typing, whereas larger Mixture-of-Experts models achieve the strongest open-weight results on taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relationship extraction remains difficult across model scales, particularly for the Materials Data Science ontology. Performance differences across matched Qwen variants and proprietary GPT releases further indicate that architecture and model lineage can outweigh nominal parameter count. These findings show that model size alone is an insufficient selection criterion for OL and provide empirical guidance for reproducible LLM-assisted ontology engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a controlled evaluation of 13 LLMs (spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants from Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 lineages and proprietary GPT releases) for ontology learning tasks using a standardized RAG pipeline. The study finds that model scale's effect on performance is non-monotonic and task-dependent: larger dense models improve precision more than recall, dense 27B models outperform larger sparse models on term typing, and architecture/lineage can outweigh nominal parameter count—concluding that model size alone is an insufficient selection criterion for ontology learning.
AI.motivation: The relationship between LLM scale and ontology learning performance is poorly understood, and this characterization gap prevents informed model selection for LLM-assisted ontology engineering.
AI.method: A controlled evaluation of 13 models spanning Qwen3.5 dense (3 sizes), Qwen3.6 dense and Mixture-of-Experts variants, and proprietary GPT releases, all evaluated with the OntoLearner retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. All models share identical embedding models, retrieval configurations, prompt templates, decoding settings, datasets, and metrics. Evaluation covers term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relationship extraction across four biomedical and materials science ontologies.
AI.result: Increasing parameter count in dense Qwen3.5 models primarily improves precision over recall, with the largest gains between 9B and 27B. Scale effects are non-monotonic and task-dependent: 27B dense models outperform larger sparse models on term typing, while larger MoE models excel at taxonomy discovery. Non-taxonomic relationship extraction remains challenging across all scales, and matched Qwen variants and GPT releases show that architecture and lineage can outweigh parameter count.
AI.conclusion: Model size alone is an insufficient criterion for selecting LLMs for ontology learning. The findings provide empirical, reproducible guidance for choosing models based on task-specific requirements and architecture considerations in LLM-assisted ontology engineering.

title: OntoAligner-Ensemble: Voting-Based Fusion across Heterogeneous Ontology Alignment Techniques
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, accepted for OM-2026 workshop at ISWC 2026
summary: Ontology alignment (OA) has evolved through several methodological paradigms, ranging from lexical and structural aligners to knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models and, more recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches. Although modern OA frameworks provide unified ecosystems for deploying these heterogeneous aligners, mechanisms for systematically reconciling their complementary and sometimes conflicting predictions remain relatively underexplored. We present OntoAligner-Ensemble, a modular and aligner-agnostic framework that combines candidate correspondences through a configurable two-stage process comprising voting-based fusion strategies followed by post-fusion selection policies. The framework supports any aligner implemented within OntoAligner that produces candidate correspondences, enabling diverse alignment paradigms to be integrated through a unified decision process. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we instantiate the framework using representative lightweight string-aligner, KGE-based, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation aligners powered by both open-weight and API-based LLMs. We evaluate individual aligners and ensemble configurations across eight benchmark tasks from five OAEI tracks spanning biomedical to beyond-equivalence. The results show that ensemble fusion consistently improves the balance between precision and recall and frequently outperforms standalone aligners across diverse domains. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that ensemble composition directly affects the precision-recall trade-off: heterogeneous cross-paradigm ensembles generally improve precision, whereas homogeneous LLM ensembles more often achieve higher overall F1-scores. These findings demonstrate that systematic ensemble learning offers a robust and reproducible strategy for OA while providing practical guidance for selecting ensemble compositions under different alignment scenarios.

AI.tldr: OntoAligner-Ensemble is a modular, aligner-agnostic framework that combines heterogeneous ontology aligners (lexical, KGE-based, and LLM-based) through a configurable two-stage ensemble process of voting-based fusion and post-fusion selection. Evaluated across eight OAEI benchmark tasks, the framework consistently improves precision-recall balance, with cross-paradigm ensembles favoring precision and homogeneous LLM ensembles achieving higher F1-scores.
AI.motivation: While modern OA frameworks provide unified ecosystems for deploying diverse aligners, there is a lack of mechanisms for systematically reconciling the complementary and sometimes conflicting predictions produced by these heterogeneous aligning paradigms.
AI.method: A two-stage ensemble pipeline: (1) voting-based fusion strategies to combine candidate correspondences from multiple aligners, followed by (2) post-fusion selection policies. The framework is aligner-agnostic and supports any aligner implemented within OntoAligner. It was instantiated with lightweight string-aligners, KGE-based aligners, and RAG-powered LLM aligners (both open-weight and API-based).
AI.result: Across eight benchmark tasks from five OAEI tracks (biomedical to beyond-equivalence), ensemble fusion consistently improved precision-recall balance and frequently outperformed standalone aligners. Heterogeneous cross-paradigm ensembles generally improved precision, while homogeneous LLM ensembles more often achieved higher overall F1-scores.
AI.conclusion: Systematic ensemble learning provides a robust and reproducible strategy for ontology alignment, with ensemble composition directly influencing the precision-recall trade-off, offering practical guidance for selecting ensemble configurations under different alignment scenarios.
